names.name: Agnus Dei
names.th: อักนุส เดอี (ลูกแกะของพระเจ้า)

etymology.root: Latin Agnus Dei, 'Lamb of God' — from John 1:29, where John the Baptist says of Jesus, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!"
etymology.note: The same two words name three different things: the prayer sung at Mass, the music written for it, and this object. Only the object is an amulet, and confusing the three is the commonest mistake made about it.

text.what: A disc of wax, round or oval, with a lamb pressed into one face. The lamb carries a cross or a flag; the reverse usually takes a saint, or the name and arms of the reigning pope. The wax is made from what is left of the previous year's paschal candle. It hangs at the neck, or it is kept somewhere safe and looked at.
text.story:
The oldest sacramental in the Roman Church is a lump of recycled candle.

Herbert Thurston, writing the Catholic Encyclopedia entry in 1907, puts the ninth-century practice like this: the archdeacon made the Agnus Deis early on Holy Saturday morning out of clean wax mixed with chrism, and handed them out to the people on the Saturday following. What changed later is who does the blessing. The great consecration of Agnus Deis takes place only in the first year of a pontificate and every seventh year after it — a rule Thurston says was still followed in 1907 — and it is the pope who performs it. That schedule is the whole economics of the object: a papal Agnus Dei is scarce by design.

The claims Thurston records are stated plainly and stated wide: protection "from all malign influences", and specifically "perils from storm and pestilence, from fire and flood, and also of the dangers to which women are exposed in childbirth". He also records the reported results rather than asserting them: "Fires are said to have been extinguished, and floods stayed." That is the exact grammar this atlas uses, arrived at independently and a century earlier.

The Agnus Dei is also where the Roman habit of blessing an object and attaching indulgences to it got started, or at least where the Catholic Encyclopedia says it got started. Writing on devotional medals, the same encyclopedia dates the sixteenth-century practice of giving a papal blessing to medals — and then enriching them with indulgences — to a usage "long previously in vogue in the case of Agnus Dei (discs of wax impressed with the figure of a lamb and blessed at stated seasons by the Pope, which could be worn suspended round the neck)". *Inference —* every struck medal later in this batch descends from this wax disc, procedurally if not physically.

The Church's line between a sacramental and an amulet runs straight through it. A sacramental, by the Catholic Church's own definition, is a sacred sign that works by the Church's prayer and "does not confer the grace of the Holy Spirit in the way that the sacraments do"; it disposes a person to receive grace rather than acting on its own. Set that beside a wax disc credited with stopping a flood and the tension is not hypothetical. The 2001 Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy names the boundary in general terms: popular piety "may never incorporate rites permeated by magic, superstition, animism, vendettas or sexual connotations", and elsewhere it warns against keeping blessed palms as amulets or for therapeutic or magical purposes. Both positions are the Church's. This atlas prints both and settles neither.
text.how: Cast from the remains of the previous year's paschal candle, mixed with chrism, impressed with the lamb, and blessed by the pope in the first year of his pontificate and every seventh year after. Distributed by the pontiff, often through envoys, and usually in a case or a cloth mount when worn. It is not renewed on a cycle and it is not burnt at retirement; it is kept.
text.today: This project has read nothing dated later than the 1907 encyclopedia entry on whether the seven-year consecration still happens, and it will not guess. Old Agnus Deis survive in Catholic households, in reliquary frames, and in museum and papal-artefact collections. That is what can be said: the object exists, its present manufacture is unverified here, and a reader who needs to know should ask a diocese.

names.name: Akua'ba
names.th: อาคัวบา (ตุ๊กตาไม้ของชาวอาคาน)

text.what: A small wooden figure with a large flat disc for a head, a ringed neck and a short body, usually with arms out to the sides. The head is the whole signature: a smooth circle or oval, set on a cylinder, with the features low on the face.
text.story:
Akua'ba come from western Ghana and nearby, and are particularly associated with the Fanti, part of the Akan group of peoples in Ghana and Ivory Coast. Young women seeking to conceive carry them, and carry them also so that the children they have will be good-looking.

When the figure is not in use it is not put away: it is ritually washed and cared for in the homestead, which is why writers describing the practice reach for the phrase sympathetic magic — the doll is treated the way the wanted child would be.

Other peoples in the region carve their own. The Kru and the Igbo have distinctive styles of fertility figure, used in similar ways.

The form crossed the Atlantic. Akua'ba were taken to the Americas by enslaved Africans, where they stood for a connection to home and were used as good-luck charms.

*Inference —* the collecting came early and it came in volume. Europeans visiting Africa in the 1800s were highly interested in Fante dolls, and that interest is why the figure is in so many European museums; what a museum case holds here, as with the Kongo material, is a record of nineteenth-century European taste as much as of Akan practice.
text.how: Carved in wood. Washed and cared for in the homestead when not being carried. The sources read here name no maker's restriction and no consecration rite, and this record does not supply one from a neighbouring tradition.
text.today: Both things at once, and the tradition's own account says so. Akua'ba are now more commonly seen as mass-produced works of art or souvenirs than as heirlooms in ritual use — and traditional use continues in some areas among the Fante and other Akan peoples. The shape has also become a general sign of good luck, detached from conception.

names.name: Ankh amulet
names.said: ANK, a modern guess at the Egyptian ꜥnḫ
names.th: เครื่องรางอังค์

etymology.root: Egyptian ꜥnḫ, three consonants that spell 'live', 'life', and also 'mirror', 'floral bouquet' and 'oath' — Egyptian oaths opened with a form of the word 'live'. The Coptic stage of the language gives ⲱⲛϩ, ōnh.
etymology.note: Egyptologists do not agree on what object the sign draws. Gardiner filed it with items of clothing, just after the sandal, and read it as a sandal strap used as a rebus; Schäfer and Fischer read it as a knot of cloth or reed worn as an amulet, close kin to the tyet. Gordon and Schwabe argued it is a bull's thoracic vertebra. James Allen, writing in 2014, still assumes the sandal strap.

text.what: A T with a loop on top, the loop shaped like a droplet. As an amulet it is small and strung at the neck; the earliest ones are gold or electrum, the alloy of gold and silver, and later ones are mostly faience — quartz paste glazed blue or green in the kiln. Painted versions in tomb and temple art are blue or black. The Coptic variant, the crux ansata, swaps the droplet for a circle.
text.story:
The ankh is everywhere in Egyptian art and rare as an amulet, and the gap is the interesting part. Amulets cut in the shape of a hieroglyph were meant to hand the wearer whatever the sign meant, and this sign meant life itself; yet ankh-shaped amulets first appear only late in the Old Kingdom, around 2700 to 2200 BCE, and stay uncommon right through to the late first millennium BCE. The composite amulet — ankh, was and djed run together, 'life, dominion and stability' — was more widespread than the ankh on its own.

On walls the sign is a thing gods hold. They carry it by the loop, they hold it up to the king's nose as the breath of life, and in scenes of purification the zigzag lines that usually mean water are replaced by chains of ankhs poured over the king's head. Before the end of the Middle Kingdom almost nobody but the pharaoh is shown receiving one. Because the same three consonants spelled 'mirror' and 'floral bouquet', mirrors, mirror cases and bouquets were made in the sign's shape.

It travelled. Syria and Canaan took it up in the Middle Bronze Age, about 1950 to 1500 BCE, and of all the Egyptian hieroglyphs they borrowed it was by far the most common. Anatolian hieroglyphs absorbed it for the word 'life'. Minoan artists on Crete combined it, or the related tyet, with the double axe. Meroitic Nubia used it heavily in temples, in funerary art and on pottery. A clay seal of King Hezekiah of Judah, about 700 BCE, found in Jerusalem in 2015, carries ankhs on either side of a winged sun.

Then Christianity kept it. When Christians were pulling down the Serapeum in Alexandria in 391 CE, according to Socrates of Constantinople, cross-like signs turned up cut into the stone blocks; the pagans present said the sign meant 'life to come' and the Christians said the sign was theirs. Egyptian Coptic Christians used the crux ansata in many media, especially on textiles. There is little evidence for it in the western half of the Roman Empire.
text.how: Cut from gold or electrum in the earliest examples, moulded in faience later — that ceramic is usually blue or green, and the colour is read as life and regeneration, which may be why it took over. Pierced and strung, or built into the composite ankh-was-djed amulet. On a wall it is painted blue or black.
text.today: Worn worldwide. The sign came back through the counterculture of the 1960s and its interest in ancient religions, and it is now a standard design for jewellery and tattoos. People of African descent in the United States and Europe wear it as a sign of African cultural identity; Kemetism, a group of movements built on the religion of ancient Egypt, uses it as its symbol; the goth subculture adopted it, tied to vampires, after an ankh pendant featured in the 1983 film The Hunger. In the twenty-first century it is the most widely recognised symbol of Egyptian, and more broadly of African, origin in the Western world. Unicode encodes it twice: U+2625 ☥ and U+132F9 𓋹.

names.name: Anting-anting
names.th: อันติง-อันติง (เครื่องรางฟิลิปปินส์)

etymology.root: Tagalog anting-anting, from Javanese anting-anting, 'ear-hanging ornament'; the wider family includes Indonesian and Malay gantung, 'hanging'. Agimat is the other Filipino word for the same thing, with virtud (virtue) and galing (prowess) as general terms
etymology.note: The ornament sense carries the claim with it: in the polytheistic mythology the word comes out of, such ornaments were worn by gods in the ear hook or the earlobe, where they were held to be strongest.

text.what: Most often a flat pendant on a necklace — round, triangular or cross-shaped, in gold-coloured metal, its face crowded with figures and Latin words. But the class is wider than the pendant. An anting-anting can be a stone said to have come out of the sky, or a fulgurite fang left where lightning struck, pangil ng kidlat, or a mutya, a drop of liquid taken from the heart of a banana tree at midnight, which is swallowed rather than worn. It can be a garment with words written on it. It usually comes with a small book of incantations, orasyon, which has to be read on Good Friday or another set date for the thing to work at full strength.
text.story:
The Philippine occult tradition matches an agimat to a department of life. The commonest kinds remove hexes and drive out spirits. A gayuma is the love charm, which makes its owner more attractive. Most of the amulets carry Latin inscriptions, and most of the dealers set up near a church — in the courtyard or in the market beside it — of which the Quiapo district in Manila is the example everyone names.

The written record starts with the colonisers. The earliest reports of anting-anting come from Spanish priests in the early colonial period, which in the Philippines begins with Miguel López de Legazpi's settlement of 1565. Trinidad Pardo de Tavera defined the thing in Spanish: amuleto que salva la vida, da poder sobre natural — an amulet of supernatural power that saves lives. As Christianity took hold, the anting-anting took on the new religion's forms, and later took in the esoteric symbols of Freemasonry as well. An Islamic version exists in the southern Muslim islands.

The charm has a political history, which is unusual in this atlas. Filipino fighters wore anting-anting against the Spanish and then against the Americans. Macario Sakay wore a vest carrying religious images and Latin phrases, to stop bullets. Ferdinand Marcos claimed that Gregorio Aglipay had given him an anting-anting — a sliver of wood inserted into his back before the Bataan campaign in 1942 — that could make him invisible. Whose claim that was, and what it was for, is left standing here as his.

The subtypes are named by what they do. Kabal, also kunat, makes the skin proof against cuts and sword slashes. Pamako nails an entity in place so it cannot move. Tagabulag turns the wearer invisible to an enemy, or blinds them. Tagaliwas turns a bullet aside.

Filipino cinema took all of it and went further: on screen the wearer gains strength, invisibility, healing, flight, telekinesis, the power to stop a bullet in the air. Ramon Revilla Sr., playing Nardong Putik, carried one that made him invulnerable. The 1939 film The Real Glory shows Moro characters saying theirs will stop bullets and knives. Screen and street are not the same object and this record keeps them apart.
text.how: Cast or cut, then charged by reading: the orasyon that comes with the amulet has to be recited on Good Friday, or on another appointed date, for the piece to reach full power. Other routes to getting one are described and are not gentle — taking the liquid drained from an exhumed body, or setting out food and drink for the spirits in a cemetery at midnight on Holy Wednesday or Holy Thursday. A mutya is swallowed. Bought at a stall by a church, most often.
text.today: Still sold from stalls around Quiapo Church in Manila and at markets beside other churches, as of the accounts this project has read. Quiapo is a major Catholic shrine, which is the point: the trade stands in the churchyard rather than away from it.

names.th: อาซาบาเช (เครื่องรางหินเจ็ต)

etymology.root: Spanish azabache, from Arabic sabaj, the black stone — the amulet is named for its material, jet, and not for its shape
etymology.note: The fist form is also called a higa in Spanish, figa in Galician and Portuguese, and cigua in Asturleonese.

text.what: A piece of jet — fossil wood, black, warm to the touch, light in the hand — cut either as a small clenched fist with the thumb pushed between the first two fingers, or as a faceted black bead. Edward Tabor, writing in Hektoen International in 2023, measures the fist at about 8 mm long and the polyhedron at 3 to 4 mm across, each with a small red bead at the end of the chain. It is pinned to a baby's clothing or worn on a bracelet.
text.story:
Jet has been cut for amulets since the Neolithic, and in Spain the trade had a centre: the deposits are in Asturias, but by the end of the Middle Ages the working of jet religious objects and amulets was concentrated at Santiago de Compostela and sold to pilgrims on the Camino. The Asturian version handed to small children was, and is, a higa — the jet fist.

Tabor's account follows the object across the Atlantic. He traces the form to Muslim North Africa, citing Washington Irving's 1829 description of a comparable jet hand among "the Moors of Barbary", into Spain during the Moorish period of 711 to 1492, and then into the Spanish Caribbean colonies. Puerto Rican, Cuban and Dominican families put one on an infant within days of birth, and Tabor found that the practice continues into adulthood.

What parents told Tabor it is for is specific: the evil eye, and with it diarrhoea, respiratory infections, deformities, and above all sudden infant death. He reports that 29% of the wearers he surveyed had chosen the fist and 71% the polyhedron. He gives a price: US$3 to US$10 in a botánica, a folk-medicine shop, and US$9 to US$55 online at the time he wrote in 2023.

*Inference —* the red bead is worth noting. Red thread and red beads run with black stone across the whole Mediterranean, and the pairing here is the same pairing Naples makes with coral. This project files that as a family resemblance and not as a descent.
text.how: Cut and polished from jet, which is soft enough — Mohs 2.5 to 4 — to work with hand tools but chips if the carver pushes detail. Strung with a red bead, then pinned to the baby's shirt or fastened as a bracelet. It is given, usually by a grandmother or godparent, not bought by the wearer. Nothing in the sources read here describes a blessing; the giving is the act.
text.today: Sold in botánicas and online across the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, Spain and the United States. Tabor's 2023 figures — US$3 to US$10 in a shop, US$9 to US$55 online — are the last dated prices this project has read. Much of what is sold now is moulded black resin rather than cut jet; jet takes a brown streak on unglazed porcelain and burns like coal, which is how a buyer tells.

names.name: Bagua mirror
names.th: กระจกปากั้ว (กระจกแปดทิศ)

etymology.root: Chinese 八卦 bāguà, 'eight trigrams', + 鏡 jìng, 'mirror'
etymology.note: A trigram is three stacked lines, each broken or unbroken for yin or yang; two states across three lines give eight figures, which is where the eight comes from.

text.what: An octagonal or circular plaque with the eight trigrams set around a mirror at its centre. The mirror is flat, convex or concave, and which one it is decides what the object claims to do. It is screwed or hung above a front door or a window, facing out. It resembles a luopan, the feng shui compass, but it is not an instrument — nothing is read off it.
text.story:
The thing it answers is a direction, not a person. In feng shui, sharp corners of neighbouring buildings and an open road running at a house count as sources of poison-arrows — Sha Qi, 煞氣 — and a bagua mirror is hung to deal with the arrow rather than the archer. A flat mirror is held to reflect it, a convex one to disperse it, a concave one to converge or absorb it, and so to alter the feng shui of the residence.

Modern bagua mirrors are described as evolved from ancient bronze-cast versions used by Taoist masters to perform Mirror Techniques, 鏡術, said to reveal or destroy evil spirits, or even to overcome natural calamities. The household version is the cheap end of that: an inexpensive, often self-administered quick fix to a specific feng shui concern.

Which is exactly where the trouble is. Whatever the mirror sends back goes in the direction the mirror faces, so pointing one at a neighbour's home is generally considered offensive and is a feng shui taboo — and the do-it-yourself nature of the object makes it easy to misuse for a private vendetta. Conflicts caused by offensive installations are well known in dense Chinese communities such as Hong Kong, and feng shui mirror feuds have been parodied in popular culture. *Inference —* this is one of the few charms in this atlas whose recorded quarrels are between neighbours rather than between believers and sceptics; the argument is not whether it works but where it is aimed.
text.how: Bought ready-made and mounted by the householder, above a door or a window, facing the corner or the road that is the problem. No consecration is described in the source read, and no specialist is required — which is the difference between this and the bronze mirrors of the Taoist masters it is said to descend from.
text.today: Sold in hardware shops, feng shui shops and online across the Chinese-speaking world as of 2026, in plastic and wood as often as in metal. A mirror over a doorway is also read by neighbours, which is why some cities treat their appearance as news.

names.name: Bes amulet
names.th: เครื่องรางเทพเบส

etymology.root: Uncertain. 'Bes' means 'cat' in Nubian, which fits a god regularly drawn with feline features; the name may instead come from the hieroglyphs bs 'flame' or bz 'to be initiated, to introduce', the latter possibly pointing at masks used in his cult.

text.what: A squat bearded figure with a lion's face, a feathered crown, a protruding tongue and bandy legs, shown full-face when every other Egyptian god is shown in profile. He is ithyphallic, sometimes in a soldier's tunic, sometimes brandishing a knife. He comes as an amulet, as a mask, moulded onto faience baby bottles, cut into the legs of furniture and headrests, painted on storage jars, and inked into skin.
text.story:
Bes faces you. That is the whole design argument: Egyptian gods are drawn in profile, and Bes is drawn head-on, dressed for a fight, so that anything approaching the house meets him looking straight at it.

He is a household god, not a temple one. What he is for is specific and domestic — killing snakes, driving off evil spirits, watching children, and standing with Taweret at a birth to fight off what comes for women in labour. Because he drove off harm he also came to stand for the good things: music, dance, sexual pleasure.

His origin is southern. People in Upper Egypt venerated him long before Lower Egypt did, his sub-Saharan features and his feathered crown point at Kush or the C-Group, and Donald Mackenzie in 1907 called him a Middle Kingdom import from Nubia whose cult only spread from the start of the New Kingdom. That story has since been complicated: thirteen Bes-like figurines were found at Tell el-Farkha in deposits from the predynastic Naqada period.

He travelled further than most. His image reaches Syria in the north and the Balearic Islands in the west, then the Roman and Achaemenid empires. From the end of the sixth century BCE Bes spreads across the Achaemenid empire while Egypt is part of it; he turns up at Susa and as far as central Asia, and over time gets redrawn in Persian clothes and a Persian headdress. Beset, the female form, was more popular on Minoan Crete; the male form took with the Phoenicians and the Cypriots.

He was also worn under the skin. A wall painting from the workmen's village at Deir el-Medina, Nineteenth Dynasty, shows a dancing Bes tattooed on the thigh of a female musician playing her instrument; New Kingdom tattoos of Bes are recorded on the thighs of dancers, musicians and servant girls. A female mummy from Aksha in Nubia, fourth century BCE, carries a Bes on her thigh.

He lasted. In the Ptolemaic period chambers were built at Saqqara painted with Bes and Beset, which Egyptologists take to have been for curing fertility problems or for general healing. A Bes-vase of the second century BCE has been found to carry traces of Peganum harmala and of the blue water lily, Nymphaea nouchali var. caerulea. The latest evidence the source names is a jug showing Bes from Tell Edfu, dated to the tenth century CE — Coptic Egypt, long after the temples closed.
text.how: Moulded in faience, carved, or painted on. Kept in the house rather than worn only on the body: a statue set up as a doorkeeper, a face on the jar, a face on the bed, a face on the baby's bottle. Tattooed on the thigh in the New Kingdom. Nothing in the sources read here restricts who may own one.
text.today: Not made as a household god. Bes turns up now as a museum object, as a character in fiction and games, and as a tattoo design. As of 2026 this project has read no account of anyone standing a Bes at a door for what the Egyptians stood him there for.

text.what: A small cross woven from straw or rushes, defined by its material rather than its shape. The National Museum of Ireland sorts them into seven classes: diamond, single or multiple; the swastika type, with four arms or three; the wheel type; the interlaced type; plain Latin crosses made of straw or rush; bare wooden crosses in the Latin or Greek style bound with straw; and a miscellaneous class. The commonest is the diamond or lozenge: two sticks crossed to make a frame, with straw woven into a diamond at the centre, and sometimes further diamonds on each of the four arms.
text.story:
The cross is woven on 1 February, the feast day of Brigid of Kildare and the date of Imbolc in pre-Christian Ireland, and hung from the rafters to bring the saint's blessing and protection for the rest of the year. The practice of making them is first attested in the seventeenth century.

Brigid herself left no historical record; she was born around 450 in Leinster, and almost everything about her comes from a hagiography written by the monk Cogitosus some two hundred years later. The story attached to the cross is a deathbed conversion: telling a pagan chieftain — in some versions her father — about the Crucifixion, Brigid gathered rushes from the floor and wove them into a cross, and the chieftain asked to be baptised. In another story she was handed a poisoned drink by a woman who meant her harm, and wove the cross to neutralise it.

The household version has a timetable. Families gathered rushes on 31 January. After the evening meal the head of the household supervised the rest of the family weaving, the finished crosses were left out overnight to receive Brigid's blessing, and on 1 February they went up in the main dwelling, the outhouses and the stables. Some households took the old ones down and replaced them each year; others let them accumulate between feasts. Discarded crosses were burned or buried, burial preferred, because of Brigid's associations with agriculture. The weaving was not confined to the feast: friends gave each other crosses to strengthen a bond, and newly married couples were given womb crosses to hang over the door, Brigid being a patron of fertility too. Outside Ireland, the crosses are hung in Glastonbury, on a local legend that Brigid visited the town in 488, and Irish families send them to relatives abroad or carry one when they leave.

The shape carries arguments. Some historians compare the central lozenge to the Mexican god's eye and to the Eurasian magic square. The swastika type, with its arms set at right angles off a central diamond, reads as a wheel in motion and may have originally stood for the sun; in parts of Ulster the same motion is made with three arms, which has been compared to the triskelion.

Its second life is national. After the Irish Free State gained independence in 1922 the cross became one of the motifs artists used to build a cultural identity separate from Britain's, alongside the shamrock and the harp. It went into the logo of the Irish Department of Health in the 1950s and, as of 2024, was still part of the logo of the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Ireland. It was chosen as the first station identification marker for Raidió Teilifís Éireann in 1962 — Alice Curtayne wrote that it was picked to evoke "the image of quiet, serene places in the springtime of our history, of rush-bordered rivers in a serene arcadian landscape" — survived nine redesigns, and was dropped in 1995 in favour of what the broadcaster called "a clean striking piece of modern design". Carol Coulter wrote in The Irish Times that Saint Brigid's cross had lost its place as a symbol of national identity, at least as far as the national broadcaster was concerned.
text.how: Gather rushes or straw on the eve of the feast, 31 January. Weave after the evening meal, the household together. Leave the crosses out overnight for the saint's blessing. Hang them on 1 February in the house, the outhouses and the stables. Take them down and replace them at the next feast, or leave them to accumulate. Retire by burning or, preferably, burying. The direction they were hung in is not recorded — but the centre is described as a lozenge rather than a square, which suggests the cross was displayed as a saltire rather than upright.
text.today: Still woven. The weaving declined through the twentieth century, partly because house renovations made the crosses hard to hang in the old way, and 1 February has since been declared a national holiday in Ireland. In 1942 the Irish Folklore Commission ran a questionnaire on the Feast of Saint Brigid and collected several hundred crosses; in 2022 twenty-one of them went on display at the National Museum of Ireland – Country Life in Castlebar.

names.name: Brown Scapular
aliases: Scapular of Our Lady of Mount Carmel
names.th: สกาปูลาร์สีน้ำตาล

etymology.root: Latin scapula, 'shoulder' — the garment hangs from them
etymology.note: The monastic scapular was at times called scutum, 'shield', because it covered the head; and jugum Christi, 'the yoke of Christ', because taking it off meant throwing off obedience. The Carmelite constitution of 1281 required it to be worn in bed; the constitution of 1369 excommunicated a Carmelite who said Mass without one.

text.what: Two small rectangles of brown wool, a few inches across, joined by two cloth bands. One rectangle sits on the chest, the bands run over the shoulders, the other rectangle hangs down the back. Some carry an image or a line of scripture; some are wood or laminated paper instead of cloth. It is worn under the clothes and it is meant not to show. The rule is that it must be in good repair with both bands intact, and a damaged one is replaced rather than mended.
text.story:
Start with the full-sized version, because the small one is a quotation of it. The monastic scapular is a length of cloth hanging front and back from a monk's or nun's shoulders, and item 55 of the Rule of Saint Benedict refers to it in the seventh century. It began as an apron. Over centuries it hardened into the mark of the religious life the way a stole marks a priest, and a long scapular still identifies its wearer as a member of an order.

The small one is how lay people got a share of that. Tertiaries — lay members affiliated to the mendicant orders — were not permitted the full habit, so they were given a shrunken version, and over time it shrank again to two rectangles on bands. In 1883, in Misericors Dei Filius, Leo XIII ruled that the miniature form earned the same indulgences as the medium-sized one. The Catholic Encyclopedia lists eighteen approved small scapulars with their dates: white for the Most Blessed Trinity in 1193, brown for Our Lady of Mount Carmel in 1250, black for the Seven Sorrows of Mary in 1255, and on down to white for St Dominic in 1903. The brown one is the best known of them, and by 1912 Joseph Hilgers could write in the Catholic Encyclopedia that "Like the rosary, [the Brown Scapular] has become the badge of the devout Catholic".

What carried it was a promise. Carmelite tradition holds that the Virgin appeared to Simon Stock at Cambridge in 1251 and — as the National Catholic Register puts the tradition — told him that "whoever wore the scapular would be saved from the fires of hell". A second promise, the Sabbatine privilege, held that the wearer would be released from purgatory on the first Saturday after death.

And here the object's own order is the one taking it apart. The Discalced Carmelite Friars' Catechesis on the Brown Scapular states that the Simon Stock vision "cannot be seen as historical events", that the earliest written account of it appears around the fourteenth century, roughly 150 years after the date it claims, with nothing contemporary behind it. On the Sabbatine privilege it is blunter: the 1322 vision attributed to John XXII rests on a papal bull "forged in Sicily", and in 1613 the Holy See declared the privilege unfounded. What the Order asks for instead is a list of obligations — Mass and Communion, reading and meditating on scripture, at least part of the Liturgy of the Hours — and it says why: "to wear the scapular without accepting the responsibilities attached to it would be to reduce this precious sacramental to the status of a charm or good-luck piece." Fr Robert Colaresi, of the Carmelite Spiritual Center, says the same thing shorter: "The scapular is not a magic charm of protection, an automatic guarantee of salvation or an excuse for not living a Christian life." Fr Patrick McMahon, the Carmelite provincial delegate quoted in the same 2001 report, gives the reason the Order bothered: "Many people were beginning to realize that if we clung to pious legend, instead of sound theology, there would be no future for any devotion to the scapular."

*Inference —* this atlas prints that argument at length because it is the clearest case it has of a tradition arguing with its own object in public, in writing, and losing. The scapular is still worn by the million on the strength of the promise the Order has spent decades qualifying. Both halves are the record. Neither is settled here.

The brown one keeps turning up at the hinge of things. In the reported 1917 apparitions at Fátima the Virgin appears "with a Rosary in one hand and a scapular in the other", and Sister Lúcia said she was told "The Rosary and the Scapular are inseparable". Scapular Magazine in the United States enrolled a million Americans to pray the rosary on the strength of the Fátima messages. John Paul II said he received his first Brown Scapular at ten and wore it into the papacy. The 2001 Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy lists it among approved practices and describes it as an external sign of a filial relationship with Mary — which is a careful sentence, and the carefulness is the point.
text.how: Invested, not bought. A scapular tied to a confraternity must be given by an ordained representative of that group; one tied to a devotion may be blessed by a priest and handed over. The benefits attach only while it is worn, they lapse while it is set aside, and they resume when it goes back on. If it wears out it is replaced, and the wearer is not reinvested — the Church's own reasoning being that the devotion of the wearer, not the object, is what carries the benefit. In 1911 Pius X sanctioned wearing a blessed medal in place of the brown and other scapulars.
text.today: Still worn under the shirt across the Catholic world in 2026, still stocked beside the Miraculous Medal and the St Christopher medal, and still sold in the metal-medal substitute Pius X allowed. The Carmelite catechesis is a click away and most wearers have not read it. No dated retail price was read for this record.

dating.period: the high Middle Ages to now
dating.label: listed from 1250; the garment in the Carmelite habit from the late thirteenth century; worn now
dating.note: 1250 is the date the Catholic Encyclopedia's list of approved small scapulars gives for the Brown Scapular of Our Lady of Mount Carmel. Carmelite tradition dates the Simon Stock apparition to 1251; the Discalced Carmelite Friars' own catechesis says that vision cannot be treated as a historical event and that the first written account is about 150 years later. The cited Wikipedia article says only that the scapular has been part of the Carmelite habit since the late thirteenth century. The monastic full-length garment is older again: item 55 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, seventh century.

etymology.root: Korean 부적, from Sino-Korean 符籍 — fu, a tally or talismanic mark, plus a register; the same fu that stands at the head of the Chinese fulu
etymology.note: The Chinese Daoist talismanic script fulu is named as the ancestor of both the Japanese ofuda and the Korean bujeok.

text.what: A paper talisman drawn by a mudang, the ritual specialist of Korean vernacular religion. The figures on it are built out of Hanja, the Korean forms of Chinese logograms, worked into shapes that are not ordinary writing. It goes one of two ways: folded into a small brocade bag and carried on the person, or pasted onto an interior wall of the client's house.
text.story:
Bujeok descend from fulu, the Daoist talismanic script of China — the same stock that produced Japan's ofuda. Fulu are described by their own scholars as deliberately hard to read: Yang Zhaohua notes that the earliest Taoist talismans were simple and legible and that later ones became cryptic to signal their divinity, and Ge Zhaoguang of Fudan University calls their unreadability a linguistic archaism designed so that only qualified clergy can produce them. A bujeok inherits that logic in Hanja.

Who draws one matters more than what is on it. Mudang — the majority of them women — are the specialists of Musok, and they hand these out to the people who attended a gut, the large rite that is their central work, at the end of it. Korean vernacular religion also runs ritual specialists who divine and make amulets without performing gut at all.

The practice has been under pressure for six hundred years and is still here. Under the Joseon dynasty Confucian elites taxed and prosecuted the mudang: they were one of eight outcast groups expelled from the capital, the Gyeonggukdaejeon prescribed a hundred public lashes for anyone who supported them, a mudang was beheaded in 1398, and the Jeju governor Yi Hyŏngsang purged the island's simbang in 1702, destroying 129 shrines. The ritual taxes ran until the Kabo reforms of 1895. In 1896 police arrested mudang, pulled down shrines and burnt their equipment. Suppression continued in the mid-twentieth century through Syngman Rhee's New Life Movement and Park Chung Hee's Saemaul Undong, with a surge of police action against mudang in the 1970s.

Then it turned. From the late 1970s the mudang were re-read as carriers of Korean cultural identity, several were tied to the minjung pro-democracy movement, and from the 1980s the South Korean government designated certain mudang Human Cultural Treasures. By 2009 ten regional gut styles were on the national intangible heritage register, and one of them — the Yŏngdŭng gut of Ch'ilmŏri Shrine on Jeju — went onto UNESCO's Representative List that year. Disapproval has not gone away: the anthropologist Chongho Kim's account and the survey this record draws on both record that mudang are still widely regarded in South Korea as charlatans, Christians especially.
text.how: Drawn by a mudang, in figures built from Hanja. Distributed to those present at the end of a gut, or made on commission. Then either sealed into a small brocade bag and kept on the body, or pasted up on the inside wall of a house. This project has read no published account of the drawing itself — what is used, in what order, with what said over it — and prints none.
text.today: South Korea holds over 200,000 mudang as of the survey this record draws on, and practitioners work abroad as well. Mudang have advertised on the internet since the 1990s and have been steadily visible on South Korean television since the 2010s, which has improved their standing. Paper talismans are sold in tourist and antique districts too, Insadong among them.

text.what: A locket on a neckchain: a round hollow pouch with something shut inside it, usually a phallus. What it was made of tracked the family's money — gold or gold foil at the top, lead, leather or cloth further down. It was given to a freeborn Roman boy nine days after he was born and he wore it until he stopped being a boy.
text.story:
The bulla has an end date built into it. Before a young man put on the toga virilis, the toga of manhood, he handed his boyhood bulla to the household's Lares, the family's own gods, and it stayed with them. The girls' version, the lunula, came off on the eve of a wedding, together with her childhood toys.

Who could wear one was not open. The bulla marks a freeborn Roman boy and a Roman citizen in the making; the object and the status are the same statement. Some modern readers take a single line in Macrobius about an amulet worn by a general in his triumph as evidence that the childhood bulla was also standard triumphal regalia. The cited account reports that reading without endorsing it, and so does this record.

*Tradition holds —* the amulet inside was usually a phallus, a shape the cited account calls a bringer of good luck in antiquity. The container is the interesting part. The protection is real enough to be worth wearing and private enough to be shut in a case: nobody is meant to see what is working.

Ireland has bullae too, and they are not these. A small number of Late Bronze Age objects, roughly 1150 to 750 BCE, are called bullae because they look like the Roman ones — base metal or clay under a folded-over sheet of gold foil, incised with geometry, hung round the neck by a cord through a hole below the flat top. Whether they were ornament, amulet or something else is unclear, and that is why Ireland does not appear in this record's country list.

text.what: A stamped metal medal clipped to a sun visor or glued to a dashboard, or a miniature statue standing on it, showing a giant wading a river with a child on his shoulder. The same image is worn as a pendant, fixed to a bracelet or carried in a pocket. Medals are aluminium, tin, brass or silver, usually 15 to 30 mm across; dashboard statues are painted resin.
text.story:
The image is legible before the text is. The Golden Legend, the thirteenth-century compendium of saints' lives, tells how Christopher, after his conversion, spent his life carrying travellers across a river; one day a boy asked to be carried, grew heavier with every step as the water rose, and on the far bank revealed himself as Christ. From that story various Christian denominations made him the patron saint of travellers, and small images of him are worn at the neck, on a bracelet, carried in a pocket or placed in a vehicle. Miniature statues are frequently displayed in automobiles. He is named patron of motorists and drivers alongside mariners, ferrymen, archers, bookbinders and gardeners.

The medals say out loud what they are for. The widespread French phrase is "Regarde St Christophe et va-t-en rassuré" — look at Saint Christopher and go on reassured. The Spanish medals and holy cards carry a harder promise: "Si en San Cristóbal confías, de accidente no morirás" — if you trust in Saint Christopher, you will not die in an accident. This atlas prints those two sentences as what the object says of itself, names who says it, and stops there.

The Church's own position moved under the object. Christopher's commemoration was of relatively late date, around 1550; by 1954 it had been extended to all Masses; in 1970 it was dropped from the general calendar of the Roman rite and restricted to particular calendars. *Inference —* the medal did not go with it. A devotional object with a working use outlived the liturgical decision that demoted it, which is the ordinary pattern for this whole class and not a Catholic peculiarity.

He is not alone on the dashboard. Japan's shrines sell a kōtsū-anzen omamori specifically for traffic safety, and it hangs from the same mirror in Nagoya that the medal is clipped under in Marseille.
text.how: Bought at a church shop, a shrine stall, a service station or online, and fixed where the driver can see it: clipped to the visor, adhered to the dash, hung from the mirror, slipped behind a licence plate. A medal may be blessed by a priest as a sacramental; nothing requires it to be. It stays with the car more often than with the driver, and is passed on with the vehicle.
text.today: Still sold and still fixed in cars across Catholic Europe and the Americas in 2026, and still stocked alongside the Miraculous Medal and the scapular in the same shops. No dated price was read for this record.

names.name: Caul
names.th: คอล (เยื่อคลุมหน้าทารกแรกเกิด)

text.what: A piece of birth membrane that comes away with a newborn and clings to the head and face — usually the thin translucent inner lining, the amnion. The midwife lifts it off, presses it onto a sheet of paper, and it dries there. That sheet is the amulet. Birth with a caul occurs in fewer than one in 80,000 births, a figure that includes en-caul births, in which the whole infant is delivered inside the intact sac.
text.story:
In medieval Europe a caul on a newborn was read as good luck and as an omen that the child was destined for greatness, and gathering the caul onto paper was an important part of the birth: the midwife rubbed a sheet across the baby's head and face and presented the result to the mother, to be kept as an heirloom. Some early modern European traditions connected caul birth to the power to defend fertility and the harvest against witches and sorcerers — the benandanti of Friuli are the named example.

The caul's main career was at sea. Folklore held that possessing a baby's caul brought its bearer luck and protected them from death by drowning, and cauls were therefore prized by sailors. Medieval women sold them to sailors for large sums; a caul counted as a valuable talisman. Charles Dickens opened David Copperfield in 1850 with the narrator's own: "I was born with a caul, which was advertised for sale, in the newspapers, at the low price of fifteen guineas." Copperfield then follows the thing through a decade of resale and raffle. Fifteen guineas is a price in a novel, printed in 1850, and this record quotes it as that and not as a market rate.

The idioms carried the belief further than the objects did. Polish w czepku urodzony, 'born in a bonnet'; Italian nato con la camicia, 'born with a shirt'; French né coiffé, 'born with a hat on'; Russian родился в рубашке, 'born in a shirt' — all of them mean someone who is very lucky, and the Russian phrase is still applied to people who walk away from disasters, as if the caul persisted as armour.

Not every tradition reads it as good. In Romanian folklore babies born with a caul are said to become strigoi on death. In England the same birth was also read as the mark of someone destined to hang, on the proverb that he who is born to be hanged will never drown. In Jamaican folklore duppies are powerless against a person born with a caul. The 16th-century Dutch physician Levinus Lemnius, who wrote The Secret Miracles of Nature, was unconvinced by the claims made for preserved cauls; the 19th-century comic writer Thomas Hood ended his poem "The Sea-Spell" with a drowning sailor's charm failing him.
text.how: Not made and not chosen. The midwife, physician or parent removes the membrane at birth and presses it onto paper; a thicker chorionic caul has to be cut across the nostrils so the child can breathe and then eased off, and taken too fast it leaves scars. The dried sheet is kept in the family, given to the child, sold, or inherited. There is no rite over it.
text.today: Not a living trade. Cauls are still removed at birth, as a medical routine, and research in the 2020s has found that delivering severely premature infants with the caul intact can improve their chances, which is a use of the membrane with nothing folkloric in it. *Inference —* what remains of the amulet is the language: the Russian, Polish, Italian and French idioms for a lucky person are still in everyday use by speakers who have never seen one.

names.name: Challenge coin
names.th: เหรียญชาเลนจ์คอยน์ (เหรียญประจำหน่วย)

etymology.root: English challenge, from the demand — the 'coin check' — that every member present produce theirs
etymology.note: The rules of the challenge are not written down anywhere central. There is no formal rule for how a challenge may be made or what the penalty is, and organizations differ; buying a round is the usual forfeit.

text.what: A struck metal disc the size of a large coin, bearing a unit's insignia or an organization's emblem, carried in a pocket. Modern ones come in other shapes and sizes and take pop-culture figures as readily as regimental crests. Defacing one — drilling it for a keyring, say — is widely held to stop it counting, which is the only design rule the tradition enforces.
text.story:
This one is here for an unusual reason: its claim is not protection. A challenge coin proves you belong. Somebody calls a coin check; everyone present produces theirs; whoever cannot buys the round. That is the whole mechanism, and it is a membership test with a drinking forfeit attached, not a charm against anything.

The origin is contested, and this atlas reports the contest and picks no winner. The cited account is explicit that "the historicity of these stories is unclear", and there are at least five:

Roman soldiers who did well in battle were given a bonus coin alongside their day's wages — specially minted, by some accounts, with the marks of their legion — and some kept them instead of spending them. Renaissance portrait medals commemorated an event for a patron and were exchanged among friends. French Huguenots, after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, carried a méreau communion token and produced it at the door of a secret service to prove they were not a state spy — which is the first instance of a coin answering an actual challenge. An American volunteer flying squadron in the First World War had a wealthy lieutenant strike bronze medallions; a pilot wearing his in a leather pouch was shot down, stripped of his identification by a German patrol, escaped, and was taken for a saboteur by the French until the squadron insignia on the medallion identified him. And a Vietnam-era bar run by infantrymen made outsiders buy a round if they could not prove combat service, the proof escalating from enemy bullets to grenades and unexploded ordnance until somebody sensibly substituted a unit-marked disc.

Against all five stands one dated object. The oldest surviving challenge coin belongs to the 17th Infantry Regiment and was minted by the then Colonel William "Buffalo Bill" Quinn between 1950 and 1958, to mark the end of a tour. *Inference —* that is the only hard floor in the whole story, and everything earlier is a claim about ancestry rather than a coin somebody can hand you.

From US units the practice went sideways into everything. The FBI's Crisis Response unit issued the Bureau's first in the late 1980s. Air Force training instructors give an airman's coin at the end of basic training. The United States Congress makes them for members to give constituents. Presidents have issued them since the late 1990s: Bill Clinton kept racks of the ones service members gave him on the credenza behind his Oval Office desk, and they are in his official portrait; Barack Obama left them on the graves of dead soldiers. In Canada the practice arrived as "an Americanism" and was pushed by General Rick Hillier as the army worked more closely with US forces; the Royal Military College issues one to every officer cadet at the end of First-Year Orientation. In Switzerland officers order and pay for their own. In the United Kingdom, after commanders tightened restrictions on drinking, the traditional coin check has largely become a collection instead.

Non-military bodies took it up wholesale: NASCAR, the NFL, Eagle Scouts, the World Series of Poker, police and fire departments, labor unions, the Utah Symphony and Opera in 2007, motorcycle clubs, television crews. *Inference —* an object that authenticates membership is useful to any group with a boundary, and the drinking forfeit travelled with it more reliably than the military content did.

Where a protective claim does attach, it is on the fire-department coins. The obverse takes the classic image of a firefighter; the reverse is engraved with the prayer text. Set that beside what Samuel Stouffer and his colleagues found among American soldiers in the Second World War, reported in the study George Gmelch cites: facing great danger and uncertainty, soldiers developed magical practices, particularly protective amulets and good-luck charms — crosses, Bibles, rabbits' feet, medals — and guarded articles of clothing they associated with past escapes. *Inference —* that is the neighbouring practice, not this one, and this record keeps them apart. The challenge coin's own documented job is the coin check.
text.how: Commissioned by a unit, a commander or an organization, struck by a commercial minter, and presented — for an achievement, a visit, a graduation, a donation, a death. Carried at all times is the rule the challenge enforces. Not blessed, not charged, not retired. A defaced coin, including one modified to make it easier to carry, generally stops qualifying for a challenge.
text.today: Issued by most units in the United States military and by a wide range of civilian bodies as of the cited account. Presidential coins have been a running controversy: the White House Communications Agency released one in May 2018 showing Donald Trump and Kim Jong-un ahead of the Singapore talks scheduled for June; Trump's own coin dropped the presidential seal, the motto E pluribus unum and the thirteen arrows, and carried a campaign slogan on both faces; Joe Biden's shows Delaware and the 261st Theater Tactical Signal Brigade, his late son Beau's unit. No dated retail price was read for this record.

etymology.root: Chinese 厭勝錢 yànshèng qián; the formal older pronunciation was yāshèng qián, 押勝錢 / 压胜钱
etymology.note: Also called 花錢 huāqián, flower coins or patterned coins, and 玩钱 wanqian, play coins. In modern China and Taiwan flower coins is the commoner name.

text.what: A cast bronze disc with a hole through it, shaped like a Chinese cash coin and never spendable as one. Where a government coin carries two or four characters, a charm coin usually carries more, and often a picture as well: a dragon, a zodiac animal, a scene, an eight-trigram diagram, a line of Taoist talismanic script. Most are cast, not struck — machine striking only reaches China in the 19th century. They have also been made in iron, lead, tin, silver, gold, porcelain, jade and paper.
text.story:
They start as coins going strange. Yansheng coins first appear in the Western Han as a variant of the Ban Liang and Wu Zhu cash then in circulation, used to speak to the dead, to pray for a favourable outcome, to terrify ghosts, or as lucky money. From the start of the Han to the end of the Northern and Southern dynasties, 206 BCE to 589 CE, most of them look like the circulating coinage; the difference is on the reverse — tortoises, snakes, double-edged swords, sun, moon, stars, famous people, the twelve zodiac animals. They were mostly privately funded and cast by wealthy families for their own ceremonies, though governments and religious orders cast some, and they circulated alongside real money because a copper-alloy disc was worth its metal.

The typologies are published and large. In Cast Chinese Amulets, 2020, the British numismatist David Hartill documented over 5,000 different types. Catalogues sort them by shape, by size, by meaning, by an emperor's name, or by any other shared feature; some deliberately refuse those categories, on the grounds that a novice cannot tell whether a given amulet is a lucky, religious, family or coin type. The standing classes run by function — good luck, safe journey, peace, burial, marriage and sex education, house, palace; by shape and design — gourd, vault protector, open-work, 24-character, spade, lock, nine-fold seal script, fish, peach, little shoe, pendant, palindrome, Ming cloisonné, money tree; and by theme — astronomy, zodiac, Eight Treasures, the Book of Changes and Bagua, five poisons, Confucian, Taoist, Buddhist temple coins, horse coins, even xiangqi pieces.

Some classes are exact enough to identify by measurement. "Laid to Rest" burial charms are bronze, 2.4 to 2.45 cm across and 1.3 to 1.4 mm thick, with the obverse inscription rù tǔ wéi ān, 'to be laid to rest', and a blank reverse; they turn up mostly in late Qing graves. They are often left out of reference books on Chinese coins and charms, because they were placed in the mouths of the dead and are considered unlucky and disturbing, and most collectors do not want them.

The five poisons charms are dated to a day: the fifth day of the fifth month, the most inauspicious in the calendar, when summer opened with dangerous animals, infectious disease and, in the account, evil spirits. The five poisons are snakes, scorpions, centipedes, toads and spiders, sometimes with lizards, the three-legged toad or the tiger, and the reasoning given is that poison can only be thwarted with poison. One example carries the legend 五日午时, 'noon of the 5th day', and the charms were worn on that day.

Peace charms have an archaeology. A find of the 1980s established that the tài píng bǎi qián was first cast by the Kingdom of Shu after the collapse of the Han, worth a hundred cash and cut in a calligraphic style closer to a charm than to the coinage of its day. Under the Qing, charms reading tiān xià tài píng — peace under heaven — became a common sight.
text.how: Cast in moulds, privately and in temples, then carried, hung, sewn on or buried. Open-work charms of the Tang and Song were used as clothing accessories, as ornament, and to decorate horses; fish charms meant to be worn at the waist come in under the Khitan Liao. House charms were set into buildings during construction, and into temples; Bagua charms decorate ridgepoles alongside red paper and cloth banners. Palace cash, which David Hartill notes were only produced at the establishment of a new reign era title, were wrapped in a rectangular cloth and given at New Year to imperial guards and eunuchs, who hung them below lamps, and were replaced with new reign titles each time an emperor died.
text.today: Collected, catalogued and reproduced. Use was revitalised in the Republic of China era, and the charms remain the best-catalogued class of amulet in this atlas — Hartill's 5,000-odd types are a finding aid a reader can actually use, which is a thing almost no other tradition here has. Feng shui coins on red cord are sold worldwide as of 2026; whether a modern cast disc is the same object as a Qing one is the same argument the dzi market has.

names.name: Cimaruta
names.th: ชีมารูตา (กิ่งต้นรูเครื่องรางอิตาลี)

etymology.root: Neapolitan cimaruta, from Italian cima di ruta, 'sprig of rue' — cima 'top, tip' plus ruta, the flowering medicinal herb the whole charm is shaped as.

text.what: A silver sprig of rue with charms on the ends of its branches. From a central stalk the branches radiate and each one blossoms into a different object: a rose, a hand holding a wand or a sword, a flaming heart, a fish, a crescent moon, a snake, an owl, a plumed medieval helmet, a vervain blossom, a dolphin, a cock, an eagle. One cimaruta might carry a key, a dagger, a blossom and a moon and no more. Most are double-sided and fairly large — some almost four inches across.
text.story:
The cimaruta is worn round the neck or hung above an infant's bed, and what it is hung against is named in Italian: mal'occhio, the evil eye. Which charms go on the branches varies by region of origin, and the form is particularly associated with southern Italy.

The piece has been studied as a structure rather than as a symbol. R. T. Günther published "The Cimaruta: Its Structure and Development" in Folk-lore in 1905, working on how the branches and their charms are put together and how that arrangement changed.

There is a live argument about whose object it is. Some practitioners of the neopagan religion of witchcraft called Stregoneria or Stregheria treat the cimaruta as a survival of an older Italian magic tradition, of the kind Charles Leland described in his 1899 Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches, which claimed a pagan witch-cult still active in Italy. Raven Grimassi, in The Cimaruta: And Other Magical Charms from Old Italy (2012), argues the cimaruta was originally a witches' charm, a sign of membership in what he calls the Society of Diana, later taken over by Italian folk magic, with Christian symbols added to the original pagan ones. Wikipedia's own account of the same material describes the cimaruta as alleged to be in borrowed use among self-identified Italian-American witches, which is a different claim about the same objects. This atlas reports both and settles neither; what is not in dispute is that the charm is worn in southern Italy and by descendants of Italian emigrants, against the eye, and that some of its branches carry Christian imagery.
text.how: Cast, commonly in silver, as a single piece: stalk, branches, and the charms that terminate them. Some modern versions are cast in bronze or pewter. Worn on a cord or chain at the neck, or hung over the bed of a child too young to wear one.
text.today: Still cast and sold, in Italy and in the Italian-American market, in silver and in cheaper alloys, and sold alongside books that make the Stregheria claim for it. *Inference —* the object's present-day buyers are not the same population as its nineteenth-century wearers, and the argument recorded above is mostly an argument between the two.

text_th.what: กิ่งต้นรู (rue) ทำด้วยเงิน ปลายกิ่งแต่ละกิ่งมีเครื่องราง กิ่งแผ่ออกจากก้านกลาง และแต่ละกิ่งผลิเป็นของต่างกัน ได้แก่ ดอกกุหลาบ มือถือคทาหรือดาบ หัวใจลุกเป็นไฟ ปลา พระจันทร์เสี้ยว งู นกฮูก หมวกเหล็กยุคกลางประดับขนนก ดอกเวอร์บีนา (vervain) ปลาโลมา ไก่ตัวผู้ นกอินทรี ชีมารูตาชิ้นหนึ่งอาจมีเพียงกุญแจ กริช ดอกไม้ และพระจันทร์ ไม่มีอื่นอีก ส่วนใหญ่ทำสองหน้าและค่อนข้างใหญ่ บางชิ้นกว้างเกือบสี่นิ้ว

names.name: Cippus of Horus
names.said: SIP-us, plural cippi, from the Latin for a small pillar or marker
names.th: ซิปปัสแห่งฮอรัส (ศิลาฮอรัส)

etymology.root: Latin cippus, a small pillar or boundary stone — an archaeologist's borrowing, not an Egyptian word for the object.
etymology.note: Museums also label the class 'Horus on the Crocodiles' after what is carved on the front.

text.what: A slab of stone carved with the child Horus standing on two crocodiles, gripping snakes and scorpions in his fists, and often an antelope by the horns and a lion by the tail. Rows of hieroglyphs cover the rest of it. Sizes run from house-sized stelae down to amulets small enough to carry: the Metternich Stela is one block of greywacke about 35.8 inches tall and 13.25 wide, and the Metropolitan Museum also holds a miniature.
text.story:
This is an amulet you drink. The instruction is on the object: water is poured over the carved spells and the carved figures, collected at the base, and given to the person who has been bitten or stung, to swallow or to wash the wound with. The words come off the stone into the water. Priests recited alongside.

The Metternich Stela is the fullest of them. It dates to about 380–342 BCE, the Thirtieth Dynasty, under Nectanebo II, and it carries thirteen spells against venomous bites and wounds and against the illnesses they cause — including the story of Isis and the Seven Scorpions, which is among the most complete versions found on any monument. The logic is precedent: Horus as a child was stung in the marshes at Khemmis and was cured, and the spell puts the patient in the child's place.

It disappeared for two thousand years and turned up in a wall excavated in a Franciscan monastery. Muhammad Ali Pasha gave it to Prince Metternich in 1828; it sat at Kynžvart Castle in Bohemia until 1950, when the Metropolitan Museum of Art acquired it.

The class runs from the Third Intermediate Period to the end of Ptolemaic rule in Egypt. Not all of them are museum monuments — some are amulet-sized, and the same image of Horus on the crocodiles is carried. The Egyptian Museum in Cairo holds the healing statue of Djedhor, the Louvre a Priest of Bastet statue, and the Brooklyn Museum another cippus; Keith Seele, Robert Ritner and Jane Draycott have written on them.

*Inference —* an amulet that is used up by being washed is a different kind of object from one that is worn, and it puts this stone closer to an Ethiopian scroll read aloud, or to a Qur'anic bowl rinsed and drunk, than to the faience beetle in the next tray.
text.how: Carved in stone with the Horus figure on the front and the spells around it. Water is poured over it, caught, and drunk or applied to the body by the person suffering the poisoning, with rites recited by priests. The large ones stay where they stand; the small ones are carried.
text.today: Not in use. Cippi are museum objects — the Metropolitan Museum shows them at The Met Fifth Avenue, and the Brooklyn Museum, the Louvre and the Egyptian Museum in Cairo hold others. As of 2026 this project has read no account of water being poured over one for a patient.

names.name: Concealed shoe
names.th: รองเท้าซ่อนในบ้าน

text.what: An ordinary worn shoe, walled into a building where nobody will see it: up a chimney, under a floor, above a ceiling, in the roof, beside a door or window frame, occasionally in the foundations. Almost all of them have been worn — 98 per cent — and many have been repaired. Most finds are single shoes rather than pairs, and about half of them belonged to children. Archaeologists call a cache of this kind a spiritual midden.
text.story:
Northampton Museum keeps the count. Its Concealed Shoe Index held more than 1,100 reports by 1998 and 1,900 by 2012, mostly from Britain but some from as far as Canada, with almost half dating from the nineteenth century. June Swann's analysis of the index, published in 1996, gives the hiding places by share: chimney, fireplace or hearth 26.2 per cent; under the floor or above the ceiling 22.9 per cent; almost as many again in the roof. The rest come from around doors and windows, under stairs and among foundations. Of the thousands reported, thirteen in Swann's analysis were in foundations, and she raised — carefully — a possible connection with the Carthaginian practice of putting infants into the foundations of buildings, with the shoe standing in for the person.

The earliest reported example was found behind the choir stalls in Winchester Cathedral, which were installed in 1308. The buildings are otherwise unremarkable: country cottages, town houses, manor houses, hospitals, workhouses, factories, public houses, two Oxford colleges — St John's and Queen's — a Benedictine monastery in Germany and a Baptist church in Cheshire. In the United States the deposits cluster in New England and the north-east, the regions first colonised from East Anglia.

What they were for is argued, and the arguers are named. The independent researcher Brian Hoggard observes that the places the shoes turn up — chimneys, floors, ceilings, doors, windows, roofs — suggest that at least some were hidden as charms protecting the occupants against evil influences such as demons, ghosts and witches. The explanation most scholars favour runs on scent: a witch is drawn by the human smell of a shoe, enters it, and is trapped, being unable to reverse. The archaeologist Ralph Merrifield suggested the belief may descend from John Schorne, an unofficial fourteenth-century English saint said to have trapped the Devil in a boot — a legend Merrifield thought might itself sit on an older folk belief the Church was trying to convert into an approved rite.

A second reading is about birth rather than defence. Shoes and fertility are linked in English custom, from the old woman who lived in a shoe to the shoe thrown after a bride and the shoes tied to a departing couple's car; Merrifield recorded that in Lancashire a woman who wished to conceive might try on the shoes of a woman who had just given birth, a custom called smickling. A third belongs to the archaeologist and architectural historian M. Chris Manning, who proposes that immuring shoes and garments may be connected to the belief in a household spirit found across northern Europe from Ireland to western Russia — the brownie and the hob of England and Scotland, who could be driven off by a gift of clothing, and the Russian domovoi, who could be drawn to a house with an old boot or bast shoe put under the stove or hung in the yard.

The custom faded through the twentieth century without quite stopping. Only fifty post-1900 instances have been recorded. In 1964 the shoe manufacturer Norvic put a pair of their women's high-leg boots into the foundations of a new factory; in 1991, at Knebworth House, an estate worker's shoe replaced an old court shoe that had been found behind some panelling.
text.how: Take a shoe somebody has actually worn — not a new one — and build it into the fabric of the house at a threshold: the chimney is the commonest choice, then the void under a floor or above a ceiling, then the roof. It is not charged, not inscribed, not renewed, and not meant to come out. The Knebworth case is the one recorded instance in this record of a replacement: the old shoe found, a new one put back.
text.today: Not a living custom in Britain, on this record's sources: it died out during the twentieth century, and the fifty recorded instances after 1900 are the exceptions that say so. The shoes themselves keep arriving, one demolition at a time, and Northampton Museum keeps adding them to the index. Apart from their folklore, they are the largest surviving body of evidence for what ordinary people actually put on their feet.

names.name: Coptic cross tattoo
names.said: in Egyptian Arabic the mark is simply the salib, the cross
names.th: รอยสักกางเขนคอปติก

text.what: A small cross tattooed on the inside of the right wrist. The usual design is the Coptic cross: two bold lines of equal length crossing at right angles, each arm ending in three points — twelve points in all. Often blue. In a Cairo studio it takes under ten minutes.
text.story:
Many Copts have the cross tattooed as a sign of faith on the inside of their right arm at the wrist. That is the whole of what the Coptic cross article says about it, and every other thing on this page had to be sourced elsewhere, which is itself worth noticing about a practice this widespread.

The Egyptian Streets writer Farah Rafik, in February 2022, traces the tattooing tradition among Egyptians to the Coptic period, and says it intensified after the Muslim conquest of Egypt around 640 CE, when Christians faced conversion or the religious tax, and some were marked with crosses on the wrist so the authorities could tell who had kept their faith. What began as a mark applied from outside became a mark applied by parents. Rafik quotes the researcher Jean-Philippe Belleau: "The fear of conversion among members of the Christian minority of Egypt has led many Coptic parents to tattoo their children with a small blue cross." The reason parents gave was blunt — a child whose parents were killed would still be recognised, and raised, among Christians. In some churches the wrist has also served as the check at the door.

The people who put it on are named and working. Girgis Gabriel Girgis has run a studio in Muqattam, the quarter above Cairo, for over thirty years, and does five to seven tattoos a day, mostly Coptic crosses. Another tattooist, Magdy Girgis, calls the practice "a sign of resistance, perseverance and solidarity".

*Inference —* this is the only amulet in this batch whose bearer cannot take it off, sell it, lose it or leave it to anybody, and the tradition's own account of why it is permanent is exactly that.

The sign has Egyptian company. The ankh survived Christianisation in Egypt as the crux ansata, an ankh with a circular loop, and Coptic Christians used that form in many media, especially in textiles. Bertran de la Farge dates the trefoil Coptic cross to the fourth century and reads it as a predecessor of the Occitan cross.
text.how: Applied by a tattooist, usually on the inside of the right wrist, commonly in childhood within Coptic families and also on adults. The design is small and fast. The sources read here name no rite, no fasting and no blessing attached to it; what they describe is a studio, a queue and a needle.
text.today: Living, and worked at daily. As of 2026 Girgis Gabriel Girgis's Muqattam studio is the one the reporting names, and the mark functions as a permanent visible sign of Christian identity. Whether a reader outside the community should wear the same design is an argument with named people in it, and this atlas reports it rather than settling it: the tattooists quoted describe the mark as resistance and solidarity, which is a claim about who is inside.

names.name: Corn dolly
names.th: ตุ๊กตาฟางข้าว (คอร์นดอลลี)

etymology.root: English corn in its British sense of grain in general — in American English this would be a grain dolly — plus dolly, a small figure. The Latin vetula, 'little old woman', is the name used for the same object among the Germanic pagans of seventh-century Flanders.
etymology.note: The names are mostly names for an old woman or a girl: Corn-mother, Old Woman, Old Grandmother in East Prussia, Carlin in Scotland, Y Wrach — the Hag — in Caernarvonshire.

text.what: A hollow shape plaited from the last sheaf of a harvest: a figure, a knot, a lantern, a crown, a fan, a horseshoe. British ones are wheat, oats, rye or barley; Irish ones are rush; in southern France they are palm leaves. In Scandinavia and the German-speaking countries the straw is tied with yarn or raffia rather than plaited. Some are whole sheaves dressed as a woman and carried home on the last waggon.
text.story:
The explanation usually given for it is a scholars' explanation, and it is worth saying so first. Writers of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries theorised that before Christianisation the spirit of the corn was held to live among the crop, and that the harvest made it homeless; the last sheaf, plaited into a shape, gave it somewhere to spend the winter until it was ploughed into the first furrow of the new season. James Frazer gave four chapters of The Golden Bough to the Corn-Mother and the Corn-Maiden in northern Europe, drawing on the enormous body of European folklore that Wilhelm Mannhardt had collected.

What Frazer's informants actually described is more concrete. Near Danzig, whoever cut the last ears made them into a doll called the Corn-mother or the Old Woman and it came home on the last waggon. In parts of Holstein the last sheaf was dressed in women's clothes, called the Corn-mother, carried home and then thoroughly drenched with water — a rain-charm, Frazer says. In the district of Bruck in Styria the Corn-mother was made by the oldest married woman in the village, a woman of fifty to fifty-five; the finest ears were plucked out and twisted into a wreath, which the prettiest girl in the village carried on her head to the squire, while the Corn-mother herself was laid down in the barn to keep off the mice. In East Prussia the reapers called out to the woman binding the last sheaf that she was getting the Old Grandmother. In Scotland, when the last corn was cut after Hallowmas, the figure made from it was sometimes the Carlin, the old woman.

The oldest dated mention is a prohibition. In seventh-century Flanders, Saint Eligius told his congregation not to make vetulas — little figures of the Old Woman — nor little deer nor iotticos, nor set tables at night, nor exchange New Year gifts.

Mechanised harvesting effectively ended the craft at the beginning of the twentieth century. It came back in Britain in the 1950s and 1960s as a craft revival: farm workers made new things, including replicas of farm implements, windmills and large figures, new shapes and new techniques appeared, and several books came out in the 1960s and 1970s. The source is blunt about what that revival did: the simple origins of the craft had been lost, and new folklore stories were added to the original ideas. Anyone reading a modern account of what a particular corn dolly means is reading something from that period unless it is sourced to Mannhardt or earlier.

The old long-stemmed, hollow-stemmed wheats the work needs were replaced by short pithy varieties bred for the combine. A number of English and Scottish farmers still grow the old sorts — Maris Wigeon, Squarehead Master, Elite Le Peuple — mainly because thatchers want them.
text.how: Cut from the last sheaf standing, at the end of harvest, by a person the local custom names — the one who cuts the last ears, the woman who binds the last sheaf, the oldest married woman in the village. Plaited hollow, or tied with yarn, or dressed as a figure. Carried home on the last waggon, set at the centre of the harvest supper, hung in the house or laid in the barn, and kept over winter. Then it goes back into the ground: ploughed into the first furrow of the new season.
text.today: Made as a craft rather than as a harvest rite, and the Heritage Crafts Association lists corn dolly making as endangered. The Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford, the Museum of English Rural Life in Reading and the Ryedale Folk Museum in Yorkshire hold collections of them from around the world.

names.name: Cornicello
names.th: คอร์นิเชลโล (เขานำโชคอิตาลี)

etymology.root: Italian corno 'horn' with the diminutive -icello: 'little horn'. The fuller name corno portafortuna is 'horn that brings luck'.

text.what: A single twisted horn, a few centimetres long, tapering to a point and pierced at the wide end for a chain. Gold, silver, plastic, bone, terracotta or red coral. The red ones look like a chili pepper, which is an accident of history: chilis only reached Europe after the Columbian exchange, and the horn shape is much older than the resemblance.
text.story:
The cornicello is worn against the evil eye — malocchio — and against bad luck in general, and historically to promote fertility and virility. The harm it answers is described precisely by the people who wear it: the eye is held to strike nursing mothers and their babies, fruit-bearing trees, milking animals and the sperm of men. Those are the forces of generation, and a horn is an answer in kind.

The shape is said to be modelled on an eland horn, for fertility, virility and strength. Its materials carry their own connections in the tradition's own telling: coral is sacred to Venus, goddess of love, fertility, sex and prosperity; silver to Luna, goddess of the moon; the phallic shape and the red colour point to Priapus, a male fertility god; the horn itself is tied to Pan, and the broken goat's horn Zeus filled with fruit and flowers became the cornucopia.

It is a regional object, not a national one. Cornicelli are most often worn by men in southern Italy, above all in Campania, then Lazio, Apulia and Basilicata, and to a lesser extent Sicily and Calabria — and by the descendants of Italian emigrants elsewhere. Dried chili peppers are hung in some southern Italian homes against the same harm, which is how the resemblance became a second charm.

The horn also has a hand. The mano cornuta, the horned hand, is an Italian gesture — and an amulet imitating the gesture — made with the hand levelled or pointing down, usually with a swivelling or oscillating motion, against the same eye.
text.how: Cast or carved: gold and silver for the good ones, red coral for the old ones, plastic for the cheap ones, bone and terracotta in between. Pierced at the broad end and hung on a neck chain. It is also hung from the rear-view mirrors of cars — a move the source ties to the older custom of hanging them on draft horses — and in houses. Nothing is recorded about charging it or retiring it.
text.today: Made and sold in enormous numbers, in gold at jewellers and in plastic at every tourist stall in Naples, and worn worldwide by people of Italian descent and by people with no connection to Campania at all. *Inference —* the horn has crossed from a charm against a named harm to a badge of origin, and the two uses are worn on the same chain by the same people without anyone being asked to choose.
