names.th: สายเปลือกหอยเบี้ย

etymology.root: Hindi कौडि kaudi, from Sanskrit कपर्द kaparda. The Italian word for the shell, porcellana, is where English gets 'porcelain', from the resemblance.
etymology.note: In Ojibwe the shells used in Midewiwin ceremonies are miigis or whiteshells, and Whiteshell Provincial Park in Manitoba is named for them. In the Kingdom of Kongo the shell currency was nzimbu or zimbo, but that was a different snail — Olivella nana, harvested at Luanda Island.

text.what: Small sea-snail shells, egg-shaped, glossy, with a long toothed slit down the flat underside. Strung on cord, sewn onto cloth, hung at the neck, or thrown in handfuls. Most run about the size of a thumbnail; the family runs from 5 mm to 19 cm across its species. The money cowrie, Monetaria moneta, is the one that travelled.
text.story:
This is the only amulet in the atlas that was also, for centuries and across three continents, money. Cowries were used as currency by Africans for centuries, and the money cowrie was almost impossible to counterfeit until the late nineteenth century. The Classical Chinese character for money, 貝, began as a stylised drawing of a Maldivian cowrie shell, and characters for money, property and wealth still carry it as a radical.

The volume matters for what follows. After the 1500s European traders, chiefly through the slave trade, moved huge numbers of Maldivian cowries into Africa; between 1500 and 1875 at least 30 billion were imported to the Bight of Benin, making up 44% of the total value of trade there. Around 1850 the German explorer Heinrich Barth found them still in use at Kano, Kuka, Gando and Timbuktu, and reported that in Muniyoma, an old division of Bornu, the king's revenue was reckoned at 30,000,000 shells, with every adult male owing 1,000 a year for himself, 1,000 for each pack-ox and 2,000 for each enslaved person he held. In parts of British West Africa cowries were accepted for tax until the early twentieth century, and their use as currency persisted in unregulated settings into the 1960s. Ghana's national currency, introduced in 1965, is the cedi, named after the shell.

What the shell does when it is not money is spread just as far. Yoruba diviners in West Africa cast cowries, as do the annual customs of Dahomey in Benin. In Brazil, as a result of the Atlantic slave trade, the shells — búzios — are cast to consult the Orixás and to hear their replies. The Kaniyar Panicker astrologers of Kerala used them among their devices. In West Bengal a cowrie is the token fare for the departed soul's ferry across the Vaitarani, and cowries are used at cremations and in the worship of Lakshmi. In Nepal sixteen are thrown in a gambling game at Tihar, and in the same festival the shells are worshipped as a sign of Lakshmi and of wealth.

As a charm it is tied to the body and to birth. In certain parts of Africa cowries were prized charms, said to be associated with fecundity, sexual pleasure and good luck. In Mende and in Kikuyu culture the shells stand for womanhood, fertility, birth and wealth. One modern ethnographic author reads the underside as a vulva or an eye — the source attributes that reading rather than asserting it, and so does this atlas.

And it goes in graves. In predynastic Egypt and the Neolithic southern Levant, cowries were placed in the graves of young girls, and modified Levantine cowries were found ritually arranged around the skull in female burials. In the Bronze Age they became more common as funerary goods, again with women and children. Egypt made an imitation of it: the cowroid, a seal amulet in the shape of a cowrie, with copies in stone or faience appearing in the early second millennium BCE.

The Ojibwe use miigis shells in Midewiwin ceremonies, and how shells from a warm-sea species reached that far inland and that far north is an open question. Oral stories and birch-bark scrolls say the shells were found in the ground, or washed up on the shores of lakes and rivers.

On the Fiji Islands, a golden cowrie — bulikula, Cypraea aurantium — was drilled at both ends and worn on a string at the neck by chieftains as a badge of rank.
text.how: Drilled at the ends or ground open on the back, then strung, sewn or hung. In divination they are not worn at all but thrown: a set number goes down and the reading is made from which ones land aperture-up. That same throw is a dice mechanism in Pachisi and Ashta Chamma.
text.today: Still worn, still cast, still sold by the sack in West African and Indian markets. The cedi is still named after it. As of 2026 this project has read no source that dates the end of any of these uses.

names.name: Crystal pendant
names.th: จี้คริสตัล

etymology.root: Greek κρύσταλλος krýstallos, 'ice' — the ancient Greek reading of clear quartz was water frozen so hard it stayed solid

text.what: A cut or tumbled stone hung at the neck, usually in a wire cage or a silver bezel: a six-sided quartz point, a rose quartz lozenge, a lump of amethyst, a polished bead of agate or turquoise. It is worn, held, placed on the body, or meditated with. The same stones are sold loose by the kilo, and the pendant is the wearable end of a trade that also fills bowls in shop windows.
text.story:
Two arguments run through this object, and they are not the same argument. This record reports the first and stays out of it, and reports the second at length because there are names and dates in it.

The first argument is whether the stones do anything. The cited account calls crystal healing "a pseudoscientific, alternative medicine practice" and says adherents "claim that these have healing powers, but there is no scientific basis for this claim". Practitioners, in the same account's words, hold that they can "boost low energy, prevent bad energy, release blocked energy, and transform a body's aura"; that physical properties — shape, colour, markings — decide what a stone can treat, with published lists of the correspondences; and, at the same time, "that crystals have no intrinsic qualities but that, instead, their quality changes according to both" the participants, which the account itself flags as a paradox. Stuart McLean calls the practice "the middle-class New Age healing activity par excellence". Against all that, Christopher French of the anomalistic psychology research unit at the University of London and colleagues from Goldsmiths College ran eighty volunteers meditating with either a quartz crystal or an indistinguishable placebo stone, reported typical crystal effects either way, and concluded at the British Psychological Society Centenary Annual Conference in 2001: "There is no evidence that crystal healing works over and above a placebo effect." Every sentence in this paragraph belongs to somebody named. This atlas does not add one.

The second argument has coordinates. Worldwide retail sales of crystals were estimated at more than US$1 billion a year in 2019. India, China, Brazil and Madagascar are the main producers. In Madagascar most crystals come out of unsafe, non-industrial mines — "homemade", in the cited account's word — dug with shovels by parents and children working together in pits and tunnels. Miners are paid between 17 and 23 US cents per kilogram for rose quartz, which is roughly 8 to 11 cents a pound; a miner's income may be 0.1 per cent of the final retail price. The reporting behind those figures is Tess McClure's, published in The Guardian on 17 September 2019 under the title "Dark crystals: the brutal reality behind a booming wellness craze"; this project could not fetch the original and read it instead through Aaron Gilbreath's Longreads piece of 25 September 2019, which gives the rose quartz village as Anjoma Ramartina, puts the going rate at 800 ariary — about 23 US cents — per kilo, enough to buy a cup of rice at the village market, and quotes one mine worker, Rakotondrasolo: "I was afraid, and was afraid for my children because of this soil. It can collapse on them."

On why the pay is that low, the cited account gives both industry answers and endorses neither: "Some people in the industry say that the low pay for miners is because customers in developed countries want low retail prices; others say that it is due to shops in developed countries wanting to be more profitable." Those are the two sides, in the trade's own mouths, and this atlas prints them and stops.

One further hazard is documented and belongs to whoever handles the stone rather than to whoever mined it: some crystals sold in the trade, shungite among them, frequently contain heavy metals and carry a toxicity risk for people handling them over long periods or ingesting anything that has been in contact with them.

*Inference —* the useful thing about this object for the rest of the atlas is that its supply chain is documented and a Bronze Age bead's is not. What a reader can see here — a wage, a village, a named miner, a retail figure, a 0.1 per cent — is the thing every other record in this collection would want and cannot have.
text.how: Mined, tumbled or faceted, wire-wrapped or set, and sold in mineral shops, gift shops, wellness retailers and online. Practitioners select stones by colour or by the qualities they attribute to them and place them on parts of the body; the pendant version keeps one stone at the sternum permanently. There is no consecration and no restriction on who may make or wear one. Nothing is said in the sources read here about retiring one.
text.today: Sold everywhere in 2026, in every price band, alongside reiki, flower essences and homeopathy in the same shops. The sourcing argument has been in print since 2019 and this project has read nothing showing it changed the supply chain. The worry stone record points here for exactly this reason: it is the same stones, the same trade, the same question.

names.name: Curse tablet
names.th: แผ่นคำสาป (คาตาเดสมอส)

etymology.root: from the Greek and Latin words for 'pierce' and 'bind' — katadesmos from katadeō, to bind down; defixio from defigere, to fix or nail down

text.what: A very thin sheet of lead with tiny letters scratched into it, then rolled, folded, or pierced through with a nail. It goes into the ground: buried in a grave or tomb, thrown down a well or a pool, shut in an underground sanctuary, nailed to a temple wall. Some are found with small bound figurines, hands and feet tied, sometimes pierced too. Some have hair or a scrap of clothing folded into them.
text.story:
This is the amulet turned around, and the atlas keeps it here on purpose. Everything else in this batch is written to keep a harm off a person. A defixio is written to put one on. Same lead, same scratched letters, same divine names, same burial in a grave — and the target is a named human being.

About 1,600 of them have been found, most in Greek, 220 from Attica alone. The first set came from Selinus in Sicily: twenty-two tablets, mostly early fifth century BCE, aimed at somebody the writer was suing. The Athenian tablets are full of lawsuits — may he botch his performance in court, forget his words, become dizzy. Others are erotic binding spells, or aimed at thieves, business rivals and sporting rivals.

In 1979 and 1980, 130 tablets came out of the sacred spring at Aquae Sulis, now Bath. All but one concern the restitution of stolen goods. More than eighty similar tablets were found at a temple of Mercury at West Hill, Uley, which makes south-western Britain one of the great centres of Latin defixiones. Some scholars refuse to call these curses at all and prefer 'judicial prayers', because what they mostly do is list a crime in detail and hand the punishment to a god.

The writing is doing work beyond its sense. Voces mysticae — words in no known language — recur; Stanley J. Tambiah proposed in 1968 that they represent "the language that demons can understand". Clement of Alexandria, around 200 CE, held that human language was not fit for addressing gods at all. Tablets survive with blank spaces where a name should go, prepared in advance and finished when a customer paid.

*Inference —* the blank space is the tell. An object sold ready-made with a gap for the buyer's enemy is a product, and the professional who wrote it had the same relationship to his customers as the man selling gems with Abrasax on them two streets away.

etymology.root: Japanese 達磨, the transcription of Dharma in Bodhidharma — the fifth- or sixth-century monk credited with carrying Chan, later Zen, to China
etymology.note: The limbless shape is read back into the legend: Bodhidharma is said to have sat facing a wall for nine years until his arms and legs wasted. The tumbler body it borrows is the okiagari-kobōshi, a self-righting monk toy popular in the Kinki region in the mid-seventeenth century, itself introduced from Ming China.

text.what: A hollow papier-mâché figure, round, weighted at the base so it rights itself when knocked over, usually red, with a bearded scowling face and two oversized white eyes left blank. Sold with no pupils. The owner inks one in when they set a goal and the other when they reach it. Other colours exist: a set of five — blue, yellow, red, white, black — is sold as Goshiki Daruma, and gold ones are sold for money.
text.story:
The doll has a home town. Shorinzan Daruma Temple in Takasaki, Gunma, north of Tokyo, is where its present sense as a luck charm starts. Josef Kyburz records that the founder of that Daruma-dera drew New Year charms of Bodhidharma, which parishioners kept to "bring happiness and prosperity and ward off accidents and misfortune". The charms expired after a year, so the demand came round again every twelve months, and the ninth priest, Togaku, solved the problem near the start of the Meiwa period (1764–72) by cutting wooden block moulds and handing them to the parishioners to make their own papier-mâché charms. Kyburz notes it is not known when the Bodhidharma charm and the tumbler toy merged; by the mid-nineteenth century the two were treated as the same thing. Takasaki's families were mostly silk farmers, a crop that turns on luck, and the doll became the region's mascot.

The red has a second history. *Tradition holds —* red is the colour of a high-ranking priest's robe, and the art historian James T. Ulak has traced depictions of Bodhidharma in red robes before any doll existed. In the late Edo period red was tied to smallpox: during measles and smallpox outbreaks in Edo and nearby cities, households strung red paper strips on ropes around the house, dressed the sick child in red, and set up a small altar with daruma figures on it for the God of Smallpox. The red was to please the deity; the self-righting body was to tell the patient to get up as fast as they went down.

The eye-painting reached national television through politics. Time reported in 1967 that in the Tokyo headquarters of the Liberal Democratic Party, Premier Eisaku Satō inked the right eye of his daruma and said: "The eyes, are as big as my own." Party headquarters at election time are still photographed with a large one.

A feminine line runs alongside. Hime daruma and onna daruma — Princess and Lady Daruma — began in the Edo merchant culture that made fun of what its betters held sacred, including a version of Bodhidharma drawn as a prostitute, on the grounds that prostitutes showed the same okiagari resilience. The satire faded; the dolls stayed, wholesome.
text.how: Bought blank-eyed, often at a New Year market. The owner picks one goal, inks the left eye with a brush, and keeps the figure in view; the right eye is filled in when the goal is met. Traditionally only the head of the household did the painting. Matsukawa daruma are sold with both eyes already painted, because their job is to watch over the house rather than to track a goal. At the end of the year every daruma goes back to the temple it came from for the daruma kuyō, a burning held just after New Year's Day — the best known at Nishi-Arai Daishi in Tokyo and Dairyū-ji in Gifu — where tens of thousands are burnt together after the monks' procession, sutras and horns. Then you buy next year's.
text.today: Takasaki still holds its Daruma Doll Festival, the daruma-ichi, at the Shorinzan. The city's own website says over 400,000 people come from across the Kanto Plain to buy new dolls for the year, and that Takasaki makes 80% of Japan's daruma. The festival also carries a 24-hour reading of sutras by the Shorinzan monks for world peace. The shape is common property now: snowmen in Japanese are yukidaruma, the children's game Darumasan ga Koronda is the local Red Light Green Light, and Pokémon put out Darumaka and Darmanitan in 2010.

names.name: Djed pillar
names.said: JED, anglicised; Ancient Egyptian ḏd, Coptic ϫⲱⲧ jōt, 'pillar'
names.th: เสาเจด

etymology.root: Egyptian ḏd 'pillar', surviving into Coptic as ϫⲱⲧ jōt. The sign writes the word for stability.
etymology.note: Egyptologists read the object it draws as Osiris's spine. Erich Neumann read it instead as a tree, and pointed out that Egypt was largely treeless, so the myth may be carrying the memory of timber imported from Syria. Gordon and Schwabe, in 2004, argued it is a bull's sacrum.

text.what: A column with four flat bars stacked across its top, like a capital with too many collars. As an amulet it is small and hung at the neck; the Book of the Dead specifies a gold one for a mummy. It is also painted onto coffins, and carved life-size in wood for a ceremony that raises it upright.
text.story:
The djed is a spine that had to be set up again. In the Osiris myth, Set tricks Osiris into a coffin cut to fit him exactly and throws it in the Nile; it drifts to Byblos, a tree grows around it, the king of the land has the tree cut and stood in his palace as a pillar. Isis, searching, gets herself into the royal household, asks for that pillar, takes the coffin out of it, and then anoints the wood with myrrh and wraps it in linen. That is the pillar of djed.

So the ceremony is a resurrection staged as carpentry. At the Sed festival, the pharaoh with priests pulling on ropes hauls a wooden djed column upright at Memphis. It was read as Osiris's win over Set. The timing is agricultural: the month of Koiak, the fourth month of the Season of the Inundation, when the fields are being sown, inside the Osiris festival that ran from the thirteenth to the thirtieth of that month. A relief in Amenhotep III's Luxor temple shows the raising at his third Sed festival, in his thirty-seventh regnal year: the pillar stands in a shrine with a human body under a djed head, wedjat eyes, crook and flail, the feather crown and the sun disc; the king presents a loaded offering table; below, food-bearers weave between heavy-stepping dancers, singers give a short hymn to Ptah, and men box and do a stick dance. Sigrid Hodel-Hoenes, who describes the scene, reads the young women rattling Hathor sistra as the king's daughters, from the line of hieroglyphs above their heads: 'Children of the king praising (or charming) the noble djed pillar.'

The amulet is the private end of the same idea. It goes near the spine of a mummified body to make the resurrection happen, and the Book of the Dead gives a spell to be spoken over a gold djed hung at the mummy's neck: it promises the mummy will get the use of its spine back and be able to sit up.

*Tradition holds —* the sign starts somewhere agricultural, in a pillar of reeds or sheaves with grain piled round it, and only later attaches to Ptah and then to Osiris. Ptah was called 'the noble djed' and carried a sceptre that fused the djed with the ankh. By the New Kingdom the sign belongs to Osiris.
text.how: Cut or moulded small and hung at the neck, laid near the spine inside the wrappings, or painted on the coffin. The Book of the Dead's spell is spoken over a gold one. At festival scale it is a wooden column raised by ropes, with the king pulling and priests supporting it.
text.today: Not made and not raised; the ceremony ended with the religion. The sign survives as a museum label and as a design in jewellery sold to Egypt's visitors. As of 2026 this project has read no source describing anybody carrying a djed for what the Book of the Dead promised it would do.

names.name: Dol hareubang
names.th: ทลฮารึบัง (รูปปู่หิน)

etymology.root: Jeju language dol 돌 'stone' + hareubang 하르방 'grandfather' — stone grandfather
etymology.note: The name was children's usage and not general until recently; the Jeju Cultural Property Committee made it the official term in 1971 and it took over. Older names, probably regional, include useongmok — reportedly the commonest — museongmok, ongjungseok, beoksumeori, dolyeonggam, sumunjang, janggunseok, dongjaseok and mangjuseok.

text.what: A standing figure cut from Jeju's volcanic rock, wearing a round hat, with large eyes, a closed mouth, and one shoulder set higher than the other. Some have big ears; the hands sit in front, on the belly, or round the back. No two are alike. Many carry grooves cut into them for wooden logs — the jeongnang bars, whose position told a passer-by whether the entrance behind was open or shut. They stood at gates, and at the entrances of fortresses, which is to say at the edges of settlements, usually in pairs facing one another.
text.story:
Nobody knows when the first ones were cut, and the record before 1914 on their number and location is thin. Three theories are in play: that a sea-faring people brought them to Jeju; that they developed out of jangseung or beoksu, the wooden guardian posts set up around mainland Korea; and a third the source leaves unnamed. What is on paper is this. Around 1416 six statues, in three pairs, reportedly stood on the island. By 1754 there were reportedly 48, of which 24 were at Jeju-mok — the town that is now Jeju City — four pairs each at the fortress's west, south and east gates. There is a record that ongjungseok statues were built at Jeju-mok in 1754, and some scholars take that as the earliest appearance of the figures in their present form. The reason given for the 1754 order is specific: after several famines in the reigns of Sukjong and Yeongjo, vengeful spirits were held to be roaming and tormenting the living, and the head of Jeju-mok ordered the statues built.

They were treated badly in the twentieth century. During the Japanese colonial period of 1910 to 1945 they were disregarded and moved around, and that continued through the rapid urban development after liberation. Because they were shifted, they wore, and it became hard to say where any of them came from. Research began in the 1960s; two were moved to the National Folk Museum of Korea in Seoul in 1968.

There are 47 or 48 pre-modern ones left. Twenty-one are in Jeju City, twelve in Seongeup-ri in Seogwipo, twelve across Inseong-ri, Anseong-ri and Boseong-ri, and two in Seoul. Everything else a visitor sees is recent.

The noses are worn down. One folk belief held that a woman with fertility trouble could secretly take a piece of a statue's nose, grind it to powder and swallow it; many statues have worn noses as a result. Others hold that touching the nose is enough.
text.how: Cut from volcanic basalt, set in pairs at a gate facing each other, sometimes on a stone platform called giseok — the statues at Jeju-seong and Jeongeuihyeon-seong tend to stand on one, those at Daejeonghyeon-seong do not. Grooves take the jeongnang logs. Some people reportedly paid their respects to the statues in passing. No consecration rite is described in this project's source, and none is invented here.
text.today: The figure is Jeju's emblem, and the souvenir trade is dated: the first replica was made in 1963 by the sculptor Song Jong-Won, a 25 cm copy of the statue at the south gate of Jeju-mok. Souvenir goods now run from miniatures to full-size recreations. Full-size ones have gone out as diplomatic gifts — to Mikhail Gorbachev at the 1991 Soviet–South Korean summit on Jeju, to Laizhou in China in 2002, and to the city hall of Santa Rosa, California, in 2003. Whether the thing on the shelf and the thing at the gate are the same object is the question this atlas puts and does not answer.

names.said: asabikeshiinh, the inanimate form of the Ojibwe word for spider
names.th: เครื่องดักฝัน

etymology.root: Ojibwe asabikeshiinh, 'little net maker', the word for spider; White Earth Nation asubakacin, 'net-like'; Curve Lake First Nation bwaajige ngwaagan, 'dream snare'
etymology.note: The English name "dream catcher" was published in mainstream, non-Native media in the 1970s. The Ojibwe names do not all mention dreams; two of the three name the net.

text.what: A willow hoop with a net woven across it in sinew or plant cordage, tied off at a centre point, sometimes with feathers or beads added. Hung over a cradleboard or a bed. The mass-market version substitutes a steel or plastic ring, synthetic cord, dyed craft feathers and glass or plastic beads, and comes in sizes from earring to wall hanging.
text.story:
It is Anishinaabe, and its oldest published account is a record of a charm for infants, not for dreams. The ethnographer Frances Densmore wrote down an Ojibwe account in 1929 of Asibikaashi, Spider Woman, who looks after the children and the people on the land; when the Ojibwe Nation spread to the corners of North America she could no longer reach every child, so mothers and grandmothers wove webs for them on willow hoops. Densmore's own words are plain about the purpose: the webs hung on the hoop of a cradle board "caught any harm that might be in the air as a spider's web catches and holds whatever comes in contact with it". In the old days the netting was nettle fibre, and two webs usually went on the hoop. Basil Johnston, an elder from Neyaashiinigmiing, gives Spider as a trickster catching Snake in his web in Ojibway Heritage, 1976.

Then it travelled. Derivative forms were taken up in the Pan-Indian movement of the 1960s and 1970s as a symbol of unity across different Native American cultures, and as a general mark of identification with Native or First Nations identity. Native Languages of the Americas, which is run by a Native-language non-profit, puts the spread carefully: "Ojibway dreamcatchers started to get popular in other Native American tribes, even those in disparate places like the Cherokee, Lakota, and Navajo. So dreamcatchers aren't traditional in most Indian cultures, per se, but they're sort of neo-traditional."

The name reached mainstream non-Native media in the 1970s; by the 1980s it was a widely marketed craft item, and by the early 1990s Wikipedia's account calls it "one of the most popular and marketable" of them. Forms appeared that bear little resemblance to traditional styles and use materials that were never traditionally used, made and sold by New Age groups and individuals.

That is the argument, and it has named people on both sides of it. Nudrat Karim, writing for The Indigenous Foundation, states the objection: "The appropriation of dreamcatchers exemplifies the dismissiveness of Native American culture and the borrowing of their spirituality to accommodate settlers," and draws the line by maker, not by object — "when non-Native people make and sell dreamcatchers it is in fact cultural appropriation however, when Indigenous people choose to make and sell dreamcatchers as they always have, it is not." Native Languages of the Americas is blunter about the trade: "Most of what you see when you search for 'Native American dreamcatchers' are cheap objects mass-produced in an Asian sweatshop somewhere or glued together by non-native teenagers with eBay accounts," and points readers to the Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 and to buying from Native artists. Against that sit the pan-Indian communities for whom the hoop became a shared sign in the first place, and Ojibwe makers who sell them. This atlas prints both and settles neither.

The object is also still doing work in its own communities. A mounted and framed dreamcatcher is used as a shared symbol of hope and healing by the Little Thunderbirds Drum and Dance Troupe from the Red Lake Indian Reservation in Minnesota, who have taken it to students at other schools where shootings have happened, and passed it on.
text.how: This record does not give instructions. Named Native writers say the making is not open, and the atlas prints the restriction rather than the method. What is published and reported here is the material: a hoop of willow, and a net of sinew or of cordage made from plants, historically nettle fibre; two webs to a cradle hoop, per Densmore.
text.today: Made and sold by Ojibwe and other Native artists; made and sold in enormous volume by everybody else, worldwide, as of 2026, in craft shops, service stations and airports. The Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 governs what may be marketed as Native American-made in the United States.

names.th: หินดีซี (ลูกปัดทิเบต)

etymology.root: Tibetan gzi, 'shine, brightness, clearness, splendor'
etymology.note: In mainland China and Taiwan the bead is known as 天珠, tiān zhū, 'heaven's bead' — a name given by Taiwanese collectors, not a Tibetan one.

text.what: A tube of agate, brown to black, carrying pale ivory-white patterns that were etched into the stone rather than cut: circles, ovals, squares, waves, zigzags, stripes, lines, diamonds, dots. The surface is usually smooth and waxy from long wear. The circular marks are called eyes, and the number and arrangement of them is the first thing a buyer counts. Strung on a Tibetan necklace, a dzi is normally flanked with coral, sometimes with amber and turquoise.
text.story:
Nobody has settled where dzi come from, and this record does not pick a story. The account in the source read here says the stones first appear between 2000 and 1000 BCE in ancient India, and repeats a claim that a few hundred thousand were supposedly brought back by Tibetan soldiers from Persia during a raid. In the same passage the geographic origin is called uncertain, and the manufacturing method is called mysterious: treatments may have included darkening with plant sugars and heat, bleaching and white-line etching with natron, and masking areas with grease, clay or wax. What can be dated is narrower and firmer. Dzi-type agate beads were made in the Indus Valley in the Harappan period and at agate-rich sites in India such as Khambhat since Neolithic times, and the earliest archaeologically controlled find of an agate bead with dzi-style decoration — straight and curved lines and a circular eye — comes from a Saka-culture excavation at Uigarak in Kazakhstan, dated to the seventh to fifth century BCE, and was read as an import from India, evidence of long-distance trade with Saka or Scythian nomads.

Drilling is the one part of the making that is described in detail: the hole was made before the bead was decorated, because drilling caused most of the breakage, and a drilled bead could be strung and dipped for colouring. The earliest holes are conical, bored from both ends with solid flint tips; Neolithic beads were also drilled with hollow reed bits driven with abrasive, and copper ones in the Chalcolithic, which leave a parallel-walled hole. All of it was bow-drill work, and the time it took depended on the abrasive, from ground quartz to corundum.

*Tradition holds —* shepherds and farmers sometimes find dzi lying in soil or grassland, and some Tibetans have held on that evidence that the beads form naturally and are not made at all. In Tibetan culture the beads are said to attract local protectors, dharmapalas, deities, beneficial ghosts, ancestors or bodhisattvas, and are always treated with respect. They are handed down, which is how a single bead can pass through hundreds of wearers over centuries.

Beads also get eaten. Some carry small dig marks where a portion was scraped or ground away for use in Tibetan medicine; others show grinding and polishing from service as a burnishing tool for applying gold leaf to thangka paintings and gilded bronzes.
text.how: The bead is not made by its wearer and, for the old ones, not made by anyone alive. A new dzi is a different matter: the tradition holds it can be brought to the same standing by having a lama or guru bless it, by carrying it on pilgrimage to stupas and shrines, and by reciting mantras and taking religious vows with it. A stone thought to carry bad energy is submerged in salt water for several hours and then fanned with incense; sun-basking and herbal smudging are also named as purification, and spirit aroma offering and recitation of the Cintamani dharani as charging. New beads are held to carry one advantage the old ones cannot: none of the bad karma of a previous owner.
text.today: A market with a forgery problem at every price. Ancient beads can reach hundreds of thousands of US dollars, more for beads with more eyes and for the tiny red bloodspots that iron inclusions leave; new dzi run from about ten to two thousand US dollars by quality and lustre. The source read in September 2026 does not date those figures, so read them as undated. Modern-era dzi-style beads were made at Idar-Oberstein in Germany at least as early as the 19th century by agate cutters who had worked there since Roman times and who brought agate colouring to a science. Imitation dzi are made of glass, resin, lampwork, wood, bone, plastic, metal and non-traditional etched stones; some resin ones are filled with lead for weight; older mock dzi have collectible value of their own. At the bottom, mass-produced machine-carved beads sell for under two US dollars, often by the strand, with etching that does not penetrate the core — mostly to mainland Chinese buyers as feng shui charms. Tibetans also buy new beads, as an affordable and obtainable alternative, and whether a new bead is the same object as an old one is argued inside the tradition, not only outside it.

names.name: Ekeko
names.th: เอเคโก (ตุ๊กตาชาวแอนดีส)

etymology.root: Aymara Ekhako or Eqaqo, popularised as Ekhekho — the name of the god of fortune and prosperity in Qullasuyu; contemporary Aymara spelling Iqiqu
etymology.note: The cited source says the Ekhako was invoked when a disgrace disturbed a household.

text.what: A short, moustached man in Andean dress, above all a poncho, loaded to the shoulders with everything a household could want: bags and baskets of grain, food, pots, tools, banknotes. Most are cast plaster now; the colonial ones were clay. Modern figures have a hole in the mouth sized for a lit cigarette. Small versions go on key rings and necklaces.
text.story:
The Ekeko is the Tiwanakan god of abundance and prosperity in the folklore of the Altiplano, and in Bolivia he is the figure the Alasitas fair is built around. That fair opens on 24 January in La Paz and runs for a month; in Peru the main festival is 3 May, in Puno, on the Machallata hill. Elsewhere the Ekeko's festival falls in October under the name Calvario.

Four named scholars argue about what he was before the colony. Ernesto Cavour, in his book Alasitas, points to anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figures in stone, mud and gold found in the Bolivian departments of La Paz, Oruro and Potosí, made from basalt out of the pre-Columbian mines on the shores of Lake Poopó and andesite from the Copacabana peninsula. Carlos Ponce Sanginés works on humped, phallic figures he places in the Inca period and reads as the colonial Ekeko's predecessors. Antonio Paredes Candia takes them for the remains of summer-solstice festivals. Arthur Posnansky observed that around 22 December the Tiwanaku population offered miniatures of what they wanted to their gods.

The story Bolivians tell puts him in 1781, during the siege of La Paz. As Antonio Díaz Villamil narrates it, Paulita Tintaya, an Indigenous girl working for Doña Josefa Ursula de Rojas Foronda, had been given a small Ekeko by Isidoro Choquehuanca before she left the hacienda where they grew up. Isidoro, serving in the Indigenous army besieging the city, left food by the statue outside the house each week without saying so. Paulita and her employer survived the siege on it. *Tradition holds —* La Paz tells that story as the origin of the Ekeko's power to provide.

What the figure is offered is specific. Banknotes are clipped to him. Grain is given for good harvests. Statuettes with the mouth opening are given a lit cigarette — in the most recent form of the practice, once a year, to secure a full year of prosperity.
text.how: Cast in plaster, painted, then loaded. The Ekeko goes in a place of honour in the house and is added to rather than replaced: more miniatures, more banknotes, a cigarette on the day. Miniatures bought at Alasitas can be blessed by the men and, less often, women working the fair as shamans, and at midday on 24 January the Catholic Church blesses the gifts at the main cathedral in La Paz. Small Ekekos ride on key rings and necklaces and are not offered anything.
text.today: Sold across western Bolivia and southern Peru, and central to a fair that fills streets and parks across central La Paz every January. In March 2011 Elizabeth Salguero, Bolivia's Minister of Cultures, nominated Alasitas along with two other Bolivian festivals to UNESCO for recognition as intangible cultural heritage. In 2016 the Feast of Alasita and the miniatures of the Altiplano of Puno were declared Cultural Heritage of the Nation of Peru.

names.name: Ethiopian talismanic scroll
names.th: คัมภีร์ม้วนเครื่องรางเอธิโอเปีย (คิตาบ)

text.what: A long strip of parchment — goat or sheep hide, soaked, dried, stretched, scraped and washed until it takes ink — painted with prayers in Ge'ez and with talismanic drawings, then rolled. A personal one is cut to the height of the person it is for. Larger ones hang on a wall. The colours are black, white, red, blue, green and yellow. Crosses and eight-pointed stars recur; so does the gätsä säb'e, a face inside an eight-pointed star; so do eyes, painted in geometric pairs and rimmed in red.
text.story:
The scroll is the size of its owner. That is the first fact anybody who handles one notices, and it is the fact that explains the rest: this is not a text about a person, it is a stand-in for one.

It is made by a dabtara — an unordained cleric of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church who has gone past memorising the Psalms into poetry, liturgy and writing. In Ethiopia the power to write includes the power to write prayers and spells, so the word carries a second sense as well. The making involves the sacrifice of an animal, usually a goat or a sheep, standing for the person the scroll is for; the patron is rubbed by and bathed in the contents of the animal, and the hide becomes the parchment.

The writing is Ge'ez, the Ethiopian Orthodox Church's liturgical language. Because few speak it now, a scroll does not work by being owned: a third party literate in Ge'ez has to read it aloud to the afflicted person. *Inference —* that makes the scroll one of the few amulets in this atlas that needs another human being present to function at all.

What it is against runs from the small to the fatal. The range the source gives is bed bugs, home intruders, smallpox. It treats the spiritual cause; homeopathic medicines are used alongside it for the physical symptoms. Historical manuscripts show the majority were made for conditions of women's reproductive health.

The oldest surviving examples are sixteenth-century, though the practice is held to go back to the tenth. The Metropolitan Museum of Art holds several, including an eighteenth- or nineteenth-century scroll of parchment, pigments and cotton.
text.how: An animal is sacrificed for the person the scroll is for. The hide is soaked for several days, dried, stretched, then scraped, washed and dried again into parchment. The dabtara writes the prayers and the mystical names and paints the talismanic figures in the six standard colours. A personal scroll is cut to the owner's height, though it may be made longer. It is rolled, often kept in a leather case, and carried; a larger one hangs. To work, it is read aloud in Ge'ez by somebody who can read Ge'ez.
text.today: Still made and still commissioned, and still being collected. The Museum of Witchcraft and Magic in Boscastle publishes one, and the Metropolitan Museum publishes several. As of 2026 the split between scrolls made for a patron and scrolls made for the trade in old Ethiopian manuscripts is not something this project has read a figure for.

names.th: สร้อยข้อมือนาซาร์ (ลูกปัดตากันตาร้าย)

text.what: One or more blue-and-white eye beads on an elastic cord, a chain or a red string, sized for a wrist. The bead itself is handmade glass with concentric circles or teardrop shapes in dark blue, white, light blue and black, sometimes with a yellow or gold edge. The cheapest versions replace the glass with printed enamel, resin or a stamped metal disc. The sign has been a Unicode character since 2018: U+1F9FF 🧿 NAZAR AMULET.
text.story:
The bead is old and the bracelet is not, and it is worth keeping the two apart. Written documentation and surviving glass eye beads run back to the sixteenth century BCE, and the form spread with glassmaking from Mesopotamia to Egypt, Carthage to Greece, Phoenicia to Persia, and through the Roman empire. The bead on a stretchy cord at a checkout counter is a recent packaging of that, and this project cannot date it.

What the bead is made of is itself part of the claim. The cited account says it is made from a mixture of molten glass, iron, copper, water and salt — "ingredients that are thought to shield people from evil" — and that "according to Turkish belief, blue acts as a shield against evil and even absorbs negativity". One further explanation is given for why the colour is blue: in the Middle East and the Mediterranean blue eyes are relatively rare, so light-eyed people were held able to curse with a look.

Somebody still makes the glass ones by hand. The Kültürel Araştırmalar Vakfı records the traditional production continuing at Nazarköy, in Kemalpaşa near İzmir, where the beads are made by a few simple hand tools, mostly in blue and white glass; Görece, in Menderes, is the other village named for the craft. Set against that is the mass-produced bracelet, the volume of which is the reason most of the world's eye beads are now within anybody's reach. Whether the two are the same object is a live argument. This project did not reach a source it could cite giving the bead-makers' own account of competition from imported beads, and so does not report their side in their words here — a gap, and named as one.

The bead's own instruction for failure is the detail worth keeping. If one breaks, the account goes, a very strong nazar hit the wearer and the bead stored it all up and broke in order to protect them. *Inference —* a charm with a published failure mode that is also a success story is a charm that cannot be disproved by breaking, which is one reason the object survives packaging changes that would kill a less well-designed one.
text.how: Glass is melted in a furnace, drawn and layered — dark blue ground, white, light blue, black centre — one bead at a time, then strung. Mass-market versions are moulded or printed and strung by machine. There is no consecration and no specialist: a bracelet is bought, or given, and worn until it breaks, at which point it is replaced rather than repaired.
text.today: Sold everywhere, in every price band, in 2026: airport shops in Istanbul and Athens, market stalls from Tbilisi to Mumbai, fast-fashion chains worldwide, and as an emoji on every phone. This project has no dated price to print and no production figure.

names.name: Exam charm
names.said: gōkaku kigan, 'prayer for passing'; in Korean, the gift is yeot (엿) or chapssaltteok (찹쌀떡)
names.th: เครื่องรางสอบผ่าน (โกกากุ คิกัง)

etymology.root: Japanese 合格祈願 gōkaku kigan, from 合格 gōkaku 'passing an examination' and 祈願 kigan 'prayer, petition'
etymology.note: The commercial category is gōkaku kigan shōhin, goods for the prayer to pass. The Kit Kat leg of it runs on a different mechanism: きっと勝つとぉ kitto katsutoo, a Kyushu phrase meaning 'you shall surely win', which is what キットカット Kitto Katto sounds like.

text.what: Four different objects doing one job. A brocade pouch a few centimetres long, the shrine's name woven into it, a paper or wooden prayer sealed inside and not to be opened. A wooden plaque about 15 by 9 centimetres, written on and hung at the shrine. A two-finger chocolate bar in a printed wrapper. A stick of boiled-down grain taffy. The first two come from a shrine; the last two come from a supermarket, and a student carries any of them into the same room.
text.story:
Japan's examination charm has a god, and he was a real man. Sugawara no Michizane was a Heian-period scholar and poet who was exiled to Kyushu and died there; he is enshrined as Tenjin, god of scholarship and learning — and of natural disasters, which is a detail worth keeping. Dazaifu Tenmangū, the shrine built where he was exiled, states it plainly on its own English page: "As Tenjin is the deity of learning, amulets for academic success are one of the most popular items to take home from Dazaifu Tenmangu." Many of the amulets carry the plum flower, which the shrine says Michizane loved and which is its symbol. The shrine's own framing of the exchange is careful and worth quoting as printed: "At Shinto shrines you can receive an omamori, or amulet, to bring good luck, for a small donation." Received, for a donation. Not bought.

The omamori for this is gakugyō-jōju, education and passing examinations, one of a standard list that also runs to traffic safety, safe childbirth, a good marriage, business prosperity and family peace. The rule is the same as for every omamori: do not open it, and return the old one to the shrine it came from — traditionally to be burnt rather than binned, out of respect to the deity that carried you through the year.

The second Japanese object is the Kit Kat, and the wordplay has to be got right. キットカット, Kitto Katto, is what the brand is called in Japanese. Kitto means surely. Katsu means to win. The Kyushu phrase is きっと勝つとぉ, kitto katsutoo, 'you shall surely win', and that is the thing the brand name sounds like. Peter Davis, writing for Japan House at the University of Illinois, gives the figure: "In fact, one in three students in Japan will buy a Kit-Kat in anticipation of entrance examinations." The English Wikipedia article is more guarded and says the marketing "is believed to have benefited from the coincidental false cognate", and that market research shows the brand strongly correlated with good-luck charms among students ahead of exams. *Inference —* the two accounts differ on how much of this Nestlé made and how much of it Nestlé found, and this project does not have the internal documents to settle that. What is dated is the marketing: the 'Lucky Charm' campaign won the Asian Brand Marketing Effectiveness Award in 2005, and in 2009 Nestlé and Japan Post ran a campaign letting people write on the bars and post them from 20,000 post offices — which won the Media Grand Prix at Cannes Lions in 2010.

Korea works the same joke on a different verb. Families and friends give a student 엿, yeot — a taffy boiled down from steamed rice, glutinous rice, sorghum, corn or sweet potato — and 찹쌀떡, chapssaltteok, glutinous rice cake, before the Suneung university entrance examination. Both are sticky. The Korean verb for sticking to something is also the verb for passing an exam, so the gift says what it means without saying it. The English Wikipedia entry on yeot confirms students receive it before examinations and otherwise concentrates on the same word's career as an obscenity, which is the other thing a Korean reader knows about it.

The shrine end of the trade has been argued about in public, with a date attached. In 1979 two shrines dedicated to education sold ema — the wooden prayer plaques — for examination success; after public outcry, the funds were turned into a scholarship in 1980. *Inference —* that is the cleanest instance this atlas has of a charm trade answering a complaint by converting the takings into the thing the charm was asking for.
text.how: An omamori is received at the shrine office for a donation, carried on the person or tied to a bag, not opened, and returned to the same shrine at the New Year to be burnt. An ema is bought at the shrine, written on, and hung on the rack until it is ritually burnt at a ceremony — the burning treated as freeing the wish. A Kit Kat is bought at a convenience store, sometimes posted, and eaten. Yeot and chapssaltteok are given by family and friends and eaten. Nothing consecrates the last two, and nobody claims anything does.
text.today: Running every winter. Japanese entrance-examination season and the Korean Suneung both fall in the cold months, and the shelves change accordingly. As of 2026 the shrine goods, the exam-season chocolate packaging and the taffy all coexist, with the shrine goods carrying a deity's name and the other two carrying a pun. No dated price was read for any of them, and neither Dazaifu Tenmangū's page nor the sources on the Korean gifts print one.

text_th.what: ของสี่อย่างที่ต่างกัน แต่ทำหน้าที่เดียวกัน อย่างแรกคือถุงผ้าแพรยกดิ้นยาวไม่กี่เซนติเมตร มีชื่อศาลเจ้าทอไว้บนถุง ข้างในมีคำอธิษฐานเขียนบนกระดาษหรือไม้ผนึกไว้ และห้ามเปิด อย่างที่สองคือแผ่นไม้ขนาดประมาณ 15 x 9 เซนติเมตร เขียนข้อความแล้วแขวนไว้ที่ศาลเจ้า อย่างที่สามคือช็อกโกแลตแท่งคู่ในห่อพิมพ์ลาย อย่างที่สี่คือแท่งลูกอมที่เคี่ยวจากธัญพืช สองอย่างแรกมาจากศาลเจ้า สองอย่างหลังมาจากซูเปอร์มาร์เก็ต และนักเรียนพกอย่างใดอย่างหนึ่งเข้าไปในห้องเดียวกัน

text.what: A phallus, worn. Usually cast in bronze, often winged, pierced or looped for a cord; also cut as finger rings, carved in relief on walls, made into lamps and into wind chimes called tintinnabula. The soldiers' type adds a clenched fist at the base of the shaft, pointing away from the glans, and on several examples the fist is making the manus fica, the fig sign. Some combine vulvar imagery with the rest.
text.story:
Pliny called the fascinus a medicus invidiae — a doctor, a remedy, for invidia. Invidia is envy, and it is built from a word for looking upon. That is the whole theory of the object in two Latin words.

Rome put it everywhere. The Vestal Virgins tended the cult of the fascinus populi Romani, a sacred phallus counted among the tokens of the state's safety alongside the Palladium; when a general celebrated a triumph, the Vestals hung an effigy of it under his chariot to protect him from invidia. Augustine, reading Varro, reports the phallus carried on a little trolley through the countryside crossroads at the festival of Father Liber and then into the city, to secure the growth of seeds and "repel enchantment (fascinatio) from the fields".

On the body it was mostly for children, and mainly boys. Varro records hanging a phallic charm on a baby's neck, and phallus-bearing rings survive that are too small for anyone but a child to wear. There are very few Roman images of a person actually wearing one. A 2017 experimental archaeology project found that some pendant types were designed to stay pointing outwards, in the wearer's direction of travel, facing whatever was coming.

The imagery is not shy about the mechanism. Reliefs from Leptis Magna in present-day Libya and several instances on Hadrian's Wall show the phallus ejaculating towards a disembodied eye; a first-century BCE terracotta figurine shows "two little phallus-men sawing an eyeball in half". The largest known collection of fist-and-phallus amulets comes from Camulodunum, the Roman colony under modern Colchester.

*Tradition holds —* the protective force is usually explained by the virile and regenerative power of an erect phallus. The cited account puts a second explanation beside it and does not choose: in most cases what diverts the evil eye is the emotion the obscenity produces — shame, or laughter.

etymology.root: Latin ficus, 'fig' — Italian far le fiche, 'to make the fig'; Spanish higa, Galician and Portuguese figa, Asturleonese cigua
etymology.note: Early Christians called the gesture the manus obscena, the obscene hand. Ancient Greek sykophantes, 'one who shows figs', is the root of English sycophant; the cited source gives the connection to the gesture as one explanation among several, not a settled one.

text.what: A closed fist with the thumb pushed up between the index and middle fingers, carved small and drilled for a cord. In Asturias it is cut from jet; elsewhere from coral, silver, gold, bone or moulded resin. Worn at the neck or wrist, or pinned on a small child.
text.story:
The gesture came first and it was rude. In ancient Rome the manus fica was made by the pater familias during the Lemuria, the festival of the restless dead, to drive the dead spirits off. The ancient Greeks wore amulets of the same gesture around the neck against the evil eye and used it in their artwork: what they took to be an overtly sexual gesture was expected to distract an evil spirit from doing harm. Early Christians called it the manus obscena.

In Italy it stayed rude. Fica in mano, far le fiche, comparable to the finger; Dante puts it in Inferno, Canto XXV; medieval painters give it to the tormentors in a Man of Sorrows. The gesture there has long since fallen out of use.

What survived, and where, is the point. In Portugal, Brazil, and parts of Spain — Galicia and Asturias especially — the fig is a gesture of good luck and a ward against the evil eye, and an amulet of a hand making it is worn for exactly that. In Asturias the amulets are jet, and it is usual to give one to a young child. The same hand shape, in Britain, Ireland, France, Germany, Argentina, Uruguay and the United States, carries no charge at all and is the joke where an adult steals a child's nose.

*Inference —* one hand shape, running simultaneously as an obscenity in Turkey, a refusal in Poland, a sexual invitation in Denmark and a child's amulet in Asturias, is the clearest case this atlas has of a sign whose meaning is entirely local while its form is continent-wide. The eye travels with its reading attached. The fist does not.
text.how: Carved from jet, coral, precious metal or bone, pierced at the wrist end, strung on a cord — red, where the tradition uses red. Given to a child rather than bought by one. No consecration is described in the source read here.
text.today: Sold in Portugal, Brazil, Galicia and Asturias as jewellery and as a child's charm, and made in every grade from cut jet to moulded resin. Whether the resin one does the same job as the jet one is an argument with people on both sides of it, and this atlas reports it without joining.

names.name: Four-leaf clover
names.th: ใบโคลเวอร์สี่แฉก

etymology.root: English four-leaf clover; Italian quadrifoglio, 'four-leaf'.
etymology.note: Four-leaf is botanically a misnomer. A clover plant carries many leaves, each made of a varying number of leaflets, usually three; what is being counted here is leaflets, not leaves.

text.what: A clover leaf with four leaflets instead of three, usually white clover, Trifolium repens. It is a mutation, not a species. Found ones are pressed flat in a book or sealed in plastic; grown ones are sold the same way. Collectors in Ireland prize the five-leaflet version, which they call a rose clover.
text.story:
The arithmetic is the whole appeal, and it has been measured. A 2017 survey of about 5.7 million clovers across six European countries put the frequency at roughly one four-leaf clover in every 5,076 — around 5,000 to one, which is almost twice as common as the 10,000-to-one figure people usually quote. The same survey gives 24,390 to one for five leaflets and 312,500 to one for six.

The luck attached to it goes back to at least the seventeenth century. A description from 1869 splits the practice by who is doing it: the clovers were "gathered at night-time during the full moon by sorceresses, who mixed it with vervain and other ingredients, while young girls in search of a token of perfect happiness made quest of the plant by day." Eight years later an eleven-year-old girl put the folk version in a letter to St. Nicholas Magazine: "Did the fairies ever whisper in your ear, that a 4-leaf clover brought good luck to the finder?" Some traditions assign a meaning to each leaflet — Christians have used them for hope, faith, love and luck — and others say the clover grants the power to see fairies.

The charm's condition is that you find it, and industry has been steadily dissolving that condition. There are reports of farms in the United States producing as many as 10,000 a day, sealed in plastic and sold as lucky charms, by introducing a genetically engineered ingredient that encourages the aberration. Cultivars that reliably throw extra leaflets have existed for a long time — Trifolium repens "Purpurascens Quadrifolium", "Quadrifolium", and a cultivar actually called "Good Luck". A 2009 study exposed white clover flowers to gamma radiation during pollination and produced a cultivar yielding up to 60 per cent four-leaf clovers. Phosphate fertiliser and the plant hormone auxin both raise the rate.

Finding them is also a sport. Guinness World Records lists the clover with the most leaflets ever found at 63, discovered by Yoshiharu Watanabe of Nasushiobara, Tochigi prefecture, Japan, on 2 August 2023, beating a 56-leaf clover found by Shigeo Obara of Hanamaki, Iwate prefecture, on 10 May 2009. Both men bred for it. An expert finder interviewed by the New York Times described the technique as scanning a patch for ruptures in the pattern: three leaflets make a triangle, four make a square.
text.how: Found, in spring, before the first mowing. Picked, pressed flat between the pages of a book or laminated, and carried in a wallet or a pocket. Nothing is said or done over it. There is no retirement rite; it fades.
text.today: Carried as a personal charm, farmed by the thousand and sold sealed in plastic, and used as a corporate emblem by organisations that have nothing to do with either. Alfa Romeo has used the quadrifoglio on its racing and performance cars since the driver Ugo Sivocci painted a green clover on a white ground for the 1923 Targa Florio. SpaceX has embroidered a four-leaf clover on every mission patch since the first successful Falcon 1 launch in 2008, which the company describes as being for luck. *Inference —* a charm whose whole claim rests on being rare is the charm most exposed to being manufactured, and the farm and the meadow versions are sold in the same packet.

names.name: Fu talisman
names.th: ยันต์ฮู้ (ฝูลู่ ยันต์เต๋า)

etymology.root: Chinese 符 fú — instructions for deities and spirits, symbols for exorcism, and recipes for potions or charms used to treat ailments — with 籙 lù, a registry of the memberships of priests that also lists the skills they are trained in
etymology.note: The writing itself is asemic: strokes that resemble Chinese characters without being readable as them. The 符 fu of a talisman is a different character and a different word from the 福 fu of good fortune pasted upside-down on doors at New Year.

text.what: A sheet — usually paper, sometimes cloth, sometimes a coin's face — written over in a script nobody is meant to read. The strokes are irregular and resemble Chinese characters, often stretching an existing word out of shape and mixing in marks that are not characters at all. Taoist priests are the main interpreters of this writing, and the characters differ from sect to sect.
text.story:
The illegibility is the design, and it has a history. Yang Zhaohua notes that a number of the earliest known Taoist talismans were simple and legible, and that later examples became deliberately cryptic in order to signal their divinity. James Robson and Gil Raz have argued that the incomprehensibility of the written forms is central to a talisman's perceived authority and efficacy, and is one of talismanic script's defining features. By the Eastern Jin dynasty, 317 to 420, it was already held unnecessary for a user to be able to decipher the writing: Ge Hong wrote in the Baopuzi that as long as the inscription was correct, use did not depend on the user reading it. Ge Zhaoguang, of Fudan University, calls the unreadability a kind of linguistic archaism, built to be incomprehensible — "a veil of unfathomable otherwordliness" that lets only a small number of qualified clergy produce them properly.

The writing has been medicine for as long as it has been anything. Known in medical writings as zhuyou, the use of talismans ran alongside drugs, meditation, acupuncture, astrology and massage; the Way of the Taiping was healing patients with it at least as far back as the Eastern Han. Zhuyou held official support from the Sui to the late Ming, and declined when acupuncture was recognised by the imperial court as a medical discipline in the sixth century. It is rejected by traditional Chinese medicine and still widely used by folk healers, and in the twentieth century, as Western psychology arrived, it began to be read as a Chinese counterpart of hypnosis.

The script also travelled. Fulu are not confined to Taoism: they were taken into several forms of Chinese Buddhism, and they lie behind the ofuda used in Japanese Buddhism and Shinto and the bujeok of Korean shamanism. On coins, fulu usually open and close the inscription of a Taoist coin charm, and most of those charms ask Lei Gong, the god of thunder, to protect the carrier from evil spirits and misfortune. Many coin talismans in the script have not been deciphered; in one specimen talismanic script was written side by side with Chinese characters that may be its gloss.

The Daozang records the fulu sect's history in the second chapter of each of its three grottoes, where fulu are said to originate in the condensation of clouds in the sky.
text.how: Written by a priest of the fulu pai, an informal grouping of priests from different schools of Taoism. The way of writing the characters is passed down in secret from a Taoist priest to their disciples and treated as a special craft for communicating with local deities and spirits; style, incantations and the mudras used in making them differ from sect to sect, and even the invocations for a single deity vary. This atlas prints that and no script.
text.today: Still written. Zhuyou continues to be widely used among Chinese folk healers, and paper talismans are issued at temples across the Chinese-speaking world — the Taiwanese peace charm is the everyday form. Whether a talisman works has never been the question a priest is asked; the question is who wrote it.

etymology.note: Before the nineteenth century the word attached to inanimate objects — a lock of hair, a ship's figurehead — rather than to a costumed person on a touchline.

text.what: Whatever was in the room the last time it went well. A pair of borrowed baseball shoes. A round rock picked up off a field. A uniform number. A cap turned inside out and worn backwards. A crucifix touched before every at-bat. A stick of gum, a yellow sandal, a particular arrangement of footwear in a locker. The object is ordinary and the selection rule is the only thing that is not: it gets chosen by what it was present for.
text.story:
The best-documented charm in this atlas is a pair of shoes a man borrowed because he forgot his own.

George Gmelch, an anthropologist at Union College who played professional baseball before he wrote about it, defines the class flatly: "Fetishes or charms are material objects believed to embody 'supernatural' power that can aid or protect the owner. Good luck charms are standard equipment for some ballplayers." His list runs from coins, chains and crucifixes to a favourite hat. And the origin rule is the interesting part: "The fetishized object may be a new possession or something a player found that happens to coincide with the start of a streak and which he holds responsible for his good fortune." Alan Foster, playing in the Pacific Coast League, left his baseball shoes behind on a road trip and borrowed a teammate's. He pitched a no-hitter that night, attributed it to the shoes, bought them off the teammate afterwards, and they became a fetish.

Mark LaRosa, a farmhand in the Montreal Expos system, gave Gmelch a different account of the same kind of object: "I found it on the field in Elmira after I had gotten bombed. It's unusual, perfectly round, and it caught my attention. I keep it to remind me of how important it is to concentrate. When I am going well I look at the rock and remember to keep my focus, the rock reminds me of what can happen when I lose my concentration." *Inference —* that is a charm whose owner says out loud it is a memory aid and not a power, and it sits in the same pocket as the shoes. Both accounts are the wearers' own and this atlas prints both without deciding which kind of object it is.

Numbers work the same way. Ricky Henderson paid outfielder Turner Ward US$25,000 in 1993 for the right to wear number 24 when he joined the Blue Jays. Vida Blue switched from 35 to 14 — his high-school quarterback number — at the Oakland A's, and switched back when it produced nothing. Jack Clark went from 25 to 00 to break a slump, got four hits in a doubleheader that day, hurt his back, and was hit in the cheekbone by a batting-practice ball three days later. Larry Walker of the Colorado Rockies wore 33, took three practice swings, showered from the third nozzle, set his alarm three minutes past the hour and married on 3 November at 3:33 p.m. Gmelch notes there is no consensus on number 13: some refuse it, some do not care, a few ask for it.

On the fan's side of the rail the same logic produces the rally cap — a baseball cap worn inside out and backwards, or otherwise wrongly, to turn a game around; the team's logo has to show for it to work. The documented instances start early: on 23 August 1887 a Giants mascot turned his cap inside out during a close game against Pittsburgh and outfielder George Gore followed. Detroit Tigers fans recalled players doing it in the 1940s without the comeback meaning attached. The Texas Rangers used it in 1977 and 1978. Mets fans at Shea Stadium were wearing caps inside out in 1985, and the practice reached national attention during the 1986 World Series when Mets players wore rally caps in the dugout in Game 6. The genre has since branched: rally chew, rally gum during Detroit's 2006 run, and a yellow Birkenstock worn on a fan's head before the Mariners' 10–9 comeback on 8 October 2022.

Gmelch's own explanation is borrowed twice over and he says so. From Bronisław Malinowski: Trobriand islanders used no magic for lagoon fishing, where skill was enough, and a great deal of it for the open sea, where it was dangerous and the catch varied — and Gmelch maps that onto baseball, where magic clusters around pitching and hitting rather than fielding. From B. F. Skinner: a pigeon rewarded on a fixed timer starts repeating whatever it happened to be doing, and one of Skinner's birds hopped side to side ten thousand times without a pellet before giving up. Gmelch's closing sentence gives his own verdict, and it is his and not this atlas's: the rituals "do not make a pitch travel faster or a batted ball find the gaps between the fielders, nor do the Trobriand rituals calm the seas or bring fish. What both do, however, is give their practitioners a sense of control, with that added confidence, at no cost."

*Inference —* the phrase worth keeping from him is "standard equipment". A charm nobody in the trade regards as remarkable is the hardest kind for an atlas to find, because nobody writes it down. Gmelch wrote it down because he had been in the clubhouse.
text.how: Not made and not bought. Retained. An object acquires the status by having been present at a win, and keeps it by being carried, worn or arranged the same way every time. Clothing gets the same treatment: Jim Davenport found he had missed a buttonhole the day he hit two home runs and left the same button undone for the rest of his career; Brian Hunter switched between high-top and low-top shoes by which pair had failed to get a hit; Bo Kennedy told the clubhouse boys never to move his shoes, wanting the Ponys in front and the turfs to the right, each pair touching. The object is dropped when the streak ends, which is the one respect in which Gmelch says ballplayers beat pigeons.
text.today: Live in every clubhouse and half the stands. The published record this atlas relies on runs to Gmelch's 2000 revision and the rally-cap instances up to 2022; no survey newer than that was read for this record, and no dated price, because almost nothing here is bought.

text.what: A metal box worn shut. Himalayan Art Resources calls the type a portable shrine, generally made from metal worked in repoussé — hammered from the back so the design stands out at the front. Small ones are round or oblong and hang at the neck on a cord; medium ones come in three parts, a metal container, a cloth outer cover and the contents, and usually carry a window with an image behind it; the largest are shrine-shaped, too big to carry, and stand on a household or temple altar. Men's boxes run from about an inch to over fourteen inches tall. What is inside is the point, and it is not on show.
text.story:
James Gentry, writing for Project Himalayan Art at the Rubin Museum in 2023, catalogues one box closely enough to see into it. It was made in Kathmandu in the first decade of the twenty-first century, measures 9 × 8 × 4 cm, and is a golden nimbus-shaped box built to imitate a Buddhist reliquary, with the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel above its window and offerings below. Behind the window sits an amulet diagram wrapped in five-coloured cords with three dark brown pills; also inside are two reddish brown pills composed of relics said to be from the eighth-century Indian tantric master Padmasambhava, and two small golden pills of unknown composition. The box shows the diagram through the window and keeps the rest concealed behind it.

The contents were handselected by Chokling Rinpoche, who prepared them and consecrated the box, and the box was a personal gift from the Tsike Chokling, Fourth Karma Mingyur Dewe Dorje (1953–2020), to two of his students. That chain — a named lama fills it, a named lama gives it, a named student wears it — is what the object is. A gau bought empty is a case.

More broadly the boxes hold miniature statues, photographs of lamas, votive plaques, amulets, Sanskrit mantras written on small pieces of paper, relic pills, and materials taken from sacred sites; Himalayan Art Resources adds small texts, blessing cords and consecrated medicine, and notes they are typically carried on pilgrimage or on long business trips, with larger ones serving as makeshift shrines while travelling.
text.how: Assembled and consecrated by a lama, then closed. Smaller boxes hang from a cord or strap at the neck; larger ones are worn over the chest or under the arm on a leather strap or a cloth band. This atlas does not print how a gau is filled or what is said over it: the filling is a lama's work, done for a particular wearer, and the rite belongs to a body of practice Tibetan Buddhism restricts to those who have received empowerment.
text.today: Made and worn across the Tibetan-Buddhist world as of 2026 — Tibet, Bhutan, Nepal, Ladakh, Sikkim, Mongolia — and made for sale in Kathmandu, where Gentry's example was made. Empty gaus are also a standard item in the Himalayan visitor trade, sold as jewellery, and whether an empty one is the same object is a question the tradition answers by asking who filled it.

restricted.note: What goes inside a gau is selected, prepared and consecrated by a lama for a particular wearer, and the box is kept closed — the published example shows one item through its window and conceals the rest. This atlas prints what a named lama's published catalogue entry shows and stops. It does not reconstruct a filling or a consecration, because those belong to tantric practice, and Tibetan Buddhism holds that without having gone through initiation one is generally not allowed to practise the higher Tantras.

names.name: Gorgoneion
names.th: กอร์โกเนออน (ศีรษะกอร์กอน)

text.what: A face, not a body: wild eyes, tusks, tongue out, snakes for hair. It is moulded, cut or struck onto whatever needs guarding — a shield boss, a temple pediment, a terracotta roof antefix, a coin, the bottom of a drinking cup, a pendant. The archaic ones are hideous on purpose. From the fifth century BCE the face begins to be carved beautiful instead, and the Medusa Rondanini, a Roman copy of a Greek original, is the earliest such gorgoneion named in the literature.
text.story:
Homer had already fixed what the thing was for. On Agamemnon's shield in the Iliad sits "the Gorgon, grim of aspect, glaring terribly, and about her were Terror and Rout"; on Athena's aegis the same head makes the aegis proof against Apollo's spear and Zeus's thunderbolt alike. Hector at his most frightening has "the eyes of the Gorgon". Odysseus, standing in the underworld and determined to stay, bolts at the thought of meeting "the head of the Gorgon, that awful monster".

Over six hundred Gorgon representations are catalogued in the Lexicon Iconographicum Mythologiae Classicae, and of all the depictions of Greek demons, the gorgoneion is by far the most frequent. The consensus among classicists is that its function was apotropaic — a device for turning unwanted things away — and that it began as a mask worn by a dancer. Jane Ellen Harrison put that view in the form everyone still quotes: the gorgoneion is "a ritual mask misunderstood".

Her argument runs backwards through the myth. What came first, she wrote, was "a grinning mask with glaring eyes and protruding beast-like tusks and pendent tongue", known in ritual. Then: "How did this Gorgoneion come to be? A hero had slain a beast called the Gorgon, and this was its head." The object comes first; the monster is invented to explain it; the hero is supplied to kill the monster. Two seventh-century BCE groups of terracotta Gorgon-like masks support her — wearable helmet masks from Tiryns, and votive masks, not wearable, from the Sanctuary of Orthia at Sparta.

*Inference —* the gorgoneion is the clearest case in the atlas of a charm that works by being looked at. Everything the sources say it does, it does to a viewer: terror, rout, flight. That is the same mechanism a Neapolitan coral horn or a blue glass bead is described as using, with the volume turned up.

names.name: Gris-gris
names.th: กรีกรี (ถุงเครื่องรางแอฟริกาตะวันตก)

etymology.root: From the Mande languages spoken by the Mandinka and Bambara peoples of West Africa, where it is taken to mean 'magic'.
etymology.note: Non-Muslims in the region who wore the sacks called them saffis. In nineteenth-century Louisiana the word did double duty: it meant both the amulet and the act of bewitching.

text.what: A small cloth pouch, worn on the body, usually at the neck. Inside: verses of the Qur'an written on pieces of paper, herbs, and a set number of small objects. In West Africa the writing is the point — some charms were the written sheets themselves, carried by scholars without any bag at all.
text.story:
Two lines run out of this object and they need keeping apart, because the sources that cover one do not cover the other.

The first line is West African and Muslim. The gris-gris originates in the Muslim Mande communities of far West Africa. Travellers through the Volta Basin, in what is now Ghana, reported Mande speakers such as the Dyula distributing Islamic charms they called gris-gris, and the practice spread to other Muslim peoples, among them the Dagomba, who wrote extensive Arabic manuscripts with magic formulae and prescriptions for preparing amulets. Among Mande Muslims the craft has a name and a course of study: Karamokobara, which divides into seli, prayer, and siri, path. Those who take seli become scholars of Qur'anic law, karamokos; those who take siri become scholars of the written talismans, marabouts. Some cross over. The tools of the siri side are spoken prayers, numerical squares called katemi, and written inscriptions from the Qur'an.

The second line is American, and the word changes on the way. Atlantic slavery carried the gris-gris to the Americas with enslaved Muslims, and it was kept up by practitioners of the traditions Wikipedia names "Louisiana Voodoo" and Haitian Vodou. In Haiti it held its original sense: an amulet with good intentions. In the United States it went the other way. It came to be thought of as something brought down on a victim; enslaved people used gris-gris against their owners, and gris-gris were found in burials. New Orleans court cases of 1773 convicted enslaved people of using gris-gris to kill those who held them, and those are among the earliest legal mentions of the tradition in Louisiana. Enslaved conjure women made gris-gris to start rebellions, and the bags were held to have guided people to freedom on the Underground Railroad and shielded them on the way. In October 1849 authorities arrested an enslaved man for carrying a human finger wrapped in flannel that he believed brought good luck; people in New Orleans sought human remains from tombs for this work, and gravesites were disturbed for it. In Cajun communities the term means black magic and ill fortune. Against that, Gris-Gris doctors have worked in the Louisiana Creole community for centuries and are looked on favourably by the Black community at large. Both of those are reported here and neither is settled here.

It is also, in West Africa now, an everyday object with a measured place in public health data. A 1982 survey found gris-gris among the top three methods of contraception known to women in Senegal — the three named were abstinence, roots and herbs, and charms. Over 60% of women reported knowing such traditional methods; the pill, the best known modern method, was known to a little over 40%. Gris-gris are worn across the whole of society, the source says, "from wrestlers to soldiers to housewives, and can feature anything from monkey to snake to mouse".
text.how: Written, then bagged. A marabout or another literate specialist writes Qur'anic verses, or a numerical square, on paper; the paper goes into a small cloth sack with herbs and a set number of small objects; the sack is worn, usually at the neck. In the American line the contents shift with what the conjurer has and what the job is, and the bag is kept on the body.
text.today: Living on both sides of the Atlantic, and not the same object on each. As of 2026 this project has read no figure for how many are made by marabouts and how many are sold over a counter.
