names.name: Hagstone
names.said: HAG-stone; the Welsh name is said glyne NAY-dir
names.th: หินรู (แฮกสโตน)

etymology.root: English hag 'witch' + stone; the parallel English name adder stone comes from the claim that snakes made it. Welsh Glain Neidr is 'snake's gem', Cornish milpreve, Scots adderstane, and northern Scottish Gaelic Gloine nan Druidh 'Druids' glass'. In Germany the same stones are Hühnergötter, 'chicken gods'.
etymology.folk: Pliny the Elder records the Druids' account: massed snakes make the egg out of slime and spit, and eject it into the air with their hissing. A second folk account has it come from a serpent's head, a third from an adder's sting.

text.what: A stone with a hole worn right through it by water, usually flint, usually glassy. Nobody makes one: a hagstone is found, on a beach or in a field, and a stone holed by human hand does not count. Most are hung on a loop of string or red ribbon and put where the hole can be looked through.
text.story:
The oldest account is Roman and second-hand. In Natural History book XXIX, Pliny the Elder reports what the Druids of the Gallic provinces told about the anguinum: snakes twist together in summer, the slime and foam they secrete hardens into an egg, and their hissing throws it into the air, where a man must catch it in a cloak before it touches the ground and then flee on horseback until a river is between him and the snakes. They said it could be tested by setting it in gold and seeing whether it floats upstream. Pliny says he has seen one — round, about the size of a moderate apple, its shell cartilaginous, covered in cup-like marks. He also says what it was carried for, and how that ended: "The possession of it is marvellously vaunted as ensuring success in law-suits, and a favourable reception with princes", and a Roman of equestrian rank from the territory of the Vocontii was put to death by Tiberius for having one in his bosom during a trial.

The English record is about sleep. English folklore collectors record the same use of a holed stone hung over a person or a horse against nightmares, attested from at least the fifteenth century. Reginald Scot printed the cure in The Discoverie of Witchcraft in 1584: hang over the bed "a stone, which stone hath naturallie such a hole in it, as wherein a string may be put through it, and so be hanged over the diseased or bewitched partie; be it man, woman, or horsse." Thomas Blundeville had already written it into a 1565 book on horsemanship, citing an older English writer, with a verse to be written on paper and hung up with the stone.

The practice did not stop. Edward Lovett, collecting folklore in Surrey and Sussex, reported in 1928 that the favourite objects for warding off nightmares were horseshoes and natural perforated stones, common on the beach at Brighton, and that the stones were usually on a loop of red ribbon or string, "or are occasionally simply hooked on to one of the knobs of the bedstead." A woman in Essex told researchers in 1984: "I still keep stones with holes in them on my window-sill for luck. I used to pick them up as a child from the beach in South Shields, and all my family still pick them up--because we think they're lucky."

The same stone does other work elsewhere. In Welsh folklore the Glain Neidr are made by a congress of snakes in spring, most auspiciously on May Eve. In Russian folklore the holed stones housed spirits called Kurinyi Bog, the chicken gods, who guarded hens and were set in farmyards against the Kikimora.
text.how: Found, not made. Picked off a beach or out of a ploughed field, strung on string or red ribbon, and hung: over a bed, over a horse, on a door, on a windowsill. Several sources say the stone works best used together with a spoken or written charm about Saint George. Nothing is done to charge it and nothing is recorded about retiring it; a hagstone is kept.
text.today: Still picked up and kept, and sold online and in shops that sell crystals and folk charms. The Hastings legend attached to it is live enough to name: the town is said to be under Crowley's Curse, which compels anyone who has lived there to return, and which can only be broken by taking a stone with a hole through it from Hastings beach.

etymology.root: Arabic khamsa, 'five' — the five fingers; Maghrebi variants khmisa and khmisa; Hebrew hamesh, also 'five'; Berber afus, 'hand'
etymology.note: 'Hand of Fatima' is a colonial nickname rather than an Arabic term: Europeans in French colonial North Africa popularised Main de Fatma, and in colonial-era French 'fatma' meant a Muslim or Arab woman. The Arabic phrase yad Fatima is rare in pre-modern usage. Levantine Christians call it kef Miryam, the Virgin Mary's hand; Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews call it the Hand of Miriam.

text.what: An open palm, usually made symmetrical so it has a thumb on both sides, in silver more often than anything else, historically also carved in jet. An eye is often set in the palm. Fingers spread turns evil away; fingers together brings luck; pointing up wards off, pointing down blesses. The most stylised versions stop looking like a hand at all and become five circles around a sixth. It is also painted in red on house walls, sometimes with the blood of a sacrificed animal, and hung on the doorway of a room where a woman is expecting or a baby has just arrived.
text.story:
The open hand is old in the Near East and the line back from the modern object is argued rather than established. Amulets of the hand of Ishtar were used in Mesopotamia and Babylon to keep evil or disease out of a building. An Iron Age tomb at Khirbet el-Qom in Judah carries an engraved hand beside an inscription, generally read as protective in a funerary setting, though the exact meaning is debated. Another line runs to the Mano Pantea, known to ancient Egyptians as the Two Fingers, where the two fingers are Isis and Osiris and the thumb is Horus, used to call a parent's protection over a child.

Eva-Maria von Kemnitz traces the medieval route in one sentence: "the Berbers brought the khamsa to al-Andalūs. Later, the expelled Muslim and Jewish population took it back to North Africa, introducing different motifs and techniques." In al-Andalus its use as an amulet is well documented from the thirteenth century on. Among the Moriscos of Granada, khamsa pendants were described as large engraved medals with a hand inscribed with letters — likely Qur'anic verses. A reform council banned them as Islamic symbols in 1526 and ordered crosses in their place; the Synod of Guadix renewed the prohibition in 1554. Christians wore them anyway, and a Nasrid-period gold pendant survives inscribed Ave Maria gratia plena.

The disagreement is live and it is not between insiders and outsiders. Von Kemnitz, citing Bruno Barbatti, calls the hamsa the most important apotropaic sign in the Islamic world. Salafi authorities reject it: one fatwa states that hanging the khamsa is impermissible, and another lists hands of Fatima among prohibited amulets. In Shia Islam the five fingers are read as the panjtan — Muhammad, Ali, Fatimah, Hasan, Husayn — with invocations written on the fingers, and the open palm became an emblem in Muharram processions and on ʿalams. In Judaism the hand doubles as the letter shin, first letter of Shaddai; Shalom Sabar suggests Jews exiled from Spain in 1492 carried it as protection into the countries they reached, while noting the assumption is hard to prove.

What people say while using it is the plainest evidence of what they take it for. Khamsa fi ainek — 'five [fingers] in your eye' — said while raising the right palm, fingers slightly apart, to blind the aggressor. Khamsa wa-khamis, 'five and Thursday'. Or the whole formula with the spitting sound: "Khamsa, Khamsa, Khamsa, tfu, tfu, tfu."
text.today: The hamsa is one of Algeria's national symbols and appears in its emblem. In Egypt it is the most popular amulet against the evil eye, ahead of the eye itself and the hirz; women in baladi quarters make khamaysa, five objects — peppers, hands, circles, stars — hung from hooks on a child's hair or black apron. Its use fell away in some places during periods of modernisation and came back as a secular good-luck charm: necklaces, keychains, postcards, lottery cards, advertisements, tilework, wall decorations. It was added to Unicode as U+1FAAC in 2021.

names.name: Heart scarab
names.said: the Egyptian word for the heart is ib; the object is named for where it lies
names.th: สคารับหัวใจ

text.what: An oval beetle, larger and heavier than the scarabs of the living, cut from a dark green or black stone — green jasper, serpentine, basalt — and usually not drilled for suspension. New Kingdom examples run four to five centimetres long. The base carries Chapter 30B of the Book of the Dead, cut into the stone or onto a gold plate fixed to it. It is hung at the mummy's neck on gold wire, the stone held in a gold frame, and laid over the heart.
text.story:
The spell on the base is an instruction to an organ. At the Weighing of the Heart the dead person's heart goes on one pan of the scales and a single feather from Ma'at's headdress on the other. A heart lighter than the feather lets its owner start the journey to Aaru; a heart heavy with wrongdoing tips off the pan into the jaws of Ammit, and the soul is left restless in the Duat. Chapter 30B commands the heart not to give evidence against its owner. The scarab is there to hold it to that, or to speak in its place.

That is why the heart, alone among the organs, stayed in the body. Egyptians held it to be the seat of the mind, so the embalmers took out the other viscera and preserved them separately and left the heart where it was — with the stone beetle on top of it.

The first known depictions are Sixteenth or Seventeenth Dynasty, about 1690 BCE, though the amulet was in use as early as the Eleventh Dynasty. Until the Eighteenth Dynasty it stayed close to Theban royalty; then it turns up in other people's burials. In the Twenty-first Dynasty it is an important piece of protection among the priesthood of Amun. After that it thins out of human burials and attaches to particular gods instead.

The object shrank. New Kingdom heart scarabs are large, four to five centimetres. By the Third Intermediate Period a smaller variant appears, two to four centimetres — and because it is small it is left uninscribed. These small ones are not laid over the wrappings but put inside the chest cavity, next to the real heart. *Inference —* a spell-bearing amulet that stops bearing its spell is a change worth naming: the shape is doing the work the words used to do.

The Book of the Dead specifies a stone it calls nmhf, nemehef. Nobody has identified it.
text.how: Cut from dark stone, inscribed on the base with Chapter 30B, set in a gold frame and hung at the neck on gold wire, or — in the smaller late form — put into the chest cavity beside the heart during mummification. Some were worked into pectorals, the rectangular chest ornaments laid on a mummy's breast.
text.today: Not made and not used; the practice ended with the religion that needed it. Heart scarabs sit in museum cases, and the Israel Museum and the British Museum both publish examples. As of 2026 what a reader is most likely to meet is a photograph of one, captioned with a spell about a heart being asked to keep quiet.

names.name: Hei matau
names.th: เฮย์ มาเตา (จี้ตะขอเบ็ดเมารี)

etymology.root: Māori hei, 'to wear around the neck', + matau, 'fish hook'

text.what: A heavily stylised fish hook, carved in bone or pounamu — the Māori term for the hard green stones, chiefly nephrite jade, found only in the South Island — and worn at the neck on a cord. Most modern pieces are not working hooks. Older matau were, and came in several forms, some plain and utilitarian, some highly ornate, some composite, and some whose function is no longer known.
text.story:
The shape carries a story about the country it is worn in. Māui caught the North Island out of the sea using a woven line and a hook made from his grandmother's jawbone; the Māori name for the North Island, Te Ika a Māui, the fish of Māui, holds the account, and the shape of Hawke's Bay is where the hook caught in the fish's side.

For Māori the hei matau is taonga, a cultural treasure. Wikipedia's summary of what it stands for is not a list of wishes: it represents the land, and prosperity, fertility and safe passage over water; it marks the importance of fishing to Māori and their relationship to Tangaroa, god of the sea. Matau were worn as pendants for safekeeping and were often treasured family heirlooms.

Material is where the modern record gets complicated. Traditionally matau were carved from bone, ivory, shell, wood or pounamu. Today most are cattle bone. Some Māori carvers still work whale bone, valued for its beauty, its cultural and historical weight and its scarcity; under current law against whaling they must use ancient stock, pre-existing supplies, or bone from whales that strand. New Zealand tradition and law give Māori first claim on part of the skeleton of any whale that strands and cannot be refloated, which is a very limited supply.

And then there is the other production line. Manufacturers in China mass-produce items resembling hei matau for the New Zealand visitor market, usually in a paste of bone and resin, and, in the words of the cited account, "have attracted criticism for their appropriation of Māori designs". That criticism is reported here with its subject named and is not adjudicated.
text.how: Carved from bone, whale bone, shell, wood or pounamu, worked down and polished, drilled and strung. Pounamu work is slow: the stone is smoothed by abrasion and bored with sticks and water. A hei matau is worn, given and inherited, not retired.
text.today: Carved by Māori artists and by collectives established by iwi that export their work, and worn by Māori and by other New Zealanders who take the hook as a New Zealand sign. Viggo Mortensen wore one after filming The Lord of the Rings, which the cited account names as part of a wider international interest in Māori art. The Chinese-made bone-and-resin versions sell on the same tourist market.

text.what: A pendant of a human figure, head tilted, hands on thigh and chest or both on the thighs, carved from pounamu and suspended on a plaited cord fastened with a loop and toggle. Pounamu is the Māori term for several hard, tough stones found only in the South Island — nephrite jade in the varieties Māori classify by colour as kahurangi, īnanga and kawakawa, and the translucent bowenite called tangiwai. A hei-tiki is a taonga: a treasure with whakapapa, an ancestral line of its own.
text.story:
Hei-tiki are, in Te Papa's summary of Māori adornment, the most famous and most highly prized of Māori personal ornaments. Two readings of the figure are given by Horatio Gordon Robley in A History of the Maori Tiki: that they are memorials to ancestors, or that they represent Hineteiwaiwa, the goddess of childbirth. Both have practices attached. A hei-tiki was often buried when its kaitiaki, its guardian, died, and retrieved later to be brought out at tangihanga, the mourning. And because of the connection with Hineteiwaiwa, hei-tiki were often given to a woman by her husband's family if she was having trouble conceiving.

The mana of one is not in the carving. Dougal Austin's 2014 thesis, supervised by Peter Adds and based on Te Papa's hei-tiki collection with early-contact pieces in overseas collections, finds that the mana of hei-tiki comes from the "agency of prolonged ancestral use", and that the form was "highly developed ... from the outset to conform to adze-shaped pieces of pounamu". Pounamu taonga gain mana as they pass between generations; the stone is held to take on the mana of past owners, and heirloom pieces are named after former owners. That is why the most prized taonga are the ones with known histories running back many generations, and why they were given to seal agreements.

The collections are large and their history is not neutral. Te Papa holds over 200 hei-tiki and the British Museum about 50; some were exchanged or gifted to European travellers and sailors at the earliest point of contact, and, in Wikipedia's words, "the majority were stolen or improperly obtained through colonial processes".

One story sits oddly beside the rest and is reported here as somebody else's reading, not this atlas's. The captain of HMS New Zealand, a battlecruiser funded by the New Zealand government in 1911, wore a hei-tiki and a piupiu into three First World War battles; the crew attributed the ship's lack of casualties to it and called her a lucky ship. That is a Pākehā crew's account of a taonga, and it is what a taonga becomes when it is read by people outside the whakapapa it belongs to.

In 1997 the Crown returned ownership of all naturally occurring pounamu to Ngāi Tahu, the South Island iwi, under the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement.
text.how: The stone was first cut roughly as a small adze — pounamu is hard and valuable enough that a carver removes as little as possible, which is why the head tilts. It is then smoothed by abrasive rubbing, shaped and bored with sticks and water, and polished over a long time. Finished, it is hung on a plaited cord with a loop and toggle. It is not retired; it is inherited, and its history is the point of it.
text.today: Carved by Māori artists, including collectives set up by iwi that export jewellery and carvings, and worn by Māori and by other New Zealanders as a mark of identity. Retailers also sell visitor versions in jade, other stone, plastic and other materials; the Wikipedia account of pounamu notes that much of the carved "greenstone" in souvenir shops is jade sourced overseas. As of 2026 the two trades run side by side, and this atlas reports the difference without ranking the buyers.

names.name: Hex sign
names.th: เฮ็กซ์ไซน์ (ป้ายดาวบนโรงนา)

etymology.root: English hex sign, from Pennsylvania German hex (German Hexe, Dutch heks), 'witch'. The compound is not old: the term was not used until the twentieth century, after Wallace Nutting's Pennsylvania Beautiful appeared in 1924.
etymology.note: Nutting was not a Pennsylvanian; he interviewed farmers about their barn decoration. Before his book there was no standard term, and Pennsylvania German farmers called the designs Blume or Sterne — flowers or stars. One farmer used Hexefoos, witch foot. The name then became popular with Pennsylvania Germans themselves during the growth of the southeastern Pennsylvania tourist trade.
etymology.folk: A competing account has English settlers mispronouncing sechs, the German word for six, as hex — the signs were traditionally adorned with six-pointed stars.

text.what: A painted disc on the side of a barn: usually a star inside a circular border, in bright colour on white. The later commercial ones are separate discs, screen-printed and mounted, carrying stars, compass roses, hearts, tulips, a tree of life, or the stylised bird called a distelfink. They are found on Pennsylvania Dutch barns in central and southeastern Pennsylvania, densest in Berks, Lancaster and Lehigh counties. The Amish do not use them.
text.story:
Two schools of thought exist about what these are, and this atlas's job here is to give both. One ascribes a talismanic nature to the signs. The other holds that they are purely decorative. Both schools accept that "there are sometimes superstitions associated with certain hex sign themes", and neither ascribes strong magical power to them.

The decorative side has a name and a date: Alfred L. Shoemaker, whose 32-page Hex, No! came out from the Pennsylvania Dutch Folklore Center in Lancaster in 1953 and whose title is its argument. *Inference —* this record has read that book's catalogue record and not its pages, and takes the phrase usually quoted from it, "chust for nice", from accounts of it rather than from the text. The scholarship the argument has run through since is Thomas E. Graves's 1984 doctoral dissertation at the University of Pennsylvania, The Pennsylvania German Hex Sign: A Study in Folk Process, and Hex Signs: Pennsylvania Dutch Barn Symbols and Their Meaning, by Don Yoder and Graves, published by Stackpole in 2000.

The chronology matters to the argument, because it is short. Barn painting of this kind is a late development in Pennsylvania Dutch folk art. Before the 1830s the cost of paint meant most barns went unpainted; the stars-in-circles began to appear in the early nineteenth century and became widespread decades later, when commercial ready-mixed paint became easy to buy. Barn decorating peaked in the early twentieth century, when there were many artists who specialised in it, drawing on a large repertoire and combining elements. The geometric patterns of quilts show up in the designs; the hearts and tulips are the ones found on fraktur, the elaborately lettered birth, baptism and marriage certificates of the same community.

The mountable sign is a documented commercial invention. Jacob Zook of Paradise, Pennsylvania, claimed to have originated it in 1942, based on traditional designs, to be sold in souvenir shops along the Lincoln Highway; Edward Buchak of Gilbertsville designed and screen-printed many of the Zook signs. William Schuster, Milton Hill, Johnny Ott and Johnny and Eric Claypoole also worked in that revival. It is the modern artists who tend to stress meanings: a horse head to protect animals from disease and the building from lightning, a dove for peace and contentment. The Pennsylvania Bureau of Radiation Protection built the international radiation symbol into a yellow-and-red hex sign design for its official logo.

Two more readings have names attached. Lee R. Gandee, in Strange Experience: The Autobiography of a Hexenmeister (1971), called hex signs "painted prayers". Others read the designs as decorative markers of ethnic identity, possibly arising in reaction to nineteenth-century government attempts to suppress the Pennsylvania German language. In recent years the signs have been taken up as talismans for folk magic by people who are not Pennsylvania Dutch, and neopagans have taken up making them, working other pre-Christian signs into the designs on the argument that the hex designs are of pre-Christian Germanic origin and related to Alpine German work — a circled rosette is called the Sun of the Alps in the Po Valley. Anabaptist sects in the region, the Amish and the Mennonites, take a negative view of hex signs, and the signs are rarely if ever seen on their farms.
text.how: Painted directly onto barn siding, in a circular border, by a specialist barn painter working from a repertoire of designs. The commercial version since 1942 is screen-printed on a separate disc and mounted on a barn or hung indoors. Nothing in this record's sources describes a blessing, a consecration, or a retirement.
text.today: Still painted, still sold, and still argued over. *Inference —* the argument is unusually hard to settle because the commercial sign arrived in 1942 with an explicit set of meanings attached for the buyer, which means most published lists of what a hex sign means postdate the tourist trade rather than the barns.

etymology.root: Arabic حرز ḥirz, from a root meaning to guard or fortify — the word means fortification, and implies a search for protection.
etymology.note: The same object is called a ta'wiz further east and a muska in Turkish; the difference is the carrier and the region, not the contents.

text.what: A small case on a chain, rectangular or cylindrical, holding verses of the Qur'an written on paper inside. Usually silver. The case may hang from a plain silver chain or sit at the centre of an elaborate necklace strung with beads, coins and other pendants; smaller versions are worn as hair ornaments or built into a headdress. The example the National Museum in Muscat publishes is silver with geometric and silver-leaf work, 30.6 cm long and weighing 152.9 g, and is dated to the fourteenth century AH — the early twentieth century CE — under the Al Bu Said dynasty.
text.story:
The case is the amulet's body and the verse is its content, and Islamic talismanic practice is clear about which of those is doing the work. Talismans in this tradition usually carry Qur'anic verses, pious phrases or invocations, and one description quoted in the literature calls the result "a supercharged prayer". Virtually all Muslim scholars permit a talisman that invokes God or one of His intercessors; addressing jinn or demons is prohibited. That is the line this object sits on the safe side of, and it is why the hirz differs from European charms, which often address minor deities or demons rather than God.

The verse most often named for protection is Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse, al-Baqara 2:255, the 255th verse of the Qur'an's second chapter, widely memorised and widely displayed. A hadith says reciting it wards off devils, shayatin, and fiends, afarit. Al-Suyuti narrates that a man and a jinn met and wrestled, and the jinn, as a reward for being beaten, taught the man a verse which, recited, keeps no devil able to enter his house with him — the Throne Verse.

*Inference —* the case, then, is a solution to a practical problem: paper in a hot, dusty, sweaty place does not last, and a verse that must stay legible has to be shut into metal. The jewellery around it is a second solution, to a different problem: what is worn every day has to be worth wearing.

The form is widespread on the Arabian Peninsula. Old Yemeni silver amulets called hirz were made to keep Qur'anic verses inside, and this sort of pendant is found across Oman, Yemen and the peninsula.
text.how: A case is cast or worked in silver and given a hinge or a sliding end. Verses are written on paper and folded into it. It is hung at the neck, or worked into a larger necklace, or scaled down for the hair or a headdress.
text.today: Made and worn, and also collected. The National Museum in Muscat publishes one through the Discover Islamic Art database of Museum With No Frontiers, and the form is sold new by silver dealers across the Gulf. As of 2026 this project has read no figure for the split between pieces made for wearers and pieces made for buyers.

names.name: Holy rider pendant
names.th: จี้นักบุญขี่ม้า

text.what: A small disc or pendant, bronze on the early Byzantine examples and lead on the medieval ones. One face carries the scene: a standing figure whipping a bound kneeling woman, or — on the later type — a horseman trampling her under the hooves. The other face often carries a whirling face-like device read as a womb, the hystera, sometimes ringed by an ouroboros, a snake biting its own tail. Everybody in the scene is labelled.
text.story:
The woman on the pendant is Abyzou, the demon blamed for miscarriage and infant mortality, and said to be driven by envy because she is infertile herself. She is Alabasandria in Coptic Egypt and Gylou in Byzantine Greek, and in the texts she has more names than anyone can count. In the Testament of Solomon she tells the king she never sleeps, that she walks the world looking for women about to give birth, and that she will strangle a newborn if she gets the chance.

The amulets take the healing-charm grammar of the late antique Mediterranean — address the affliction by name and order it out — and apply it to her. One bronze amulet labels the standing figure Arlaph and reads "The Seal of Solomon [is] with the bearer; I am Noskam." The reverse, written inside the ouroboros, reads: "Flee, flee, Abyzou, [from] Sisinios and Sisinnia; the voracious dog dwells here."

Who does the driving off varies: Solomon, or Arlaph — called Afarof in the Testament of Solomon and identified with the archangel Raphael — or, on Christian examples, Saint Sisinnios. On one medieval piece the rider is Sisinnios, the demon is named twice over as Abizou and Anabardalea, and an angel called Araph stands by with one wing raised.

The same scene exists in paint. At the monastery of St Apollo in Bawit, in Egypt, a wall painting shows the childbirth demon named Alabasandria trampled under a horse; the rider wears a belted tunic and trousers in the Parthian style, and the inscription, faded by the time it was read, was read as Sisinnios. Round the central image are a centaur, the piercing of the evil eye, and the demon's winged, reptile-tailed daughter, named in her own inscription.

*Inference —* the amulets are usually described as protecting women in childbirth and their infants, and Jeffrey Spier's survey notes that some of the names of the people seeking protection on surviving examples are men's. Whatever these pendants were understood to be doing, they were not only for mothers.

names.name: Horseshoe
names.th: เกือกม้า

text.what: A U of iron, drilled with nail holes, that spent its first life nailed to a hoof. As a charm it is the used one: worn thin at the toe, still carrying nail stubs, fixed over a doorway. Traditionally it is held up by seven nails. Model shoes in card and plastic are given at weddings, and paper ones go into confetti.
text.story:
The object arrives late and the charm arrives after it. Historians differ on the origin of the nailed shoe, partly because worn iron was valuable and got reforged; there is no hard evidence that the Druids invented it. Four bronze horseshoes with apparent nail holes were found in an Etruscan tomb in 1897, dated around 400 BCE, and a horseshoe complete with nails came out of the tomb of the Frankish king Childeric I at Tournai, dated to the fifth century CE. Written references are later: the earliest clear record of iron horseshoes is a mention of "crescent figured irons and their nails" in 910, with occasional mentions by 973. Around 1000 CE cast bronze shoes with nail holes were common in Europe; the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries brought widespread iron manufacture, and during the Crusades iron was valuable enough that horseshoes were accepted in lieu of coin to pay taxes.

Why this piece of scrap and not another: they were made of iron, a material held to turn away evil spirits, and they were held on with seven nails, seven being the luckiest number. Worn shoes were put above or beside doorways to guard houses, barns and stables, a custom whose remnants can still be seen across Italy, Germany, Britain and Scandinavia. In the Middle East the same shape is made as blue-glazed terracotta plaques; in Turkey metal or blue glass horseshoes are combined with the all-seeing eye.

Then there is the argument about which way up. In much of Europe, the Middle East and Latin America the shoe is hung facing downward, so that blessing pours onto whoever passes beneath. In parts of Ireland and Britain it is hung upward, so the luck is caught and cannot run out. Both went to the United States with their emigrants: English and Irish descent hangs it up, French, German, Italian, Spanish and Balkan descent hangs it down. Other conditions get attached in some traditions and not others — that the shoe must have been used and not new, that it must have been found and not bought, that any luck belongs to the owner of the shoe rather than to whoever hung it.

The Christian version names a blacksmith. Saint Dunstan, who worked as a smith before becoming Archbishop of Canterbury in 959, is said to have been asked by the Devil to shoe his horse, and to have nailed the shoe to the Devil's own foot instead, removing it only on a promise that the Devil would never enter a household with a horseshoe nailed to the door.

One English town has been collecting them since the fifteenth century. Every noble visiting Oakham, the county town of Rutland, presents a horseshoe to the Lord of the Manor, and it is nailed to the wall of Oakham Castle; the oldest of that accumulation date from the 1400s. The county flag is a golden horseshoe on a field of acorns.
text.how: Found, not bought, in the strictest versions. Nailed up over a door, a barn or a stable, points up or points down according to which tradition you inherited, ideally with seven nails. Nothing is done to charge it. It is not retired: it stays on the door until the door goes.
text.today: Still nailed over doors across northern Europe and North America, still sold new in gift shops as a wedding token, and still hung as a decorative wall piece with no claim attached. Edward Lovett found them on Sussex bedsteads in 1928, beside holed stones, against nightmares. *Inference —* a new shoe bought for luck breaks two of the tradition's own rules at once, and the people who sell them and the people who quote the rules are rarely the same people.

names.name: Illa
names.th: อิยา (รูปสัตว์หินแอนดีส)

text.what: A small carved animal, usually a llama or alpaca, cut from hard stone — the Dallas Museum of Art's Inca example is green and black — with a cylindrical hole sunk into the back between the shoulders. It sits in the hand. The hole is the working part: it is a container, not a decoration.
text.story:
Dana Olesch, writing for the Dallas Museum of Art in 2017 about a camelid-form vessel made between 1400 and 1540, describes what the hole was for: "Inca religious leaders likely inserted a mixture of llama fat, blood, and other ceremonial objects into the hole located at the top of this vessel during various fertility rituals." The point was agricultural and pastoral fertility. Several Inca-related groups ended the rite by placing the illa in a pasture.

That is the whole logic of the object, and it is not the logic of a pendant. An illa is not worn where somebody can see it; it is fed and then put into the ground the herd walks over. The charm is a deposit.

*Inference —* an object that is buried is an object that is found, which is why museums hold so many of them and why nearly every one has left the corral it belonged to. This atlas notes that as a fact about collections rather than about the Andes.

Olesch writes that highland communities in the Andes still use illa in fertility rituals for their camelid herds. The word travels with variants — conopa, canopa in colonial Spanish sources, inqaychu and enqa in Quechua-speaking herding communities — and the objects under those names are not all the same object.
text.how: Carved from hard stone with hand tools, the cavity drilled. Charged by filling: llama fat, blood, and other offerings placed in the hole. Then set in a pasture or field, or kept in the house and brought out for the rite. The illa is not retired; it is refilled.
text.today: Still in use in Andean highland herding communities as of the account cited here, and held in numbers by museums in Europe and North America. This project has read no dated field report of a present-day rite and does not describe one.

names.name: Incantation bowl
names.th: ชามคาถา

text.what: A plain earthenware bowl with writing inside it. The text is inked in a spiral that starts at the rim and winds inward to the centre, most often in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, sometimes Mandaic, Syriac, Arabic or Persian. Then the bowl is turned upside down and buried — under a threshold, in a courtyard, in the corner of a house where somebody has just died, in a cemetery. Around one in ten carries no real language at all.
text.story:
John Charles Arnold sets out the mechanism the way its users described it: "When placed upside down under each corner of a house, demons would follow the inscribed charms that spiraled from the outer rim inward, only to be caught in the center."

The bowls belong to Sasanian Mesopotamia, sixth to eighth century, in a population that was Christian, Manichaean, Mandaean, Jewish, Zoroastrian or still Babylonian in religion, and largely Aramaic-speaking whatever else it was. They were commissioned across those lines. Nearly eighty Jewish bowls survive from Babylon under Sasanian rule, most from the Jewish settlement at Nippur, where almost every excavated house had them buried in it. They name what they are against: the evil eye, Lilith, Bagdana. Their inscriptions quote scripture and rabbinic texts alike, which scholars read as evidence that the rabbinic material was held to carry the same power as the biblical.

Two things follow that are worth stating plainly. The bowls often call themselves amulets, and the Talmud, which was being written in the same place and period, discusses the use of amulets to drive away demons — so the text on these bowls is the only written material documenting Jewish language and religion recovered from that time and place. And the corpus is a scandal: about 2,000 bowls are registered as archaeological finds, while the trade digs them up freely, so there may be tens of thousands in private hands.

There is an Islamic branch. In the medieval period, talismanic bowls did the same work in metal rather than clay, covered in Arabic — Qur'anic verses, a hadith, sometimes numerology or astrology — and used for healing by drinking water left standing in them overnight.

names.said: the Inuit terms vary by group and are not collapsed into one here

text.what: Small worked or unworked pieces of animal and bird — bone, claw, tooth, skin, feather — sewn to clothing or carried, one amulet to one spirit. There is no single form. The class is defined by the relation, not the shape: published ethnography states that the effect of an Inuit amulet is attributed to the spirit that corresponds to it.
text.story:
Two numbers in the ethnographic record say more about this practice than any description of an object does.

The first is 80. Wikipedia's summary of the published ethnography of Inuit religion records that the Netsilik used a great many amulets — even dogs could have them — and gives one recorded instance of a young boy who had eighty, so many that he could hardly play. The second is 17: one man carried seventeen names taken from his ancestors, and the names were themselves intended to protect him. Beside that sits the Iglulik, who used few.

Amulets sit inside a system with other parts. Inuit religion holds that human illness can be caused by offending the spirits, and that fear of retribution produces caution; to avoid giving offence, people have observed rules and taboos, offered prayers and songs, worn amulets, and consulted the angakkuit, the ritual specialists who mediate between people and spirits. An amulet might be made by an angakkuq, but lay people made them too.

*Inference —* an eighty-amulet child and a seventeen-name man describe a practice where protection is cumulative rather than singular, which is a different logic from the one-charm-one-neck traditions that fill most of this atlas. This project states that as its own reading of the published record and not as anybody's account of their own practice.

This record prints what published ethnography and Inuit and Greenlandic institutions have made public, and no more. It does not reconstruct which animal answers which spirit, and it does not fill the gaps from a neighbouring tradition.
text.how: Selected and attached: sewn to a parka, hung at the neck, set into a hood. An amulet corresponds to a spirit, and the rest of the making is not printed here. Names function alongside objects — a name taken from an ancestor is described in the ethnography as protective in itself.
text.today: Inuit amulet practice is documented by twentieth-century ethnographers working in the Canadian Arctic and Greenland; Inuit religious practice continues alongside Christianity across the Arctic. This project has read no dated present-day account it can cite, so no claim is made here about what any community carries in 2026.

names.name: Jimat
names.th: จิมัต (เครื่องรางมลายู)

etymology.root: Malay and Indonesian azimat, borrowed from Arabic عزيمة ʿazīmah, 'determination, firmness of resolve'; shortened in Indonesian to jimat. The Malay synonym is tangkal (Jawi تڠكل); the Arabic-derived tamimah is also used
etymology.note: Malay Wikipedia defines azimat as an object held to give tuah — luck — and protection to its owner. Indonesian Wikipedia defines jimat as an object or piece of writing hung on the body, a vehicle or a building.

text.what: A class rather than a shape. Jimat covers any object or piece of writing hung on a body, a vehicle or a building to keep its owner from harm. Inside the class, three things are described in detail by the sources this record uses: a rajah, a charm written out in inscribed characters; a baju rajah, a garment carrying that writing; and the cast coin-charms of Java and Bali, flat discs of copper and brass with a square hole, made like Chinese cash coins but never spent.
text.story:
The coin-charms are the part of this class with dates on it. Indonesian collectors call them uang gobog, gobog wayang or koin gobog; in Bali they are pis bolong; Dutch sources called them Indonesische tempelmunten, Indonesian temple coins. The first gobog amulets in Java appeared during the Majapahit Empire. Gobog wayang in copper and brass were produced in the eighteenth century, and evidence for making them at scale runs only from the beginning of the twentieth.

They left the island early. Sir Thomas Stamford Raffles took 106 gobog wayang cash coins with him from Java to Britain, and they are in the British Museum. Joe Cribb built the standard catalogue on them: Magic coins of Java, Bali, and the Malay Peninsula, 13th century to 20th century — A Catalogue based on the Raffles Collection of Coin-shaped charms from Java in the British Museum, published in 1999. That subtitle is also the clearest published statement of the span.

What the pieces are held to do is stated type by type. A Yogyakarta numismatist describes the function of gobog amulets as "a complement to the requirements or ritual offerings in Java". In Bali they remain in use in Hindu rites, as tokens of faith and as bringers of good fortune, and individual types carry individual claims — the Pis Anoman is said to give its holder strength and energy like the wind.

The class carries an argument inside it. Indonesian Wikipedia's article on jimat states the Islamic position flatly: "Penggunaan jimat di dalam ajaran Islam adalah perbuatan terlarang. Hal ini dikarenakan perbuatan tersebut merupakan bentuk meminta perlindungan dan penyembuhan kepada selain Allah" — using a jimat is forbidden in Islamic teaching, because it amounts to seeking protection and healing from other than God — and adds that the practice belongs to pre-Islamic society and should not be followed. The same article illustrates the baju rajah as a thing people wear. Both statements sit on the same page. That is where the word stands in Indonesian and Malay now, and this atlas reports it without settling it.
text.how: Cast, for the coins: metal of a composition close to Chinese cash, in moulds, with wayang figures on the face. Written, for the rajah: characters inscribed on paper or onto cloth, as in the baju rajah. Then hung — on the body, on a vehicle, on a building — or set out with ritual offerings, which is the use a Yogyakarta numismatist names for the gobog in Java. This project has read no published account of the making rite for either, and prints none.
text.today: Still in use in Bali in Hindu rites as of the accounts this project has read, and still argued over in Indonesian-language religious writing, where the class is described as forbidden by Islamic teaching and illustrated at the same time. The Raffles pieces remain in London.

dating.note: The span is Cribb's: his catalogue is subtitled '13th century to 20th century'. The source also states that the first gobog amulets in Java appeared during the Majapahit Empire, that copper-and-brass gobog wayang were produced in the 18th century, and that large-scale production is evidenced only from the start of the 20th. The dates belong to the coin-charms; the wider class of jimat is not dated here.

text.what: A written amulet: a small sheet of parchment, paper or thin metal, inscribed in Hebrew with divine and angelic names, sometimes laid out as a grid of letters or numbers, then folded or rolled and carried, hung at a bed, or fixed in a house. What is written on it is the object; the case, where there is one, is a case.
text.story:
The practice has a name in its own tradition — Kabbalah Ma'asit, practical Kabbalah — and that tradition mostly forbids it.

Gershom Scholem's point about it is the historical one: a large part of the content of practical Kabbalah predates speculative Kabbalah and does not depend on it. What ended up under the label was an agglomeration of all the magical practices that developed in Judaism from the Talmudic period through the Middle Ages, and the doctrine of the Sefirot hardly ever played a decisive role in them. Amulet-making using the esoteric names of angels dates from Talmudic times.

The split between contemplative and practical Kabbalah was complete by the beginning of the 14th century, and most of the writing of the practical branch was never published. Abraham Abulafia condemned it. One tradition of it flourished in Spain in the second half of the 15th century, before the Alhambra Decree, around a text called Sepher ha-Mashiv; Moshe Idel describes its practitioners as interested in demonology and in coercive incantations to summon demons, angels and even God, in order to hasten the Messianic Age. Joseph Della Reina's failure at that was held up by later Kabbalists as a warning.

Then Isaac Luria, in 16th-century Safed, forbade his students to write amulets at all, and because Luria is the central teacher of modern Kabbalah and the foundation for later Hasidism, that prohibition carries authority rather than opinion. His reasoning was about purity: without the Temple and the ashes of the Red Heifer to purify with, the pursuit of practical Kabbalah by a person with an impure body is very detrimental.

It kept going anyway, at the border. The Baal Shem healers worked with methods between practical and meditative Kabbalah, amulets among them — Elijah Ba'al Shem of Chelm (1550–1583), the Baal Shem of London (1708–1782). Yisrael Baal Shem Tov (1698–1760) began as one, used amulets, and by the end of his life wrote only his own name on them, Yisrael ben Sara or Yisrael ben Eliezer, and no names of God at all. In the 1750s Jacob Emden accused Jonathan Eybeschütz of being a secret Sabbatean, chiefly on his reading of some amulets Eybeschütz had written. Rabbi Hirsch Fraenkel was imprisoned in Germany in 1713 for owning a library said to contain oaths and amulets for overcoming demons, seeing the future and speaking to the dead.

*Inference —* a practice whose own authorities forbid it and whose writings were mostly never published is a practice an atlas can describe and should not demonstrate. This record names who restricts it and stops there; see the restricted note below.

One word of warning about the name. In Western ceremonial magic, 'kamea' also means the planetary number squares that Cornelius Agrippa expounded in De Occulta Philosophia in 1531, used as grids on which to trace the sigils of spirits by converting a name to numbers. That is a different object with a borrowed Hebrew word, and the atlas keeps them apart.

restricted.note: Practical Kabbalah is restricted inside its own tradition. It was held to be permitted only to an elite who could keep its spiritual source separate from the realms of evil, and only under conditions of holiness and purity; most Kabbalists have taught that its use is forbidden outright. Isaac Luria forbade his students to write amulets and taught that, in generations without the Temple and the ashes of the Red Heifer, its pursuit by a person with an impure body is very detrimental. This atlas therefore prints no formula, no arrangement of divine or angelic names, and no construction for any kame'a. What is above is history and prohibition; the working content is not published here and is mostly not published anywhere.

etymology.root: Old Javanese kris, 'dagger'; keris ꦏꦼꦫꦶꦱ꧀ in the Javanese ngoko register, dhuwung in krama, wangkingan in krama inggil. Pusaka is a sanctified heirloom
etymology.note: The blade has a different name at each level of Javanese politeness, which is a measure of what kind of object it is. Malay, Sundanese, Balinese and Sasak spell it keris; Minangkabau karih; Buginese and Makassarese sele.

text.what: An asymmetrical dagger in three parts: blade (bilah), hilt (hulu) and sheath (warangka). The blade is forged from alternating laminations of iron and nickelous iron, and the contrast between them stands out on the finished surface as pamor, a pattern. Many blades are wavy — the waves are luk — and many are straight. Each part is worked: carved wood, ivory, brass, iron, silver or gold, set with stones. A blade is described by its dhapur, the form, of which there are around 60 variants; by its pamor, of which there are around 250; and by its tangguh, which is its age and origin. Worn in the belt at the back.
text.story:
The kris is a weapon that is also a member of the family. Javanese calls a heirloom blade tosan aji, sacred heirloom weapon, and counts it a pusaka. Blades are handed down through generations and worn at weddings and other ceremonies. A kris given by a Javanese king to a noble or a subject carried the king's confidence with it and was a great honour; the property the blade confers is piyandel, which means to add self-confidence. A Javanese groom wears one with a chain of jasmine wound round it, and the flowers say he should not be quick to anger.

The smith is the point. Making a kris was the work of an empu — 'possessor' — the honorary title in Java for an ironsmith with the skill to forge one, as against a pandai besi who makes tools and peasants' weapons. A kris empu was held to need knowledge, technical skill and spiritual prowess together, because the blade has a physical and a spiritual presence. The metal is layered from different iron ores and meteorite nickel, folded dozens or hundreds of times on a high-quality blade. Some take a short time; some take years. Empu are described as craftsmen who also know literature, history and the occult.

The blade is treated as alive and, more to the point, as not necessarily friendly. Kris are held to be vessels for spirits, good or bad. A blade can be tested: cuts on a leaf, read against the blade's width, say whether it is a good one; or the owner sleeps with it under the pillow and reads the dream — a bad dream and the blade has to go, a good one and it stays. A blade bad for one person is not bad for another, and the fit between weapon and owner is what matters. Types carry their own claims: Beras Wutah was held to grant its possessor a life without famine, and was given mainly to officials paid in foodstuffs. Pointing a kris at someone means they will die soon, so silat practitioners touch the blade tips to the ground before a demonstration.

The legends have names and centuries. The Pararaton tells of Mpu Gandring, the smith killed by his impatient customer Ken Arok in the last days of Kediri in the thirteenth century, who cursed the unfinished blade to kill seven men, Ken Arok among them. The Sejarah Melayu of Tun Sri Lanang tells of Taming Sari, made by a Javanese empu, won in a duel by the Melakan admiral Hang Tuah in the fifteenth century, and so well made that whoever held it could not be beaten. Setan Kober, 'devil of the grave', forged with thirteen luk by Empu Bayu Aji and disturbed at its charging by a crying djinn from the graveyard, made its wielders overly ambitious and impatient and finally killed Arya Penangsang in the sixteenth century.

Colonial law disarmed it. Firearms came into the archipelago in the sixteenth century; the forging of edged weapons fell away as sultans and rajas were subjugated, and in some regions carrying cutting and stabbing weapons was banned. The turning point in Java was 1830, when Prince Diponegoro, defeated at the end of the five-year Java War, handed his kris to the Dutch. The early twentieth century brought a ban on carrying edged weapons in the Dutch East Indies. The ceremonial and protective use continued anyway, in the kraton and istana of Indonesia, Malaysia and the Muslim-inhabited southern Philippines.

It is a live object still, with the danger that implies. In the Balinese Barong dance the segment called the keris dance has male dancers in trance stabbing themselves in the chest with their own blades and coming away unhurt. In February 2021 a 16-year-old kris dancer was stabbed to death in the heart by his own kris during a Rangda dance in Denpasar.
text.how: Forged by an empu from layers of different iron ores and meteorite nickel, folded and folded again, the pamor raised by the contrast between the laminations. The smiths carried out old rites that were held to put power into the blade; this project's sources do not print them, and nor does this record. A kris needs a yearly cleaning, called jamasan in Javanese, which is part of what is owed to it — the repeated cleanings leave old blades worn and thin. Repairs used whatever was to hand locally, so a blade from Java can end up with a hilt from Bali and a sheath from Madura. Warriors made offerings to their kris at a shrine.
text.today: In 2005 UNESCO put the Indonesian kris on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Making it had nearly stopped by the 1990s, under economic pressure and changing values; concerned specialists pushed a revival and craftsmanship picked up. Smiths still work in Madura, Surakarta, Yogyakarta, Makassar and Palembang, but their numbers are falling sharply and successors are hard to find. The craft survives in villages such as Banyu Sumurup in Imogiri, Bantul, near Yogyakarta, where a blade is made either as a sacred amulet ordered by an enthusiast who wants its spiritual power, or as a souvenir for a visitor — the same workshop, two customers, and the argument about whether those are the same object sits inside the trade rather than outside it.

names.name: Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls
names.th: ม้วนแผ่นเงินเคเทฟฮินโนม

text.what: Two sheets of silver, tiny, rolled tight, each scratched with a passage of the Priestly Blessing from the Book of Numbers. They were found rolled and had to be opened; the method for doing it without losing them took three years to develop. They hold what may be the oldest surviving text of the Hebrew Bible.
text.story:
Ketef Hinnom is the shoulder of rock where the Valley of Rephaim meets the Valley of Hinnom, on the old road from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, beside St Andrew's Church. Gabriel Barkay reported the first season there in 1975: a salvage excavation on the hill between the church road and the road down into the valley, prompted by a block of stone 2.80 m long lying on the surface, which turned out to be a threshold still in place in a monumental complex. Underneath were rock-cut burial chambers in natural caverns, Iron Age Judahite, of the seventh and sixth centuries BCE.

In 1979 the two silver scrolls came out of one of those chambers. The excavation report describes them as apparently once used as amulets. They are dated to the First Temple period, late seventh to early sixth century BCE, before the Babylonian Exile. They are now in the Israel Museum.

*Inference —* two things about this object are unusual for the atlas at once. It is a written charm that survives from before the tradition it belongs to had a canon to quote from, and it is a charm whose text is not a spell but a blessing. Whether the people who rolled them up would have called them amulets is a question the excavation cannot answer, and the cited report does not claim more than 'apparently'.
text.how: Silver, hammered thin, inscribed, rolled, and worn or carried. How they were suspended is not published in what this project read; what is documented is where they ended up, which is a burial chamber.

names.name: Ladanka
names.th: ลาดันกา (ถุงกำยานออร์โธด็อกซ์)

etymology.root: Russian ладан, 'incense, frankincense', plus a diminutive — the little thing you keep incense in
etymology.note: The same word once named a small brass censer, a sphere with a cross on top, set before the icons in the red corner of a house. The neck-worn pouch is the sense that survived.

text.what: A small pouch or a small hinged case hung at the neck on the same cord or chain as a baptismal cross. Cloth for the old kind, stamped or cast metal for the kind sold now, often with an icon on the lid. Inside goes incense, or a fragment of a relic, or a written prayer — commonly the Lord's Prayer, Psalm 90 or the Jesus Prayer. It is worn next to the skin and it is not opened for show.
text.story:
The Orthodox reference portal Azbyka very defines it in one line: a ковчежец со священными реликвиями в виде иконы, носимый на шее — a small reliquary with sacred relics, in the form of an icon, worn at the neck. The Russian encyclopedic entry adds the older layer: a fabric pouch, worn on the body, holding ладан, incense, and sometimes a bone from a saint's remains. Ivan Shmelev, in Bogomolye, gives it in a child's voice: "У бабушки ладанка из Иерусалима с косточкой... от мощей..." — grandmother has a ladanka from Jerusalem with a little bone in it, from the relics.

The positional rule is the first thing every Orthodox source states, and it is the whole argument in miniature. Её принято носить вместе с ним, но не вместо него: it is worn together with the cross, never instead of it. The cross is the baptismal object and cannot be displaced by this one.

The second thing every Orthodox source states is what a ladanka is not. Azbyka very is categorical: никаких оберегов и амулетов православный христианин носить на себе не должен — an Orthodox Christian should wear no protective charms and no amulets at all. The same entry says that wearing a ladanka with a prayer inside carries no sacred meaning without knowledge of the prayer and a personal appeal to God, and that treating an object with Christian symbolism as an amulet does the soul no good. The Russian encyclopedic account, describing what people do rather than what the Church teaches, records the object as functioning as both талисман and амулет, and notes that the pouches have carried protective signs.

*Inference —* set those two paragraphs side by side and this is the Orthodox twin of the Catholic argument on this shelf. In Rome the Church built a legal category — the sacramental — that lets a blessed object be devotional without being magical, and then spent centuries policing the edge of it. Here there is no such category to stand on; the instruction is simply not to. The object is still sold, still filled, still worn under the shirt, and the instruction is still printed.

The trade has moved with the money. Monastery and church shops sell ladanki in sterling silver and gold with enamelled icons on the lid; one Moscow Orthodox shop's catalogue page, read on 17 September 2026, listed twenty-five of them priced between 5,377 and 50,037 roubles. The cloth pouch with incense in it costs a fraction of that and is the older thing.
text.how: Bought at a church or monastery shop, or given. Filled with incense, a relic fragment, or a written prayer, and hung on the cross cord at the neck. The Orthodox sources this record cites do not describe a consecration rite for the pouch itself and this project has not gone looking for one; what they describe instead is where the relic or the incense came from, which is what carries the weight. Nothing is said about retiring one.
text.today: Sold in Russian church and monastery shops in 2026 in every price band, from a fabric pouch to a gold locket. The Orthodox reference portal that explains what it is spends most of the entry explaining what it must not be taken for, which is a fair description of the object's position now.

names.name: Lamashtu plaque
names.th: แผ่นเครื่องรางลามัชตู

text.what: A small plaque, pierced or looped so it can hang, carrying the figure of the demon it is aimed at. Lamashtu is cut on it as a composite: a lion's or dog's head, donkey's teeth, bare breasts, bird-of-prey talons, a serpent gripped in each hand. She stands on a donkey in a boat; a dog and a piglet suckle at her. Her seven names, and an incantation telling her to keep away, run across the object in cuneiform. Bronze is the material of the big Neo-Assyrian examples; smaller ones are fired clay and cut stone.
text.story:
Lamashtu is the daughter of the sky god Anu, and she acts on nobody's instructions but her own — the reason Assyriologists argue she is a goddess rather than a demon, and the reason her name is written with the cuneiform sign that marks deity. Her victims are the unborn and the newly born. She touches a pregnant woman's stomach seven times to kill the baby, or takes it from the wet nurse. Adolescents, adults and the old are on her list too, as a bringer of disease.

The incantations open by addressing her directly. One amulet, catalogued as AO 8184, runs through her names — 'Dimme', 'Daughter of Anu', 'Who was named by the gods', 'Victoria, heroine among ladies' — and then delivers the whole point of the object: "you must not approach (this) person." The names matter because knowing them is the hold.

The largest surviving pieces are scenes rather than signs. The Neo-Assyrian plaque in the Louvre known as the Plaque des Enfers sets divine symbols above a sickroom: a patient on a bed, ritual specialists at work, and in the bottom register Lamashtu on her donkey in the boat with the serpents in her fists, while Pazuzu drives her off down the river.

*Inference —* the object is not a picture of the demon so much as a place to put her. Iconographic studies distinguish an earlier threatening figure with raised hands, a middle type holding a comb and spindle, and the elaborate serpent-holding compositions of the first millennium BCE; what stays constant across all three is that she is shown named, held, and on her way out.

names.name: Lung ta prayer flag
names.th: ธงลุงตา (ธงมนต์ม้าลม)

etymology.root: Tibetan rlung-rta, 'wind horse' — rlung wind, rta horse
etymology.note: The vertical kind is darchog, dar-lcog, 'flagstaff'.

text.what: A square or oblong of coloured cloth, printed from a woodblock, sewn along its top edge to a long string with others. Flags come in sets of five and always in the same order of colours: blue for sky and space, white for air and wind, red for fire, green for water, yellow for earth — the five elements, whose balance Tibetan medicine reads as health. Strings are hung on a diagonal, high to low, between two fixed points: a rock and a pole, a roof and a tree, the top of a temple, a stupa, a mountain pass. The vertical kind, darchog, is a single large rectangle fixed along its side to a pole and planted in ground, cairns and rooftops.
text.story:
The centre of the printed field is a horse carrying three flaming jewels on its back. The horse stands for speed and for the turning of bad fortune into good; the three jewels are the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha. Around the horse run versions of some four hundred traditional mantras, each addressed to a particular deity, including mantras of Padmasambhava, Avalokiteśvara — Chenrezig, patron of the Tibetan people — and Manjusri. The four corners carry the Four Dignities: the dragon, the garuda, the tiger and the snow lion. Prayers for a long life of good fortune are often added for whoever puts the flags up, and wishes are written on them.

The flags are held to have come out of Bon, where shamanistic Bonpo used plain flags in primary colours. Sutras first written on cloth banners travelled as prayer flags; legend ascribes the origin to the Buddha, whose prayers were written on the battle flags the devas carried against the asuras. That knowledge reached Tibet by 800 CE, and the flags themselves no later than 1040 CE, where they were modified further; the Indian monk Atisha (980–1054) brought the Indian practice of printing on cloth flags to Tibet and Nepal.

What the flags do is stated in the negative as often as the positive. They do not carry prayers to gods — the source calls that a common misconception. As wind passes over the cloth the air is held to be purified and sanctified by the mantras, and the blessings are carried to all beings. The printed images fade with exposure, and the fading is not decay in this reading: the prayers become a permanent part of the universe as the images go, and new flags are mounted beside the old ones, which is read as a welcome to life's changes.

During the Cultural Revolution prayer flags were discouraged but not eliminated, and many traditional designs may have been lost.
text.how: Printed from woodblocks onto the five colours, strung, and raised. Timing matters: some hold that flags hung on inauspicious astrological dates may bring negative results for as long as they fly, and the best time to put new ones up is the morning of a sunny, windy day. Because the symbols and mantras are treated as sacred, flags are not to be put on the ground or used on clothing. In Tibet old flags are replaced with new ones every year at the Tibetan New Year, and old flags should be burned.
text.today: Strung across passes, roofs, bridges and monastery courtyards throughout the Tibetan world as of 2026, and sold worldwide as decoration, often in the right five colours and the wrong order, and often hung where nothing is renewed and nothing is burned. Different styles can now be seen across the Tibetan region.

names.name: Lunula
names.th: ลูนูลา (จี้พระจันทร์เสี้ยวโรมัน)

text.what: A crescent moon on a chain, usually gold, worn by girls in ancient Rome. Isidore of Seville defines it exactly: "Lunulae are female ornaments in the likeness of the moon, little hanging gold bullae." It came off on the eve of her marriage, with her childhood toys and the rest of her child's clothes, and she put on women's dress.
text.story:
Two lines of Plautus are most of what a reader can hold onto. In Epidicus, the speaker asks the girl Telestis: "Don't you remember my bringing you a gold lunula on your birthday, and a little gold ring for your finger?" In Rudens, Palaestra says her father gave her a golden bulla on the day she was born. Girls got a crescent, boys got a locket, and the plays treat both as the ordinary furniture of a childhood.

The cited account is direct about what Romans wore amulets for: against evil forces, demons and sorcery, and especially against the evil eye. It also draws a map line worth keeping. Lunulae were common right across the Mediterranean; the bulla, the boys' version, was mostly an Italian object. This record lists Italy alone in its countries because Italy is where the source names the practice; the wider Mediterranean spread is stated in the source without countries attached to it.

*Inference —* an amulet with a removal ceremony is doing two jobs. It guards a child, and it counts. Take it off and something has ended — a wedding in this case, a toga in the boys'. The atlas has a small class of these, and the Bulgarian martenitsa, which comes off when the wearer sees a stork, belongs to it.

text.what: A cut stone between one and three centimetres across, engraved on both faces and often round the edge as well. One face carries a figure — most famously the cock-headed, serpent-legged anguipede named Abrasax, holding a shield and a whip. The other carries names and lines of letters, many of them in no known language. It was set in a ring or pierced and hung. The Campbell Bonner Magical Gems Database, which catalogues them, describes gems "designed to bring their owners health, prosperity and love".
text.story:
The name Abrasax, or Abraxas, appears on nearly all the legends on these gems, sometimes filling the whole face on its own. It turns up in the same breath as other names across the Greek magical papyri and on Greek metal curse tablets: "I conjure you by Iaō Sabaōth Adōnai Abrasax, and by the great god, Iaeō." E. A. Wallis Budge described the composite figure as a Pantheus, an All-God, "with the head of a cock (Phœbus) or of a lion (Ra or Mithras), the body of a man, and his legs are serpents which terminate in scorpions".

The stones were classed and re-classed for three centuries by collectors who wanted to know whose they were. Antiquarians sorted them into Abraxas proper, taken as Basilidian and Gnostic; Abraxastes, older forms adapted; and Abraxoïdes, unconnected to Basilides altogether. The cited account is blunt about where that got them: no attempt to identify the figures on existing gems with the personages of Gnostic mythology has succeeded, and Abrasax is the only term in the legends that is not already known from other religions.

What can be said is that the gems and the magic papyri reflect the same ideas, and that the papyri contain directions for making and using gems with similar figures and formulas — which is why, as the cited account puts it, it can scarcely be doubted that many of these stones are amulets and instruments of magic.

*Inference —* this is the atlas's clearest case of a corpus without a findspot. The Campbell Bonner database lists contributing institutions across fifteen countries and a string of galleries and auction houses; the whole corpus is estimated at around 5,600 pieces. The countries on this record are where the gems were made and used according to the cited accounts, not where they were dug up, because for most of them nobody recorded that.

etymology.root: Japanese maneki 招き 'beckoning' + neko 猫 'cat' — the beckoning cat
etymology.note: The gesture is a Japanese beckon, not a wave: hand up, palm down, fingers folding towards the caller. Figures made for Western markets often turn the paw palm-up instead, because the Japanese gesture reads as goodbye elsewhere.

text.what: A seated cat, one forepaw raised palm-down in a beckoning fold, usually holding an oval koban coin in the other. The classic figure is a calico Japanese Bobtail. Ceramic or plastic now; antique ones are carved wood, stone, cast metal or handmade porcelain. It sits near the entrance of a shop, a restaurant, a pachinko parlour, a laundromat, a bar, a hotel, and in houses. Some have a mechanical paw that swings, driven by a battery or a solar cell through a coil and a magnet.
text.story:
The dated record starts in 1852. The Bukō nenpyō, a chronology of Edo, carries an entry for that year; Utagawa Hiroshige's print Joruri-machi Hanka no zu, also 1852, shows the marushime-neko — a variant of the beckoning cat — being sold at Sensō-ji in Asakusa. A Meiji newspaper picked it up in 1876, kimono-clad ones were handed out at an Osaka shrine around then, and by a 1902 advertisement the thing was established.

Behind that lies clay. Potting clay was found at Imado in Asakusa during the Tenshō era of the Azuchi-Momoyama period, local people started making Imado ware, potters from Mikawa Province moved in and developed it, and in the Genroku era (1688–1704) Imado dolls appear — which is the lineage most accounts give the beckoning cat.

*Tradition holds —* four different origin stories, each with a temple attached. Ii Naotaka's hawking party shelters at Gōtoku-ji in the Kan'ei era after a cat beckons them in at the gate, a thunderstorm breaks, and the Ii clan makes the temple its own. Ōta Dōkan, lost and outnumbered at Ekodahara, is beckoned into Jishōin and wins. A poor old woman near Imado Shrine dreams of the cat she had to give up, makes an Imado-ware figure of it, sells it at Asakusa Shrine and prospers. The courtesan Usugumo of Miuraya in Yoshiwara loses her cat to a rumour and a sword; the severed head kills the snake in the privy that would have killed her, and a customer gives her a wooden cat in its place. Each temple claims the birthplace.

It is routinely taken for Chinese. It is made and sold in China too, as zhāocáimāo, and in Chinatowns abroad it is often labelled a Chinese lucky cat or a golden cat. That is a fact about where the object circulates, not an error to be corrected off the page.
text.how: Bought, not consecrated: this is a shop-counter object with no shrine rite behind it, though shrines and temples sell them. Which paw is up carries a reading, and the reading varies with time and place — a raised left paw for more customers, a raised right for more money; hence also the saying that the left is for a business and the right is for a house. Colour was added later, in combination with feng shui: the original white is for good fortune generally, black to turn away evil, red for health, yellow or gold for wealth, pink for romance. It is not retired, renewed or burnt. It sits by the till until it breaks.
text.today: Mass-produced worldwide as of 2026, in ceramic, plastic, keychains, piggy banks, air fresheners and pots. Hikone City's mascot Hikonyan is drawn from the Gōtoku-ji story and the Ii clan; the cat has been worked into Pokémon's Meowth and into the card game Balatro; a Trinidad and Tobago party ran one in an election advertisement in 2015, waving goodbye to the incumbent prime minister.

names.th: มาร์เตนิตซา

text.what: Twisted white and red yarn, most often made into two small wool dolls: Pizho, the male one, mostly white; Penda, the female one, mostly red and wearing a skirt. It is pinned to clothing or tied at the wrist or neck from Baba Marta Day, the first of March. Modern ones take other shapes and add coloured beads.
text.story:
Two rules govern the object, and both are about other people and about time. It is always given, never bought for oneself — to family, friends, anyone you feel close to. And it comes off on a sign, not a date: the wearer takes it off on first seeing a stork, a swallow returning from migration, or a tree in blossom. Failing all three, the end of March.

Baba Marta means Grandma March, and Bulgarian and Macedonian folklore makes her a bad-tempered old woman whose mood turns fast. Wearing her colours is described as asking her for mercy, so that winter passes and spring comes; the first stork or swallow says she is in a good humour and about to retire.

Taking it off has its own local rules. Some tie the martenitsa to the branch of a fruit tree, giving the tree the health and luck the wearer has had while wearing it. Others put it under a stone and look the next day: a larva or a worm means a healthy, successful year; an ant means the same but with hard work for it; a spider means trouble.

On where it comes from, the cited account offers several accounts and settles none. The custom is tied to the pre-Christian history of the Balkans and to agricultural cults of nature; the twisted white-and-red woollen threads specifically are said to suggest Thracian, possibly Hellenic or Roman origins. Some ethnographers trace it to the Eleusinian Mysteries, with the ancient equivalent of the Greek mártis being the kroke; the custom is mentioned in Photios' Lexicon, which records that the priests wrapped a red thread round the right hand and foot. At that time red and other coloured threads were used to protect children and young people from evil spirits and witchcraft. An early twentieth-century Bulgarian story puts the first martenitsa at the seventh-century Battle of Ongal: after the Bulgar victory, Khan Asparuh sent doves with white threads to carry the news, and the threads turned bloody in flight.

*Inference —* the ethnographers' colour readings are worth quoting rather than choosing between. White for the purity of melting snow, red for the setting sun growing stronger as spring comes; white for purity, red for life and passion; the two together for the cycle of life and death, for good and evil, for sorrow and happiness, for the male and female beginnings and the balance between them. A charm that means that many things at once is a charm doing social work, and the rule that it must be given rather than bought says so out loud.
