names.said: me-zu-ZAH, plural mezuzot; the word means 'doorpost'
names.th: เมซูซา

etymology.root: Biblical Hebrew mezuzah, 'doorpost' — the upright that carries the lintel; it takes on the meaning 'inscribed parchment' only in post-Biblical Hebrew, from the Deuteronomy commandment to write the words on the doorposts
etymology.note: The root is disputed. One reading takes it from z-w-z, 'to move or shift', the doorpost being what lets the door move. Another takes it from Akkadian mazzāzu, 'stand', from izuzzu, 'to stand' — the fixed part as against the revolving door, which matches the Septuagint's σταθμός. Some researchers doubt the Akkadian borrowing.

text.what: A strip of parchment, handwritten by a trained scribe in indelible black ink with a quill, carrying Deuteronomy 6:4–9 and 11:13–21. It is rolled, put in a case, and fixed to the right-hand doorpost, in the upper third at about shoulder height, within about eight centimetres of the opening. The case can be anything — silver, wood, stone, ceramic, pewter, polymer clay — and the case is not the point; a photocopy on paper inside a beautiful case is not a valid mezuzah.
text.story:
Jewish law does not class a mezuzah as an amulet, and the atlas has to say so before it says anything else. It is a mitzvah, a commandment, one of the 613, and its stated purpose in the verses that command it is educational: to keep God's words in front of a person, taught to their children, spoken of at home and on the road.

The objection is on the record and it is old. Maimonides, in the Mishneh Torah, allows writing Shaddai on the outside of a mezuzah and then draws the line hard: "Those, however, who write the names of angels, other sacred names, verses, or forms, on the inside [of a mezuzah] are among those who do not have a portion in the world to come." And the reason: "Not only do these fools nullify the mitzvah, but furthermore, they make from a great mitzvah ... a talisman for their own benefit." A commandment converted into a charm stops being a commandment.

So why is it in an atlas of amulets? Because people have in fact used it that way, in writing, for a very long time, and that argument is itself documented. The cited account states that in later generations the mezuzah began to be interpreted as an apotropaic device protecting the house from evil, and names early rabbinic sources that explicitly witness a belief in an anti-demonic function: Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 4:12, Babylonian Talmud Bava Metziya 102a, Babylonian Talmud Pesahim 113b. It also notes that some Jewish sources construe the mezuzah as a guard against divine anger and that others vehemently reject that reading. In the 1970s, after a series of attacks at Ma'alot, Chabad began a campaign to have mezuzot systematically checked, on the assumption that keeping the mitzvot would guarantee personal safety. And sociological research summarised in the cited article reports that about three-quarters of adults in Israel hold that the mezuzah guards their houses.

That is the record this atlas prints: a tradition that calls it a commandment, a legal authority who wrote down exactly why calling it a talisman degrades it, and a large documented practice of treating it as protection anyway. The atlas does not settle it.

Karaite Jews read the Deuteronomy verse as metaphor and traditionally use no mezuzah, putting up instead a small plaque shaped like the two Tablets of the Law with the Ten Commandments — though in Israel many Karaites also fix a mezuzah so as not to make other Jews uncomfortable. Samaritans read the commandment as displaying any selected text from the Samaritan Torah, on marble, wood, parchment or good paper, above the door or on a prominent wall inside; stone plaques of the Ten Commandments from the Byzantine and early Muslim periods survive, and are in the Israel Museum. For Samaritans, the more of them in a house, the better.
text.how: Written on klaf, parchment, by a sofer stam — a scribe trained both in the relevant laws and in Ktav Stam calligraphy — in indelible black ink, with a quill made from a feather or, rarely now, a reed. On the back it is customary to write Shaddai, a name of God which also reads as an acronym for Shomer Daltot Yisrael, Guardian of Israel's doors; many cases carry the letter shin for the same reason. Ashkenazi custom adds a second line that is a one-letter Caesar shift of three words of the Shema, written on the back opposite the words it shifts; Sephardi custom, following the Shulchan Aruch and the Rambam, leaves it out. It is held against the spot, a blessing is said, and it is fixed. Where the doorway is wide enough, many Ashkenazim tilt it — a compromise proposed by Rabbi Jacob ben Asher between Rashi, who held it should be vertical, and his grandson Rabbeinu Tam, who held it horizontal. Most Sephardi, Mizrahi and other non-Ashkenazi Jews fix it vertically. Many observant Jews have a scribe check the parchments for tears or faded letters at least twice every seven years. Torn or damaged wording invalidates it.
text.today: Contested in American housing law, repeatedly, since 2001. A condominium association at Shoreline Towers in Chicago banned objects outside unit doors and management removed tenants' hallway mezuzot; complaints went to the Chicago Commission on Human Relations, the Illinois Attorney General and the US Department of Housing and Urban Development. Alderman Burton Natarus drafted a city ordinance making it illegal to prohibit a religious sign, symbol or relic on a door, doorpost or entrance; it passed that December with a maximum $500 fine, the first such legislation in North America. A federal judge found in 2006 that the rule did not violate the Federal Fair Housing Act, the district court upheld that in 2008, the Seventh Circuit reversed in 2009, and the disputes settled confidentially in 2011. Illinois amended its Condominium Property Act in 2006, effective 1 January 2007; Florida followed in 2008 after a Fort Lauderdale case; Texas passed HB1278 in June 2011 after a Houston couple lost in federal court in 2008. A national bill introduced by Congressman Jerrold Nadler in 2008 never became law.

names.name: Milagro
names.th: มิลาโกร (แผ่นโลหะแก้บน)

etymology.root: Spanish milagro, 'miracle' — the word for the answered prayer, used for the token that asks for it or thanks for it

text.what: A small flat metal shape of the thing you are praying about — a leg, an eye, a heart, a lung, a kneeling man, a cow, a house, a car. Most are stamped tin or silver a few centimetres long, pierced or pinned so they can be fastened to a saint's robe, a shrine rail or a retablo; some are modelled in the round. Gold, silver, tin, lead, wood, bone and wax all turn up, depending on what the local trade works in.
text.story:
Milagros are religious folk charms used for healing and as votive offerings in Mexico, the southern United States, other parts of Latin America, and parts of the Iberian Peninsula. They are pinned to altars, shrines and sacred objects, and bought in churches and cathedrals or from vendors outside them.

The custom is traced to the ancient Iberians of the Spanish coast and travelled with the Spanish into Central and South America. It has thinned since, but it holds in rural Spain — Andalusia, Catalonia and Majorca — alongside its American forms.

A milagro is offered to a saint's image either as a reminder of what the petitioner needs or in thanks for a prayer already answered. The shape does the pointing. But the code is local, not universal: a leg can mean a leg that hurts or a journey to be made; a heart can mean a heart condition, a romance, or something else again. *Inference —* that ambiguity is the interesting part. The object is precise enough to aim a prayer and loose enough that only the petitioner and the saint need know what it is about, which is a useful property for a token left in public on a church wall.

Milagros also get carried rather than pinned, for protection and luck, and the same stampings end up as earrings and necklace charms. They correspond almost exactly to the tamata of the Eastern Orthodox churches — the same body parts, in the same thin metal, on the same kind of icon.
text.how: Stamped, cast or cut, then pinned, wired, glued or nailed to the image. A vendor's tray outside a shrine is sorted by body part. Nothing is consecrated before it is offered; the offering is the act. Old milagros accumulate on a much-visited image until the metal is a second garment, and are periodically taken down and stored or sold by the church.
text.today: Still sold at church doors and in markets across Mexico, the southwestern United States and rural Spain as of the most recent accounts this project has read. They also sell as craft jewellery to buyers with no shrine in mind, which is the same argument this atlas reports about every charm that reached a gift shop, and does not settle.

names.name: Miraculous Medal
aliases: Medal of Our Lady of Graces
médaille de la rue du Bac
names.th: เหรียญอัศจรรย์

etymology.root: French médaille miraculeuse, 'miraculous medal' — a nickname the public gave it, not the name it was struck under
etymology.note: It was minted as the Medal of the Immaculate Conception. The cited account says the present name was earned in the decades after cures were reported during a cholera pandemic.

text.what: An oval stamped medal, worn at the neck on a chain. The front shows a woman standing on a globe, crushing a serpent's head, rays coming from rings on her hands, inside an oval of words that reads "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee", with 1830 struck below. The back has a bar and a cross over a large letter M, twelve stars around the rim, and two hearts beneath — one crowned with thorns, one pierced by a sword. Aluminium at the cheap end, silver and gold at the other.
text.story:
This one has a date, a witness and a goldsmith, which almost nothing else in this atlas does.

Catherine Labouré, a novice with the Daughters of Charity in the rue du Bac in Paris, said that on 18 July 1830 a child's voice woke her and led her to the convent chapel, where the Virgin Mary told her: "God wishes to charge you with a mission [...] You will be contradicted, but do not fear, you will have grace." On 27 November the same year, she said, Mary returned during her evening meditations, standing on a globe inside an oval frame, wearing rings that shed light — the rays, Mary told her, were "the graces I shed upon those who ask for them", and the gems that stayed dark "are the graces for which souls forget to ask". The frame turned, and the reverse design appeared. Then the instruction, which is the whole point of the object: have a medal struck after this model, and "all who wear them will receive great graces".

Her priest watched her ordinary daily behaviour for two years before taking it to Archbishop Hyacinthe-Louis de Quélen of Paris. Approval came; the goldsmith Adrien Vachette made the die; the first 1,500 medals were minted on 30 June 1832. Then the arithmetic gets strange. The Daughters of Charity distributed them during a deadly cholera pandemic, cures were reported, and the public renamed the object. Over 500,000 had been distributed by 1834. By 1835, more than a million worldwide. By 1839, over ten million. By Labouré's death in 1876, more than a billion had been produced. *Inference —* a devotional object that reached a billion within a single lifetime is an industrial fact as much as a religious one, and the cholera years are where the curve bends.

On the Church's side the object sits inside a category. The Miraculous Medal is a sacramental — by the Catholic Church's definition a sacred sign that works "through the intercession of the Church", which prepares a person to receive grace and disposes them to cooperate with it, and which does not act by itself the way a sacrament does. The Enchiridion Indulgentiarum of 2004 grants a partial indulgence to the faithful who use a crucifix, a crown, a scapular or a medal blessed by a priest. The 2001 Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy lists Marian medals among approved practices while holding that popular piety "may never incorporate rites permeated by magic, superstition, animism, vendettas or sexual connotations". *Inference —* the medal's own promise, struck into it, is that wearing it brings graces; the doctrine is that the wearing disposes rather than delivers. Both sentences are on the record, they are not the same sentence, and this atlas does not decide between them.

One wearer's account is famous enough to be in the liturgy. In 1842 Marie-Alphonse Ratisbonne, a Jewish man, took a bet to wear the medal on a trip to Rome, entered the basilica of Sant'Andrea delle Fratte, and reported a vision of the Virgin exactly as the medal depicts her. He converted, became a Jesuit, and the event has its own canonical inquiry behind it and a place in the Feast of the Miraculous Medal. Maximilian Kolbe, founding the Militia of the Immaculate in 1917 under this Virgin's patronage, handed the medals out and called them his "ammunition".
text.how: Struck from the 1832 die design by religious-goods manufacturers worldwide. Bought or given; the giving is the commoner route, and the Daughters of Charity have handed them out free since the first batch. A priest may bless one, which is what attaches the indulgence; nothing requires it. Worn at the neck under clothing more often than over it. Never retired — a lost one is simply replaced.
text.today: Still struck to the 1830 design, still sold and given at the rue du Bac chapel, where Catherine Labouré's body lies, and in religious-goods shops everywhere the Catholic Church is. In 2026 it shares a counter with the St Christopher medal and the Brown Scapular. No dated retail price was read for this record.

names.name: Mjölnir pendant
names.th: จี้มโยลเนียร์ (ค้อนธอร์)

etymology.root: Old Norse Mjǫllnir, from Proto-Norse *melluniaR. Historical linguists disagree on where it goes next: one derivation links it to Old Church Slavonic mlŭnuji and Russian molnija 'lightning', giving 'lightning-maker'; a second to Old Norse mjǫll 'new snow', giving 'shining lightning weapon'; a third to Old Norse mala 'to grind', giving 'the grinder'.
etymology.note: The name belongs to the god's weapon. The pendant borrows it, and no Viking-Age wearer left us a word for the pendant itself.

text.what: A small hammer worn head-down at the throat: short haft, wide splayed head, a suspension loop or ring where the handle should end. Most are plain iron or silver; about a hundred of the thousand or so known carry ornament. Wear one and the weapon hangs upside down, which is how you tell it from a cross at arm's length.
text.story:
Around a thousand hammer pendants have come out of the ground in what are now the Nordic countries, England, northern Germany, the Baltic states and Russia. As of 2004, a tenth of the finds came from graves, nearly all cremations, and those burials are often identified as women's. The rest turn up in hoards and in the dirt of trading towns.

The pendants appear to have grown out of an older north Germanic habit of wearing pendants, and scholars have connected them to the club-of-Hercules amulet worn by other ancient Germanic peoples. Their surge in popularity during the Viking Age, and some of the shapes that surge produced, may have been an answer to Christian cross pendants, which were appearing in the same region as Christianisation advanced. Two signs, two workshops, one neck.

What the hammer was for is said out loud on one object. The Kvinneby amulet, an 11th-century copper plate from Öland in Sweden, was likely worn at the neck and carries a Younger futhark inscription that runologists Mindy MacLeod and Bernard Mees translate: "May Thor protect him with his hammer which came from out of the sea. Flee from evil!" The poems agree on the hammer's second job. In Þrymskviða, Mjölnir is fetched to hallow a bride; in Gylfaginning, Thor consecrates Baldr's burning ship with it. A hammer that kills is also a hammer that blesses.

In 1999 the German archaeologist Jörn Staecker proposed a typology of the finds by decoration and material — amber, iron, silver. In 2019 the American scholar Katherine Suzanne Beard extended it by hammer shape and suspension type and launched Eitri, an online database of hammer finds with their composition and discovery context.

The second span starts much later. The hammer is worn again today by adherents of Heathenry, and scholars Jenny Blain and Robert J. Wallis wrote in 2006 that Thor's hammer is the most common of heathen sacred artefacts. In the United States the National Cemetery Administration issues the Hammer of Thor as emblem #55 for veterans' headstones. The symbol has also been taken up in white nationalist and neo-Nazi circles: the Anti-Defamation League's symbol database records that white supremacists sometimes build swastikas and other hate symbols into the decoration, while noting that its traditional origins are non-racist. Beard's position is that "most people who wear hammer pendants today do so for cultural, religious, or decorative reasons and maintain absolutely no ties to any racist groups or beliefs". The dating block below covers the excavated Viking-Age span only; the revival is a separate, living span that this record describes in prose rather than folding into the same bar.
text.how: Cast or cut in iron or silver, occasionally amber, pierced or looped at the haft end, and strung. In Viking-Age cremation graves around Mälaren, in Åland and in Russia, archaeologists also find Thor's hammer-rings: iron rings hung with several amulets, many but not all of them hammers, recovered from cinerary urns and found in graves of both sexes but more often women's. Their exact function is unknown, and this atlas leaves it unknown.
text.today: Made and sold worldwide as of 2026, in silver, steel and pewter, by museum shops, by Heathen craftworkers and by mass-market jewellers. Whether a cast reproduction is the same object as an excavated one is the argument this atlas reports rather than settles; so is who gets to wear the sign, and the ADL entry and Beard's sentence above are the two ends of it.

names.name: Navaratna ring
names.th: แหวนนพเก้า

etymology.root: Sanskrit nava 'nine' + ratna 'gem'
etymology.note: The same compound travels: Navaratnam in Malayalam, Nabaratna in Bengali and Odia, Navaratinam in Tamil, Nawaratna in Malay and Nepali, Nawarat or Noppharat in Thai, Nawarat in Burmese.

text.what: Nine stones set together in gold or silver, one for each of the nine bodies of Hindu astrology, with a ruby at the centre for the Sun. The traditional arrangement runs clockwise from the top: diamond, natural pearl, red coral, hessonite, blue sapphire, cat's eye, yellow sapphire, emerald. Nothing but a ruby or a red spinel goes in the middle, because the Sun sits at the centre of the system the ring is a model of. It is made as a ring, a pendant, a necklace and a star worn on the chest.
text.story:
The nine are fixed and the list is old enough to be quoted rather than explained. A Sanskrit sloka attributed to the Brihat Jataka, and repeated in the Mani-mala and the Jataka Parijata, assigns ruby to Surya, pearl to Chandra, red coral to Mangala, emerald to Budha, yellow sapphire to Brihaspati, diamond to Shukra, blue sapphire to Shani, hessonite to Rahu, the ascending lunar node, and cat's eye to Ketu, the descending one. The late Thai astrologer Horacharn Thep Sarikabutr gives the same nine in his Parichad-Jataka, chapter 2, verse 21: "Top quality and flawless ruby is the gem for the Sun, natural pearl for the Moon, red coral for Mars, emerald for Mercury, yellow sapphire for Jupiter, diamond for Venus, blue sapphire for Saturn, hessonite for Rahu (ascending lunar node), and cat's eye for Ketu (descending lunar node)."

The sloka's two words that matter most are sujatyam-amalam — high-born and flawless. The Garuda Purana, chapter 68, verse 17, has Sri Suta Goswami say that "Pure, flawless gems have auspicious powers which can protect one from demons, snakes, poisons, diseases, sinful reactions, and other dangers, while flawed stones have the opposite effect." The Agni Purana, chapter 246, agrees in the negative: a gem that is cracked, fissured, dull, rough or sandy "should not be used at all".

*Inference —* that is an unusual clause for an amulet. Most charms in this atlas work whatever they look like; this one is cancelled by a flaw, and a flaw is a thing only a dealer can price. The prescription and the trade are the same sentence.

In Thailand the nine gems are a state emblem. The king awards the Noppharat Ratchawaraphon, the Ancient Auspicious Order of the Nine Gems, in a single class: a Pendant of the Nine Gems on a yellow sash trimmed red, blue and green, worn over the right shoulder to the left hip by men and on a silk ribbon at the front left shoulder by women; a Star of the Nine Gems on the left chest; and a Gold Ring of the Nine Gems, for men, on the right ring finger.
text.how: Prescribed before it is made. In Hindu astrology the placement of the navagrahas in a person's sidereal horoscope is read first, and either a single gem or a combination of compatible stones is advised — to draw on a beneficial planet or to counter a harmful one — which is why the tradition says to consult an astrologer before wearing one. Paramahansa Yogananda, writing in Autobiography of a Yogi, adds a weight and a placement: "the proper jewels, metals, or plant preparations are valueless unless the required weight is secured, and unless these remedial agents are worn next to the skin", and puts the floor at faultless jewels of not less than two carats.
text.today: Made and sold across southern and southeastern Asia as of 2026, in gold for the wealthy and in small stones for everyone else, and worn regardless of religious difference — the arrangement is treated as auspicious in India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Singapore, Myanmar, Cambodia, Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia. The claimed astrological or piezoelectric benefit of wearing or donating gems has not been scientifically quantified, and this atlas does not adjudicate it either way.

text_th.what: อัญมณีเก้าเม็ดฝังรวมกันบนตัวเรือนทองหรือเงิน หนึ่งเม็ดต่อดาวหนึ่งดวงในเก้าดวงของโหราศาสตร์ฮินดู โดยมีทับทิมอยู่ตรงกลางแทนดวงอาทิตย์ การจัดวางตามประเพณีเรียงตามเข็มนาฬิกาจากด้านบน: เพชร ไข่มุกธรรมชาติ ปะการังแดง เฮสโซไนต์ (โกเมนชนิดหนึ่ง) ไพลิน ไพฑูรย์ บุษราคัม มรกต ตรงกลางใส่ได้แต่ทับทิมหรือสปิเนลแดงเท่านั้น เพราะดวงอาทิตย์อยู่ตรงกลางของระบบที่แหวนวงนี้จำลองไว้ ทำเป็นแหวน จี้ สร้อยคอ และดาราสำหรับติดที่อก
text_th.story:
อัญมณีทั้งเก้าถูกกำหนดไว้ตายตัว และรายการนี้เก่าพอที่จะยกมาอ้างแทนการอธิบาย ศโลกภาษาสันสกฤตบทหนึ่งซึ่งว่ากันว่ามาจากพฤหัตชาดก (Brihat Jataka) และถูกกล่าวซ้ำในมณีมาลา (Mani-mala) และชาตกปาริชาต (Jataka Parijata) กำหนดทับทิมให้สุริยะ ไข่มุกให้จันทรา ปะการังแดงให้มังคละ มรกตให้พุธ บุษราคัมให้พฤหัสบดี เพชรให้ศุกร์ ไพลินให้ศนิ เฮสโซไนต์ให้ราหู จุดตัดขาขึ้นของวงโคจรดวงจันทร์ และไพฑูรย์ให้เกตุ จุดตัดขาลง โหราจารย์เทพ สาริกบุตร ผู้ล่วงลับ ให้อัญมณีทั้งเก้าชุดเดียวกันไว้ในปาริชาตชาดก (Parichad-Jataka) บทที่ 2 โศลกที่ 21: "ทับทิมเนื้อเลิศไร้ตำหนิเป็นอัญมณีแห่งดวงอาทิตย์ ไข่มุกธรรมชาติแห่งดวงจันทร์ ปะการังแดงแห่งดาวอังคาร มรกตแห่งดาวพุธ บุษราคัมแห่งดาวพฤหัสบดี เพชรแห่งดาวศุกร์ ไพลินแห่งดาวเสาร์ เฮสโซไนต์แห่งราหู (จุดตัดขาขึ้นของวงโคจรดวงจันทร์) และไพฑูรย์แห่งเกตุ (จุดตัดขาลงของวงโคจรดวงจันทร์)"

สองคำในศโลกที่สำคัญที่สุดคือ สุชาตยัม-อมลัม (sujatyam-amalam) — กำเนิดสูงและไร้ตำหนิ ครุฑปุราณะ บทที่ 68 โศลกที่ 17 ให้ศรีสูต โคสวามี (Sri Suta Goswami) กล่าวว่า "อัญมณีบริสุทธิ์ไร้ตำหนิมีพลังอันเป็นมงคล ซึ่งปกป้องผู้สวมจากอสูร งู พิษ โรคภัย ผลแห่งบาป และอันตรายอื่น ๆ ขณะที่อัญมณีที่มีตำหนิให้ผลตรงกันข้าม" อัคนีปุราณะ บทที่ 246 เห็นพ้องในด้านกลับ: อัญมณีที่ร้าว แตก หมอง หยาบ หรือมีเนื้อทราย "ไม่ควรใช้เลย"

*ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* นั่นเป็นเงื่อนไขที่แปลกสำหรับเครื่องราง เครื่องรางส่วนใหญ่ในแอตลาสนี้ทำหน้าที่ของมันได้ไม่ว่าหน้าตาจะเป็นอย่างไร ชิ้นนี้ถูกยกเลิกด้วยตำหนิ และตำหนิเป็นสิ่งที่มีแต่พ่อค้าอัญมณีเท่านั้นที่ตีราคาได้ ข้อกำหนดกับการค้าคือประโยคเดียวกัน

ในประเทศไทย นพรัตน์เป็นเครื่องหมายของรัฐ พระมหากษัตริย์พระราชทานเครื่องราชอิสริยาภรณ์อันมีเกียรติยศยิ่งนพรัตนราชวราภรณ์ ซึ่งมีชั้นเดียว: ดวงตรานพรัตน์ห้อยกับสายสะพายสีเหลืองขลิบแดง น้ำเงิน และเขียว สะพายจากบ่าขวาเฉียงลงสู่สะเอวซ้ายสำหรับบุรุษ และห้อยกับแพรแถบที่บ่าซ้ายด้านหน้าสำหรับสตรี ดารานพรัตน์ประดับที่อกเบื้องซ้าย และแหวนทองนพรัตน์ สำหรับบุรุษ สวมที่นิ้วนางข้างขวา
text_th.how: ถูกกำหนดก่อนจะถูกทำ ในโหราศาสตร์ฮินดู ตำแหน่งของนวเคราะห์ในดวงชะตาแบบนิรายนะของบุคคลจะถูกอ่านก่อน แล้วจึงแนะนำอัญมณีเม็ดเดียว หรือชุดอัญมณีที่เข้ากันได้ — เพื่อดึงพลังจากดาวที่ให้คุณ หรือเพื่อแก้ดาวที่ให้โทษ — ซึ่งเป็นเหตุที่ประเพณีนี้บอกให้ปรึกษาโหรก่อนสวม ปรมหังสา โยคานันทะ (Paramahansa Yogananda) เขียนไว้ในอัตชีวประวัติของโยคี (Autobiography of a Yogi) โดยเพิ่มเรื่องน้ำหนักและตำแหน่งที่สวมว่า "อัญมณี โลหะ หรือตัวยาจากพืชที่ถูกต้อง ไม่มีค่าอะไรเลยหากไม่ได้น้ำหนักตามที่กำหนด และหากไม่ได้สวมสิ่งที่ใช้แก้เหล่านี้ให้แนบกับผิวหนัง" และกำหนดขั้นต่ำไว้ที่อัญมณีไร้ตำหนิไม่ต่ำกว่าสองกะรัต
text_th.today: ณ ค.ศ. 2026 ยังมีการทำและขายทั่วเอเชียใต้และเอเชียตะวันออกเฉียงใต้ เป็นทองสำหรับผู้มีฐานะ และเป็นพลอยเม็ดเล็กสำหรับคนทั่วไป และสวมกันโดยไม่แบ่งแยกศาสนา — การจัดวางแบบนี้ถือเป็นมงคลในอินเดีย เนปาล ศรีลังกา สิงคโปร์ เมียนมา กัมพูชา เวียดนาม อินโดนีเซีย ไทย และมาเลเซีย ประโยชน์ทางโหราศาสตร์หรือทางไฟฟ้าจากแรงกด (piezoelectric) ที่อ้างกันจากการสวมหรือบริจาคอัญมณียังไม่เคยถูกวัดเป็นตัวเลขทางวิทยาศาสตร์ และแอตลาสนี้ไม่ตัดสินไม่ว่าทางใด

names.th: เครื่องรางนาซาร์ (ลูกปัดตาสีฟ้า)

etymology.root: Arabic naẓar, 'sight' or 'looking' — the same word for the look that does the harm and for the bead that answers it; Turkish nazar boncuğu adds boncuk, Turkic for 'bead'
etymology.note: The word travels: Albanian, Azerbaijani, Bengali, Hebrew, Hindi–Urdu, Kurdish, Pashto, Persian, Punjabi, Sindhi and Turkish all use it. Greek calls the object máti, 'eye'. In India and Pakistan the phrase nazar lag gai says somebody has been hit by it.

text.what: A handmade glass bead: concentric circles, or a teardrop, in dark blue, white, light blue and black, sometimes rimmed in yellow or gold. The Turkish boncuk is blue glass with a blue, white and black dot set on a white or yellow centre. It hangs at a neck, on a wrist, over a door, from a mirror, above a till, on a cradle.
text.story:
The bead is older than any of the countries that sell it. Glass eye beads are documented and extant from as early as the 16th century BCE, and the design spread with glassmaking itself — Mesopotamia to Egypt, Carthage to Greece, Phoenicia to Persia, and right through the Roman imperial period.

The explanations people give for the colour are specific. "According to Turkish belief, blue acts as a shield against evil and even absorbs negativity." And the materials are part of the claim, not just the manufacture: "The bead is made of a mixture of molten glass, iron, copper, water, and salt, ingredients that are thought to shield people from evil." A second explanation in the cited account runs the other way round — in the Middle East and the Mediterranean, blue eyes are relatively rare, so people with light eyes were held able to curse with a look, and the Assyrians already had turquoise and blue-eye amulets.

The bead also has a rule for its own death. If one breaks, a very strong nazar has hit the wearer, and the bead stored it all up and broke in order to protect them. That is the only retirement instruction in this batch that the object gives itself.
text.today: Mass-produced and sold everywhere: the Grand Bazaar in Istanbul, Monastiraki in Athens, airport shops, phone cases. A Turkish budget airline, Fly Air, carried the nazar boncuğu on the tail fins of its aircraft. The bead was added to Unicode as U+1F9FF 🧿 NAZAR AMULET in 2018, which makes it one of the very few amulets in this atlas that a reader can send in a message. Whether a factory bead is the same object as a lampworked one is argued by sellers and buyers alike; this atlas reports the argument and describes both the same way.

etymology.note: The wider class word is nazar battu, from nazar, the harmful look, in Hindustani.

text.what: A lime and seven green chillies threaded on a string and hung at a doorstep, over a shop counter or from the back of a vehicle. Nothing is worn and nothing is written. The thing rots in the sun, browns, and is replaced.
text.story:
Two explanations of the same string circulate, and they disagree about who the string is for.

In Hindu households, especially in northern India, hanging a lime and seven green chillies at the doorstep is a ritual to either ward off or acknowledge Alakshmi, the goddess of misfortune and grief, whose name means not-Lakshmi. One version holds that the sourness of the lime and the pungency of the chillies together make a smell even Alakshmi cannot tolerate. The other holds that Alakshmi is pleased by sour and spicy offerings, and will take her share standing at the door — which makes the string a payment at the threshold rather than a barrier across it. Alakshmi is not named in Vedic, Upanishadic or early Puranic literature; she is named in the Linga Purana, the Padma Purana and the Śrī Sūkta.

The string also belongs to a wider North Indian and Pakistani class, the nazar battu, whose logic is spoilage. A nazar battu is often a deliberate blemish introduced to prevent perfection: a black mark on the face or neck of a loved one, a flaw built into an otherwise faultless house, a stitching or colouring error put into an expensive carpet or sari. Mothers lightly spit to the side of their children to imply disparagement, and children are marked with a black spot on the cheek, because excessive admiration — even from well-meaning people, even a mother's own love — is held to draw nazar.

*Inference —* a lime and chillies at a shop door belong to that logic rather than to the eye-against-the-eye logic of the Mediterranean. The object is not looking back. It is either an imperfection hung where the perfect thing is, or a plate left out for the guest nobody wants inside.
text.how: Bought made up, at the price of a lime. Threaded so the chillies hang below the fruit, tied at a lintel, a counter, a bumper or a dashboard. It is a household act, not a specialist's: no source read here names a priest, a mantra or a consecration for it.
text.today: Ordinary street furniture in North Indian and Pakistani towns as of 2026, on shopfronts, new cars and trucks. The phrase nazar battu has also gone idiomatic: commentators in North India and Pakistan use it for a person or thing that is unwanted but has to be tolerated, as some of the press did of Pervez Musharraf during Pakistan's transition to democracy at the 2008 general election.

names.name: Nkisi
names.said: n-KEE-see; plural minkisi, and also mikisi, zinkisi, nkisi
names.th: เอ็นกีซี

etymology.root: From the Proto-Njila root *-kitį, an ancient subdivision of the Bantu language family, meaning a spiritual entity or the material object it inhabits.
etymology.first_attested: early seventeenth century in Kikongo dialects, transliterated into Dutch as mokissie — the mu- prefix of the noun class was still being pronounced
etymology.note: Dutch visitors to Loango, in what is now Cabinda, used it in the 1668 book Description of Africa for both the material item and the spirit inside it. When the Kingdom of Kongo converted in the sixteenth century, the Kikongo Catechism of 1624 used ukisi — a substance having the characteristics of nkisi — to translate 'holy'.

text.what: A container with a spirit in it. The container can be a ceramic vessel, a gourd, an animal horn, a shell, a cloth bundle — anything that will hold spiritually charged substances — and it can also be a carved wooden figure, human or animal, with a cavity cut in the belly, the head, or a pouch at the neck. The cavity is closed with a mirror or a disc of reflective glass fixed in resin, and the eyes are often mirrors too. On the aggressive class, nkondi, the surface bristles with nails and blades hammered in. The word names the spirit and the object at once.
text.story:
The first thing to get right is the word for the person, not the object. A nganga — plural banganga — is a healer, diviner and mediator who defends the living against harmful workings and supplies remedies against sicknesses caused either by them or by the demands of the bakisi, the spirits who are emissaries from the land of the dead. Banganga harness those powers by making minkisi. Nothing here happens without one.

The substances that go inside are bilongo, singular nlongo, a word usually translated 'medicine'. Wyatt MacGaffey's objection to that translation is the useful one: bilongo are not applied to the sick or swallowed, so 'therapeutic substances' is closer. They are chosen by metaphor. Bird claws go in to catch a wrongdoer. Minerals come from places associated with the dead — earth from graves, earth from riverbeds. White clay matters because white carries dead skin, moral rightness and spiritual positivity against the black of negativity, and red ochre where the powers of the dead are being mediated. Some minkisi have been described as portable graves, and many contain earth or relics from the grave of a powerful person as a prime ingredient.

The nails are not decoration. Nkondi comes from -konda, 'to hunt'; a nkondi hunts. The phrase used for hammering a nail in is koma nloka, to attach or hammer in a curse, from two ancient Bantu roots — one whose field includes hammering, one that covers witchcraft and cursing. According to Kongo testimony of the early twentieth century, people drive the nails in as a petition: for help, for healing, or as a witness to a contract or a pledge. Each nail stands for a vow, a signed treaty, an effort to abolish an evil. The purpose is to wake the nkisi, and sometimes to enrage it, for the task in hand. An oath-taker may declare himself open to the sickness a particular nkondi causes should he break the oath, and a person who falls ill with that sickness consults the nganga who mediates with that spirit to find out how to be cured. Kindoki, from the same root, covers any action that enlists spirits to harm others: used privately and selfishly it is condemned as witchcraft, used publicly by a village, a tribe or political leaders, or defensively by innocent people, it is not.

The nailed figures are narrower in time and place than the museum trays suggest. Minkisi nkondi have probably been made since at least the sixteenth century, but the nailed ones were probably made mainly in the northern part of the Kongo cultural zone in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Nailed minkisi are not described by missionaries or anyone else writing in the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries. MacGaffey, reading the late seventeenth-century Capuchin missionary Luca da Caltanisetta, notes that banganga then sometimes banged minkisi together, and suggests nails — which he argues were first being made around that time — eventually replaced the metaphor. Other scholars think Portuguese missionaries' images of Christ nailed to the cross and of Saint Sebastian influenced the practice; MacGaffey argues against that, on the grounds that nailing is tied up with too many other Kongo concepts to be a misreading of a missionary's picture. The earliest firmly dated nailed nkondi is one Commodore A. P. Eardley Wilmot acquired in 1864 while suppressing Solongo piracy at the mouth of the Congo River; another, named Mabiala mu ndemba and described as a thief-finder, is illustrated in the notes of the German Loango expedition of 1873–76.

How they got to Europe is part of the object. European collectors wanted the nailed ones as soon as the German Loango expedition published them. Robert Visser, a German trader and diplomat, collected a great many for German museums, especially Berlin and Stuttgart. In the nkondi entry's own words, "Many were purchased, others confiscated or removed by colonial authorities, and often found their way to museums, but many also remain in private hands." In the art world they arrived as a stimulus: the source says Bantu themes "previously considered primitive or gruesome were now viewed as aesthetically interesting" — a sentence about European taste, not about the objects. MacGaffey's counter is that the banganga's intentions were practical, the characteristics of the object dictated by the work it had to do, and the nails never decorative.

The argument about where they should be now is live and has names on it. The 2018 Report on the Restitution of African Cultural Heritage by Felwine Sarr and Bénédicte Savoy set out the case for return and moved the debate onto moral rather than only legal ground. In Belgium the Royal Museum for Central Africa holds more than 180,000 cultural and natural history objects, mainly from the former Belgian Congo, and has run its first major renovation in more than a century as a decolonisation programme. The Pitt Rivers Museum has built its own programme on four tenets — provenance, transparency, repatriation and redress — and in 2020 joined Savoy and other art historians at Technische Universität Berlin in a research project called Restitution of Knowledge. The British Museum has consistently refused to return objects, citing the British Museum Act 1963.

*Inference —* the European label for these objects entered this atlas as a term, not as a description. This record files the word under fetish-word for that reason, and writes about it there.
text.how: The nganga gathers the bilongo and assembles them, most often into a carved figure with a cavity cut for them, and then either becomes possessed by the spirit or leaves the finished object in a graveyard or another place spirits frequent. Once it is charged it can be handed to the client. Nkondi are often composed at the edge of the village, on the reasoning that a village, like a body, must have its entrances guarded; the nganga works isolated in a hidden camp and returns covered in paint and behaving strangely, to show he has come back from the land of the living's far side. Personal minkisi are kept in a private house. Community ones are put where the village can see them, though often inside their own enclosure by day.
text.today: Contested, and split across three places: Kongo communities, European and American museum stores, and private hands. Artists have taken the form up — Renee Stout, whose exhibition Astonishment and Power at the Smithsonian paired her own versions with commentary by MacGaffey; Tania Bruguera, who in 1998–99 performed Destierro in a suit made to resemble a nailed nkondi and then went looking for people who had broken promises; Kara Walker, Dread Scott, Karen Seneferu, Wesley Clark, Stephanie Dinkins, Michael MacGarry, Andrew Lamprecht, Justin Par. The Republic of the Congo painter Trigo Piula made a New Fetish series and said of it: "is a way of engaging with my community and a way of denouncing things that I believe are impacting us, like television for example". As of 2026 this project has read no count of how many minkisi sit in European collections.

etymology.root: Japanese fuda 札 'slip of paper, card, plate', with the honorific prefix o-/go-; the Buddhist and Daoist-derived synonym is gofu 護符, 'guarding tally'
etymology.note: The form descends in part from the Chinese Daoist lingfu, which reached Japan through Onmyōdō, and in part from the woodblock-printed Buddhist texts and images temples produced from the Nara and Heian periods.

text.what: A flat talisman issued by a shrine or a temple: a sheet of paper, a thin rectangular plaque in a paper sleeve, or a wooden tablet, carrying the name of the shrine or of the deity enshrined there and stamped with the shrine's seal. Paper ones are kamifuda, wooden ones kifuda. It is not carried on a person. It stands on a household altar, or goes on a wall above eye level, or is fixed at a gate, a doorway, a kitchen or a ceiling.
text.story:
Two lines run into the ofuda. One is Daoist: the lingfu, the talismanic script of China, which reached Japan through Onmyōdō. The other is print — the woodblock sheets of Buddhist text and image that temples were turning out from the Nara and Heian periods on. In the medieval period the three Kumano shrines in Wakayama stamped their paper talismans with stylised crows and called them Kumano Goōfu, Ox King Talismans; oaths and contracts were written on the blank side, so the sheet held the agreement and the sanction at once.

The standard modern form comes from Ise. Wandering preachers attached to the Ise shrines, the oshi, handed out purification wands called Oharai Taima as a sign that prayers had been said on a devotee's behalf. The wand came folded into paper shaped like a sword blade — kenharai — or boxed. Distribution started in the Muromachi period and peaked in the Edo: a document of 1777 records that eighty-nine to ninety per cent of households in the country held an Ise talisman. That is close to universal coverage, three centuries before mass media.

Then the state took it over. An imperial decree of 1871 abolished the oshi and moved production of the talisman, renamed Jingū Taima, to the shrine's own offices. In 1900 a new Department of Priests, the Kanbesho, took over; in 1927 the National Association of Shinto Priests; after the Second World War, the Association of Shinto Shrines, which still distributes Jingū Taima to affiliated shrines across Japan. *Inference —* an object whose issuing body is renamed four times in seventy-five years is an object the state has an opinion about.
text.how: Received at a shrine or temple counter, in exchange for hatsuhoryō, a first-fruit offering rather than a price. Shinsatsu are set on a kamidana, a household Shinto altar, or on a stand; failing that, upright in a clean space above eye level, facing east, south or south-east. The Association of Shinto Shrines recommends three per household: the Jingū Taima from Ise, the ofuda of the tutelary kami of where you live, and the ofuda of a shrine you are personally attached to. In a three-door altar the Ise one goes in the middle. Other ofuda go elsewhere in the house — hearth deities in the kitchen, a talisman of the Buddhist figure Ucchuṣma in the toilet, the horned Tsuno Daishi, the Tendai monk Ryōgen drawn as a yaksha, on a doorway. They are replaced annually, ideally before the year turns, and the old ones are burnt at the Sagichō or Dondoyaki fire in mid-January. Most shrines will take back another shrine's ofuda; many will not take a Buddhist one.
text.today: Issued year-round by shrines and temples with permanent staff, and distributed nationally through the Association of Shinto Shrines as of 2026. Japan has around 100,000 public shrines, about 80,000 of them affiliated with the Association and roughly 20,000 unaffiliated, which is the network the Ise talisman travels down.

names.name: Ojo de venado
names.th: โอโฮ เด เวนาโด (ตากวาง)

etymology.root: Spanish ojo de venado, 'deer's eye' — a name for the look of the seed, not for its plant
etymology.note: The seed is a Mucuna, a climbing legume; México Desconocido lists ojo de buey, ojo de toro and ojo de caballo as the same seed under other animals' eyes.

text.what: A hard round seed of a Mucuna vine, dark and glossy with a broad black band across it, which is why it reads as an eye at arm's length. Sellers dress it: a red cord or ribbon, often a tuft of coloured wool, sometimes a tiny image or a bead glued to the face. It is sold loose on a string, as a bracelet, or on a cord long enough to hang from a rear-view mirror.
text.story:
Wikipedia's account of the Mercado de Sonora in Mexico City puts it in one line among the market's magical stock: crosses of ocote wood for good luck, chains of garlic to ward off evil, and a seed called "deer's eye" to protect against the "evil eye".

México Desconocido traces the seed's career as a good-luck amulet to Xichú, a municipality in the northeast of Guanajuato, and notes that Mucuna also grew in Chiapas, Oaxaca, Puebla, San Luis Potosí and Veracruz, so other regions may have reached the same use independently. Newborns get one against mal de ojo; adults take one up for a hard stretch; drivers hang one where they can see it.

The object has a public opponent. The priest Eduardo Hayen Cuarón condemned it as "un amuleto y por tanto una práctica esotérica, maligna y 'obra de Satanás'" — an amulet, and therefore an esoteric practice, malign, and the work of Satan. *Inference —* a charm that draws a priest's condemnation by name is a charm being carried by people who also go to Mass, which is where most of this atlas's Latin American material sits. Both statements are reported here; neither is settled here.

The seed reached national pop culture too: the band Caifanes put it on their 1988 debut album.
text.how: Gathered from the vine, dried, drilled or bound, and finished with red thread. No consecration is published in the sources this project read. Wearers say a seed that cracks or splits has taken a hit meant for the person carrying it — the same account Turkish sellers give of a broken nazar bead — and it is replaced rather than repaired.
text.today: Sold across central and southern Mexico in markets, at church doors and online as of 2026, and hung in cars as often as worn. No dated price was read for this record, so none is printed.

names.th: โอมาโมริ (เครื่องรางญี่ปุ่น)

etymology.root: Japanese mamori 守り 'protection', with the honorific prefix o- (sonkeigo) — 'the honoured protection'
etymology.note: The same character stands behind ofuda's shinsatsu vocabulary; omamori shares its origin with ofuda and is described as the smaller, portable version of it.

text.what: A small brocade pouch, a few centimetres tall, drawn shut at the top with a cord and printed with the name of the shrine or temple that issued it. Inside is a slip of paper or a chip of wood carrying a prayer or an invocation. The pouch stays shut: nobody who carries one opens it. Most hang from a bag, a school satchel, a phone strap or a car mirror rather than round the neck.
text.story:
Omamori are issued by Shinto shrines and by Buddhist temples alike, dedicated to particular kami or to Buddhist figures, and sold to anyone regardless of what they believe. The shrine consecrates the contents by rite; a Shinto one is described as holding busshin, spiritual offshoots of the deity, a Buddhist one kesshin, manifestations.

The folklorist Yanagita Kunio dated the thing a reader now recognises to the Tokugawa period at the earliest. Writing in 1969 he put it this way: "Japanese have probably always believed in amulets of one kind or another, but the modern printed charms now given out by shrines and temples first became popular in the Tokugawa period or later, and the practice of a person wearing miniature charms is also new. The latter custom is particularly common in cities." Two claims sit in that sentence — the printed charm is early modern, the pocket-sized charm is later still, and urban.

The demand outgrew the shrines. Where a popular shrine or temple cannot keep up, it orders omamori from a factory, and priests have objected to the quality and to what they call the "authenticity" of the factory product. Both halves of that get reported here: the factory pouch and the hand-finished one come off the same counter, and the argument over whether they are the same object is an argument inside the tradition.

*Inference —* a charm designed to be replaced every twelve months is a charm with a business model, and the New Year crowds are the year's trade. Fushimi Inari-taisha alone drew 2.69 million worshippers over three days at the New Year in 2006, a police figure and the largest in western Japan. No source this project has read publishes what any shrine takes in omamori money, so no figure is given here.
text.how: Received, not bought — the verb the tradition uses is sazukaru, to be granted, and the money handed over is hatsuhoryō, a first-fruit offering. If a visitor cannot find one for their need, they may ask a priest to have one made; if enough people ask for the same one, the shrine starts stocking it. The pouch is then carried, tied to a bag or a strap, and not opened; opening it loses what is in it. It is customarily swapped for a new one once a year. The old one goes back to the shrine or temple it came from, usually on or just after New Year, and is burnt rather than thrown out, at the Sagichō or Dondoyaki fire held at the Little New Year on 14 or 15 January. Most Shinto shrines will accept another shrine's omamori; many will not accept a Buddhist one, and the reverse holds too.
text.today: Still issued by nearly every shrine and temple in Japan as of 2026, in a spread of categories a buyer picks from: kōtsū-anzen for the road, gakugyō-jōju for exams, shōbai-hanjō for trade, en-musubi for finding a partner, anzan for a safe delivery, kanai-anzen for the household, yaku-yoke against a bad year. Alongside them, shops sell omamori-shaped goods with Mickey Mouse, Hello Kitty, Snoopy or Kewpie on them, issued by no shrine and consecrated by nobody — a separate product that borrows the shape.

etymology.root: Japanese kuji 籤 'lot, drawn slip', with honorific mi- and o-; literally 'the sacred lot'
etymology.note: Kuji carries two senses at once: chance used to make a verdict impartial, and chance used to consult a deity's will. The same word covers drawing straws for an office and asking a kami.

text.what: A narrow strip of printed paper drawn at random from a box at a shrine or temple, for a small offering. It carries a graded verdict at the top — great blessing down to misfortune — then a run of short readings for particular departments of a life: auspicious directions, a wish, a person being waited for, a lost article, travel, business, study, market speculation, disputes, love, moving house, childbirth, illness, a marriage proposal. It is not a charm anybody wears. It is filed in this atlas because of what happens next: a bad slip is folded and tied to a pine branch or to a rack of wire in the grounds, and left behind. The disposal is the charm-act.
text.story:
The dating here is unusually firm for a paper object. A wooden container of oracular lots dated 1409 survives at Tendai-ji in Iwate Prefecture, which puts the method in Japan before the Muromachi period. The system it belongs to was modelled on the Chinese kau chim — a tube of bamboo sticks read against a numbered sequence of printed oracles — and the hundred five-character quatrains used in Japanese Buddhist temples descend from a Southern Song set, the Tiānzhú língqiān.

Those hundred verses are attributed to Ryōgen (912–985), the Tendai monk known posthumously as Ganzan Daishi, and the sequence is called the Ganzan Daishi Hyakusen after him. *Tradition holds —* Avalokiteśvara revealed the verses to him. The attribution itself has a date and an author: Tenkai (1536–1643) is credited with attaching Ryōgen's name to the set, and a story from one of Tenkai's disciples has Ryōgen appear to Tenkai in a dream to reveal that the hundred quatrains, lost for centuries, still existed. Copies duly turned up at Togakushi Shrine in Shinano. The sequence spread through the Edo period into temples of every school, Tendai or not, and publishers put out books explaining what the oracles meant.

The pine is a pun. Matsu 松, pine, is a homophone of matsu 待つ, to wait: tie the bad fortune to the tree and the bad luck waits there instead of following you home. A good fortune can be tied up too, to make it work harder, or kept.

Omikuji still do public work beyond personal fortune. Provincial festivals use the same drawing to pick the tōnin, the person responsible for a coming year's religious duties: names go on slips, and the choice is settled by a ritual strike of a gohei wand.
text.how: Make a small offering, shake or draw from the box, take the slip you get. Read the grade first. The standard Ganzan Daishi sequence runs great blessing (dai-kichi), blessing (kichi), small blessing (shō-kichi), half-blessing (han-kichi), future blessing (sue-kichi), future small blessing (sue-shō-kichi), misfortune (kyō); other sequences add middle blessing, great misfortune, or a grade that says the outcome is still undetermined and depends on what you do. A bad slip is folded and knotted onto a pine or onto the wire racks set up for it. A good one is either tied up as well or pocketed.
text.today: Available at shrines and temples across Japan as of 2026; since 2024 vending machines dispense them in some places. The paper fortune in a Western fortune cookie may descend from this: the claim is made by Seiichi Kito of Fugetsu-Do, and rests on evidence that American fortune cookies derive from nineteenth-century Kyoto crackers called tsujiura senbei.

names.th: องกอน

text.what: Two things under one word. An ongon is a spirit in the shamanic belief of Mongolia — after death, shamans become shamanic souls, ongod — and it is also the made object that stands for that spirit in the physical world, put together by a shaman and central to the ritual that calls on the spirit's protection. Idols can be consecrated to a dead shaman within three years of the death, and are kept in the house, as a home ongon, or out in the open in a shelter, as a field ongon.
text.story:
The objects are described one at a time in the ethnography, and this record keeps them that way. For the Tuvan shamaness Yamaan, an ancestor spirit is represented in the handle of a drum: a carved figure with a pink head and chest, a black crown, and red eyes and forehead, with a wire for arms and, on a second wire, suspended holbogo standing for the spirit's earring.

Some ongod are not made at all but inhabited. Agaaryn Khairhan, a mountain in Khövsgöl Province, carries the name of one of the most powerful shamanesses of the Darkhad clan — Agaaryn Khairhan, also called Bagdan Udgan — who lived on that mountain in the eighteenth century.

Among the Darkhad in present-day Northern Mongolia, clusters of ongod stand in transitional places: the mouths of rivers, the border between taiga and steppe. That border is also a religious one, with the taiga and the mountains the traditional ground of shamanism and the steppe the ground of Buddhism. Many Darkhad households own lineage talismans, yazguur ongod, or household talismans, geriin ongod, which both contain and attract spirits.

The ongon matters most in black shamanism: the main job of the khar talynkh, the black shaman, is to bring people into contact with the ongon, whose spirit they call up while drumming in a trance. Otgony Purev records that in late-nineteenth-century Mongolia yellow shamans revered ongod as well, and that every three years they gathered at Dayan Deerh monastery in Khövsgöl Province to renew these ancestral spirits. Dayan Deerh is itself one of the well-known ongod.
text.how: Made by a shaman, not by a household member, and consecrated to a particular dead shaman. The renewal Purev records for yellow shamans ran on a three-year cycle at a named monastery. This atlas does not print how an ongon is made or what is said over it: the sources read describe particular objects among particular peoples — a Tuvan shamaness's drum handle, Darkhad household talismans — and do not publish a procedure, and neither a Darkhad practice nor a Tuvan one stands in for the other.
text.today: Recorded in the Darkhad Valley of Northern Mongolia in the ethnography of the 2010s, with household and lineage talismans in ordinary houses and clusters of ongod at the edges between taiga and steppe. Morten Axel Pedersen's Not Quite Shamans, 2011, and Ágnes Birtalan's 2011 study of Dayan Deerh are the recent published accounts this record leans on; Dmitry Zelenin's Культ онгонов в Сибири, 1936, is the old one.

names.name: Palad khik
names.th: ปลัดขิก

etymology.root: Thai ปลัดขิก; the phrase is rendered in English as 'honorable surrogate penis' — palad, a deputy or stand-in, and khik
etymology.note: The name states the function: it stands in for the wearer's own, and takes what is aimed at him.

text.what: A carved phallus, from a couple of inches to several feet long, in wood, metal, bone, horn or ivory, usually with sacred inscriptions cut into it. The small ones are worn by men and boys on a cord round the waist, under the clothes, hanging to one side of the wearer's own. Wearing several at once is ordinary. The large ones are not worn at all: they stand in shops, restaurants and other premises, often by the till. Cast metal ones do not always carry the inscriptions; some carry animal figures instead.
text.story:
The form came from India, tied to Shiva, who is represented by the linga; the Cham carried it into Southeast Asia and it stayed. Where the linga is set with a yoni, the pair stands for creation and destruction together, and the Chinese yang is named as the comparable idea. As a phallic representation of Shiva, the palad khik is also an animist fertility sign. In Thailand a penis amulet hanging in a convenience store or a restaurant, or sold by an older woman on the street, is unremarkable.

Who wears one and why is documented, and it is not what the outside write-ups usually make of it. Men wear them for three named reasons: to attract women, for luck in gambling, and for protection from dangerous objects — bullets and knives are the two the source names. Women in Thailand carry one in a purse against rape and mugging. Shopkeepers set one by the cash register to protect the business and to bring in sales.

The rule that tells you what kind of object this is has nothing to do with sex. A palad khik can be taken into places counted as lowly or unclean — a bar, a gambling house, a brothel. An amulet carrying the Buddha cannot. It is the charm you can take where the Buddha may not go, and that, not the shape, is its place in the Thai kit.
text.how: Carved by monks who specialise in the form. Cutting the sacred inscriptions is treated as a rite in itself and can take days. The piece is then empowered by the repetition of incantations Thais call Kata Bucha, from the Sanskrit ghata puja; which kata depends on the maker's lineage and school. Worn on a waist cord under the clothing, off-centre; carried in a bag; or stood by a till. It is not renewed on a cycle and not retired.
text.today: Still carved, still sold, still hanging by tills in Thailand as of the accounts this project has read — and routinely written up abroad as a curiosity, which is a fact about the writers rather than about the charm. This atlas describes it the way the trade does: an object with a stated function, a named maker, a lineage of incantation, and a waist cord.

text_th.what: รูปองคชาตแกะสลัก ยาวตั้งแต่สองสามนิ้วไปจนถึงหลายฟุต ทำจากไม้ โลหะ กระดูก เขาสัตว์ หรืองาช้าง มักมีอักขระศักดิ์สิทธิ์จารไว้ อันเล็กผู้ชายและเด็กผู้ชายสวมกับเชือกคาดเอว ไว้ใต้เสื้อผ้า ห้อยอยู่ข้างใดข้างหนึ่งของอวัยวะจริงของผู้สวม การสวมหลายอันพร้อมกันเป็นเรื่องปกติ อันใหญ่ไม่ได้ใช้สวมเลย แต่ตั้งไว้ในร้านค้า ร้านอาหาร และสถานที่อื่น ๆ มักอยู่ข้างเครื่องเก็บเงิน ปลัดขิกแบบหล่อโลหะไม่ได้มีอักขระเสมอไป บางอันมีรูปสัตว์แทน
text_th.story:
รูปแบบนี้มาจากอินเดีย ผูกอยู่กับพระศิวะ ซึ่งมีศิวลึงค์เป็นสัญลักษณ์ ชาวจามนำเข้ามาในเอเชียตะวันออกเฉียงใต้ และคงอยู่สืบมา ในที่ที่ศิวลึงค์ตั้งอยู่บนโยนี ทั้งคู่หมายถึงการสร้างและการทำลายไปพร้อมกัน และหยางของจีนถูกยกเป็นแนวคิดที่เทียบกันได้ ในฐานะรูปองคชาตแทนพระศิวะ ปลัดขิกยังเป็นเครื่องหมายความอุดมสมบูรณ์ตามคติวิญญาณนิยม (การนับถือผี) ด้วย ในประเทศไทย ปลัดขิกที่แขวนอยู่ในร้านสะดวกซื้อหรือร้านอาหาร หรือที่หญิงสูงวัยขายอยู่ริมถนน ไม่ใช่เรื่องแปลกอะไร

ใครสวมและสวมเพราะอะไรมีบันทึกไว้ และไม่ใช่อย่างที่งานเขียนของคนนอกมักตีความ ผู้ชายสวมด้วยเหตุผลสามข้อที่ระบุไว้: เพื่อดึงดูดผู้หญิง เพื่อโชคในการพนัน และเพื่อคุ้มครองจากของอันตราย — กระสุนและมีดคือสองอย่างที่แหล่งข้อมูลระบุ ผู้หญิงในไทยพกไว้ในกระเป๋าถือเพื่อกันการข่มขืนและการจี้ชิงทรัพย์ เจ้าของร้านตั้งไว้ข้างเครื่องเก็บเงินเพื่อคุ้มครองกิจการและให้ค้าขายดี

กฎที่บอกว่าวัตถุนี้เป็นของประเภทใดไม่เกี่ยวกับเรื่องเพศเลย ปลัดขิกนำเข้าไปในสถานที่ที่ถือว่าต่ำหรือไม่สะอาดได้ — บาร์ บ่อนการพนัน ซ่องโสเภณี พระเครื่องที่เป็นรูปพระพุทธทำเช่นนั้นไม่ได้ ปลัดขิกคือเครื่องรางที่พาไปได้ในที่ที่ไม่อาจนำพระพุทธรูปเข้าไป และสิ่งนั้น ไม่ใช่รูปทรง คือที่ทางของมันในชุดเครื่องรางของคนไทย
text_th.how: แกะโดยพระสงฆ์ที่ชำนาญการสร้างปลัดขิกโดยเฉพาะ การจารอักขระศักดิ์สิทธิ์ถือเป็นพิธีในตัวเองและอาจใช้เวลาหลายวัน จากนั้นจึงปลุกเสกด้วยการสวดคาถาซ้ำ ๆ ที่คนไทยเรียกว่าคาถาบูชา จากคำสันสกฤต ฆฏปูชา (ghata puja) คาถาบทใดขึ้นอยู่กับสายและสำนักของผู้สร้าง สวมกับเชือกคาดเอวใต้เสื้อผ้า เยื้องจากกึ่งกลาง พกไว้ในกระเป๋า หรือตั้งไว้ข้างเครื่องเก็บเงิน ไม่มีการเปลี่ยนใหม่ตามรอบ และไม่มีการปลดระวาง
text_th.today: ตามบันทึกที่โครงการนี้ได้อ่าน ปลัดขิกยังคงถูกแกะ ยังคงถูกขาย และยังคงแขวนอยู่ข้างเครื่องเก็บเงินในประเทศไทย — และมักถูกเขียนถึงในต่างประเทศในฐานะของแปลก ซึ่งเป็นข้อเท็จจริงเกี่ยวกับผู้เขียนมากกว่าเกี่ยวกับเครื่องราง แอตลาสนี้บรรยายมันแบบที่วงการบรรยาย: วัตถุที่มีหน้าที่ระบุไว้ มีผู้สร้างที่มีชื่อ มีสายคาถา และมีเชือกคาดเอว

names.name: Patuá
names.th: ปาตูอา (ถุงเครื่องรางบราซิล)

text.what: A small sewn packet, worn at the neck or carried, closed over whatever was put inside it. The example catalogued by Duke University's Sacred Arts of the Black Atlantic project is 43 by 35 by 11 mm: cloth and blue vinyl, wood pieces, white thread, and a cowrie shell. It is not meant to be opened.
text.story:
Duke's catalogue entry is blunt about what the object is for: "This amulet, called a pátua, used the power of the Brazilian goddess Iemanjá to protect the owner."

The construction is a set of claims stitched into cloth. Iemanjá's name is embroidered in white thread on blue vinyl — her colour — in twenty-one stitches, a number the catalogue says is sacred to her. Wood pieces reference Catholic relics. A Star of David sits on the back. A cowrie is set in, the shell that is both an instrument of divination and, in Candomblé, a body the gods are present in. The entry reads the combination as sacred colour, sacred number, and references that follow the trade routes between West Africa and Brazil.

*Inference —* the Catholic relic and the Star of David on an Iemanjá packet are the record of a religion that spent centuries being illegal and learned to be legible in more than one language at once. This atlas states that as its own reading and not as the catalogue's.

What this record cannot do is tell a reader how a patuá is filled, closed or charged. That happens inside a terreiro, a Candomblé house, under people entitled to do it; this project has read no published account of the procedure that it can cite, and does not fill the gap from a neighbouring tradition. The entry stops here.
text.how: Sewn shut. The Duke example is closed with a counted number of stitches carrying the name of the orixá it belongs to. Beyond that, the making is not described here — see the note above. A patuá is worn under clothing at the neck, or carried in a bag, wallet or car.
text.today: Patuás are made and sold in Brazil, in terreiros and in shops selling to Umbanda and Candomblé practitioners, and are a regular subject of Brazilian religious-goods retail online as of 2026. This project has no dated price and no maker's name for the current trade.

names.name: Pazuzu head
names.th: เศียรปาซูซู

text.what: A head, cast or carved, with a hole or a loop through the top for a cord. The face is the point: gazelle horns, human ears, a dog's muzzle, bulging eyes, wrinkled cheeks. Terracotta is the common material; bronze, iron, gold, glass and bone examples survive too. Some heads were fixed to cylinder seals or worn as brooches; larger stone versions hung on a wall. The full figure, where it appears, has a scaled canine body, two pairs of wings, a scorpion's tail, bird talons, right hand up and left hand down.
text.story:
Pazuzu is a demon employed as a doorman. He is the south-western wind, he carries plague, and the texts that address him call him "Agony of Mankind" and tell him to stay out of the house — and the same culture hung his face over the bed. In the bilingual Compendia he introduces himself: "I am Pazuzu, son of Ḫanbu, king of the evil lilû-demons. I was enraged (in violent motion) against the strong mountains and ascended them."

What he is for is Lamashtu. She snatches babies; he forces her back to the underworld. Ritual texts from Uruk direct that a woman be given a bronze Pazuzu necklace so that Lamashtu cannot make her miscarry; a Late Babylonian incantation against Lamashtu tells the reader to make a Pazuzu necklace and hang it round the afflicted person's neck; an Assyrian ritual text prescribes a Pazuzu head to banish sickness. Franz Wiggermann dates the figure's sudden appearance to the Early Iron Age, with the first images in the eighth century BCE from the tombs at Nimrud, the first texts in the seventh, the bulk of the finds in the seventh and sixth, and the latest under the Seleucids.

One of the large wall amulets was found where it fell. At Dur-Katlimmu, a Neo-Assyrian town, it lay on the floor of the main reception room, facing the entryway it had been hung to watch.

*Inference —* the heads are uniform and there are a great many of them. Eckart Frahm's study finds the appearance barely changes across his history. An object that looks the same everywhere and turns up everywhere was made in quantity by people who were not improvising, which is what the cited scholarship means when it calls the representations mass-produced.

names.th: สายห้อยมือถือ

etymology.root: Japanese 携帯 keitai, 'portable', used on its own for a mobile phone, plus English strap borrowed as ストラップ sutorappu
etymology.note: The Japanese account calls the strap 現代の根付 — the netsuke of the present day, after the carved toggle that anchored a cord to a kimono sash. That is the tradition's own comparison, not this project's.

text.what: A small figure, bead, tassel or brocade pouch on a thin cord, knotted with a lark's head through a hole in a phone or a case. Where a handset has no hole, it goes on a silicone plug pushed into a jack port, a lobster clasp, a circle cotter or a lanyard. The cord is the object; what hangs on the end of it is negotiable.
text.story:
This started as a safety feature and turned into a charm rack, and the sequence is documented.

The Japanese account gives the mechanism first: handsets carried a ストラップホール, a strap hole, and a thin loop was passed through it. One explanation it records for why straps spread in Japan is the Product Liability Law of 1995: carriers told users to put a hand through the strap so the phone would not be dropped. 落下防止 — fall prevention. That is a claim about gravity, and it is the only claim in this record that nobody argues with.

Then the hole filled up. By the late 1990s and early 2000s, hanging ten or more straps at once was a fashion among young people in Japan, to the point where the straps could outweigh the phone. The English account says phone charms "first originated in Japan and later in the United States", and spread from there to the United Kingdom and Ireland. When the iPhone 3GS arrived in 2008 without an attachment slot, a Korean company answered with hanging charms fixed by screws. The British designer Anya Hindmarch put charms into a collection called Pimp Your Phones in 2018.

What gets hung there is the reason this object is in an amulet atlas rather than an accessories one. Omamori — the brocade pouches Japanese shrines and temples issue, with a prayer or an invocation sealed inside and a rule against opening them — are, in the cited account's words, "often spotted on bags, hung on cellphone straps, in cars, etc." The shrine's range is specific about what each is for: kōtsū-anzen for traffic safety, gakugyō-jōju for passing examinations, en-musubi for finding a partner, anzan for a safe delivery, shōbai-hanjō for business. Dazaifu Tenmangū sells a keychain amulet for safe travel and a bracelet amulet, which is the same shift in fastening. *Inference —* a charm designed to be tied to something found a phone waiting with a hole already drilled in it, and the reason there was a hole had nothing to do with the charm.

The argument attached to this object is the usual one and the shrines are on record in it. The cited account notes that when demand outruns what a shrine can make, popular shrines and temples turn to factories, and that "priests have been known to complain about the quality and authenticity of the products made by factories". It also records the other end: generic omamori sold in ordinary Japanese shops with Mickey Mouse, Hello Kitty, Snoopy or Kewpie on them, issued by no shrine and typically not spiritual in nature. That is two named positions, and this atlas reports both and settles neither.

*Inference —* the strap is also the clearest case in this atlas of a charm losing its mounting. The flip phone had a hole; the slab phone mostly does not, and the workarounds — the jack plug, the screw, the case with a loop moulded in — are all later inventions answering the same problem. What happens to a carried charm when the thing it was tied to changes shape is a question this collection will keep meeting.
text.how: Bought at a phone shop, a shrine office, a souvenir counter, a convenience store, or given away with a drink or as promotional merchandise. Attached with a cow-hitch or lark's-head knot through the strap hole, or by whatever adapter the handset forces. An omamori on a strap follows the omamori rules: not opened, replaced about once a year, returned to the shrine it came from to be burnt. A character strap follows no rules at all.
text.today: Still sold in 2026, and still standard on Japanese shrine counters, where the strap format is one of several the same prayer is sold in. No dated price was read for this record, and neither the Japanese nor the English account this project read publishes a market figure.
