names.th: ทามา (แผ่นโลหะถวายของกรีก)

etymology.root: Greek τάμα, plural τάματα — the vow itself, used for the metal thing that carries it
etymology.note: Same move as Spanish milagro, where the word for the miracle becomes the word for the tin leg pinned under the saint. The vow and the object share a name in both languages.

text.what: A small metal plaque, base metal or precious, with an image embossed on it: a heart, an eye, a hand, a leg, a whole kneeling figure, a house, a baby, a ship. A ribbon runs through it. It gets hung on a pole or a hook beside the icon of a saint, and it is left there.
text.story:
Go and stand in front of a much-visited Greek icon and you will not see the icon. You will see silver.

A tama is offered either as a reminder of what the petitioner needs or in thanks for a prayer already answered — the cited account puts both uses on the same object and does not separate them, and the offering is usually made with a prayer and sometimes with a votive candle lit beside it. The shape aims it. A heart may mean a heart condition or it may mean love. Eyes mean an eye affliction. Hands or legs mean maladies of the limbs.

The Spanish-speaking world's milagro is the same object and the atlas says so on that record. Here is what a reader standing on this page gets that the milagro page cannot give: the tama has a named origin story with a hand in it. John of Damascus, serving as vizier to the caliph al-Walid I, was falsely accused of treachery and had his hand cut off. Praying before an icon of the Theotokos, he found the hand restored. In thanks he had a silver replica of it made and fixed it to the icon. That icon, called Trojeručica — the Three-handed — is preserved at Hilandar Monastery on Mount Athos, and it is the reason the story is not just a story: the object it describes is still on the wall.

*Inference —* the difference between the two traditions is where the metal goes, not what it means. A milagro hangs on a robe or a retablo in a Catholic church and also, sometimes, gets carried in a pocket for luck. A tama goes onto the icon, and the icon is not a picture of a saint in Orthodox practice but the place the saint is met. The plaque is therefore pinned to a person, in the tradition's own terms, rather than to a painting of one.

Tamata are not the only thing left. Orthodox Christians also offer candles, prosphora — the bread baked for the liturgy — wine, oil and incense, and many leave something of their own worth instead: jewellery, a pectoral cross, a military decoration. *Inference —* a medal a man was given for war, hung on an icon because a prayer was answered, is the most compressed object in this whole atlas.

They are bought in shops selling Greek Orthodox religious goods, and the practice runs beyond Greece: the cited account records tamata in Italy too, particularly in the south, where they stand next to the Catholic ex-voto trade rather than instead of it.
text.how: Stamped or cast, pierced, threaded with a ribbon, and hung on a pole or a hook by the icon — the hanging done by the petitioner, with a prayer, sometimes with a candle. Nothing consecrates the plaque before it is offered; the offering is the act. They accumulate. What a church does with a wall of them after some years is not described by the sources read here, and this record does not guess.
text.today: Still sold in Greek Orthodox religious-goods shops and still hung on icons in Greece and in southern Italy, and wherever the Greek diaspora has built a church. No dated price was read for this record.

names.name: Ta'wiz
names.said: ta-WEEZ; Arabic taʿwīdh, Urdu and Hindi ta'wiz, Hindi तावीज़
names.th: ตะอ์วีซ

etymology.root: Arabic taʿwīdh, 'amulet' or 'charm', from the verb ʿawwadha, 'to fortify someone with an amulet or incantation'; Urdu and Hindi take the word from the Arabic
etymology.note: In Islamic contexts the object is also called hafiz, protector, or himala, pendant.

text.what: Writing, folded up and worn. A ta'wiz can be a paper packet in a black pouch, a scroll in a tubular pendant case, letters carved into metal, or a framed dua on a wall. The text is Qur'anic verses, names of God, names of prophets and companions, hadith, religious narratives, or duas. In Central and West Asia the packet is often triangular and pinned to a baby's clothes.
text.story:
The trade in these has a documented shape. Texts packaged in ta'wiz were most often pre-made for the public; a literate wearer could change the verse at his own discretion. Scrolls with Qur'anic quotations, prophetic references and sacred symbols were common in war in the Ottoman Empire, carrying verses such as 'victory is from God and conquest is near', Qur'an 61:13, worn in combat.

One of the oldest surviving examples is a printed object, not a written one. Diminutive amulets made in the medieval Mediterranean Islamic world were executed with a block print or die, called tarsh, and folded down small enough for a tiny box or tubular case. The Aga Khan Museum in Toronto holds an Egyptian block-printed amulet of the tenth or eleventh century, ink on paper, 7.2 by 5.5 centimetres; the last line of its text is Qur'an 20:46, "So God will safeguard you from them. He is All-Hearing and All-Knowing". Such text amulets were housed in lead cases stamped with surat al-Ikhlas, with lugs so the packet could be sewn to clothing or hung from the body. The cases were kept sealed, so the printed contents were invisible to an owner who could not afford a handwritten one.

Whether a Muslim should wear one at all is disagreed about, by name, and this atlas reports both sides without joining either. Some hadith condemn the wearing of talismans, and some Muslims, notably Salafis, hold that amulets and talismans are forbidden and that using them is shirk — associating a partner with God. Other hadith support their use, and some denominations count it permissible magic, usually on conditions: that the wearer holds the talisman to help only through God's will. The formulation reported for Sunni practice is that a ta'wiz may be worn as long as it consciously strengthens the wearer's bond with Allah, and not out of a belief that the ta'wiz itself cures or protects. Set against that, virtually all Muslim scholars are described as permitting talismans that invoke God or an intercessor — Muhammad, Ali, the saints — while addressing jinn or demons is prohibited. Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab treated sorcery as one of the few sins carrying a divinely sanctioned death penalty; Muhammad Nasiruddin al-Albani held that those convinced sorcery has effect of its own accord, rather than by God's decision and will, will not enter paradise; the Wahhabi preacher Bilal Philips has tried to draw the line by way of a hadith in which a sura with supernatural properties was recited but not written down and used as a charm.

The numbers are surveyed. A Pew Research Center survey of Muslims worldwide in 2011–2012 found belief in talismans, witchcraft and spiritual healers ranging from about a quarter to a half of Muslims in the Middle East and North Africa, Turkey, South Asia and Southeast Asia — less widespread than belief in jinn. Ta'wiz use is reported at 41 per cent of Muslims in Pakistan and 39 per cent in Albania.

*Tradition holds —* a ta'wiz worn by Hindus often carries the sacred Om symbol instead, which is the plainest evidence in the atlas that the container and the writing can come apart.

names.name: Taweret amulet
names.said: ta-WER-et, from Ancient Egyptian tꜣ-wrt, 'she who is great'; Greek Θουέρις, Thouéris
names.th: เครื่องรางเทพีทาเวเรต

etymology.root: Egyptian tꜣ-wrt, 'she who is great' or simply 'great one' — a pacificatory address, the form of words used to calm a dangerous deity rather than to describe a kind one.
etymology.note: Her sister goddesses are named the same careful way: Ipet, 'the Nurse'; Reret, 'the Sow', from the Egyptian classification of hippopotami as water pigs; Hedjet, 'the White One', whose sense is less clear.

text.what: A hippopotamus standing upright on two legs, with a lion's limbs and paws, a Nile crocodile down her back and tail, human breasts and a pregnant belly. She usually holds the sa sign, the hieroglyph that means 'protection'. She comes as a pendant, as a face on furniture, chairs, stools and headrests, on children's feeding cups, and as a vessel whose spout is a nipple.
text.story:
Egypt made two decisions about hippopotami and kept both. The male was chaos, hunted down by kings to show divine power. The female was the opposite, because she guards her young with everything she has — so the protective goddesses of the household are female hippopotami, and amulets in their likeness are among the oldest in the country. They start before 3000 BCE, in the Predynastic period, and the making and wearing of them runs the whole length of Egyptian history into the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, to about 390 CE.

Her amulet peaks in popularity at the very end. In the Ptolemaic and Roman centuries, when the temples were changing hands and the old state religion was thinning out, household amulets of Taweret and her fellow hippopotamus goddesses sold better than ever.

She worked at both ends of a life. In the Middle Kingdom her image is carved onto a class of curved implement made from hippopotamus ivory that Egyptologists call a wand or a knife; tomb paintings show these in the hands of nurses, and wear on the tips indicates they were used to draw protective patterns in the sand. Taweret is on almost all known wands. The other figures on them are the gods who escort the sun through the underworld at night. At the same time hippopotami decorated with marsh flora were being put in tombs, which Egyptologists read as the same goddess helping a dead person be reborn the way she helped a living one be delivered.

She survived Akhenaten. Objects bearing Taweret were found at Amarna, from a reign, about 1352–1336 BCE, when the worship of the traditional gods was proscribed in favour of the sun disc. *Inference —* what people keep when the state tells them to stop is a good measure of what an object is for, and a birth charm is not easy to give up.

She travelled by trade. Middle Kingdom contact with the Levant carried her into the religions there in the same maternal role. From the Levantine coast she reached Crete, where Minoan artists redrew her in their own style as the figure Aegean archaeologists call the Minoan Genius, and from Crete the image reached the mainland and appears in palace art at Mycenae. Nubia took her into its pantheon in the late Middle Kingdom, and she features in royal rituals at Kerma.

Do not confuse her with Ammit. Ammit is also a composite hippopotamus and she is there to eat the unjust at the weighing; Taweret and her kin nourish and help.
text.how: Moulded or carved as a pendant, cut into furniture, moulded onto feeding cups, and poured from: New Kingdom vessels in her shape are taken to have purified the liquid poured out of them, since one of her epithets is 'She of the Pure Water', and some have their openings through the nipples. The hippopotamus-ivory wands were drawn with, in sand, by the nurse.
text.today: Not made as a birth charm. She is a museum object, a name in Egyptology, and a character in a television series. As of 2026 this project has read no account of anybody in Egypt using a Taweret at a birth.

etymology.root: Mishnaic Hebrew plural of tefillah; Jastrow connects it to Syriac tefiltha, 'attachments' or 'hangings'. In the Hebrew Bible the objects are totafot, 'headband' or 'frontlet', from a reduplicated root ṭ-p-ṭ-p meaning 'to encircle'
etymology.note: The resemblance to Hebrew tefillah, 'prayer', is coincidental. The English word phylactery is from Greek phylaktērion, 'guarded post, safeguard, security', and in later Greek 'amulet' or 'charm' — it enters European languages from its single appearance in Matthew 23, not from anything Jewish usage calls these.
etymology.folk: Rabbi Akiva, in Sanhedrin 4b, read totafot as two foreign words for 'two' — tot in Coptic and fot in 'Afriki' — making 'two and two', for the four compartments of the head tefillah. The cited article calls this an early attempt at etymology.

text.what: Two small black leather boxes with long black straps. The arm box goes on the upper non-dominant arm and its strap winds down the forearm, round the hand and round the middle finger; the head box sits between the eyes at the hairline. Each box is made from a single piece of hide, cubical, on a wider base, with a passage at the back for the strap. On both sides of the head box the letter shin is moulded — with four branches on the wearer's left instead of three. The head strap's knot forms a dalet, the arm strap's a yud; with the shin those three letters spell Shaddai. Inside are parchment scrolls with four Torah passages: Exodus 13:1–10, Exodus 13:11–16, Deuteronomy 6:4–9 and Deuteronomy 11:13–21. Three thousand one hundred and eighty-eight letters, and a scribe can take as long as fifteen hours to write a set.
text.story:
Like the mezuzah, tefillin are a commandment and not an amulet, and the tradition guards that distinction itself. The cited account puts it exactly: tefillin are sometimes mentioned together with amulets in the Talmud because of certain similarities of form, but they are never identified as such — they are specifically differentiated from them. Maimonides counts the arm box and the head box as two separate positive commandments. His account of what they do is about the wearer's mind: as long as they are on the head and the arm of a man, "he is modest and God-fearing and will not be attracted by hilarity or idle talk". The Sefer ha-Chinuch, in the 14th century, adds that they help subjugate worldly desire. Joseph Caro, in the 16th, explains the positions: next to the heart and above the brain, to show both organs willing to serve.

The argument that they are also apotropaic is made, and made by named people. Yehudah B. Cohn argues that tefillin should be read as an invented tradition, aimed at countering the popularity of Greek amulets with a Jewish one. Joshua Trachtenberg took every ornament worn on the body, whatever its declared function, to have begun as an amulet. And the early rabbinic sources are explicit enough on their own: Numbers Rabbah 12:3 has tefillin defeating "a thousand demons" coming up on the left side; rabbis Yohanan and Nahman use their sets to repel the demons of privies; Elisha the Winged, scrupulous in this mitzvah, is saved from Roman persecution. Tefillin are also credited with lengthening life, and are listed in one breath with objects that are amuletic in nature.

So the atlas includes them and states the objection rather than dissolving it. The object is dated: Jews were wearing physical tefillin by at least the first century CE, which is shown by the finds at Qumran and by the reference in Matthew 23. Karaite Judaism reads the commandment as metaphor and does not.

Who wears them is governed. The obligation rests on Jewish males from thirteen; women are exempt, as they are from most time-bound positive commandments, and since Rema in the 16th century the prevalent practice among religious Jews has strongly discouraged women from wearing them. Claims that Rashi's daughters and the wife of Chaim ibn Attar wore tefillin have no historical evidence behind them. In Orthodox practice it remains a male obligation; Conservative women often wrap; SAR High School in Riverdale allowed girls to wrap at morning prayer from 2013, probably the first Modern Orthodox high school in the United States to do so; a Jerusalem District Court judge ruled in 2013 that Women of the Wall wearing tefillin at the Western Wall did not violate 'local custom'; in 2018 students at Hebrew College in Boston made a series of videos teaching female and transgender Jews to wrap.
text.how: Cubical boxes from a single piece of hide, in three grades — peshutim, made with several pieces of parchment forming the inner walls of the head box; dakkot, stretched from one thin piece; and the more durable gassot. Painted black by custom now, though the archaeological finds do not show that this was always so. Straps must be black on the outside and any colour but red inside. The four passages go on one strip in the arm box, which has a single compartment, and on four separate scrolls in the head box, which has four — because the verses name the hand device in the singular and the head device in the plural. Written by a scribe in Ashuri script in one of three lettering styles: Beis Yosef for Ashkenazim, Arizal for Hasidim, Velish for Sefardim. The letters must be written in order; a mistake found later cannot be corrected, because the replacement would be out of sequence, and the set is invalid. Talmudic commentators disagreed on the order of the scrolls: Rashi held to the order the passages appear in the Torah, Rabbeinu Tam switched the last two. Most follow Rashi; some also lay Rabbeinu Tam briefly, a custom of the Ari taken up by Hasidim, many Sephardic communities and some Ashkenazim. The Vilna Gaon, who wore Rashi's, rejected the stringency, pointing out that there are 64 possible arrangements and one cannot put on 64 sets. Worn during Shacharit on weekdays and removed after morning services; Jewish men once wore them all day.
text.today: Worn daily wherever weekday morning prayer is kept, as of 2026. The live question inside the tradition is gender, and it is being answered differently by different communities — see the story above, which names the rulings and the dates.

etymology.root: Japanese teru 照る 'to shine', doubled, + bōzu 坊主 'Buddhist monk' — 'shine, shine, monk'
etymology.note: The doll's head is read as a monk's shaved head, which shines in sun; the name is also the request. A children's rhyme addresses the doll directly as the fine-weather priest.

text.what: A small handmade doll of tissue paper or cloth, white, a ball of stuffing for a head with the cloth falling loose below it and a string tied round the neck. It hangs outside a door or a window, made the day before a day the maker wants dry. Children make them; most Japanese meet one in kindergarten or daycare.
text.story:
The practice came from China and changed sex on the way. In the Chinese version, Saoqing Niang 掃晴娘, the figure is a young girl with a broom, set on the end of a broom to sweep the sky clear; the story attached has a girl ascending to the heavens in a heavy rainfall to sweep the clouds off and save her city, and paper cut-outs of her hung outdoors afterwards in her memory. Japan took the practice up in the Heian period, inside an older weather-watching culture, hiyorimi, that runs with certainty from the Heian period through the Edo.

The Japanese doll seems to come out of the resemblance between origami dolls and the names recorded in mid-Edo literature. The reference this project can name is Kiyū Shōran, written in 1830 by Nobuyo Kitamura, a scholar of Japanese classical literature: "If the weather becomes fine, I write my pupils on the paper, offer sake to the gods, and pour it into the river." Painting in the eyes after the sun comes out, and the libation, and the river — the whole disposal is in that one sentence.

It became popular in the Edo period among city dwellers, whose children made them the day before and chanted, "Fine-weather priest, please let the weather be good tomorrow." A warabe uta released in 1921 fixed the modern version, and children sing it while making the doll. The song is not soft: it promises the doll plenty of sake if the wish comes off, and decapitation if it does not.
text.how: Tissue paper or a scrap of white cloth, gathered over a ball of stuffing, tied at the neck with string, hung from an eave, a window frame or a door on the eve of the day in question. The face is often left blank and drawn on afterwards, when the weather has behaved. If the day comes up fine, a libation of sake is poured over the doll and it is floated away in a river. Hanging one upside down is the reverse request, for rain — a use this project has not read in a cited source and so does not assert here.
text.today: Still made by Japanese children in 2026, taught through the 1921 nursery rhyme. Ikeda in Nagano Prefecture has built its town mascot on the shape.

text.what: A metal disc, brass, copper or bronze, ornamented on one face and polished on the other, worn on a shaman's body. Small ones are sewn onto the deel or the apron in quantity, laid like overlapping scales; large ones hang at the neck and over the chest. Worn together they are armour, and they are described that way.
text.story:
The counts are recorded people by people, and this record keeps them apart. Among the Daur, small toli were set on the costume like overlapping scales, with eight large mirrors and one medium one to protect the heart — the neker-toli, which might be plated in nickel. In Hure Banner, shamans wore nine mirrors, and nine is a number of particular weight in Mongolian religion and mythology. The practice is also recorded among the Buryats in the Republic of Buryatia and among the Tsaatan in Mongolia.

Walther Heissig, documenting shamans in Hure Banner in the 1940s, recorded that the toli held the white horses of the shamans and served as a vehicle for the shaman.

What the mirrors are said to do beyond armour: purify and empower water or vodka; collect and trap hostile spirits; give helper spirits somewhere to live. In Mongolia they are described as vessels for the shaman's spiritual power, the wind horse, and as collecting and storing the power of blessings. A toli also says what its wearer is — the mirrors signify the shaman's authority and role, and how many of them there are is read as a measure of standing.

*Inference —* a polished disc worn at the chest does two jobs at once that this atlas usually finds split between two objects: it faces outward like a door charm and it is worn like a pendant. The Chinese bagua mirror does the first from a wall. This one walks.
text.how: Worn on the costume and at the neck, in numbers. The sources read describe what the mirrors are and what they are for, and do not publish how one is made, charged or passed on; this record stops where they stop and does not borrow a procedure from a neighbouring people.
text.today: Still worn by practising shamans in Mongolia, Buryatia and among the Daur, as the published ethnography describes them; the atlas has not read a survey dated to 2026 and does not claim numbers. Bronze mirrors of this kind also circulate as collectibles, which is a different object with the same shape.

names.name: Agadez cross
names.said: tanaghilt (tanaɣilt), or tasagalt — 'cast in a mould'; the plate-shaped kind is talhakim
names.th: กางเขนอากาเดซ

etymology.root: Tamashek tanaghilt / tasagalt, 'cast in a mould' — the name is a description of the method, not of a shape. Talhakim covers jewellery resembling a plate or a plate shield. Zakkat is the general Tamashek word for pendants; kaulé is widespread across the Sahel.
etymology.note: The European name calls it a cross after the town of Agadez. Only a few of the pieces actually resemble one.

text.what: A cast pendant, usually silver, with a ring or loop at the top and a flared, spreading body below — sometimes a cross, more often a shape between a cross and a shield. Blacksmiths cast it by the lost-wax process and never hammer the metal. The plate-shaped kind, talhakim, is cut from soft stone or from platelets of copper, aluminium or another metal; the tanaghilt is made in stone or copper.
text.story:
This is the best-known category of Saharan Berber jewellery, made especially by the Tuareg of Niger — and its use is narrower than its fame. Current use of tanaghilt and talhakim is restricted to a few Tuareg groups, the Kel Aïr and the Kel Geress, and to non-Berber peoples across Niger who have taken it up: Songhai, Zarma, Fulani, Hausa. Other Tuareg barely use them. Worn as ornaments, the pieces hang at the neck; a tanaghilt is also fixed to a woman's veil or to her forehead, and fixed upside down.

Ask the people wearing them what the shape means and the answers go vague. The source says so flatly: any question about their symbolism put to the users generally elicits only vague answers. Some name it a grigri; some call it a reserve of wealth.

The ethnologists Germaine Dieterlen and Ziedonis Ligers recorded one occasion that does give the object a sentence of its own. A father handed the jewel to his son at the age of virility, marriage and nomadism, and said: "My son, I give you the four directions of the world, because we do not know where you will go to die."

A Tuareg elder's narration gives another origin. A young nomad wanted to declare his love to a girl shut up at home and out of reach. The village blacksmith had an important place in Tuareg society and the right to enter the houses of all the families he traded with, so the young man had a jewel forged that combined the two syllables of the Tamashek word tara, love, written ⵜⵔ in Tifinagh, and sent the blacksmith in with it.

*Tradition holds —* the image may go back to ancient stylised images of the Carthaginian goddess Tanit. The source offers that as a possibility and this atlas leaves it there.
text.how: Cast by a blacksmith in silver by the lost-wax process — a wax model, a mould, the wax melted out, the metal poured in — and never hammered. The stone and platelet kinds are cut. Worn at the neck, or fixed to a woman's veil or forehead, upside down.
text.today: Made and worn, and also the standard thing a visitor to Niger brings home. As of 2026 this project has read no figure for the split between the two, and no source that says Tuareg smiths object to either.

names.name: Tupilaq
names.th: ทูปิลัก

text.what: Two different things share this name, and a reader should hold them apart. The first is what the word originally named in Greenland: an avenging creature assembled by an angakkuq from animal parts — bone, skin, hair, sinew — and, in the accounts, from parts taken from the bodies of children, brought to life by chants and sent into the sea after a named enemy. None survive; they were made in secret, in isolated places, out of materials that rot. The second is the carved figure: a small grotesque cut from sperm whale tooth, and today from narwhal and walrus tusk, wood and caribou antler, a few centimetres high, made to be looked at and bought.
text.story:
The second object exists because of the first. Early European visitors to Greenland were fascinated by the accounts they heard and wanted to see what a tupilaq looked like, so Inuit began carving representations of them out of sperm whale teeth. That carving is now an important part of Greenlandic Inuit art and is prized by collectors. It is a picture of a thing, made for an audience that had asked. That is not the same as the thing.

The first object came with a risk attached. Sending a tupilaq at somebody with greater power than the maker could turn it back on its maker — and the escape from that was public confession of the deed. The published ethnography places this inside a wider Greenlandic logic in which concealment carries magical consequences and confession neutralises them: a concealed miscarriage or infanticide could produce a monster called an anngiaq, a concealed breach of taboo could bring harm on the whole community, and angakkuit resolved a taboo breach by getting the breacher to confess in public. A young hunter's first kill was neutralised the same way, by making every adult share in it.

The word also does not mean the same thing across the Arctic. At Igloolik a tupilaq was an invisible ghost, the restless soul of a dead person whose death taboo had been breached, visible only to the angakkuq, and it drove the game away until the angakkuq scared it off with a knife. Among the Kivallirmiut it was an invisible chimera with a human head and parts of different animals, dangerous to the settlement, which the angakkuq fought and devoured with helping spirits. Among the Copper Inuit, the Inuinnait, tupilak came to mean something close to the Christian devil. Only in Greenland is it primarily a physical, human-made object.

*Inference —* the tupilaq is the clearest case in this atlas of a word that a museum label flattens. A tray of carved tupilait in a gift shop in Nuuk and a sentence in Knud Rasmussen's notebooks are not describing the same category, and the difference is not one of quality.
text.how: The carved figure is cut from tusk, tooth, antler or wood with hand tools and polished; it is signed and sold. How the older object was made is not printed here. See the note below.
text.today: Carved tupilait are made in many shapes and sizes in Greenland from narwhal and walrus tusk, wood and caribou antler, form an important part of Greenlandic Inuit art, and are highly prized as collectibles. This project has read no dated price and names no living carver.

names.name: Tyet
names.th: ทิเยต (เครื่องรางปมอียิปต์)

etymology.root: Egyptian tjt. The sign is usually translated 'welfare' or 'life', which is close to what the ankh means.
etymology.note: It looks like a knot of cloth, and may have started as a bandage used to absorb menstrual blood — which is why one of its names is the blood of Isis.

text.what: A looped knot with two arms hanging down and a tail below — an ankh whose crossbar has drooped. Cut small and laid in the wrappings, usually on the upper torso. Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead calls for one of red jasper at the mummy's neck, and the surviving ones are red jasper, carnelian or red glass, or else green faience, whose colour Egyptologists read as the renewal of life.
text.story:
The sign is older than the goddess it belongs to. An early tyet comes from a First Dynasty tomb at Helwan, dug by Zaki Saad in the 1940s; it predates the first written references to Isis, so at that point it was probably not hers. Later it attaches to her, and to the healing that is a central part of her character.

As an amulet it starts in the early New Kingdom, about 1550 BCE, with the earliest examples in the reign of Amenhotep III. From then to the end of dynastic Egypt, few people were buried without one placed inside the mummy wrappings. That is an unusually strong statement to be able to make about any amulet anywhere: not that it was common, but that its absence was rare.

Chapter 156 gives the words. The red jasper tyet is laid at the neck and the spell says the power of Isis will be the protection of the mummy's body, and that the amulet will drive away whoever would commit a crime against him.

A second knot gets confused with this one. From the Late Period, Egyptian women wore a large knot in a mantle, and because it turns up on Hellenistic and Roman statues of Isis it picked up the name 'Isis knot' — but Robert Bianchi's 1980 paper is titled 'Not the Isis-Knot', and apart from the name the two have nothing to do with each other. Elsewhere the comparison runs the other way: the Minoan sacral knot at Knossos, a knot with a loop projecting from it, is close enough in shape that Egyptologists set the two side by side.
text.how: Cut from red jasper, carnelian or red glass, or moulded in faience, and placed inside the wrappings on the upper torso — Chapter 156 puts it at the neck. Egyptian funerary texts carry spells to be recited over amulets, and this one has its own.
text.today: Not made and not placed. The sign is in Unicode's hieroglyphic block and in every Egyptology textbook, and it sells as jewellery in Cairo and online alongside the ankh and the wedjat. As of 2026 this project has read no account of anyone using one the way Chapter 156 describes.

text_th.what: ปมเป็นห่วง มีแขนสองข้างห้อยลงและมีหางอยู่ด้านล่าง เหมือนอังค์ที่คานขวางห้อยตกลง ตัดเป็นชิ้นเล็กและวางไว้ในผ้าห่อศพ ส่วนใหญ่ที่ลำตัวส่วนบน บทที่ 156 ของคัมภีร์ผู้ตาย (Book of the Dead) กำหนดให้วางชิ้นที่ทำจากแจสเปอร์แดงไว้ที่คอมัมมี่ ชิ้นที่หลงเหลือมาเป็นแจสเปอร์แดง คาร์เนเลียน หรือแก้วสีแดง หรือไม่ก็เฟย็องส์สีเขียว ซึ่งนักอียิปต์วิทยาตีความสีว่าหมายถึงการฟื้นคืนของชีวิต

names.name: Wedjat eye
names.th: ตาเวดจัต (ดวงตาแห่งฮอรัส)

etymology.root: Egyptian wḏꜣt, feminine of wḏꜣ 'whole, sound, uninjured' — the eye after it was healed, not before
etymology.note: Egyptologists pair the left wedjat with the moon and the right with the sun; texts use the two almost interchangeably.

text.what: A stylised human eye with a falcon's cheek-mark curling below it, cut or moulded small enough to string at the throat. Most surviving examples are faience — quartz paste, glazed blue-green in the kiln — and run a few centimetres across. Egypt made more of these than of any other amulet shape, for the living to wear and for the dead to be wrapped in.
text.story:
The eye comes out of a fight. Set tears out Horus's eye; Thoth, or another god, puts it back; Horus gives the restored eye to his dead father Osiris, and the offering keeps Osiris going in the afterlife. That is why the sign stands for an offering as much as for an eye, and why it turns up on temple walls beside the meat and bread.

As an amulet it runs from the Old Kingdom to the Roman period — roughly 2686 BCE to the seventh century CE, which is close to three thousand years of continuous use, and the longest run of any object in this atlas. Coffins of the First Intermediate Period and the Middle Kingdom carry a pair of eyes painted on the side, positioned so the mummy inside could look out through them. Boats carried them on the bows. *Tradition holds —* the eye also travelled: Syria, Canaan and especially Nubia took the sign up from Egypt, and Nubian versions are common enough that a museum tray of them is rarely all Egyptian.

*Inference —* the arithmetic on the shelf is worth stating plainly. An object that was cheap to mould, buried by the thousand, and made of a material that does not rot is an object that survives; the reed, cloth and dough charms that stood beside it did not. What a museum drawer holds is a record of what lasts, not a census of what Egypt wore.
text.how: Moulded in faience or cut from carnelian, lapis, gold or glass, pierced at the top or through the back, and strung. Size was the variable, not the design — the same eye scaled from a bead to a pectoral. In mummification the eye went into the wrappings, and one class of it covered the embalmer's incision.
text.today: Nobody makes a wedjat as a wedjat any more in Egypt's ancient sense; the practice ended with the religion. It is made by the million as jewellery, sold in Cairo, Luxor and every airport shop that sells to Egypt's visitors, and worn worldwide by people with no connection to Osiris. As of 2026 the sign is also standard tattoo flash. Whether the mass-market version is the same object is an argument this atlas reports and does not settle.

names.name: Witch bottle
names.th: ขวดแม่มด

text.what: A stoppered vessel filled with the afflicted person's urine and with sharp iron — pins, needles, nails — then hidden. The earliest documented ones are salt-glazed stoneware Bartmann jugs, also called Bellarmines or Greybeards, brown or grey, embossed with a bearded face; later ones are ordinary glass bottles and small vials. It is not worn and not seen: it goes under the hearth, inside a wall, or into the farthest corner of the property, and it is supposed to stay there.
text.story:
The earliest surviving description is a story about a bird. In 1681 Joseph Glanvill printed it in Saducismus Triumphatus: a Suffolk man tells a travelling old man that his wife has been long in a languishing condition and is haunted by a thing in the shape of a bird that flurrs near her face. The old man tells him to take his wife's urine, cork it in a bottle with pins, needles and nails, and set it to the fire. The cork blows out with a report like a pistol and the wife is no better. The old man comes back and changes the instruction: bottle it the same way and bury it in the earth. She recovers. Then a woman arrives from a town some miles off crying that they have killed her husband, who told her on his deathbed that he was a wizard and had bewitched the man's wife.

That is the logic the whole class runs on. A witch bottle is countermagic: it draws in harm aimed at its owner and holds it. Folk magic contends that the bottle protects against evil spirits and magical attacks and counteracts spells cast by witches. It stays active as long as it stays hidden and unbroken, which is why people took so much trouble over the hiding — bottles buried under fireplaces have turned up only after the rest of the building was pulled down.

The bottles keep being found. In 2016 a glass bottle dug out of the threshold of a Cornish house appeared on Antiques Roadshow, filmed at Trelissick; the glass specialist Andy McConnell tasted a little of the contents and guessed port or wine, noting a rusty flavour and the nails. A 2019 episode gave the laboratory answer: Loughborough University found it contained "urine, a tiny bit of alcohol, and one human hair", along with brass pins dating from the late 1840s, and an ostracod. In 2020 a sixteenth-century jug used against witchcraft was found during the renovation of the De Zwarte Ruiter pub in Turnhout, Belgium — reported as the first witch bottle found in Europe outside England.

In the United States fewer than a dozen possible witch bottles have been identified. The archaeologist Marshall Becker was the first to identify one in an archaeological context: the Essington witch bottle, recovered during excavations on Great Tinicum Island in Delaware County, Pennsylvania. A mid-nineteenth to early twentieth-century slave or tenant site in Dorchester County, Maryland, yielded a buried bottle whose cork stopper bristled with straight pins. In 2016 a bottle filled with nails came out of the hearth of a Civil War site in Virginia.
text.how: A white witch or folk healer prepared it. The historical fill is the victim's urine, hair or nail clippings, or red thread from sprite traps; later bottles take rosemary, needles and pins, and red wine. Other recorded fills include sand, stones, knotted threads, feathers, shells, herbs, flowers, salt, vinegar, oil, coins and ashes; sea water or earth stand in for urine. Then it is corked and buried — at the farthest corner of the property, beneath the hearth, or somewhere inconspicuous indoors. Carriers describe the mechanism: evil is drawn in, impaled on the pins and needles, drowned by the wine, and sent away by the rosemary. One variant is destructive rather than protective: throw the bottle into a fire, and when it explodes the spell is broken.
text.today: Still made. Modern practitioners bottle and bury them, and the historical ones surface at a steady rate during building work in England and, now, Belgium. *Inference —* the finds are a function of demolition as much as of belief: a charm designed never to be found is only counted when a wall comes down.

names.name: Worry stone
names.th: หินคลายกังวล

text.what: A smooth polished gemstone, usually an oval with a thumb-sized dish worn into one face, about 3 centimetres across. It is held between index finger and thumb, and the thumb is moved back and forth across the dish. That motion is the whole of the object's use.
text.story:
There is no single origin claimed for it, and the sources do not pretend otherwise. Variations are traced to ancient Greece, to Tibet, to Ireland and to several Native American peoples; the Greek ones were stones the sea had smoothed, and the concept begins, as the cited account puts it, with the simple act of picking up a smooth stone and fiddling with it. A worry stone is one of the few objects in this atlas that anybody can find on a beach.

What it claims is unusually narrow, and the cited source hedges it in the same breath: the motion "is thought to reduce stress, but there is no conclusive scientific evidence to support this". This atlas does not test that and does not settle it.

Where it is documented most precisely is in a clinic. Writers on cognitive behavioral therapy treat the worry stone as one of a set of folk practices that work as psychologically healthy self-soothing exercises, taught early in treatment to displace familiar but destructive coping habits — nail-biting, scratching, lip-biting — and to ready a patient to face anxiety or trauma safely. The cited account singles out short-term treatment of refugees, where complexity and unfamiliarity are the constraints and a stone is simple and intuitive enough to be useful. Later, once a patient has learned a fuller relaxation script, the stone becomes a reminder of it: the impulse to reach for it is itself the signal that the person is anxious.

*Inference —* that last function is the interesting one for this atlas, because it is the only charm here whose stated job is to tell its carrier something rather than to keep something away. The stone reports.
text.how: Tumbled and polished, or picked up already smooth. Sold in a box with a card, or handed over in a session, or found. There is no consecration, no maker's restriction and no retirement rite. A lost one is replaced.
text.today: Sold worldwide in mineral shops, gift shops, pharmacies and therapy-supply catalogues, and given out in clinical settings. The stones are the same stones the crystal trade sells, which means the same sourcing questions attach to them; that argument is set out on the crystal pendant record and is not repeated here.

names.name: Yantra plate
names.th: แผ่นยันต์ (ยันตระ)

etymology.root: Sanskrit yantrá, from the root yam 'to sustain, support' with the instrument suffix -tra: literally a machine or contraption
etymology.first_attested: Rigvedic Sanskrit, in the sense of an instrument for restraining or fastening — a prop, a support, a barrier
etymology.note: The literal sense survives in Sushruta's medical vocabulary, where a yantra is a blunt surgical instrument such as tweezers or a vice. The sense of a mystical or occult diagram arises in the medieval period, in the Kathasaritsagara and the Pancharatra.

text.what: A geometric diagram, drawn on paper, painted, or engraved into a sheet of metal, and usually smaller and less coloured than a mandala. Shapes radiate from a centre point, the bindu: triangles, hexagrams, circles, lotus petals numbering anything from two to a thousand, and an outer square standing for the four directions, often with a doorway cut in each side. Sanskrit mantras are written into the design. A downward triangle is read as Shakti and an upward one as Shiva; white, red and black stand for the three gunas — sattva, rajas and tamas. Plates are hung on a wall, set under a lamp or a vessel, or carried.
text.story:
Yantras belong mainly to the Tantric traditions of the Indian religions, and are used for worship in temples and at home, as an aid to meditation, and — the reason they are in this atlas — as charms. Gudrun Bühnemann sorts them into three by use: yantras laid under a ritual implement such as a lamp or a vessel; yantras used in regular worship, the Sri Yantra among them, energised with mantras and often carrying written mantras in the design; and yantras made for a specific desire-driven rite, which are often drawn on birch bark or paper and can carry flowers, rice paste or ashes.

How old the form is depends on who is asked, and the source read here does not settle it. Representations of the yantra in India have been claimed to go back 11,000 to 10,000 BCE. G. R. Sharma, who excavated it, considered the Baghor stone the earliest example — a triangular stone with triangular engravings on one side, found daubed in ochre at what was read as a worship site in the Son River Valley, in an Upper Paleolithic context dated to 25,000–20,000 BCE. Kenoyer, also on the excavation, associated it with Shakti, and the triangle resembles the Kali Yantra and the Muladhara Chakra. Against that, the word's occult sense is medieval. *Inference —* a triangle scratched on a Paleolithic stone and a Tantric diagram consecrated with a seed syllable are separated by a gap this record cannot bridge with the sources it has, so it reports both claims and dates neither.

The Sri Chakra, which represents the goddess Tripura Sundari and includes Shiva as well, is the best-known form. The largest ever drawn covered 67,400 square feet on the ground at Cranbury, New Jersey, under the guidance of Guru Karunamaya.
text.how: Drawn, then woken. Yantras are traditionally consecrated and energised by a priest, using the mantras tied to that deity and that diagram; practitioners hold that a yantra not energised with a mantra is lifeless. Colour is not decoration — each colour denotes an idea or an inner state, and texts disagree about which colours belong to which yantra. As a talisman a yantra is treated as standing in for a deity who can be called on at will. In Sri Lankan Buddhism, practitioners are required to keep the yantra of the deity with them once the deity has shown acceptance of their prayer.
text.today: Engraved copper plates and printed paper sheets sell across India and Nepal, in temple shops and online, and the Sivali yantra, used mainly in Southeast Asian Buddhism, is bought for wealth and good luck. Designers now depart from the patterns in the older texts, and designers in the West copy elements from Nepali and Tantric imitations rather than from the texts — which is an argument about what a yantra is, running inside the tradition and outside it at once.

text_th.what: แผนภาพเรขาคณิตที่วาดบนกระดาษ ระบายสี หรือสลักลงบนแผ่นโลหะ มักเล็กกว่าและมีสีน้อยกว่ามณฑล (mandala) รูปทรงต่าง ๆ แผ่ออกจากจุดศูนย์กลางที่เรียกว่า พินทุ (bindu): สามเหลี่ยม รูปดาวหกแฉก วงกลม กลีบบัวตั้งแต่สองกลีบไปจนถึงพันกลีบ และกรอบสี่เหลี่ยมด้านนอกที่แทนสี่ทิศ มักมีช่องประตูเจาะไว้ทุกด้าน มีมนต์ภาษาสันสกฤตเขียนอยู่ในลวดลาย สามเหลี่ยมคว่ำอ่านความหมายว่าเป็นพระศักติ และสามเหลี่ยมหงายว่าเป็นพระศิวะ สีขาว แดง และดำ แทนคุณะทั้งสาม — สัตตวะ รชัส และตมัส แผ่นยันต์ใช้แขวนบนผนัง วางไว้ใต้ตะเกียงหรือภาชนะ หรือพกติดตัว
text_th.story:
ยันตระส่วนใหญ่เป็นของธรรมเนียมตันตระในศาสนาของอินเดีย ใช้บูชาในเทวาลัยและที่บ้าน ใช้เป็นเครื่องช่วยในการทำสมาธิ และ — ซึ่งเป็นเหตุที่อยู่ในแอตลาสนี้ — ใช้เป็นเครื่องราง กุดรุน บึห์เนอมันน์ (Gudrun Bühnemann) แบ่งยันตระออกเป็นสามประเภทตามการใช้: ยันตระที่วางไว้ใต้เครื่องใช้ในพิธี เช่นตะเกียงหรือภาชนะ ยันตระที่ใช้ในการบูชาเป็นประจำ ซึ่งรวมถึงศรียันตระ ที่ได้รับพลังจากมนต์และมักมีมนต์เขียนอยู่ในลวดลาย และยันตระที่ทำขึ้นสำหรับพิธีเฉพาะที่มุ่งให้สมความปรารถนา ซึ่งมักวาดบนเปลือกต้นเบิร์ชหรือกระดาษ และอาจมีดอกไม้ แป้งข้าว หรือเถ้าอยู่ด้วย

รูปแบบนี้เก่าแก่เพียงใดขึ้นอยู่กับว่าถามใคร และแหล่งข้อมูลที่อ่านในที่นี้ไม่ได้ตัดสินเรื่องนี้ มีการอ้างว่าภาพแทนยันตระในอินเดียย้อนไปถึง 11,000 ถึง 10,000 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. จี. อาร์. ชาร์มา (G. R. Sharma) ผู้ขุดค้น ถือว่าศิลาบาโฆร์ (Baghor stone) เป็นตัวอย่างที่เก่าที่สุด — เป็นหินรูปสามเหลี่ยมที่มีรอยสลักรูปสามเหลี่ยมด้านหนึ่ง พบโดยมีดินเทศ (ochre) ป้ายอยู่ ณ จุดที่ตีความว่าเป็นที่บูชา ในหุบเขาแม่น้ำโสน (Son River) ในบริบทยุคหินเก่าตอนปลาย ที่กำหนดอายุไว้ 25,000–20,000 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. เคโนเยอร์ (Kenoyer) ซึ่งอยู่ในการขุดค้นด้วย เชื่อมโยงศิลานี้กับพระศักติ และสามเหลี่ยมนั้นคล้ายกาลียันตระและมูลาธารจักร ในอีกด้านหนึ่ง ความหมายทางเวทมนตร์ของคำนี้เป็นของยุคกลาง *ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* สามเหลี่ยมที่ขีดไว้บนหินยุคหินเก่า กับแผนภาพตันตระที่ปลุกเสกด้วยพีชาขระ (พยางค์เมล็ดพันธุ์) ห่างกันด้วยช่องว่างที่บันทึกนี้เชื่อมไม่ได้ด้วยแหล่งข้อมูลที่มีอยู่ จึงรายงานทั้งสองข้ออ้าง และไม่ระบุอายุให้ทั้งสองอย่าง

ศรีจักระ ซึ่งแทนพระแม่ตรีปุรสุนทรี และรวมพระศิวะไว้ด้วย เป็นรูปแบบที่รู้จักกันดีที่สุด ศรีจักระที่ใหญ่ที่สุดเท่าที่เคยวาดมีพื้นที่ 67,400 ตารางฟุต บนพื้นดินที่แครนเบอรี (Cranbury) รัฐนิวเจอร์ซีย์ ภายใต้การแนะนำของคุรุ การุณามยะ (Guru Karunamaya)
text_th.how: วาดก่อน แล้วปลุกให้ตื่น ตามธรรมเนียม ยันตระได้รับการปลุกเสกและเสริมพลังโดยนักบวช ด้วยมนต์ที่ผูกกับเทพองค์นั้นและแผนภาพนั้น ผู้ปฏิบัติถือว่ายันตระที่ไม่ได้รับพลังจากมนต์นั้นไร้ชีวิต สีไม่ใช่การตกแต่ง — แต่ละสีบ่งบอกความคิดหรือสภาวะภายใน และตำราต่าง ๆ เห็นไม่ตรงกันว่าสีใดเป็นของยันตระใด ในฐานะเครื่องราง ยันตระถูกปฏิบัติเสมือนเป็นตัวแทนของเทพที่เรียกหาได้ตามต้องการ ในพุทธศาสนาแบบศรีลังกา ผู้ปฏิบัติต้องเก็บยันตระของเทพไว้กับตัว เมื่อเทพองค์นั้นแสดงว่ารับคำอธิษฐานของเขาแล้ว
text_th.today: แผ่นทองแดงสลักและแผ่นกระดาษพิมพ์มีขายทั่วอินเดียและเนปาล ทั้งในร้านค้าของเทวาลัยและทางออนไลน์ และยันต์พระสีวลี ซึ่งใช้มากในพุทธศาสนาในเอเชียตะวันออกเฉียงใต้ มีผู้เช่าบูชาเพื่อความมั่งคั่งและโชคลาภ ผู้ออกแบบในปัจจุบันเบี่ยงออกจากแบบแผนในตำราเก่า และผู้ออกแบบในโลกตะวันตกลอกองค์ประกอบมาจากของเลียนแบบแบบเนปาลและแบบตันตระ แทนที่จะลอกจากตำรา — ซึ่งเป็นข้อถกเถียงว่ายันตระคืออะไร ที่เกิดขึ้นทั้งภายในและภายนอกธรรมเนียมไปพร้อมกัน

th_fields.etymology.root: สันสกฤต ยนฺตฺร (yantrá) จากรากศัพท์ ยมฺ (yam) 'ค้ำจุน รองรับ' กับปัจจัยบอกเครื่องมือ -ตฺร (-tra): ตามตัวอักษรคือเครื่องจักรหรือกลไก
th_fields.etymology.first_attested: ภาษาสันสกฤตสมัยฤคเวท ในความหมายเครื่องมือสำหรับยึดรั้งหรือผูกมัด — ไม้ค้ำ สิ่งรองรับ สิ่งกีดขวาง
th_fields.etymology.note: ความหมายตามตัวอักษรยังคงอยู่ในศัพท์การแพทย์ของสุศรุตะ (Sushruta) ซึ่งยันตระหมายถึงเครื่องมือผ่าตัดชนิดไม่มีคม เช่น แหนบหรือปากกาจับ ความหมายว่าแผนภาพลึกลับหรือทางไสยศาสตร์เกิดขึ้นในสมัยกลาง ในกถาสริตสาคร (Kathasaritsagara) และปัญจราตระ (Pancharatra)
th_fields.dating.period: ประเพณีตันตระสมัยกลางจนถึงปัจจุบัน ข้ออ้างว่าย้อนไปถึงยุคหินเก่ายังเป็นที่โต้แย้ง
th_fields.dating.note: ข้ออ้างสามข้ออยู่ในแหล่งข้อมูลเดียวกัน และประสานกันไม่ได้จากแหล่งนั้น: ความหมายทางไสยศาสตร์ของคำนี้เป็นของสมัยกลาง มีการอ้างว่าภาพแทนย้อนไปถึง 11,000–10,000 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. และ จี. อาร์. ชาร์มา (G. R. Sharma) กำหนดอายุหินบาฆอร์ (Baghor) ซึ่งเขาถือว่าเป็นตัวอย่างเก่าที่สุด ไว้ที่ 25,000–20,000 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. การใส่ข้อที่เก่าที่สุดลงในเส้นเวลาจะเป็นการบอกสิ่งที่หลักฐานไม่ได้บอก บันทึกนี้จึงไม่มีปี
th_fields.object.made_by: วาดโดยผู้ปฏิบัติหรือโรงงาน ปลุกเสกโดยนักบวชด้วยมนตร์ของเทพองค์นั้น
th_fields.object.inscription: มนตร์ของเทพองค์นั้น เป็นภาษาสันสกฤต วางอยู่ภายในรูปเรขาคณิต
th_fields.object.note: เปลือกต้นเบิร์ชเป็นวัสดุรองรับอีกอย่างที่แหล่งข้อมูลระบุ สำหรับพิธีที่มุ่งผลตามความปรารถนา และไม่มีหมวดในรายการวัสดุของแอตลาสนี้ ไม่ได้ให้ขนาดไว้ เพราะรูปแบบนี้ย่อขยายได้ตั้งแต่จี้ห้อยคอไปจนถึงผืนพื้น
th_fields.object.colour: ขาว · แดง · ดำ
th_fields.against.0.who: บทสรุปของแหล่งข้อมูลเรื่องยันตระทางไสยศาสตร์ ซึ่งระบุการขับไล่ผีไว้ในบรรดาการใช้งาน
th_fields.against.1.who: บทสรุปเดียวกัน ซึ่งระบุการแพทย์เชิงป้องกันไว้
th_fields.against.2.who: ผู้ใช้ยันตระทางไสยศาสตร์ ซึ่งใช้เป็นเครื่องรางนำโชคและป้องกันสิ่งชั่วร้าย
th_fields.against.3.who: ผู้เช่าบูชายันต์พระสีวลี ซึ่งใช้ในพระพุทธศาสนาในเอเชียตะวันออกเฉียงใต้เป็นหลัก เพื่อเรียกทรัพย์และโชคลาภ
th_fields.confusable_with.0.tell: ถ้าอยู่บนผิวหนังก็คือสักยันต์ ส่วนแผ่นยันต์คือลวดลายตระกูลเดียวกันบนโลหะ กระดาษ หรือเปลือกไม้

dating.period: medieval Tantric traditions to the present; a Paleolithic claim is disputed
dating.label: undated here — see the note
dating.note: Three claims sit in one source and cannot be reconciled from it: the occult sense of the word is medieval; representations are claimed back to 11,000–10,000 BCE; and G. R. Sharma dated the Baghor stone, which he considered the earliest example, to 25,000–20,000 BCE. Putting the earliest of those on the timeline would say something the evidence does not, so this record carries no years.

object.inscription: the mantras of the deity, in Sanskrit, set inside the geometry
object.note: Birch bark is the other support named in the source, for desire-driven rites, and has no key in this atlas's materials list. No measurement is given because the form scales from a pendant to a floor.

users of occult yantras, for whom they serve as good luck charms and to ward off evil
buyers of the Sivali yantra, used mainly in Southeast Asian Buddhism for the attraction of wealth and good luck

kin.as: the word, from a Sanskrit term for a machine, and the road it took to mean a drawn sign

kin.as_th: ธรรมเนียมที่ปลุกเสกแผ่นยันต์ และตัดสินว่าใครทำได้

kin.as: the step that makes it work at all, in the practitioners' own account: unenergised, they say, the diagram is lifeless
kin.as_th: ขั้นตอนที่ทำให้มันทำงานได้เลย ตามคำบอกเล่าของผู้ปฏิบัติเอง: หากไม่ได้รับพลัง พวกเขาว่าแผนภาพนั้นไร้ชีวิต

kin.as: the making itself — the mantra written into the geometry rather than beside it
kin.as_th: การสร้างเอง — มนต์ที่เขียนลงไปในเรขาคณิต ไม่ใช่เขียนไว้ข้าง ๆ

kin.as: the Himalayan neighbour — a printed deity diagram folded and wrapped in thread rather than hung flat
kin.as_th: เพื่อนบ้านในหิมาลัย — แผนภาพเทพที่พิมพ์ขึ้น พับและพันด้วยด้าย แทนที่จะแขวนแบน ๆ

kin.as_th: แผ่นรวมแบบที่ช่างสักใช้เป็นต้นแบบ ซึ่งคือแผนภาพเหล่านี้ที่วาดขึ้นสำหรับผิวหนัง

etymology.root: Quechua illa, a term for the small carved stone figures used in herding and household rites; colonial Spanish sources call them conopa or canopa, and Quechua-speaking herding communities also say inqaychu and enqa
etymology.note: The variants are not synonyms for one object. The atlas keeps them as a family of related terms and does not flatten them.

text.what: A practice of making the small thing stand for the large one. Its oldest form is the illa: a carved stone llama or alpaca, palm-sized, with a cylindrical hole sunk into the back between the shoulders — a container, fed with a mixture and then set in a pasture. Its most visible modern form is the Alasitas fair, where people buy miniature houses, cars, banknotes, tools and diplomas to give to somebody else, on the understanding that the full-size version follows within the year.
text.story:
The Dallas Museum of Art's Inca camelid vessel, made between 1400 and 1540, is the object this record is named from. Dana Olesch, writing for the museum in 2017, describes what the hole was for: Inca religious leaders likely inserted a mixture of llama fat, blood and other ceremonial objects into it during fertility rituals. The aim was pastoral and agricultural fertility, and several Inca-related groups ended the rite by placing the illa in a pasture. Olesch records that highland communities in the Andes still use illa in fertility rituals for their camelid herds.

The second half of the practice is a fair with a date on it. Alasitas runs for a month from 24 January in La Paz, honouring Ekeko, the Aymara god of abundance, and takes its name from the Aymara for 'buy from me'. Its pre-Columbian ancestor, according to the account, is an Aymara event called Guyatt, at which people prayed for good crops and exchanged basic goods; Arthur Posnansky observed that in the Tiwanaku culture, around 22 December, the population worshipped their deities for good luck by offering miniatures of what they wished to have. The colonial move is dated precisely: during the 1781 siege of La Paz, Sebastián Segurola re-established the celebration and shifted it from October to 24 January, as a gesture of gratitude to Our Lady of Peace. Transactions were made with stone coins; the cult of Ekeko was slowly reintroduced, appearing first modelled in clay, and cast in plaster now.

The figure himself carries the logic on his body: Ekeko is a moustached man in Andean dress, loaded with bags and baskets of grain and food, household objects and currency notes, and modern statues have a circular opening in the mouth so that a lit cigarette can be put in as an offering. Banknotes are clipped to him. Grain is offered for good harvests. He is placed in a good spot in the house.

The calendar is shared with the Church and both sides turn up. At midday on 24 January the Catholic Church blesses the gifts at the main cathedral in La Paz; before or after that, men and, less often, women acting as shaman bless the miniatures at the fair. In March 2011 Bolivia's Minister of Cultures, Elizabeth Salguero, nominated Alasitas to UNESCO alongside two other Bolivian festivals. In 2016 the Feast of Alasita and the miniatures of the Puno Altiplano were declared Cultural Heritage of the Nation of Peru.

*Inference —* the practice is the atlas's clearest case of buying being the rite rather than the preliminary to it. In most traditions here, purchase is how you acquire an object that a separate act then charges. At Alasitas the transaction is the ritual gesture: you buy the small thing, you give it away, and the claim is lodged. The illa says the same in the other direction — the object is fed and buried rather than worn, so the charm is a deposit and never an ornament.
text.how: For the illa: a figure is carved from hard stone with a cavity in the back, a mixture is put in, and it is set in the pasture the herd walks over. For Alasitas: a miniature is bought from a stall, blessed — by a person acting as shaman at the fair, by the Church at the cathedral at midday on 24 January, or by both — and given to somebody else. For Ekeko: the figure is placed in a good spot at home and fed. Banknotes go on him; grain is offered for harvests; a lit cigarette goes in the mouth of the versions built to take one, in the most recent form of the practice once a year.
text.today: Live, urban, and on two heritage registers. Alasitas fills streets and parks across central La Paz with smaller fairs in the neighbourhoods; other Bolivian fiestas fold alasitas into their own observances, including the feasts of the Virgin of Copacabana and the Virgin of Urkupiña; in Peru the main Ekeko festival is held on 3 May at Puno, on the Machallata hill, and elsewhere the Ekeko fair falls in October under the name Calvario. The Mercado de las Brujas on Calle Linares in La Paz supplies the year-round trade, with roughly 60 per cent of its sales falling in October, when Pachamama offerings cluster.

restricted.note: Two limits are stated rather than assumed. names.name: Bakongo nkisi craft
names.said: the maker is an nganga, plural banganga; the object is an nkisi, plural minkisi
names.th: งานสร้างนคิซีของชาวบาคองโก

text.what: The practice, among the Bakongo of the Congo Basin and the Songye of Kasai, of assembling containers that a spirit inhabits. The maker is an nganga: a healer, diviner and mediator. The container is an nkisi: a pot, a gourd, a horn, a shell, a bundle, a carved figure — or a grave, since the dead are what the practice draws on. The substances inside are bilongo. Everything else follows from those four words.
text.story:
Close communication with ancestors, and confidence in what they can do, is what minkisi are for. Among the peoples of the Congo Basin, exceptional human powers are held to come from some kind of communication with the dead, and banganga are the people who do that communicating — working as healers, diviners and mediators, defending the living against harmful workings and supplying remedies against sicknesses caused either by those workings or by the demands of the bakisi, the spirits who are emissaries from the land of the dead.

The substances are chosen by metaphor, not by pharmacy. Wyatt MacGaffey's correction is the one this record follows: bilongo is usually translated 'medicine', but they are not applied to the sick or swallowed, so 'therapeutic substances' is closer. Bird claws to catch a wrongdoer. Fruit, charcoal, mushrooms. Minerals from places associated with the dead — grave earth, riverbed earth. White clay, because white carries dead skin, moral rightness and spiritual positivity against the black of negativity; red ochre where the powers of the dead are being mediated. Many minkisi contain earth or relics from the grave of a powerful person as a prime ingredient, which is why the objects have been described as portable graves.

The practice sorts itself. Minkisi and the afflictions that go with them are classed 'of the above' and 'of the below'. The above are the sky, rain and thunderstorms, counted masculine, tied to violence and violent forces, used to maintain order, serve justice and seal treaties; their motifs are birds of prey, lightning, weapons, fire, and they affect the upper body, so head, neck and chest pains are attributed to them. The below are the earth and the waters on land. Some figures are animals — most often dogs, kozo, sometimes carved with two heads, because a dog lives in two worlds at once, the village of the living and the forest of the dead. Na monanga minkisi are made carefully, with tranquil expressions, and are associated with a powerful person of great reasoning who brings happiness and fortune; npezo figures are made to look menacing and their power is held to be weakened by laughter. Personal minkisi are anonymous and kept in a private house; community ones are placed to be seen, often overlooking the village, though kept in their own enclosure by day.

The word is old in writing and older in use. Its earliest attestations are in Kikongo dialects in the early seventeenth century, transliterated into Dutch as mokissie; Dutch visitors to Loango used it in 1668 for both the object and the spirit in it; when Kongo converted in the sixteenth century, the Kikongo Catechism of 1624 used ukisi to translate 'holy'.

The practice crossed the Atlantic. Aspects of Kongo spirituality reached the Americas with the slave trade, and Hoodoo and Palo carry them; the art historian Robert Farris Thompson has been the influential identifier of Kongo elements in African-descended populations of the Americas. The Kikongo word mooyo, the cavity in an nkisi where charged items sit, is where the American word mojo comes from. Archaeologists working at the African Burial Ground in Lower Manhattan found Kongo-related material — minkisi and nkisi bundles — buried with African remains.

The objects left. Collectors wanted the nailed figures as soon as the German Loango expedition published them in the 1870s; Robert Visser, a German trader and diplomat, supplied Berlin and Stuttgart. Many were purchased, others confiscated or removed by colonial authorities, and often found their way to museums, while many also remain in private hands. Where they should be now is an argument with names attached: the 2018 Report on the Restitution of African Cultural Heritage by Felwine Sarr and Bénédicte Savoy, which moved the debate onto moral rather than only legal ground; the Royal Museum for Central Africa in Belgium, holding more than 180,000 objects mainly from the former Belgian Congo and rebuilt around decolonisation; the Pitt Rivers Museum's four tenets of provenance, transparency, repatriation and redress, and its 2020 Restitution of Knowledge project with Savoy and colleagues at Technische Universität Berlin; and the British Museum, which has consistently refused to return objects, citing the British Museum Act 1963.

*Inference —* the European word for these objects came out of Portuguese traders on the West African coast in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and was applied to Central African things from outside. This atlas treats it as a term with a history, filed under fetish-word, and does not use it to describe what an nganga makes.
text.how: The nganga gathers the bilongo and assembles them, most often into a carved figure with a cavity cut for them at the belly, the head, or in pouches at the neck, closed with a resin-fixed mirror. He then either becomes possessed by the spirit or leaves the object in a graveyard or another place spirits frequent. Nkondi are often composed at the edge of the village, on the reasoning that a village, like a body, must have its entrances guarded; the nganga works isolated in a hidden camp and comes back covered in paint and behaving strangely. Before use he recites invocations to wake the nkondi. Banganga paint themselves for performances — white circles around the eyes to see past the physical world, white stripes on participants — dress unlike anyone else, wear ornate jewellery and work knots into their clothing, knots being tied to closing up or sealing spiritual forces.
text.today: Contested, and split three ways: Kongo communities, museum stores in Europe and North America, and private hands. Artists have taken the form up — Renee Stout, Tania Bruguera, Kara Walker, Dread Scott, Karen Seneferu, Wesley Clark, Stephanie Dinkins, Michael MacGarry, Andrew Lamprecht, Justin Par. The Republic of the Congo painter Trigo Piula made a New Fetish series against what he called the rebuffing of traditional objects, and described the work as "a way of engaging with my community and a way of denouncing things that I believe are impacting us, like television for example". As of 2026 this project has read no count of how many minkisi are held outside Central Africa, and no source dating an end to the practice inside it.

restricted.note: This record prints no bilongo recipe and no invocation. Both belong to the nganga, and the tradition's own arrangement puts them out of sight: the nganga assembles and charges the object isolated in a hidden camp, away from the village, and learns its proper use and its songs before bringing it back. What is printed here is the class of substances, the reasoning that selects them, and what Kongo testimony says the nails and the mirrors are for.

etymology.root: Latin sacramentalia, the plural of sacramentale, from sacramentum — the word used for the seven sacraments, which these objects and rites deliberately resemble without being.
etymology.note: The Church's own vocabulary separates two things this atlas tends to run together: a sacramental is a sacred sign, a ritual act or a ceremony; rosary beads, scapulars, medals and religious images are, in the Church's words, more accurately termed devotional articles.

text.what: The class of blessed objects and rites the Catholic Church puts around the sacraments: holy water, blessed candles given out at Candlemas, blessed palms, blessed ashes, blessed salt, a crucifix, a cross necklace, a headcovering, holy cards, a scapular, a medal. The Catechism sorts sacramentals into three kinds — blessings, consecrations and dedications, and exorcisms. They are also recognised, in their own forms, by the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches, the Church of the East, the Lutheran churches, the Old Catholic Church, the Anglican churches and Independent Catholic churches.
text.story:
This is the one tradition in this atlas that has published a boundary against being in it, and the boundary is the record.

The Church's own definition: sacramentals are "sacred signs which bear a resemblance to the sacraments: they signify effects, particularly of a spiritual nature, which are obtained through the Church's intercession." The machinery is deliberately different from the sacraments'. Sacramentals do not confer the grace of the Holy Spirit the way the sacraments do; by the Church's prayer they prepare a person to receive grace and dispose them to cooperate with it. Unlike the seven sacraments, which the Church holds were instituted by Christ, sacramentals were instituted by the Church, which can change their form and number; and they do not act ex opere operato, by the working of the work, but ex opere operantis, by the working of the one who does it. The Catechism puts the distinction in an example: the water of baptism causes the forgiveness of sins within the sacramental celebration, while holy water, which recalls baptism, has no effect in itself and depends on the faith of the person who crosses themselves with it at the church door.

That is the line. On the other side of it, in the same Catechism, comes the condemnation. Paragraph 2111 defines its terms — "Superstition is the deviation of religious feeling and of the practices this feeling imposes" — and says that attributing a magical importance to otherwise lawful practices, or crediting the efficacy of prayers to their external performance apart from the interior dispositions they require, falls under it. Paragraph 2117 is blunter: after condemning magic and sorcery as gravely contrary to the virtue of religion, it adds four words — "Wearing charms is also reprehensible."

And on the third side there is what people do. The Miraculous Medal was distributed by the Daughters of Charity during a cholera pandemic and passed a billion copies within fifty years. Saint Christopher medals are sold with the promise printed on them in French and Spanish. The Agnus Dei, a papal wax disc, was carried against storm, pestilence, fire, flood and the dangers of childbirth. The Brown Scapular carries a promise of salvation to those who wear it piously. The 2004 Enchiridion Indulgentiarum grants a partial indulgence to the faithful who use a crucifix or cross, a crown, a scapular, or a medal blessed by a priest — so the Church attaches a benefit to wearing the object, by its own procedure, in the same book of rules that says wearing charms is reprehensible.

The distinction the Church draws is between an object that disposes a wearer toward grace and an object worked to compel a result. This atlas prints that distinction, prints the condemnation, prints the promise, and prints what a driver with a medal on the dashboard says the medal is for. It does not rule on which of them is describing the same object.

names.name: Fulu — Taoist talismanic craft
names.th: ฝูลู่ (ศาสตร์ยันต์เต๋า)

etymology.root: Chinese fu (符), instructions for deities and spirits, symbols for exorcism, and recipes for potions or charms; lu (籙), a register of priestly membership listing the skills a priest is trained in
etymology.note: The compound names both halves of the craft at once: the writing, and the licence to do the writing. Two different characters are romanised fu in this atlas — 符, the talisman, and 福, good fortune, the one pasted upside down at New Year. They are unrelated words.

text.what: Writing that is not meant to be read. Fulu are Taoist talismanic characters — strokes that resemble Chinese characters, often an existing word elongated, with non-character symbols worked in, sometimes two characters stacked into one — painted or written on paper, cloth or metal by a Taoist priest. The same craft supplies the charm coins, the mirror that hangs over a doorway, and the New Year slips pasted on a door.
text.story:
The unreadability is the point, and its own scholars say so. Yang Zhaohua notes that a number of the earliest Taoist talismans were simple and legible, and that later examples became deliberately cryptic in order to signal their divinity. James Robson and Gil Raz hold that the incomprehensibility of the written forms is central to a talisman's perceived authority and is one of talismanic script's defining features. Ge Zhaoguang of Fudan University calls it a linguistic archaism, a veil of unfathomable otherworldliness designed so that only a small number of qualified clergy can produce them.

That had already settled by the Eastern Jin (317–420). Ge Hong wrote in the Baopuzi that successful use of a talisman did not depend on whether the user could decipher the script, so long as the inscription itself was right. By then illegibility was a sign of divine authority rather than a defect.

Style varies by sect, and so does everything else: the characters differ from sect to sect, each sect has its own incantations and its own mudras for making them, and even the invocations used for a single deity vary between sects. The method of writing is passed in secret from a Taoist priest to their disciples and treated as a craft for communicating with local deities and spirits. The fulu pai — the informal grouping of priests across schools who work this way — take their name from it.

The medical strand has an institutional history. Talismanic technique has been used in China alongside medicine, meditation, acupuncture, astrology and massage, at least as far back as the Eastern Han, when the Way of the Taiping used it to heal. In medical writing it is called zhuyou, and it held official support between the Sui and the late Ming, declining after rival acupuncture practices were recognised by the imperial court as a medical discipline in the sixth century. Traditional Chinese medicine rejects zhuyou; Chinese folk healers still use it widely; and with the arrival of Western psychology in the 20th century it began to be read as a Chinese counterpart to hypnosis.

The craft also travelled, and two other traditions in this atlas are downstream of it. Fulu were incorporated into Chinese Buddhism; they inspired Japan's ofuda, by way of Onmyodo; and Korea's bujeok comes out of the same stock. Coin talismans carry fulu at the beginning and the end of the inscription, and many of them have not been deciphered — one specimen has talismanic script written beside Chinese characters suspected to be its gloss.

The household end of it is a different character and a different logic. Fu (福), good fortune, is mounted on doorways at Chinese New Year, printed on a square of red paper or stitched in fabric, and hung upside down: in nearly all varieties of Chinese the words for 'upside-down' and 'to arrive' are homophones, so an inverted fu reads as 'good luck arrives'. The practice dates to at least the Song dynasty and the account describes it as universal among Chinese people regardless of income.
text.how: Structure only, because the making is transmitted in secret. A priest of a particular sect writes the characters, using that sect's forms, incantations and mudras, on paper, cloth or metal. The result is displayed, carried, burnt, or — in the medical use — dissolved or otherwise administered. A lu, a register, records which priests hold which skills, so the entitlement to write one is a matter of record inside the tradition rather than of talent. Coin charms carry the script cast into metal instead of brushed, with fulu opening and closing the inscription.
text.today: Live in Taiwan, mainland China and the Chinese diaspora, in temples and in folk healing. Popular accounts of fulu are published for general readers, including by Taiwanese temple-culture sites, while the sect-specific forms stay inside the sects. The New Year fu on a red square is everywhere Chinese New Year is kept. Museum and numismatic collections hold large runs of charm coins whose inscriptions remain unread, which is the tradition's own design working on its own evidence.

names.name: Egyptian amulet craft
names.th: งานเครื่องรางอียิปต์โบราณ

text.what: The practice of making, wearing and burying small protective objects in ancient Egypt: shapes cut from stone or moulded in faience — quartz paste glazed blue or green in a kiln — pierced and strung, worn in life and packed into the wrappings at death. It ran for roughly three thousand years, produced amulets by the million, and is the single largest body of amulet evidence anywhere on earth.
text.story:
Egypt's amulets come in two economies and the same workshops served both.

The living wore them strung at the neck. The dead were wrapped in them, by rule. What went where was not a matter of taste: the funerary texts say which amulet goes on which part of the body, which stone it should be cut from, and what is to be recited over it. Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead asks for a tyet of red jasper at the mummy's neck. Chapter 30B goes on a heart scarab laid over the heart. A gold djed at the neck comes with a spell that promises the mummy the use of its spine back. That is an unusual thing for an amulet tradition to have: a manual.

The material made the scale possible. Faience is cheap, mouldable and does not rot, so a single mould turns out eyes and beetles and ankhs by the tray, and three thousand years later they are all still there. *Inference —* that is also the tradition's largest distortion. The reed, cloth, dough and wax charms that stood beside the faience ones are gone; what survives is what survives, and a museum drawer is a record of durability, not a census of what Egypt wore.

The shapes are hieroglyphs. An amulet cut in the form of a sign was meant to hand its wearer the quality the sign wrote: life for the ankh, stability for the djed, soundness for the wedjat, protection for the sa that Taweret holds. Composites run several signs together — ankh and was and djed, 'life, dominion and stability' — and were worn more often than the ankh on its own.

Not all of it was writing. Bes and Taweret are household gods with faces and bodies, moulded onto baby bottles, chairs, headrests and jars, and worn on the thigh as tattoos. The cippi are slabs you rinse and drink from. The scarab was an office seal as well as a charm.

The practice ended with the religion that needed it. Nothing in Egypt is now made to do what Chapter 156 describes. The shapes went on: the ankh survived into Coptic Christianity as the crux ansata, the wedjat into a worldwide jewellery trade, and Bes and Taweret into museum cases and fiction.
text.how: Moulded in faience or cut from stone — carnelian, lapis, green jasper, steatite fired hard — then pierced and strung, or set in gold. For the dead, placed by the embalmers at the position the funerary text specifies, with the spell recited over it. For the living, worn at the neck or the wrist, or set on a swivel ring.
text.today: Archaeological. The tradition is studied rather than practised, and the objects are concentrated in a handful of museums: the British Museum, the Metropolitan Museum's Egyptian galleries, the Petrie Museum of Egyptian Archaeology in London, the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. Flinders Petrie's excavation and sorting of amulets into classes is still the framework museums label by. The modern trade in Egyptian-shaped jewellery, sold in Cairo, Luxor and the airports and worn worldwide, is a separate thing and is described on the object records rather than here.
