names.name: Ethiopian scroll craft
names.said: the maker is a dabtara, däbtära
names.th: งานคัมภีร์ม้วนเอธิโอเปีย

text.what: The making of painted parchment scrolls by dabtaras — unordained clerics of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church — for named people, cut to their height, written in Ge'ez, and read aloud to them by someone who can read it. The craft sits beside the church without being inside its orders.
text.story:
The dabtara is the whole tradition in one job description. He is a liturgical specialist who has gone past memorising the Psalms into courses in poetry, liturgy and writing. In Ethiopia the power to write includes the power to write prayers and spells, so the same word carries a second sense.

The scroll is made for one person and stands in for them. An animal, usually a goat or a sheep, is sacrificed as a substitute for the patron; the patron is rubbed by and bathed in its contents; the hide is soaked for days, dried, stretched, then scraped, washed and dried into parchment. The dabtara writes on it and paints it, and it is cut to the same height as the person it is for, though it may be made longer. A larger one hangs on a wall instead.

The writing is Ge'ez, the church's liturgical language, and the texts combine Christian prayers invoking saints and the Trinity with mystical names of God and with incantations. Because few speak Ge'ez, the scroll does not work by being owned: a third party literate in Ge'ez must read it to the afflicted person for its properties to take effect. *Inference —* that requirement is rare in this atlas. Most charms are worn and forgotten; this one needs a second human being in the room every time it is used.

The painted signs are their own vocabulary: crosses, eight-pointed stars, the gätsä säb'e — a face inside an eight-pointed star — and eyes, in geometric pairs, rimmed in red. The palette is fixed at six colours: black, white, red, blue, green, yellow.

What the scrolls are for runs from the trivial to the lethal — the range published is bed bugs, home intruders, smallpox — and they treat the spiritual cause while homeopathic medicines are used for the physical symptoms. In the historical manuscript record, most were made for conditions of women's reproductive health.

The earliest surviving scrolls are sixteenth-century. The practice is held to go back to the tenth, which is five hundred years this project cannot put an object behind.
text.how: Sacrifice, then parchment, then writing, then reading. The animal stands in for the patron; the hide becomes the surface; the dabtara writes the prayers and paints the figures; the finished scroll is rolled, kept, and read aloud in Ge'ez when it is needed.
text.today: Living. Scrolls are still made and still commissioned, and they are also collected: the Metropolitan Museum of Art holds several, and the Museum of Witchcraft and Magic in Boscastle publishes an example in Ge'ez on vellum. As of 2026 this project has read no figure for how many dabtaras work, or for what a scroll costs.

names.name: European folk apotropaic craft
names.said: ap-oh-TROH-pay-ik, from Greek apotrepo, 'to turn away'
names.th: ศาสตร์เครื่องรางกันภัยพื้นบ้านยุโรป

etymology.root: The label is Greek — apotrepo, 'to turn away' — and it is a scholar's word, not a carrier's. English speakers inside the practice said ward, charm, luck.
etymology.note: Nobody nailing a horseshoe to a barn in Somerset called it apotropaic. The word arrives with the collectors in the 1890s and is applied backwards.

text.what: Protective objects made and kept by European households outside the church's list: iron over a door, a bottle in a hearth, a shoe in a wall, rowan bound with red thread, a cross of rushes in the rafters, a bead against a look. No priesthood, no manual, no initiation. The maker is whoever needs the thing — a farmer, a mother, a blacksmith, a child gathering rushes on 31 January — and most of it is made at home from what the house already holds.
text.story:
Start at the threshold, because the tradition does. Doorways and windows were held to be where harm gets in, and the answer went on them: grotesque faces cut over oven and kiln doors, gargoyles and sheela na gigs and hunky punks on churches and castles, a horseshoe nailed above a door, an iron knife buried under the entrance, a lantern cut from a turnip or a swede at Samhain. Everything else in this record is a variation on a guarded opening.

Iron carries most of the load. Cold iron is recorded across Britain, Ireland and Scandinavia as repelling, containing or harming ghosts, fairies and witches — hence the horseshoe on the door, hence the iron fence round a graveyard, said to hold the dead in rather than keep anything out. The horseshoe is where the tradition's internal disagreements become visible. Points up so the luck does not fall out; points down so it pours onto whoever stands beneath; in some tellings either is fine so long as the shoe was used, was found rather than bought, and can be touched. Where luck attaches to the owner and not the hanger, a stolen or borrowed shoe carries it back to the owner. One reputed origin is the story of St Dunstan, a blacksmith who became Archbishop of Canterbury in 959, nailing a shoe to the Devil's hoof and removing it only on a promise never to enter a house with one over the door.

The calendar does the rest. On 31 January Irish families gathered rushes; that night the head of the household supervised the weaving of Brigid's crosses; on 1 February they went up in the dwelling, the outhouses and the stables, and a year later they were taken down and burnt or buried, burial preferred because of Brigid's link to agriculture. The practice is first attested in the 17th century and was in decline by the 20th, partly because house renovations left nowhere to hang them. That is an unusually complete account of a folk object: a start date, a decline, and a building-trade reason for it.

*Inference —* the thing that makes this a tradition rather than a pile of customs is the absence of a gate. Every other tradition in this atlas restricts something — a script, a lineage, an initiation, a clan. This one's objects are made by the person who needs them, from rushes, rowan, a worn shoe, a bottle from the kitchen, a stone with a hole in it. That is why its evidence is so lopsided: what survives is what got walled in or thrown down a well, and what was said over it was almost never written.

It was assembled as a subject late, and by three men buying. Frederick Elworthy published The Evil Eye in 1895 and Horns of Honour in 1900, buying in Spain and Italy as he wrote. Siegfried Seligmann, a German ophthalmologist, put out the two volumes of Der böse Blick und Verwandtes in 1910 and gathered more than 1,500 amulets doing it. Edward Lovett, a bank cashier in the City of London, collected what Londoners were carrying in their pockets — a mole's foot, a dried frog, a blue bead, a caul — and published Magic in Modern London in 1925. *Inference —* the shape of every museum case of European charms follows the shape of those three men's buying, and so, to a degree this atlas cannot measure, does the shape of this record.
text.how: Made at home, from the house's own materials, usually at a fixed point in the year or at a moment of threat. Rushes woven on the eve of a feast; rowan cut and bound with red thread; a bottle filled and put under the hearth when the house was built or when somebody suspected a neighbour; a worn shoe pushed into a chimney breast during building work; a horseshoe found in a lane and nailed up. Renewal is annual where the object is vegetable and never where it is iron. Retirement is by fire or by burial, and the choice between them is itself traditional — Irish practice preferred burying a year-old Brigid's cross to burning it.
text.today: Alive and mostly unremarked. Horseshoes still go over doors, four-leaf clovers are still looked for, amber necklaces are still sold for teething in Europe and warned against by the American Academy of Pediatrics and the FDA, and Bulgarian martenitsi still go up on 1 March. The objects have largely left the farm for the souvenir shelf, and workshops like those on Via San Gregorio Armeno in Naples supply both at once. Whether a cornicello bought in a Naples lane by a visitor is the same object as one worn by the seller is a live argument with named people on both sides, and this atlas reports it on the object records rather than settling it here.

dating.label: 1308 to now, on dated objects
dating.note: 1308 is the earliest dated object any European record in this atlas carries — the shoes behind choir stalls installed at Winchester Cathedral that year. It is a floor, not an origin: the practice is plainly older, and Europe's ancient layer is filed under greco-roman-apotropaic rather than here. Written attestation clusters much later — St Brigid's crosses first attested in the 17th century, witch bottles from the 16th, hex signs from the early 19th.

object.made_by: anybody. This is the tradition's defining fact and the reason it has no restricted block: the sources describe householders, farmers, blacksmiths and children making these things, and name no gate.
object.note: There is no single object. Form and materials here are the commonest cases across the European records in this atlas.

etymology.root: Ancient Greek ἀποτρέπω, apotrépō, 'to turn away' — the whole theory of the practice in one verb
etymology.note: The Greeks had a shelf of words for these objects: apotropaia, probaskania, periammata, periapta, profylaktika, phylaktiria, antipharmaca, alexicaca, alexipharmaca, alexima pharmaca. They also gave gods the epithet Alexicacus, 'averter of evil' — Zeus, Apollo, Heracles and Leucothea among them.

text.what: A practice organised around one idea: harm arrives through a look, so the answer is to catch the look. The Greek word for it is apotrépō, to turn away. The objects are the ones that do the catching — a Gorgon face, a phallus, a bead, a crescent, a locket on a child — and the argument in the sources is about what makes a glance stop, not about what a charm contains.
text.story:
The Greeks committed the child to kourotrophic deities and hung amulets on it. They put charms in houses and wore them against the evil eye, and hung them on their animals too. Peisistratus hung the figure of a kind of grasshopper before the Acropolis of Athens. They spat into the folds of their clothes. They dressed boys as girls to avert the eye, and told the story of Achilles dressed as a girl at the court of Lycomedes as a case of it. Exaggerated eyes were painted on the drinking cups called kylikes from the sixth century BCE to the end of the classical period, perhaps to stop anything entering the mouth while drinking; fishing boats in parts of the Mediterranean still have eyes on the bows.

Rome added laughter to terror. In Roman art, envy was thought to bring bad luck to the person envied, so hosts set out images meant to make guests laugh: outsized phalluses, deformities, hunchbacks, pygmies. Pliny called the phallus a medicus invidiae, a remedy for envy. The mechanism the sources describe is not power but interruption — in most cases what turns the eye is the shame or the laughter the obscenity produces.

The literate end of the practice is the gemstones and the lead. Carved gems, many thousands of them, pair a stone with a god so the wearer takes on the associated powers; one gold amulet box from the Thetford treasure in Norfolk was found to contain sulphur, for its evil-repelling qualities. And the same hands that cut gems scratched curse tablets, which run the machinery backwards and aim it at a named person.

*Inference —* the substitutions are the argument. Illyrians used the phallus, the hand, the leg and animal teeth against the same harm the eye was used against; Romans used a winged phallus; southern Italy still cuts a horn. Nothing about a horn resembles an eye. What they share is that each of them takes a glance.

names.name: Kavacha — the Hindu armour tradition
names.th: กวจะ (เกราะคุ้มครองในคติฮินดู)

etymology.root: Sanskrit kavaca, 'armour, coat of mail'
etymology.note: Monier-Williams gives the same word three ways: armour; "an amulet, a charm, a mystical syllable (such as hum, or hūm) forming part of a Mantra used as an amulet"; and "a piece of bark or birch-leaf or any substance inscribed with mystical words and carried about as an amulet". Apte's dictionary gives the charm sense as a preservative like armour. The word covers the hymn and the object it is written on without distinguishing them.

text.what: A family of practice in which protection is armour, said or worn. A kavacha is first a hymn that covers the body part by part, naming a deity for each; it is also the written text carried on the person, and by extension the whole class of South Asian objects worn or hung because a text, a horoscope or a household rule says to. Its objects are a seed bead, nine graded stones, a diagram engraved on copper, a cylinder of folded paper on a thread, and a lime with seven chillies at a doorstep.
text.story:
The armour is a recitation before it is a thing. The Devi Kavacham runs to 61 slokas and sits in the Markandeya Purana; it is one of the subsidiary texts recited before the Devi Mahatmya, and what it claims is exactly the shape of armour — that the Kavacham protects the reader in all parts of the body, in all places and in all difficulties. The Devi Mahatmya is generally dated 400 to 600 CE, around 550 by Wendy Doniger O'Flaherty, and before the seventh century on the evidence of the Dadhimati Mata inscription of 608 CE.

The word then walks out of the text and onto the body. In Tantric practice kavaca is one of the six limbs into which a deity's mantra is divided, alongside the heart, the head and the topknot — the armour syllable. In the Pancharatra, the Jñānāmṛtasārasaṃhita speaks of amulets, kavaca, worn as a necklace and holding mantras. Monier-Williams records the object plainly: bark, birch-leaf or any substance inscribed with mystical words and carried about. The Jain Jñānārṇava, of the eleventh century, keeps the metaphor without the object: like the hero well-clad in armour, who is not pierced by arrows.

*Inference —* that is why this atlas files a seed, a ring, a plate and a lime under one head. They do not share a material, a maker or a price. They share a grammar: something is put between a person and what is coming, and a named authority — a text, an astrologer, a priest, a mother — says which something.

The authorities differ by object, and so does who may act. A yantra is consecrated and energised by a priest with the mantras of its deity, and practitioners hold that an unenergised one is lifeless. A navaratna is prescribed from a sidereal horoscope, and the tradition says to consult an astrologer before wearing one. A rudraksha needs nobody: it is strung and worn, and the texts promise merit rather than permission. The lime and chillies at a shop door need nobody either, and are hung by whoever opens the shop.

The tradition also borrows. A tawiz worn by Hindus often carries the Om sign instead of a Qur'anic verse — the Islamic container with the writing changed.
text.how: Recited, prescribed, consecrated, or simply hung. At the formal end, a priest energises the object with the mantra of a deity and the object stands in for that deity; at the astrological end, a specialist reads a chart and names a stone and its weight; at the household end, nobody is consulted at all.
text.today: Live at every level as of 2026: temple shops selling engraved copper plates and printed yantras, jewellers cutting navaratna to an astrologer's list, seed malas grown as a crop in Nepal and India, and limes and chillies at shop doors from Delhi to Karachi.

names.name: Islamic talismanic craft
names.said: tilasm, plural talasim; the object is also called hafiz, 'protector', and himala, 'pendant'

etymology.root: Arabic ṭilasm, from ancient Greek telesma, 'completion, religious rite, payment', from teleō, 'I complete, perform a rite'; French talisman carried it into English
etymology.note: The English word was lifted out of this tradition's vocabulary, which is why the atlas files the word under talisman-word and the practice here.

text.what: Writing, worn. The tradition makes protective objects out of text — Qur'anic verses, the ninety-nine names of God, names of angels and prophets, pious phrases, invocations — set on paper, parchment, metal, cloth or a bowl, and carried, folded, sewn in, hung or drunk off. The vehicle varies by region: a folded packet in a pouch on a Cairo child's shoulder, a rolled sheet in a silver tube on an Omani necklace, a whole inscribed shirt under a Mughal or Ottoman coat, a magic square engraved on a ring. One rule holds across all of it and the tradition states it out loud: the text calls on God, or on an intercessor the tradition recognises. It does not address jinn.
text.story:
The scale is not marginal. Belief and practice in magic in Islam has been described by scholars of the subject as widespread and pervasive, and as a vital element of everyday life and practice, historically and now. Sixty-six Qur'anic verses are reported to bear on the subject, and the Qur'an describes magic in a negative light — but does not forbid it or prescribe a punishment for it. Three suras carry protective use in the tradition's own account: al-Falaq (113), used as a prayer to God against black magic and, per hadith literature, revealed to Muhammad to protect him against Jann, the ancestor of the jinn; al-Fatiha (1) and an-Nas (114), held to generate barakah, blessing. Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse at al-Baqara 2:255, is the verse the tradition names as the verse of protection, and it is the one written on amulets more than any other.

The craft has a history with dates in it. Until the ninth century, talismans often reflect pre-Islamic artistry. From the 12th century, for reasons the scholarship does not settle, pre-Islamic designs drop out in favour of the pentagram, the Seal of Solomon and zodiacal signs — and above all the wafq, the magic square. The earliest are 3×3 squares of the numerals 1 to 9 summing to 15 in every line, a square the tradition associated with the four archangels; 6×6 squares are attested by the late tenth century but do not enter the magical vocabulary until the thirteenth. Thabit ibn Qurra, the tenth-century Abbasid mathematician, was treated as the authority: 'The noblest part of astronomy is the science of talismans.' Talismanic shirts survive only from the 15th century, though the tradition is held to predate them.

The argument about whether any of this is permitted is internal, old, live, and conducted by name. This atlas reports it and joins neither side. Tobias Nünlist's summary is that Muslim writers generally distinguished licit from illicit practice rather than condemning the field. Virtually all Muslim scholars are described as permitting a talisman that invokes God or an intercessor — Muhammad, Ali, the saints — while addressing jinn or demons is prohibited as shirk, associating a partner with God. Hadith allow magic for healing so long as it contains no act of shirk. Ahmad ibn Hanbal (780–855) refrained from condemning those who used it to heal. Ibn al-Nadim (932–995) conceded white magic and condemned black, tracing the licit back to Solomon and the illicit to Iblis. Ibn Khaldun separated karamat, miracles, as gifts of God from sihr worked by a person's own psychic power.

On the other side stand scholars who denied the whole thing had any reality. The Hanafi jurist Abu Bakr al-Jassas argued that if magic worked its practitioners would be rich and powerful rather than poor men working a market crowd. The Mu'tazilite rationalists held it to be image-making without reality. Al-Jahiz offered psychological explanations for encounters with jinn. And the modern hard line is named too: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab treated sorcery as one of the few sins carrying a divinely sanctioned death penalty; Muhammad Nasiruddin al-Albani held that those convinced sorcery has effect of its own accord, rather than by God's decision, will not enter paradise; Salafi authorities hold that amulets are forbidden outright and that wearing one is shirk.

Remke Kruk's fieldwork is where the two sides meet on a stall. She found the handbooks and the pamphlets attacking them sold side by side in North African markets, and recorded how fine the line has become: contacting jinn in an exorcism to threaten them is acceptable, asking their help in a healing is shirk; dissolving Qur'anic text written on paper in water is forbidden, while writing in a bowl with ink the poured water washes off is recommended by the conservative cleric Wahid 'Abd al-Salam Bali. Kruk's own stated worry is that the rise of stricter forms of Islam has produced an attack on healing practices that used to be well integrated into Islamic life. Set against that, a Pew Research Center survey of Muslims worldwide in 2011–2012 found belief in talismans, witchcraft and spiritual healers running from roughly a quarter to a half of Muslims across the Middle East and North Africa, Turkey, South Asia and Southeast Asia.

The argument has a body count in some jurisdictions and this record states that without editorial. Saudi Arabia formalised an Anti-Witchcraft Unit in 2009; in Makkah region alone that year at least 118 people were charged with practising magic or with using the book of God in a derogatory manner, and by 2011 the unit had nine bureaus and had processed at least 586 cases. Human rights workers allege the accused are often foreign domestic workers practising folk medicine from home.
text.how: Structure only, which is as far as this atlas goes. A text is chosen — a verse, a name, a square, a combination of letters. It is written by a person the client trusts to write it, in Arabic script, on paper, parchment, metal, cloth or the inside of a bowl. Where it is a packet it is folded small, sealed into a case of lead, silver or leather, and hung, pinned to a child's clothes or sewn into a garment. Where it is a bowl or a shirt it is used rather than worn hidden. Cheap ones were made at scale early: block-printed paper amulets, tarsh, are attested in the medieval Mediterranean Islamic world, sealed into cases so the contents stayed unread. The letter-and-number work that generates some of the texts is ʿilm al-ḥurūf, the science of letters, and the branch called jafr; this record names the technique and prints none of it.
text.today: Live everywhere the tradition is, and arguing with itself in print. Handbooks are on market stalls in Marrakesh and Khan el-Khalili with the pamphlets against them alongside; Salafi authorities rule against the objects by name; Pew's 2011–2012 survey found belief in talismans, witchcraft and spiritual healers running from a quarter to a half of Muslims across the regions it covered, and its 2012 figures put belief in the evil eye in the majority in 20 of the 39 countries surveyed. Museum holdings run from a 10th- or 11th-century block-printed Egyptian sheet to Ottoman and Safavid talismanic shirts. Nothing in this record should be read as this atlas taking a view on whether a Muslim should wear one; both sides are named above, and the naming is the whole of the project's contribution.

restricted.note: This tradition restricts material, and the atlas prints the restriction instead of the detail. Two lines are involved. The first is the tradition's own doctrinal one: a talisman may invoke God, angels, prophets or saints, and addressing jinn or demons is prohibited — so a formula that does the prohibited thing is not published here, and neither is a formula that does the permitted thing, because the ones in circulation are the property of the practitioners who write them. The second is the letter-and-number science, ʿilm al-ḥurūf and jafr, which this record names and does not demonstrate. No square is filled in, no name-combination is worked, no consecration wording is given. That is a deliberate blank; the reason is above it.
restricted.who_says: the tradition's own rule as reported in the cited account — virtually all Muslim scholars permit talismans evoking God or an intercessor, while it is prohibited to address jinn or demons — and the standing scholarly dispute about the objects themselves, with Salafi authorities holding that they are forbidden altogether

dating.label: block-printed amulets from the 10th century; the practice older, the argument continuous
dating.note: from_year is the earliest dated object this atlas has read a description of — a block-printed Egyptian paper amulet of the tenth or eleventh century. The cited accounts describe the practice as running from early Islam and say pre-Islamic artistry persisted in talismans until the ninth century, so the object date is a floor, not an origin.

object.made_by: a person trained to write the text: in North and West Africa a marabout; elsewhere a scholar, a healer, a shopkeeper selling pre-made packets, or the wearer if literate. A literate wearer could change the verse at his own discretion.
object.inscription: Qur'anic verses — Ayat al-Kursi above all — the ninety-nine names of God, names of angels and prophets, pious phrases, invocations, and the wafq or magic square
object.note: No measurement is given here; the one published dimension this atlas has read belongs to a single object and sits on the taweez record.

etymology.root: Japanese engi (縁起), an omen or an auspicious origin, plus mono (物), a thing — 'a thing of good omen'
etymology.note: Japanese Wikipedia's definition is functional rather than theological: engimono are objects prepared in order to pray that good things will happen.

text.what: Objects bought at a shrine, a temple or a fair to bring a named good thing: a brocade pouch for traffic safety, a paper or wooden tablet for the household altar, a red papier-mâché doll with blank eyes, a ceramic cat with a raised paw, a bamboo rake for raking in fortune, a folded paper fortune tied to a rack. Japanese Wikipedia's list runs across harvest, trade, household safety, health, long life, marital harmony and the turning-away of misfortune. Most are sold on an approach road, in a temple precinct or in the town outside the gate, and most are replaced once a year.
text.story:
The tradition is distinctive for being administered. Ofuda — the tablet for the household altar — descend from the Taoist lingfu by way of Onmyodo, and from woodblock-printed Buddhist texts and images made by temples since the Nara and Heian periods. In the medieval period the three Kumano shrines in Wakayama stamped their paper talismans with stylised crows and called them Kumano Goofu; those sheets were used for oath-taking and contract-drafting, with the terms written on the blank side.

The national distribution system is dated at every step. The shinsatsu most shrines now issue are modelled on the Ise talisman, the Jingu Taima, which began as purification wands handed out across the country by the oshi, the wandering preachers attached to Ise, as a sign that prayers had been performed on a household's behalf. Distribution of these began in the Muromachi period and peaked in the Edo: a document of 1777 indicates that eighty-nine to ninety per cent of all households in the country owned an Ise talisman. In 1871 an imperial decree abolished the oshi and moved production to the shrine's administrative offices; in 1900 a new Department of Priests took it over; in 1927 it passed to the National Association of Shinto Priests, and after the Second World War to the Association of Shinto Shrines, which distributes Jingu Taima to affiliated shrines to this day. Very few charm traditions anywhere can be traced through four changes of administrative owner.

The market is the other half. Sensō-ji granted the shops that became the Nakamise permission to trade on its main approach in 1685, in exchange for their charging local residents for sweeping the grounds — a temple licensing a shopping street and taking maintenance labour as rent. The daruma has its own annual fair: Takasaki's daruma-ichi at Shorinzan draws, on the city's own figure, over 400,000 people from across the Kanto Plain to buy the year's dolls, and Takasaki produces 80 per cent of Japan's daruma. The doll itself came out of a production problem. The charms the Daruma-dera's founder drew were good for one year, so parishioners needed new ones annually; the ninth priest, Togaku, solved the demand by cutting wooden block moulds around the beginning of the Meiwa period (1764–72) and letting the peasants make their own papier-mâché charms. Most of those households were silk farmers, a crop the account describes as needing a great deal of luck.

The beckoning cat is dated from the other end, by pictures. The earliest figurine record is the marushime-neko, an Imado ware variant of the late Edo period; the Bukō nenpyō chronicle of Edo has an entry dated 1852, and Utagawa Hiroshige's ukiyo-e Joruri-machi Hanka no zu, painted the same year, shows marushime-neko being sold at Sensō-ji. A newspaper mentioned them in 1876; a 1902 advertisement shows they were popular by then. Four temples and shrines claim to be the birthplace.

The argument inside the tradition is about manufacture, and the complainants are priests. Where a popular shrine cannot keep up with demand for a charm, it turns to factories, and priests have complained about the quality of what comes back. Separately, shops sell generic omamori carrying licensed characters — Mickey Mouse, Hello Kitty, Snoopy, Kewpie — that no shrine issued and no priest charged. *Inference —* the tradition has an unusually clean test for the argument, because its objects carry a shrine's name and seal. What a factory charm lacks is not craftsmanship but the stamp, and both sides of the argument know it.
text.how: Made or printed, then consecrated, then issued rather than sold. Omamori enclose paper or wood carrying a prayer inside a brocade bag; the practice describes them as made sacred through ritual and as holding busshin, spiritual offshoots, in a Shinto frame, or kesshin, manifestations, in a Buddhist one. They are not opened: shrines and their buyers alike hold that opening one loses the protection. Payment is treated as a donation: the objects are not bought but received, sazukaru or ukeru. Replacement is annual, customarily at or just after New Year, and the old one goes back to the shrine or temple that issued it to be burnt, as a mark of respect to the deity that helped through the year. If a visitor cannot find a charm for their need they can ask a priest to have one made, and if enough people ask for the same thing the shrine may start stocking it.
text.today: Live, and expanding into categories older shrines did not have. Kanda Myojin in Tokyo issues charms for IT equipment and electronics; Sega released free digital omamori in 2022 for success at school and work; omamori hang from phone straps, bags and car mirrors, and have been made as bumper decals, bicycle reflectors and card-shaped objects. The annual cycle holds: Japanese Wikipedia's own entry is organised as a month-by-month calendar of fairs — tori-no-ichi for the kumade rake, daruma-ichi for the dolls, hagoita-ichi for the decorated paddles. As of 2026 an engimono is still, in the tradition's own framing, something you receive at a counter, keep for a year, and bring back.

dating.note: from_year is the start of the Muromachi period, when the cited account dates the beginning of widespread Oharai Taima distribution. The underlying practice is older — medieval Kumano talismans, and temple woodblock printing since Nara and Heian — but the Muromachi date is the earliest the source attaches to distribution at national scale. names.name: Practical Kabbalah
names.th: คับบาลาห์ภาคปฏิบัติ

etymology.root: Hebrew qabbalah, 'that which is received', plus ma'asit, 'practical, of deeds' — the branch defined by doing rather than by contemplating
etymology.note: Its opposite number inside the same word is Kabbalah Iyunit, contemplative Kabbalah, which studies the nature of God and existence and makes nothing.

text.what: The branch of Jewish mysticism that makes things: amulets and incantations built from divine and angelic names, written on parchment or cut into silver, and carried, hung or worn. Its material output is small and its literature is mostly unpublished, because the tradition's own authorities spent six centuries telling it not to exist. This record prints that argument. It prints no name-formula, no seal and no square, because the tradition itself restricts them.
text.story:
Begin with what it is not. Halakha forbids divination and soothsaying, and the Talmud lists condemned divining practices at a frequency that historians read as evidence of how common they were. What became practical Kabbalah is, in Gershom Scholem's account, not an outgrowth of the speculative Kabbalah at all: historically a large part of its content predates the speculative branch and does not depend on it, being an agglomeration of the magical practices that developed in Judaism from Talmudic times through the Middle Ages, in which the doctrine of the Sefirot hardly ever played a decisive role. Amulet-making using the esoteric names of angels dates from Talmudic times.

The split is dated. By the beginning of the 14th century the mystical and the magical had been separated into Kabbalah Iyyunit and Kabbalah Ma'asit, and the great majority of Kabbalistic writing thereafter belongs to the contemplative branch; most of the practical branch's writings stayed unpublished. Abraham Abulafia condemned it outright. A practical tradition flourished in Spain in the second half of the 15th century around a text called Sepher ha-Mashiv, whose practitioners Moshe Idel describes as interested in demonology and in coercive incantations to summon demons, angels and even God, in order to hasten the Messianic Age; Joseph Della Reina's failure at that, with his students, was held up by later Kabbalists as a warning.

Then the prohibition that matters most. In 16th-century Safed, Isaac Luria opposed Kabbalah Ma'asit and forbade his students to write amulets, developing instead a form of exorcism that moved the techniques from the practical side to the speculative. His reasoning was purity: without the Temple and the ashes of the Red Heifer to purify with, pursuit of the practical realm by a person with an impure body is very detrimental. Because Luria is the central teacher of modern Kabbalah and the foundation of later Hasidism, that is not an opinion in a dispute — it is the position with authority behind it. The medieval Rabbi Yaakov ben Moshe Levi Moelin had already put a different objection: the person using a formula may lack the grounding, and the rite would then do nothing.

It continued anyway, at the border, and the people who continued it are named. The Baal Shem healers worked between the practical and the meditative, amulets included: Elijah Ba'al Shem of Chelm (1550–1583), the Baal Shem of London (1708–1782). Yisrael Baal Shem Tov (1698–1760) began as one, used amulets, and by the end of his life wrote only his own name on them — Yisrael ben Sara, Yisrael ben Eliezer — and no names of God. The Vilna Gaon recorded that he had attempted a golem in his youth and stopped when he perceived an impurity in it. In the 1750s Jacob Emden accused Jonathan Eybeschütz of being a secret Sabbatean, chiefly on his reading of amulets Eybeschütz had written; an amulet was the evidence in a dispute that split European Jewry. Rabbi Hirsch Fraenkel was sentenced to prison in Germany in 1713 for owning a library said to hold oaths and amulets for overcoming demons, seeing the future and speaking to the dead.

And there is a permission inside the prohibition, which is why the tradition never quite closed. The Talmud mentions charms used for healing, and a wide range of magical cures were sanctioned by rabbis; the ruling that any practice actually producing a cure was not to be dismissed opened the door that segullot — folk remedies — have walked through in Jewish communities across time and geography ever since.

*Inference —* two things follow for an atlas. First, this is the only tradition here whose own central teacher forbade its objects and whose objects went on being made; that is worth stating flatly rather than resolving. Second, a tradition whose writings mostly stayed unpublished cannot be described from its writings, so this record describes its argument, its people and its dates, and leaves the contents of the amulets where its authorities left them.
text.how: Structure only. A name — divine, angelic, or a combination worked from letters — is written by a person the client trusts, on parchment prepared to the standards Jewish law sets for sacred writing, or cut into silver, and then enclosed and worn or hung. Who may write one is exactly the contested question above: the elite, under conditions the tradition calls holy and pure, in one account; nobody, in Luria's. Hasidism displaced the whole apparatus with a different mechanism — the tzaddik altering the divine will through deveikut, cleaving to God — which Dov Ber of Mezeritch was at pains to distinguish from a magical process, though some Hasidic leaders kept using traditional amulets at the border.
text.today: Two distinct presents, and they should not be run together. One is the continuing use of segullot and of written amulets in Jewish communities, unbroken and largely private. The other is the retail red string, popularly attached to Kabbalah and sold to pilgrims and tourists in the Old City of Jerusalem and, from the late 1990s, to celebrities outside Israel — a wave usually linked to Philip Berg's Kabbalah Centre. The Torah, Halacha and the Kabbalistic texts contain no requirement to tie one, and Michael Laitman's published position is that practical Kabbalah has no use for red strings. Both facts belong in the same paragraph; neither is this atlas's verdict.

text_th.what: สาขาหนึ่งของรหัสยลัทธิยิวที่สร้างสิ่งของ ได้แก่เครื่องรางและคาถาที่สร้างจากพระนามของพระเจ้าและนามของทูตสวรรค์ เขียนบนหนังฟอกหรือสลักลงบนเงิน แล้วพก แขวน หรือสวม ผลงานที่เป็นวัตถุมีน้อย และวรรณกรรมส่วนใหญ่ไม่เคยตีพิมพ์ เพราะผู้มีอำนาจของธรรมเนียมนี้เองใช้เวลาหกศตวรรษบอกให้มันไม่มีอยู่ บันทึกนี้ตีพิมพ์ข้อถกเถียงนั้น แต่ไม่ตีพิมพ์สูตรพระนาม ตราประทับ หรือตาราง เพราะธรรมเนียมนี้เองจำกัดสิ่งเหล่านั้นไว้

restricted.note: This tradition restricts its own material and the atlas stops where it stops. Practical Kabbalah was held to be permitted only to an elite, and only under conditions the tradition calls holy and pure; most Kabbalists have taught that its use is forbidden; Isaac Luria forbade his students to write amulets at all. So this record prints no divine-name formula, no angelic name-combination, no seal and no square — not the wording, not a worked example, not a reconstruction from scattered sources. Maimonides' objection, written about the mezuzah and quoted on that record, is the tradition's own statement of what is at stake: writing names, verses or forms inside a sacred object turns a commandment into a talisman for the owner's benefit.
restricted.who_says: the tradition itself as reported in the cited account — practical Kabbalah reserved for an elite, most Kabbalists teaching that its use is forbidden, and Isaac Luria's prohibition on his students writing amulets, which carries authoritative force because he is the central teacher of modern Kabbalah

dating.label: amulet-making from Talmudic times; named as a branch by the 14th century; still argued about
dating.note: The cited account dates amulet-making with esoteric angelic names to Talmudic times and does not put a year on it; 200 CE is this project's conventional marker for that period and is circa. The separation of practical from contemplative Kabbalah is dated firmly, to the beginning of the 14th century. The bulk physical evidence for the ancestor practice is earlier and sits on the incantation-bowl record.

etymology.root: Korean bujeok, from Sino-Korean 符籍 — the same fu character as Chinese fulu, 'talisman', plus a register or record
etymology.note: The word arrives with the object. Bujeok descend from Taoist talismanic script in China, and are often built on Hanja, the Korean use of Chinese logograms.

text.what: Talismans drawn by a mudang, the ritual specialists at the centre of Musok, Korean vernacular religion. A bujeok is usually built on Hanja — Korean versions of Chinese logograms — worked in the same deliberately unreadable manner as its Chinese ancestor, and handed to the people who attended a rite rather than sold across a counter. Clients take them home and fix them to the internal walls of the house.
text.story:
Two facts about who makes them frame everything else. First, the makers are ritual specialists and the majority of them are women: approximately a fifth of mudang are male, with more male simbang on Jeju than on the mainland. Second, they hand the talismans out at the end of a gut — the large ritual that is the core of the practice — at the point where wandering spirits are expelled and the food is distributed. A bujeok is the take-home part of a rite, not a transaction on its own. Korean vernacular religion also runs ritual specialists who divine and make amulets without performing gut at all.

The script is inherited and the inheritance is documented. Fulu, the Taoist talismanic script, was carried into Korean practice as it was into Japanese; the scholarship on the Chinese side says the illegibility is deliberate, designed so that only qualified clergy can produce them. A bujeok takes that logic into Hanja.

What distinguishes this tradition from its neighbours is six centuries of state pressure, which it survived. Under the Joseon dynasty Confucian elites deemed the mudang's rites improper and suppressed them with taxation and legal restriction. From the late 19th century modernisers, many of them Christian, characterised Musok as misin — a Korean word the sources gloss as "superstition" — and backed its suppression. Under the Japanese occupation, nationalist folklorists began promoting Musok as Korea's ancient religion and a form of its national culture, an idea mudang themselves later took up strongly. Persecution continued in the mid-20th century, in North Korea and through the New Community Movement in the South.

Then it turned. From the late 1970s South Korean appraisal of the mudang improved, particularly as practitioners were associated with the minjung pro-democracy movement and came to be treated as a source of Korean cultural identity. There are now over 200,000 mudang in South Korea, with practitioners abroad as well.

The reversal is not complete and this record says so. Disapproval of mudang, often regarded as charlatans, remains widespread in South Korea, especially among Christians. Chongho Kim's 1990s fieldwork found most mudang he met were poor and with little formal education, and mudang have conventionally belonged to the lowest social class. Clients are mostly women — in Kim's fieldwork, in their late fifties and early sixties; in Laurel Kendall's, small entrepreneurs around Seoul; by the early 21st century, in Sarfati's account, many young people, as part of a spiritual search or for counselling. Clients do not generally regard themselves as exclusively committed to Musok and may consider themselves Buddhist or Christian.

*Inference —* that client profile is the most interesting thing about this tradition for an atlas of charms. A bujeok is not the property of a believer; it is something a Buddhist small-business owner in Seoul comes away from a rite holding. The tradition has no doctrine, no hierarchy and no central authority, and is transmitted orally, so what holds it together is the specialists and their training rather than a text.
text.how: Drawn by a mudang, generally on paper, in Hanja-based forms. Distributed at the close of a gut to the people who attended, sometimes alongside food charged with auspiciousness by its use in the rite. Clients affix them to the internal walls of the home. Training is by apprenticeship rather than by manual: an initiate who has accepted the call finds an established mudang willing to teach, becomes that person's chagŭn mudang, and the teacher is their sineomeoni, spirit mother, the apprentice a sinttal or sinadul. Each mudang keeps a personal pantheon, the chusin, which may differ from the pantheon of the mudang who trained them.
text.today: Live, with over 200,000 mudang in South Korea and a state that now protects what it once prosecuted: regional gut styles are on the national intangible heritage register, and the Yŏngdŭng gut of Ch'ilmŏri Shrine on Jeju went onto UNESCO's Representative List in 2009. Insadong in Seoul, which holds 40 per cent of the country's antique shops and art galleries, is where a visitor is likeliest to encounter the printed retail version. Korea also has a separate and much larger charm economy that runs on food rather than paper: sticky-rice cakes and toffee given to students before the national university entrance exam, on the wordplay that the sitter will stick to the school.

restricted.note: The forms a bujeok takes are a specialist's craft learned by apprenticeship, in a tradition that has no manual, no central authority and no doctrine, and that transmits orally. This record names the practitioners, the script's ancestry and where the object ends up, and prints no bujeok form, no accompanying invocation and no reconstruction of one. The Chinese parent craft states the reason plainly — the illegibility exists so that only qualified clergy can produce them — and Korean practice inherits it.

text.what: Catholic forms in lay hands, worked past the point the clergy sanctions. A tin leg pinned to a saint's robe; a jet fist tied on a newborn in the first week; a seed called deer's eye on a red cord; a Saint Christopher on the dashboard; a candle, a cleansing and a saint's image bought in the same market aisle as medicinal herbs. Nothing in the list is outside Catholicism's own vocabulary. What makes it a separate tradition is who decides where the line falls — and here the household decides, not the parish.
text.story:
The objects arrived with the ships and most of them are older than the crossing. Milagros — small metal or wax body parts offered at a shrine — are traced to the ancient Iberians of the Spanish coast, travelled with the Spanish into Central and South America, and still hold in rural Andalusia, Catalonia and Majorca alongside their American forms. Jet amulets have been cut since the Neolithic; by the end of the Middle Ages the working of jet religious objects was concentrated at Santiago de Compostela and sold to pilgrims on the Camino, and the Asturian fist for a baby went from there into the Spanish Caribbean. Edward Tabor traces that fist further back, to Muslim North Africa, citing Washington Irving's 1829 description of a comparable jet hand among the Moors of Barbary, into Spain during the Moorish period of 711 to 1492 and on to the colonies.

The local material entered the same kit. In Mexico the ojo de venado is a Mucuna seed; México Desconocido traces its career as an amulet to Xichú in northeastern Guanajuato and notes the plant also grew in Chiapas, Oaxaca, Puebla, San Luis Potosí and Veracruz, so other regions may have arrived at the use independently. Newborns get one against mal de ojo; adults take one up for a hard stretch; drivers hang one where they can see it.

The argument in this tradition is unusually well documented because the clergy write it down. The Catechism of the Catholic Church condemns attributing a magical importance to otherwise lawful practices and crediting an object's efficacy to its material form. The priest Eduardo Hayen Cuarón condemned the ojo de venado by name, as an amulet and therefore an esoteric practice, malign and the work of Satan. Set against that, a Saint Christopher medal sold in Spanish-speaking markets carries a printed promise — 'Si en San Cristóbal confías, de accidente no morirás', if you trust in Saint Christopher you will not die in an accident — which is exactly the proposition the Catechism warns against, printed on a devotional article and sold in a shop. Both facts are on the record. This atlas prints them side by side and settles nothing.

The markets are where the tradition is legible as a system. At the Mercado de Sonora in Mexico City, established with other public markets by the city government on 23 September 1957 to regulate retail trade, medicinal herbs and magical and occult goods occupy aisles at the back of a single metal-framed nave. The two categories are not separate, and the account says so. Candles, saints' images, cleansings and herbs are bought in the same visit, from the same stallholders, by customers across the income range. In Lima and La Paz the equivalent counters sell the same combination with Andean material alongside.

*Inference —* the tradition's defining move is a doubling rather than a substitution. A saint does not replace a charm and a charm does not replace a saint; the same object is both, and which one it is depends on who is asked. That is why this record sits beside catholic-sacramentals rather than inside it: the sacramental tradition is defined by the Church drawing a line, and this one by households drawing it somewhere else.
text.how: Bought rather than made, in a church, a cathedral, a churchyard stall, a botánica or a market aisle, and then put to work in a named place: pinned to a saint's image or a shrine wall, tied to an infant's wrist within days of birth, hung from a rear-view mirror, set on a home altar, carried in a pocket. Some are blessed by a priest and some are not, and the tradition does not treat that as the deciding fact. Milagros can be offered as a reminder of what the petitioner needs or in thanks for a prayer already answered, and the shape does the pointing — though the code is local, not universal, so a leg can mean a leg or a journey.
text.today: Live across Mexico, the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, the Andes, parts of the United States, and the Philippines by the same galleon route. Prices have been published for one object: Tabor gives US$3 to US$10 for an azabache in a botánica and US$9 to US$55 online at the time he wrote, in 2023, and reports that 29 per cent of the wearers he surveyed had chosen the fist and 71 per cent the polyhedron. Quiapo Church in Manila draws millions on 9 January and thousands every Friday, with the stalls outside selling the amulets alongside. The Mercado de Sonora still trades, in a building the city put up in 1957 and has maintained badly since.

names.name: Taonga Māori
names.th: ตาองกาเมารี

etymology.root: Māori taonga, a treasure; taonga tūturu, in New Zealand law, an object relating to Māori culture, history or society, made or modified in New Zealand by Māori, brought into New Zealand by Māori or used by Māori, and more than 50 years old
etymology.note: English 'treasure' undersells it. A taonga carries whakapapa — a genealogy of its own — so the word names a relationship with named people, not a valuation.

text.what: Treasures with whakapapa. A hei-tiki, a hei matau, an adze reworked into a pendant, a cloak, a carving: Te Papa's own description of taonga Māori covers ancestral carvings, personal ornaments, garments and weaponry, alongside archaeological material and contemporary Māori visual culture. The atlas files these here rather than under charms because the tradition's own account of what they do is about descent and relationship, not about luck. This record uses the tradition's words.
text.story:
Start with what mana is and where it comes from, because that is the whole difference. Pounamu taonga increase in mana as they pass from one generation to another; the stone is held to absorb the mana of its past owners, and some heirloom pieces are named after a former owner in memory of their position and authority. The most prized taonga are those with known histories running back many generations, and those are the ones given as gifts to seal important agreements. Peace between groups was cemented by exchanging carved heirlooms — a tautau pounamu, a door of greenstone — as in the saying Me tautau pounamu, kia kore ai e pakaru, ake, ake: let us conclude a peace that may never be broken, for ever and ever.

Dougal Austin's 2014 thesis, supervised by Peter Adds and based on Te Papa's hei-tiki collection with early-contact examples in overseas collections, locates the mana of a hei-tiki in the 'agency of prolonged ancestral use'. That is an argument about time and handling, not about design. A hei-tiki was often buried when its kaitiaki — its guardian — died, and brought out again at tangihanga.

The objects are also functional history. Adze blades of pounamu were wanted for carving wood and stayed in use after metal tools arrived; when they were no longer useful as tools they were often reworked into hei tiki and other taonga. Pounamu crafting and trade mattered to the economy of Ngāi Tahu, the South Island iwi, and production increased after their arrival in the South Island in the middle of the 18th century. There were a dozen major pounamu trails and many minor routes, walked in summer by parties of six to twelve.

How the collections were formed is part of the record and the sources state it plainly. Te Papa holds over 200 hei-tiki and the British Museum about 50; some were exchanged or gifted to Europeans at the earliest point of contact, and, in the cited account's own words, 'the majority were stolen or improperly obtained through colonial processes'.

Two frameworks now sit over that. Te Papa works on a stated principle: 'Mana Taonga is a recognition of the power of taonga to communicate deep truths about our people.' The museum describes itself as recognising the role of communities in the care and understanding of collections and taonga, and names among its aspirations 'the reconnection of people to their tribal taonga' and 'the reclamation of Māori knowledge, language, and customs'. It also runs a repatriation programme, Karanga Aotearoa. And New Zealand law protects the objects by category: under the Protected Objects Act 1975, ngā taonga tūturu are one of nine classes of protected New Zealand object, unauthorised export of a protected object without permission from the chief executive of the Ministry for Culture and Heritage is an offence carrying fines of up to $100,000 for an individual and $200,000 for a body corporate, and the chief executive must consult two or more expert examiners on an application. Ownership of all naturally occurring pounamu was returned by the Crown to Ngāi Tahu in 1997 under the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement.

The modern trade runs alongside all of that and is argued about by name. Most hei matau are now carved from cattle bone; carvers who work whale bone must use ancient standings, pre-existing supplies, or bone from whales that strand, since Māori have first claim under New Zealand tradition and law on part of the skeleton of a stranded whale that cannot be refloated — a very limited supply. Manufacturers in China mass-produce items resembling hei matau for the New Zealand visitor market, usually in a paste of bone and resin, and have, in the cited account's words, 'attracted criticism for their appropriation of Māori designs'. Retailers also sell tourist versions of hei-tiki in jade, other stone, plastic and other materials, and much of the 'greenstone' in souvenir shops is jade sourced overseas rather than pounamu, which occurs only in New Zealand.

*Inference —* an atlas of protective objects has to say where it has put this record and why. Taonga are here because the rest of the world meets them in the same museum cases and the same shop windows as charms, and because a reader who has just seen a hei matau on a cord deserves the tradition's own account of what it is. Calling one a lucky charm would be a category error the sources do not make, and this record does not make it either.
text.how: Carved, worn, handed on. Traditional method on a hei-tiki: the stone is first cut in the form of a small adze, smoothed by abrasive rubbing, shaped with sticks and water, the holes bored, then polished at length, and the finished pendant suspended on a plaited cord secured by a loop and toggle. The tilt of the head on one variety comes from the properties of the stone — its hardness and value make it important to remove as little as possible. Large pounamu boulders were and still are set at the entrances to significant sites as mauri stones, and visitors are invited to rub them gently with a dry or wet hand to connect with the mana of the place.
text.today: Live, and worn across New Zealand society. Bone and pounamu carvings relate to Māori cultural identity for many Māori, and are popular with young New Zealanders of all backgrounds for whom they relate to a more general New Zealand identity; several Māori tribal collectives create and export jewellery and other work. Pounamu appeared at London Fashion Week in 2013 in Kiri Nathan's collection. Te Papa charges international visitors an entrance fee and admits New Zealanders free.

restricted.note: This atlas follows the tradition's own published protocols here rather than summarising or completing them. That means three specific blanks. It prints no karakia and no rite. It prints no particular taonga's whakapapa or ancestral line — those belong to the descendants and to the iwi, not to an encyclopedia. And it does not attribute protective functions to taonga that the tradition's own publications do not attribute to them; where a source states what an object stands for, this atlas quotes the source and stops. Te Papa's stated position is that communities have a role in the care and understanding of taonga and that its aspirations include the reconnection of people to their tribal taonga; that is the framework, and the atlas works inside it.

dating.note: from_year is the middle of the 18th century, when the cited account says pounamu production increased after Ngāi Tahu's arrival in the South Island. It is the only date the sources read here attach to the craft, and it is plainly a late one: adzes, trails and taonga predate it. This atlas prints the date it can cite rather than an estimate it cannot, and flags that the bar on the timeline is shorter than the practice.

object.made_by: Māori carvers; several artistic collectives established by Māori tribal groups now create and export work. Ownership of all naturally occurring pounamu was returned to Ngāi Tahu in 1997.
object.note: Pounamu is the collective term: nephrite jade in the varieties Māori classify by colour — kahurangi, īnanga, kawakawa, kōkopu, totoweka — and the translucent bowenite called tangiwai. The article notes that the alternative English names mislead: not all pounamu is jade, and 'greenstone' is a generic term for unrelated stone from many countries.

names.name: Mesopotamian household protection
names.said: the apotropaic craft of Sumer, Akkad, Babylonia and Assyria
names.th: การคุ้มครองบ้านเรือนแบบเมโสโปเตเมีย

text.what: A craft with four moving parts: a demon with a name, a counter-power with a name, an incantation that addresses the demon directly, and a physical object — a plaque, a cast head, a figurine — placed where the danger comes in. Apotropaic ritual of this kind was practised throughout the ancient Near East, in houses rather than in state temples.
text.story:
The method is verbal before it is material. The incantations open by naming the demon and then work through her epithets — 'Dimme, daughter of Anu', 'Who was named by the gods' — because the names are the hold. The object carries the words. An amulet with Lamashtu's image on it is not a portrait; it is her, held and instructed.

The counter-power does not have to be good. Pazuzu is a wind that brings plague and a text addresses him as 'Agony of Mankind', and his head hangs over the bed anyway, because he is the one thing that sends Lamashtu back underground. That is the tradition's most distinctive move: it hires demons.

Placement is documented rather than guessed. Amulets bearing Lamashtu's image could be worn, attached to the body or to clothing, or set near beds, doorways and other vulnerable spaces. A large Pazuzu wall amulet was found on the floor of the main reception room of a house at Dur-Katlimmu, where it had hung facing the entryway. Ritual texts from Uruk prescribe a bronze Pazuzu necklace for a woman at risk of miscarriage.

The objects were made at scale. The uniformity of the Pazuzu heads and their number across sites is read as mass production, which makes this the earliest industrialised amulet trade in the atlas.

*Inference —* the tradition does not end where the language does. Six hundred years after the last Pazuzu heads, the same ground is producing incantation bowls: a named demon, an incantation addressed to it directly, an object buried at the threshold. The scripts are Aramaic and Mandaic and the demons have new names, and the method is the one described above.

etymology.root: Thai wicha, 'knowledge, subject, learned craft', from Sanskrit vidyā through Pali vijjā — the same root as the yantra word the practice inscribes
etymology.note: The word names the thing that is transmitted rather than the thing that is sold. A yant belongs to a lineage; an amulet belongs to whoever buys it.

text.what: The taught craft behind Thailand's protective objects: the designs, the scripts, the incantations and the rules that go with them. Its outputs are a pressed clay or metal tablet of the Buddha or a revered monk, a rolled metal or palm-leaf scroll in a case, a small carved phallus on a waist cord, and a tattoo. What ties them together is not the shape but the transmission — a yant and the words said over it belong to a master's lineage, and an amulet's price is set by which temple pressed it and which monk chanted over it.
text.story:
The tablets come first and they are older than the idea of a charm. Buddhism reached what is now Thailand in the Dvaravati period carrying India's votive-tablet practice, and Dvaravati tablets were made to perpetuate the religion. Under Srivijaya and Mahayana influence, tablets were pressed to dedicate merit to the dead and toward becoming a bodhisattva. By Ayutthaya they were being made for protection, and warriors carried them into battle in place of the phrajiat, the takrut or a herbal charm. In the early Rattanakosin period the protective amulet took off, the class acquired the name phra khrueang, and temples began using them to raise funds — a monk would give one as a gift in return for a donation. The term 'amulet' in this sense first appears under King Rama IV.

Takrut are older than Thai Buddhism in the sources' own account. They are the form the Khun Chang Khun Phaen epic mentions most, and after Buddhism took root monks were making them in 1200–1300 CE. The tattoo comes from the other direction: sak yant originates in the Khmer Empire around the ninth century, built on mainland Southeast Asian animist tattooing that the sources run back as far as 2,500 BCE, with the geometry drawn from Indian yantras. Cambodia writes them in Khmer script, central Thailand in Khom, northern Thailand in Shan, Northern Thai or Tai Lu, Laos in Lao Tham.

The craft states its own rules and they run on the bearer, not the object. A yant confers what it confers only while the person carrying it observes the taboos taken on with it — abstaining from a named food is the example the source gives. Break them and it stops. Three classes of effect are named: one that works on the bearer, making them more eloquent; one that protects, taken by soldiers, police, taxi drivers and people in trades they count as dangerous; one that works on everyone else, invoking fear.

And there is a live economy with dated figures. In 1987 a policeman, Khun Phantharak Rajjadej, created the Jatukham Rammathep amulet for the founding of Nakhon Si Thammarat's city pillar; it names two Srivijaya princes the city holds to be its guardians, is round, and runs about 5 cm across. It caught on in the early 2000s, hard, from the time of its creator's funeral on 5 July 2006 into mid-2007. As many as 150 series were planned for production in 2007, and the market for that one amulet reached twenty billion baht that year. In late 2007 the bubble burst: the popularity faded fast, leaving plenty of stock that could be had at low prices. The source gives no figure for what the collapse cost anybody, so none is given here.

The other prices are collectors' prices and carry what their source carries. The Benja Phakhi — Phra Somdej, Phra Rod, Phra Nang Phaya, Phra Phong Suphan, Phra Sum Kor — are valued at over 10 million baht, with no year attached in the source, so none is printed. A Phra Somdet Jitlada, one of no more than 3,000 made by King Bhumibol and awarded between 1965 and 1970 with a numbered certificate naming its recipient, was worth at least two million baht as of 2013.

*Inference —* the argument about whether this is devotion or trade is Thai, conducted in Thai, and older than any foreign observer's version of it. The atlas reports both halves: temples have funded themselves this way since the early Rattanakosin period and say so plainly, and a market that can move twenty billion baht in twelve months behaves like a market. Neither half is a debunking of the other.
text.how: Amulets are pressed from plaster, metal, wood or bone, often with ash, a monk's hair or temple relics mixed in, then chanted over and blessed in a process that can take from a week to several years, and usually cased before wear. Takrut are inscribed with yant in Khom, Lan Na Tai Tham or another script, rolled into a tube, cased, and tied to the body — at the neck, at chest level, at the waist, or over a body part the wearer wants covered. Value afterwards turns on appearance, scarcity, maker, age and reputation, which is why buyers arrive at a market with a loupe and why specialist authenticators are part of the trade. A sak yant is applied by needle by a monk, a Brahmin priest, a ruesi or a lay wicha practitioner, and the rules travel home with the bearer.
text.today: Live and internationally visible, with the frictions that brings. Angelina Jolie was tattooed by Ajahn Noo Ganpai in Old Khmer script and took a Bengal tiger yant in 2004 on acquiring Cambodian citizenship, which the source credits with the practice's popularity among women abroad. In 2011 Thailand's Culture Ministry moved against parlours inking Buddha images on non-Buddhist visitors. Wat Bang Phra in Nakhon Pathom holds its Wai Khru on the grounds once a year in March, when the tattoos of those who come are renewed. In 2021 a Thai project put monk-blessed amulets on a blockchain as NFTs. Tha Phrachan market in Bangkok still trades the tablets, and forgery is common enough that expert authentication is a standing part of the transaction.

text_th.what: วิชาที่สืบทอดกันด้วยการสอน อยู่เบื้องหลังวัตถุคุ้มครองของไทย ได้แก่ แบบลวดลาย อักขระ คาถา และข้อห้ามข้อปฏิบัติที่มาพร้อมกัน สิ่งที่วิชานี้สร้างขึ้นมีทั้งพระพิมพ์ดินหรือโลหะที่กดเป็นรูปพระพุทธเจ้าหรือพระเกจิอาจารย์ ตะกรุดที่ม้วนจากแผ่นโลหะหรือใบลานแล้วใส่ปลอก ปลัดขิกชิ้นเล็กที่แกะเป็นรูปลึงค์ห้อยสายคาดเอว และรอยสัก สิ่งที่ผูกทั้งหมดไว้ด้วยกันไม่ใช่รูปทรง แต่คือการสืบทอด ยันต์หนึ่งแบบกับคาถาที่ใช้เสกยันต์นั้นเป็นของสายครูสายหนึ่ง และราคาของพระเครื่ององค์หนึ่งขึ้นอยู่กับว่าวัดใดกดพิมพ์ และพระสงฆ์รูปใดปลุกเสก
text_th.story:
พระพิมพ์มาก่อน และมีมาก่อนความคิดเรื่องเครื่องรางเสียอีก พระพุทธศาสนาเข้ามาถึงดินแดนที่เป็นประเทศไทยในปัจจุบันในสมัยทวารวดี พร้อมกับธรรมเนียมการสร้างพระพิมพ์แบบอินเดีย และพระพิมพ์สมัยทวารวดีสร้างขึ้นเพื่อสืบต่ออายุพระศาสนา ในสมัยศรีวิชัยซึ่งได้รับอิทธิพลมหายาน มีการกดพระพิมพ์เพื่ออุทิศบุญแก่ผู้ล่วงลับ และเพื่อมุ่งสู่การเป็นพระโพธิสัตว์ พอถึงสมัยอยุธยา พระพิมพ์ถูกสร้างเพื่อการคุ้มครอง และนักรบนำติดตัวออกศึกแทนผ้าประเจียด ตะกรุด หรือเครื่องรางสมุนไพร ในสมัยรัตนโกสินทร์ตอนต้น พระเครื่องเพื่อการคุ้มครองได้รับความนิยมอย่างมาก วัตถุกลุ่มนี้ได้ชื่อเรียกว่า พระเครื่อง และวัดเริ่มใช้พระเครื่องหาทุน โดยพระสงฆ์จะมอบให้เป็นของที่ระลึกตอบแทนผู้ทำบุญ คำเรียก "เครื่องราง" ในความหมายนี้ปรากฏครั้งแรกในรัชสมัยพระบาทสมเด็จพระจอมเกล้าเจ้าอยู่หัว รัชกาลที่ 4

ตามที่แหล่งข้อมูลเล่าไว้เอง ตะกรุดเก่าแก่กว่าพระพุทธศาสนาในไทย ตะกรุดเป็นเครื่องรางที่วรรณคดีเรื่องขุนช้างขุนแผนกล่าวถึงบ่อยที่สุด และหลังจากพระพุทธศาสนาหยั่งรากแล้ว พระสงฆ์ก็สร้างตะกรุดกันในช่วง พ.ศ. 1743–1843 (ค.ศ. 1200–1300) ส่วนรอยสักมาจากอีกทางหนึ่ง สักยันต์มีต้นกำเนิดในอาณาจักรเขมรราวคริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 9 ต่อยอดจากการสักตามคติผีของผู้คนในภาคพื้นทวีปเอเชียตะวันออกเฉียงใต้ ซึ่งแหล่งข้อมูลสืบย้อนไปได้ไกลถึง 2,500 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. โดยรูปทรงเรขาคณิตได้มาจากยันตระของอินเดีย กัมพูชาเขียนยันต์ด้วยอักษรเขมร ภาคกลางของไทยใช้อักษรขอม ภาคเหนือของไทยใช้อักษรไทใหญ่ อักษรธรรมล้านนา หรืออักษรไทลื้อ ส่วนลาวใช้อักษรธรรมลาว

วิชานี้กำหนดกฎของตัวเองไว้ และกฎเหล่านั้นผูกอยู่กับผู้ถือ ไม่ใช่กับวัตถุ ยันต์จะให้ผลตามที่ว่าไว้ก็ต่อเมื่อผู้ถือรักษาข้อห้ามที่รับมาพร้อมกับยันต์ แหล่งข้อมูลยกตัวอย่างการงดกินอาหารบางอย่าง หากผิดข้อห้าม ยันต์ก็หมดผล ผลที่กล่าวถึงแบ่งเป็น 3 แบบ แบบแรกเกิดกับตัวผู้ถือ ทำให้พูดจาคล่องแคล่วน่าฟัง แบบที่สองคุ้มครองป้องกัน ซึ่งทหาร ตำรวจ คนขับแท็กซี่ และผู้ที่ทำงานที่ตนถือว่าเสี่ยงอันตรายนิยมรับ แบบที่สามเกิดกับผู้อื่นทุกคน คือทำให้เกิดความเกรงกลัว

และยังมีเศรษฐกิจที่ดำเนินอยู่จริงพร้อมตัวเลขที่ระบุปีได้ ในปี พ.ศ. 2530 (ค.ศ. 1987) ตำรวจนายหนึ่ง คือ ขุนพันธรักษ์ราชเดช ได้สร้างพระเครื่องจตุคามรามเทพขึ้นในวาระการสร้างหลักเมืองนครศรีธรรมราช ชื่อจตุคามรามเทพเป็นชื่อของเจ้าชายสองพระองค์แห่งศรีวิชัยซึ่งชาวเมืองถือว่าเป็นผู้พิทักษ์เมือง องค์พระเป็นทรงกลม ขนาดราว 5 ซม. จตุคามรามเทพเริ่มได้รับความนิยมในช่วงต้นคริสต์ทศวรรษ 2000 และนิยมอย่างรุนแรง ตั้งแต่ช่วงงานศพของผู้สร้างเมื่อวันที่ 5 กรกฎาคม พ.ศ. 2549 ไปจนถึงกลางปี พ.ศ. 2550 มีการวางแผนจะสร้างมากถึง 150 รุ่นในปี พ.ศ. 2550 และตลาดของพระเครื่องรุ่นนี้เพียงอย่างเดียวมีมูลค่าถึง 20,000 ล้านบาทในปีนั้น ปลายปี พ.ศ. 2550 ฟองสบู่ก็แตก ความนิยมจางหายไปอย่างรวดเร็ว เหลือของค้างอยู่จำนวนมากที่หาเช่าได้ในราคาต่ำ แหล่งข้อมูลไม่ได้ให้ตัวเลขว่าการล่มครั้งนั้นทำให้ใครเสียหายเท่าใด ที่นี่จึงไม่ใส่ตัวเลขไว้

ราคาอื่น ๆ เป็นราคาของนักสะสม และมีรายละเอียดเท่าที่แหล่งข้อมูลให้ไว้ พระชุดเบญจภาคี ได้แก่ พระสมเด็จ พระรอด พระนางพญา พระผงสุพรรณ และพระซุ้มกอ มีมูลค่ากว่า 10 ล้านบาท แหล่งข้อมูลไม่ได้ระบุปี ที่นี่จึงไม่ระบุปีไว้ พระสมเด็จจิตรลดา ซึ่งมีไม่เกิน 3,000 องค์ พระบาทสมเด็จพระบรมชนกาธิเบศร มหาภูมิพลอดุลยเดชมหาราช บรมนาถบพิตร ทรงสร้าง และพระราชทานระหว่าง พ.ศ. 2508–2513 พร้อมใบกำกับที่มีหมายเลขและระบุชื่อผู้ได้รับพระราชทาน มีมูลค่าอย่างน้อย 2 ล้านบาท ณ พ.ศ. 2556

*ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* ข้อถกเถียงว่าเรื่องนี้เป็นศรัทธาหรือการค้าเป็นข้อถกเถียงของคนไทย ถกกันเป็นภาษาไทย และมีมาก่อนที่ผู้สังเกตการณ์ชาวต่างชาติคนใดจะหยิบมาพูด แอตลาสนี้รายงานทั้งสองด้าน วัดต่าง ๆ หาทุนด้วยวิธีนี้มาตั้งแต่สมัยรัตนโกสินทร์ตอนต้นและพูดถึงเรื่องนี้อย่างตรงไปตรงมา ขณะเดียวกัน ตลาดที่เงินหมุนเวียนได้ถึง 20,000 ล้านบาทในสิบสองเดือนก็มีพฤติกรรมอย่างตลาด ไม่มีด้านใดหักล้างอีกด้านหนึ่ง
text_th.how: พระเครื่องกดพิมพ์จากปูน โลหะ ไม้ หรือกระดูก มักผสมเถ้า เส้นเกศาของพระสงฆ์ หรือพระธาตุลงไปในเนื้อพระ จากนั้นจึงปลุกเสกและอธิษฐานจิต ซึ่งอาจใช้เวลาตั้งแต่หนึ่งสัปดาห์ไปจนถึงหลายปี และมักเลี่ยมกรอบก่อนนำมาห้อยคอ ตะกรุดจารึกยันต์ด้วยอักษรขอม อักษรธรรมล้านนา หรืออักษรอื่น แล้วม้วนเป็นหลอด ใส่ปลอก และผูกติดตัว ที่คอ ระดับอก ที่เอว หรือทับส่วนของร่างกายที่ผู้สวมต้องการให้คุ้มครอง หลังจากนั้น มูลค่าขึ้นอยู่กับลักษณะองค์พระ ความหายาก ผู้สร้าง อายุ และชื่อเสียง ผู้เช่าบูชาจึงพกกล้องส่องพระมาที่ตลาด และผู้เชี่ยวชาญที่รับตรวจสอบพระก็เป็นส่วนหนึ่งของวงการ สักยันต์สักด้วยเข็มโดยพระสงฆ์ พราหมณ์ ฤๅษี หรืออาจารย์ฆราวาสผู้ถือวิชา และข้อห้ามข้อปฏิบัติก็ติดตัวผู้ถือกลับบ้านไปด้วย
text_th.today: ยังมีชีวิตอยู่และเป็นที่รู้จักในระดับนานาชาติ พร้อมกับแรงเสียดทานที่ตามมา แองเจลินา โจลี (Angelina Jolie) ได้รับการสักจากอาจารย์หนู กันภัย ด้วยอักษรเขมรโบราณ และสักยันต์เสือเบงกอลเมื่อปี พ.ศ. 2547 (ค.ศ. 2004) ในโอกาสที่ได้รับสัญชาติกัมพูชา แหล่งข้อมูลระบุว่าเหตุการณ์นี้ทำให้สักยันต์เป็นที่นิยมในหมู่ผู้หญิงต่างชาติ ในปี พ.ศ. 2554 กระทรวงวัฒนธรรมของไทยเคลื่อนไหวเพื่อจัดการกับร้านสักที่สักรูปพระพุทธเจ้าให้ผู้มาเยือนที่ไม่ได้นับถือพระพุทธศาสนา วัดบางพระ จังหวัดนครปฐม จัดพิธีไหว้ครูในบริเวณวัดปีละครั้งในเดือนมีนาคม และในพิธีนั้นรอยสักของผู้ที่มาร่วมจะได้รับการครอบใหม่ ในปี พ.ศ. 2564 โครงการหนึ่งของไทยนำพระเครื่องที่พระสงฆ์ปลุกเสกแล้วขึ้นบล็อกเชนในรูปแบบ NFT ตลาดพระท่าพระจันทร์ในกรุงเทพฯ ยังคงมีการเช่าบูชาพระพิมพ์ และพระปลอมก็มีมากพอที่การให้ผู้เชี่ยวชาญตรวจสอบจะเป็นขั้นตอนปกติของการเช่าบูชา

th_fields.etymology.root: คำไทย วิชา หมายถึง 'ความรู้ วิชาการ ศาสตร์ที่เรียนกันมา' มาจากภาษาสันสกฤต วิทยา (vidyā) ผ่านภาษาบาลี วิชชา (vijjā) — เป็นรากเดียวกับคำในยันต์ที่วิชานี้ลงอักขระ
th_fields.etymology.note: คำนี้เรียกสิ่งที่สืบทอดกัน ไม่ใช่สิ่งที่ซื้อขายกัน ยันต์เป็นของสายครู ส่วนพระเครื่องเป็นของผู้ที่เช่าบูชาไป
th_fields.dating.period: สมัยอาณาจักรเขมรถึงปัจจุบัน
th_fields.dating.note: ปีเริ่มต้น (from_year) คือต้นกำเนิดในอาณาจักรเขมรราวคริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 9 ที่แหล่งข้อมูลให้ไว้สำหรับการสักยันต์ ซึ่งเป็นปีที่เก่าที่สุดที่สายใดสายหนึ่งของวิชานี้มี การสักตามคติผีที่อยู่เบื้องล่าง แหล่งข้อมูลเดียวกันระบุอายุย้อนไปไกลถึง 2,500 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. แต่ในฐานะธรรมเนียมของภูมิภาค ไม่ใช่ในฐานะวิชานี้ การที่พระสงฆ์สร้างตะกรุดระบุอายุไว้ที่ พ.ศ. 1743–1843 (ค.ศ. 1200–1300) และวัตถุกลุ่มนี้ได้ชื่อว่า พระเครื่อง ในสมัยรัตนโกสินทร์ตอนต้น
th_fields.object.made_by: พระสงฆ์ พราหมณ์ ฤๅษี หรือฆราวาสผู้ถือวิชา ซึ่งทำงานอยู่ในสายครูที่ระบุชื่อได้ วัดเป็นผู้ดำเนินการกดพิมพ์และพิธีปลุกเสกหมู่ และชื่อของพระสงฆ์ผู้ปลุกเสกคือประวัติที่มาของวัตถุชิ้นนั้น
th_fields.object.inscription: ยันต์ — เรขาคณิตศักดิ์สิทธิ์พร้อมคาถาบาลีและบทสวดทางพุทธศาสนา — เขียนด้วยอักษรขอมบาลีในภาคกลางของไทย อักษรเขมรในกัมพูชา อักษรธรรมล้านนา ไทใหญ่ หรือไทลื้อในภาคเหนือ และอักษรธรรมลาวในลาว
th_fields.object.note: ขนาดเดียวที่มีระบุไว้คือของจตุคามรามเทพ กว้างราว 5 ซม. และเป็นขนาดของพระแบบนั้นเท่านั้น จึงอยู่ในส่วนเรื่องราว ไม่ใช่ที่นี่
th_fields.against.0.who: หมวดของวิชาเองคือ คงกระพัน คือความอยู่ยงคงกระพัน และตะกรุดที่ปลุกเสกไว้เพื่อคุ้มครองให้ปลอดภัย ส่วนสักยันต์เพื่อการคุ้มครองนั้น ทหาร ตำรวจ และคนขับแท็กซี่นิยมรับ
th_fields.against.1.who: คำอธิบายเรื่องพระเครื่องที่อ้างถึง ซึ่งระบุการคุ้มครองจากคุณไสยไว้ควบคู่กับภัยอันตรายและภัยพิบัติ
th_fields.against.2.who: หมวดของวิชาคือ มหาเสน่ห์ (แรงดึงดูด) และเมตตามหานิยม (ความเป็นที่รักใคร่และความสำเร็จในการค้า) พระขุนแผนได้ชื่อตามตัวละครในเรื่องเล่าพื้นบ้านที่ใช้คาถาเสน่ห์
th_fields.against.3.who: หมวดเดียวกัน — มหาโภคทรัพย์ คือการเรียกทรัพย์ — และเจ้าของร้านที่ตั้งปลัดขิกไว้ข้างลิ้นชักเก็บเงินเพื่อให้ขายดี
th_fields.against.4.who: ผู้หญิงไทย ซึ่งแหล่งข้อมูลกล่าวว่าพกปลัดขิกไว้ในกระเป๋าถือเพื่อป้องกันการข่มขืนและการจี้ชิงทรัพย์
th_fields.against.5.who: พระกริ่ง ซึ่งสร้างเป็นรูปพระไภษัชยคุรุ พระพุทธเจ้าแห่งการรักษาโรค ตามคติกล่าวว่าผู้ใดได้ยินพระนามของพระองค์แม้เพียงผ่าน ๆ หรือได้เห็นพระรูป จะหายจากโรค
th_fields.against.6.who: นักรบสมัยอยุธยา ซึ่งนำพระพิมพ์ติดตัวออกศึกแทนผ้าประเจียด ตะกรุด หรือเครื่องรางสมุนไพร
th_fields.holdings.0.what: พระพิมพ์และวัตถุทางพุทธศาสนาของไทย
th_fields.restricted.note: แบบของยันต์และถ้อยคำที่ใช้เสกยันต์นั้นเป็นของสายครูที่ถือวิชานั้นไว้ และคาถาก็ต่างกันไปในแต่ละสำนัก แอตลาสนี้ลงเฉพาะสิ่งที่ธรรมเนียมนี้เปิดเผยเอง — ผลแบ่งเป็นกี่หมวด ใครเป็นผู้ลงยันต์ และยันต์มาพร้อมข้อปฏิบัติ — และไม่ลงคาถา ถ้อยคำปลุกเสก หรือข้อห้ามเฉพาะที่อาจารย์ท่านหนึ่งกำหนดให้ผู้ถือคนหนึ่ง ทั้งไม่นำมาปะติดปะต่อขึ้นจากแหล่งข้อมูลที่กระจัดกระจายด้วย ช่องว่างนี้เว้นไว้โดยเจตนา

restricted.note: A yant's design and the words said over it belong to the master's lineage that holds them, and the incantations differ from school to school. This atlas prints what the tradition publishes — what the classes of effect are, who applies them, that rules come with them — and does not print an incantation, a consecration wording, or the specific taboos a particular master sets on a particular bearer. It does not reconstruct them from scattered sources either. The blank is deliberate.
restricted.who_says: the practice as described in the cited account: sak yant is defined by strict rules intended to maintain the tattoos' power, the incantations depend on the creator's lineage in each school, and the tattoo holds only while the bearer keeps the taboos taken on with it

dating.label: 9th century to now
dating.note: from_year is the ninth-century Khmer Empire origin the source gives for yantra tattooing, which is the earliest date any strand of this craft carries. The animist tattooing underneath it is dated in the same source as far back as 2,500 BCE, but as a regional practice rather than as this craft; monks making takrut are dated to 1200–1300 CE; the amulet class acquires the name phra khrueang in the early Rattanakosin period.

object.made_by: a monk, a Brahmin priest, a ruesi or a lay wicha practitioner, working in a named lineage; temples run the pressing and the mass consecrations, and the consecrating monk's name is the object's provenance
object.inscription: yant — sacred geometry with Pali gatha and Buddhist invocations — in Khom Pali script in central Thailand, Khmer in Cambodia, Lan Na Tai Tham, Shan or Tai Lu in the north, Lao Tham in Laos
object.script: Khom Pali, Khmer, Lan Na Tai Tham
object.note: The one measurement given is the Jatukham Rammathep's, about 5 cm across, and it belongs to that type alone; it sits in the story rather than here.

against.who: the craft's own category kong grapan, invulnerability, and the takrut blessed for safe keeping; sak yant protection is taken by soldiers, police and taxi drivers
the cited account of phra khrueang, which names protection from black magic alongside danger and disaster
the craft's categories maha sanaeh, attraction, and metta mahaniyom, popularity and business success; the Khun Phaen amulet is named for a folklore figure who used a love formula
the same categories — maha pokasap, the drawing of riches — and shopkeepers who set a palad khik by the till to bring in sales
Thai women, who the source says carry a palad khik in a purse against rape and mugging
the Phra Kring, made in the image of Bhaisajyaguru the medicine Buddha, of whom the tradition says that whoever hears his name in passing or sees his image will be healed
Ayutthaya-period warriors, who carried votive tablets into battle in place of the phrajiat, the takrut or a herbal charm
