kin.as: the same craft with the object removed: the yant goes into skin, and the rules stay on the person
kin.as_th: วิชาเดียวกันโดยไม่มีวัตถุ ยันต์ลงไปอยู่บนผิวหนัง และข้อห้ามข้อปฏิบัติอยู่กับตัวคน

kin.as: the piece of the kit that can go where the Buddha may not — a bar, a gambling house, a brothel
kin.as_th: เครื่องรางในชุดนี้ที่ไปได้ในที่ที่พระพุทธรูปไปไม่ได้ เช่น บาร์ บ่อนการพนัน หรือซ่องโสเภณี

kin.as: the drawn sheets the practitioners work from, and the rules that come attached to them
kin.as_th: แผ่นแบบยันต์ที่ผู้ถือวิชาใช้เป็นต้นแบบ พร้อมข้อห้ามข้อปฏิบัติที่ติดมาด้วย

kin.as: the step this tradition prices by: a week to several years of chanting, and the consecrating monk's name as provenance
kin.as_th: ขั้นตอนที่วิชานี้ใช้กำหนดราคา คือการปลุกเสกตั้งแต่หนึ่งสัปดาห์ไปจนถึงหลายปี โดยชื่อของพระผู้ปลุกเสกคือประวัติที่มาของพระ

kin.as: the practice that holds the lineages, the refusals and the annual renewal at Wat Bang Phra
kin.as_th: การปฏิบัติที่รักษาสายครู การปฏิเสธไม่สักให้ และการครอบรอยสักประจำปีที่วัดบางพระ

kin.as: the practice at its most monetised anywhere in this atlas — loupe, certificate, forgery, and a twenty-billion-baht year on the record
kin.as_th: การปฏิบัติที่เกี่ยวกับเงินมากที่สุดในแอตลาสนี้ มีทั้งกล้องส่องพระ ใบรับรอง ของปลอม และปีที่ตลาดมีมูลค่า 20,000 ล้านบาทอยู่ในบันทึก

kin.as: the market this tradition's economy runs through, beside Thammasat University in Bangkok
kin.as_th: ตลาดที่เศรษฐกิจของวิชานี้ไหลผ่าน อยู่ข้างมหาวิทยาลัยธรรมศาสตร์ในกรุงเทพฯ

kin.as: where the geometry comes from: the Indian yantra, arriving through the Khmer Empire and staying under a Thai name
kin.as_th: ที่มาของรูปทรงเรขาคณิต คือยันตระของอินเดีย ซึ่งเดินทางผ่านอาณาจักรเขมรเข้ามา แล้วอยู่ต่อภายใต้ชื่อไทย

kin.as: the word at the other end of that journey, shortened to yant
kin.as_th: คำที่อยู่อีกปลายหนึ่งของเส้นทางนั้น ซึ่งหดสั้นลงเหลือ ยันต์

kin.as: the long read on authentication, which is a standing cost of doing business in this tradition rather than an occasional scandal
kin.as_th: บทความยาวว่าด้วยการตรวจสอบพระ ซึ่งในวิชานี้เป็นต้นทุนประจำของการค้า ไม่ใช่เรื่องอื้อฉาวนาน ๆ ครั้ง

text.what: The protective end of Tibetan Buddhism: printed and drawn amulets consecrated by lamas, folded and bound in five-coloured cord, carried in worked-metal boxes at the neck or over the chest, hung on strings across passes and roofs, strung as agate beads, and painted as cosmological charts. Objects are made by specialists, given rather than sold, and mostly worn shut.
text.story:
The frame is old and dated. Tibetan Buddhism preserves Indian Buddhist tantric practice of the post-Gupta early medieval period, 500 to 1200 CE, along with native Tibetan developments; the Buddhist Tantras date from around the seventh century onward. In the eighth century King Trisong Detsen, who reigned 755 to 797, made Buddhism the state religion and invited Indian scholars to his court — Padmasambhava, whom Tibetans call Guru Rinpoche, and Śāntarakṣita, 725 to 788, counted as the founders of the Nyingma, the oldest school. The Bengali monk Atisha, 982 to 1054, arrived in 1042. Before all of it the predominant tradition was Bon, which prayer flags are held to come out of.

Protection is part of a lama's ordinary work, not a sideline. There has been a close association in Tibet between the religious and the secular — chos srid zung 'brel — and lamas have tended to the lay population by helping with protection and prosperity: rites for purifying karma, for avoiding harm from demonic forces and enemies, for a successful harvest, with divination and exorcism among the methods. Even the word is read that way: Tibetan Buddhists take the etymology of mantra as mind protector, and Tsongkhapa says a mantra "protects the mind from ordinary appearances and conceptions".

What the objects claim is specific. James Gentry, writing for the Rubin Museum's Project Himalayan Art, says Tibetans have used protective amulets against misfortune during travel, injury during battle, illness, harmful spirits, and any other potential calamity — and that relic pills of the kind kept in an amulet box need not be consumed to have effect, and are held to protect not only against mundane dangers but against rebirth as an animal, an anguished spirit or a hell being.

The twentieth century broke the institutions that make these things. In 1959 the fourteenth Dalai Lama and a great number of clergy and lay people left for India and neighbouring countries; the Cultural Revolution, 1966 to 1976, targeted religion, most of the several thousand temples and monasteries in Tibet were destroyed, monks and lamas were imprisoned and forced to disrobe, and much of the textual heritage went with them. Prayer flags were discouraged but not eliminated, and many traditional designs may have been lost. *Inference —* the trade in Himalayan amulets that a visitor meets in Kathmandu today sits on the far side of that break, which is one reason provenance questions in this material are so hard.
text.how: Made and consecrated by lamas; given to named people. This atlas prints what published scholarship describes — that an amulet is a geometric diagram with mantras and images, consecrated through contemplative ritual proceedings, folded, wrapped in five-coloured cords with sacred substances, and distributed — and prints no diagram, no mantra sequence and no consecration. The reason is the tradition's own: these practices sit inside Vajrayana, the Secret Mantra, where a practitioner must receive an empowerment from a qualified lama, and without initiation one is generally not allowed to practise the higher Tantras.
text.today: Practised across Tibet, Bhutan, Nepal, Ladakh, Sikkim, Mongolia and the Buryat, Tuvan and Kalmyk regions of Russia, and in the diaspora since 1959. Amulet boxes, wrapped amulets, prayer flags and dzi beads are also made for sale to buyers outside the tradition, and an object bought that way carries no record of who consecrated it — the market's standing problem, in metal, paper and stone alike.

restricted.note: The designs inside Tibetan protective amulets, the mantras written on them, and the rites that consecrate them belong to tantric practice, which Tibetan Buddhism restricts to those who have received an empowerment from a qualified lama. This atlas prints published descriptions of what these objects are and what they are carried against, and does not reproduce a design, a mantra sequence or a consecration, and does not reconstruct one from scattered sources.
restricted.who_says: Tibetan Buddhism's own rule on empowerment — without initiation one is generally not allowed to practise the higher Tantras — and the published scholarship, which stops at the same line

names.name: West African charm craft
names.said: the Fon word for a charm is bǒ; Francophone Beninese say gris gris; the Hausa-derived English word is juju
names.th: งานเครื่องรางแอฟริกาตะวันตก

text.what: Not one practice but a shelf of them, made by different specialists for different clients across Benin, Togo, Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal, Mali, Niger and Cameroon: written Qur'anic charms sewn into cloth sacks; assembled charms of plant and animal matter activated by words; carved figures; cast shells read for answers. Four different vocabularies cover them, and this record keeps them apart rather than merging them.
text.story:
Start with the words, because they belong to different peoples and get used interchangeably in English.

Bǒ is Fon, and translates as charm. Bǒ are amulets made from zoological and botanical material, activated with secret incantations in a language called bǒgbé, 'bǒ's language'. Families and individuals keep their recipes closely guarded, on a widespread belief that anyone who learns the exact ingredients gains power over the maker. Many Francophone Beninese call them gris gris. They are sold: tourists buy them for love, for wealth, or for protection while travelling, and a diviner — a bokónó — charges a rate that varies with who the client is, less for family, more for a tourist or a middle-class Beninese client.

Gris-gris is Mande, and the line behind it is Muslim and scholarly. Mande speakers such as the Dyula distributed Islamic charms under that name; the Dagomba wrote extensive Arabic manuscripts with formulae and prescriptions for preparing amulets. The craft has a curriculum: Karamokobara, divided into seli, prayer, and siri, path. Seli produces karamokos, scholars of Qur'anic law; siri produces marabouts, scholars of the written charms. The tools of the siri side are spoken prayers, numerical squares called katemi, and written Qur'anic inscriptions. Islam shows up inside non-Islamic practice too — Vodún charms occasionally use Islamic script.

Juju is from Hausa, where it means evil spirit; some derive it instead from the French joujou, a plaything. In its general English use it covers magical properties to do with luck of either kind, and it has been applied to West African traditional religions broadly. A juju man is a man vetted by local tradition and versed in traditional spiritual medicines; the practice is most often used for treating physical and spiritual ailments, and is also used to enforce a contract or ensure compliance, with the practitioner paid for the service. The same word gets attached to serious crime: the source records that crimes have been committed using the practice, human trafficking being the most extreme and prominent example, and that nineteenth-century traders and travellers in the Niger Delta and Benin published accounts of a list of practices they said they had witnessed. *Inference —* those nineteenth-century accounts were written by men with commercial and colonial interests in the region, and this atlas reports that they exist and who wrote them rather than treating them as a neutral inventory.

Cowries run through all of it as a fourth strand. They are cast in divination among the Yoruba, in Ifá, and in the annual customs of Dahomey in Benin, and in Brazil the same shells are thrown to consult the Orixás — a direct line out of this coast.

And there is a market with an address. The Akodessawa Fetish Market, Marché des Féticheurs, in the Akodessawa district of Lomé, Togo, sells the materials used in vodún practice: monkey heads, skulls, dead birds, crocodiles, skins and other products of dead animals. It is described as the largest such market in the world. *Tradition holds —* what is sold there is raw material for a specialist, not a finished charm for a buyer.
text.how: By specialist and by rule, and the rules are not the same from one strand to the next. A marabout writes; a bokónó divines and then supplies; a bǒ-maker assembles plant and animal matter and speaks over it in bǒgbé; a diviner casts cowries and reads what falls. Payment is normal and openly discussed in the sources: fees scale with the client.
text.today: Living, commercial and mixed with other religions rather than sealed off from them. Many people in West Africa draw on traditional religion, Christianity and Islam at once to deal with a problem, and a Vodún practitioner may read Jesus as a vodún. Since the 1990s there have been growing efforts to bring foreign visitors to West Africa to be initiated into Vodún, which puts the tourist inside the practice rather than outside it — an argument this atlas reports and does not settle. As of 2026 no figure has been read here for what any of this is worth.

names.name: The bell
names.said: tintinnabulum, the Roman wind chime of bells
names.th: กระดิ่ง

text.what: A small bell, hung or carried, that sounds when the air or the body it is attached to moves. The sign is audible rather than visible, which makes it the only entry in this atlas that a person could use with their eyes shut.
text.story:
Rome hung its bells at the door and put a phallus on them. A tintinnabulum is a wind chime or assemblage of bells, often taking the form of a bronze ithyphallic figure or of a fascinum, the magico-religious phallus. They were hung near thresholds at a shop or house, under the peristyles, by the bedroom or the venereum, where the wind would set them tinkling, and some were rigged to a cord and bell pull to work as doorbells. The cited account gives the Roman reason for the noise: the sounds of bells kept away evil spirits. Examples have been found at Pompeii and Herculaneum, and a number of them are in the Secret Museum collection at the Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli. The phallic charm and the bell are the same object: phallic charms, often winged, appear in Roman culture as jewellery, relief carvings, lamps and wind chimes.

Korea rings its bells to bring spirits in. During a gut, the mudang carries a fan and brass bells; the scholar Sarfati commented that these bells were "a central symbol" of Musok, and their purpose is to attract the attention of the spirits. The rite's music regularly involves cymbals, hourglass-shaped changgu drums and a gong, and the mudang dances by swirling in circles, which the same account reports as facilitating the possession trance.

*Inference —* those two uses are opposite, and that is the interesting fact about this sign. A Roman bell rings on its own, unsupervised, at a threshold, to push something out. A Korean bell is shaken by a named specialist, inside a rite, to pull something in. The noise is the same; the direction is reversed, and it is the practitioner's presence or absence that decides which way it runs. No source read here connects the two customs, and this atlas does not.
text.notes: This record is short because the sources read here document the bell in two places only. It is filed under the sound family, added to the vocabulary for it: a bell is a hollow vessel, but what it is carried for is the noise.

text.what: A round disc of copper alloy, brass or bronze with a square hole punched through the middle, the four sides of the hole framed by characters. It is the shape of Chinese money for two thousand years, and it is also the shape of a charm that was never money. Most numismatic charms imitate whatever circulating cash coin was current when they first appeared; some were cast instead as spades, locks, fish, peaches and gourds.
text.story:
The charm coin — yansheng qian, now more often called huaqian, flower coin — first appears under the Western Han as a variant of the Ban Liang and Wu Zhu cash coins. It was used to speak to the dead, to pray for a good outcome, to frighten ghosts and as lucky money. Over centuries it became a separate commodity with its own shapes and sizes. Unlike a cash coin, which carries two or four characters on a side, a charm often carries more characters, and pictures on the same side.

These were mostly privately funded and cast by wealthy families for their own ceremonies, though governments and religious orders cast some. They circulated alongside official coinage and held value because they were made of copper alloy and Chinese coins were valued by weight in bronze or brass. In periods of copper scarcity they worked as alternative currency — temple coins were issued by Buddhist temples under the Yuan when copper was short or deliberately limited by the Mongol government.

The square hole is not only an opening. It is called an eye, yǎn, and Chinese charms are built on visual puns: a gourd charm made of two Wu Zhu replicas with a bat covering the character where they meet reads as happiness is before your eyes, because bat sounds like happiness and coin sounds like before. A charm's meaning is frequently a rebus you have to hear rather than see.

The forms multiply from there. Open-work charms have irregular openings between the design elements and usually a single large round hole, or a square one where the design is a building. Lock charms are flat, have no moving parts, resemble the character 凹, and were tied around children's necks by Buddhist or Taoist priests; the hundred family lock was funded by a poor family asking a hundred other families each to give a cash coin for a newborn. Pendant charms were worn at the neck or waist from the beginning of the Han, or fixed to rafters, pagodas, temples and lanterns; fish and lock charms were worn mainly by young children and infants. Han pendant charms carry inscriptions like chu xiong qu yang, do away with evil and dispel calamity, and bi bing mo dang, avoid hostilities and ward off sickness.

Qing-era cash coins of the five emperors Shunzhi, Kangxi, Yongzheng, Qianlong and Jiaqing are strung together as a set said to bring wealth and good fortune. Strung coins are also built into swords: in feng shui, coin-swords are hung to frighten demons and evil spirits away.

Chinese charms inspired the same tradition in Japan, Korea and Vietnam, and charms from those countries are regularly mistaken for Chinese ones because the symbolism and inscriptions are close. Chinese cash coins themselves are treated as lucky charms outside China.

names.name: The crescent
names.th: พระจันทร์เสี้ยว

text.what: A moon with its middle cut out, two horns and a curved back, hung point-up at the neck. Roman ones are gold. Isidore of Seville defines them as female ornaments in the likeness of the moon, little hanging gold bullae. The shape is a lune in geometry and a crescent in heraldry only when the horns point up.
text.story:
Rome gave the crescent to girls. A lunula was worn as an apotropaic amulet — a charm meant to turn harm away — and stood as the girl's equivalent of the boy's bulla. Romans wore amulets against evil forces, demons and sorcery, and above all against the evil eye. In Plautus's Epidicus, Epidicus asks the girl Telestis whether she remembers his bringing her a gold lunula on her birthday and a little gold ring for her finger; in Rudens, Palaestra says her father gave her a golden bulla on the day she was born. Lunulae were common across the whole Mediterranean, while the bulla stayed mostly Italian.

As a sign rather than an amulet the crescent is older and travels further. It stands for the moon and for the moon deity Nanna or Sin in Akkadian cylinder seals as early as 2300 BCE. Egypt's logograph for the moon is a crescent. Phoenicians carried it as far as Carthage and Numidia in the eighth century BCE. The star-and-crescent pair arises in the ancient Near East for the moon and Ishtar as the planet Venus, often with the solar disk as a third, and was inherited in Sassanian and Hellenistic iconography. It moved into Islamic iconography from Sassanian use after the Muslim conquest of Persia, and into Marian iconography in Christianity through the Woman of the Apocalypse, with the moon under her feet.

*Inference —* two different things share this outline and this atlas does not merge them. The Roman lunula is a birth-gift to a named child; the star-and-crescent is a dynastic and then a religious emblem. Nothing read here shows the second growing out of the first.

names.name: The cross
names.th: กางเขน

text.what: Two lines crossing, usually at right angles. The variations are named and they matter: the †-shaped crux immissa, the T-shaped crux commissa or tau, the X-shaped crux decussata or saltire, the crux ansata with a loop on top. Worn as a pendant, tattooed at the wrist, woven from rushes, cast in Saharan silver, hung over a door.
text.story:
Two intersecting lines are the cheapest mark a hand can make, so the shape has no single origin. Cross-shaped incisions appear from deep prehistory, as petroglyphs in European cult caves from the beginning of the Upper Palaeolithic and right through to the Iron Age. The cross mark also turns up as a number independently — Roman X for ten, Chinese rod numeral 十 for ten, the Brahmi numeral that becomes 4 — and in the Phoenician alphabet it is taw, whose name means mark.

The Christian cross is a later, dated adoption of an existing shape. It came into use as an emblem of Christianity from the second century CE, in the Latin letter T form, after Ichthys. Clement of Alexandria in the early third century calls it the Lord's sign. Tertullian, writing De Corona in 204, says it was already a tradition for Christians to trace the sign repeatedly on their foreheads — a cross made of a gesture before it is made of metal. Crosses with intersecting beams appear in Christian art towards the end of Late Antiquity; the patriarchal cross first appears in the tenth century; heraldry multiplies the forms from the Crusades onward.

What gets hung on a neck varies by church and by craft. The Coptic cross is two bold equal bars, each ending in three points for the Trinity, twelve points in all for the Apostles, often with a circle at the centre for God's love; the trefoil form developed locally from the short Greek cross. Many Copts have a cross tattooed on the inside of the right wrist as a sign of faith. In Ireland the cross is woven: the National Museum of Ireland sorts Brigid's crosses into seven categories by build rather than by outline, including a bent-armed type and a wheel type.

The Tuareg Agadez cross is the case that resists the word. Only a few tanaghilt actually resemble a cross; most are pendants with a varied silhouette, cast by blacksmiths in silver by lost-wax and never hammered. Asked what it means, users generally give vague answers; some call it a grigri or a reserve of wealth. The ethnologists Germaine Dieterlen and Ziedonis Ligers recorded a father giving the jewel to his son at the age of virility, marriage and nomadism with the words: my son, I give you the four directions of the world, because we do not know where you will go to die.

*Inference —* filing all of these under one sign is a convenience of shape, not a claim of common descent, and the Agadez piece is here mainly to show where the convenience breaks.

text.what: A name of God, or of an angel, or a string of characters that stands in for one, written on the object and doing the work. Sometimes it is legible and sometimes it is deliberately not. On a mezuzah it is three Hebrew letters on the outside of the parchment. On an Islamic amulet it is one of the ninety-nine names, or a Qur'anic verse. On a Taoist fu it is a character that resembles Chinese writing and is not meant to be read.
text.story:
Each tradition here has its own account and this record keeps them separate.

In Jewish practice the name on the doorpost is Shaddai, written on the outside of the mezuzah parchment opposite the space between the two passages; it also reads as an acronym for Shomer Daltot Yisrael, Guardian of Israel's doors, and many cases carry just the letter shin for it. The same three letters are built into tefillin: the head-strap's knot forms a dalet, the arm-strap's a yud, and with the shin on the head-box they spell Shaddai. But the practice is contested from inside. Maimonides allows the name on the outside and then condemns what people do with it: those who write the names of angels, other sacred names, verses or forms inside a mezuzah, he writes, are among those who do not have a portion in the world to come — they nullify the commandment, and turn a great commandment about the unity of God's name into a talisman for their own benefit. A bathroom and a small closet get no mezuzah, because the name of God is forbidden there.

Practical Kabbalah, Kabbalah Ma'asit, is the branch that uses divine and angelic names for amulets and incantations. Gershom Scholem's account is that much of its content predates the speculative Kabbalah and does not depend on it, being an accumulation of magical practices from Talmudic times through the Middle Ages. The Talmud and Midrash call the theurgic technique using the Divine Name. In the Hekhalot literature the angels guarding each heavenly level are bound by formulae and seals. The tradition restricts itself: it was held to be permitted only to an elite, and only under conditions that were holy and pure, and most Kabbalists taught that its use is forbidden.

In Islamic practice the amulet usually contains one of God's ninety-nine names, or the names of angels or prophets, or a Qur'anic verse, a pious phrase or an invocation, and has been described as a supercharged prayer. Virtually all Muslim scholars permit a talisman that calls on God or on an intercessor; addressing jinn or demons is prohibited. Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse, al-Baqara 2:255, is the verse most often used: hadith say reciting it turns away devils and fiends, and it is recited before a journey, before sleep, and after every obligatory prayer. Because of that association it is also used against the evil eye. Letter-and-number work, ʿilm al-ḥurūf, combines the letters of one of the ninety-nine names with those of a desired object — the technique called jafr.

In Taoist practice the writing is meant to defeat reading. Fulu are talismanic script written on talismans by Taoist priests. Ge Hong noted in the Baopuzi, by the Eastern Jin, 317–420, that it was already unnecessary for the user to decipher the writing for it to work. Scholars including James Robson and Gil Raz argue the incomprehensibility is central to the talisman's perceived authority; Ge Zhaoguang of Fudan University calls it a deliberate linguistic archaism. The method of writing the characters is passed in secret from a Taoist priest to their disciples. Fulu were taken into forms of Chinese Buddhism and inspired the Japanese ofuda and the Korean bujeok.

Gnostic gems give the oldest surviving objects in this family that carry a name and nothing else. Abrasax, later spelled Abraxas, appears in nearly all the legends on the gems, in the Greek Magical Papyri and in Gnostic texts; the attempts to derive the name from Greek, Hebrew, Coptic or Egyptian have not succeeded. The seven letters may stand for the seven classical planets.

*Inference —* the four traditions agree on one thing only: the name is not decoration and the object is not the charm. What they disagree about is whether writing a name down is prayer, permitted craft, or an offence against the name itself.

restricted.note: Practical Kabbalah's techniques for writing divine and angelic names are restricted within the tradition itself: they were held to be reserved for an elite, to require conditions of holiness and purity, and most Kabbalists taught their use is forbidden. Isaac Luria forbade his students to write amulets. Most practical Kabbalistic writing stayed in manuscript rather than going into print. This atlas prints that position and does not reconstruct the formulae.
restricted.who_says: Gershom Scholem's account of the tradition; Isaac Luria, who forbade his students from writing amulets and from other techniques of practical Kabbalah; Moshe Idel on the Spanish tradition

names.name: The eye
names.th: ดวงตา

text.what: An eye, drawn or moulded, worn where another person will see it. It is the most widespread sign in this atlas and the only one whose logic is stated out loud by its carriers everywhere it appears: harm arrives by looking, so the answer looks back.
text.story:
Amulets against a harmful look have been found dating to around five thousand years ago, and the belief runs through the Mediterranean, the Balkans, Eastern Europe, West Asia, Central Asia, South Asia, Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America. Jewish rabbinic literature returns to it repeatedly.

The sign takes two different bodies. In Egypt it is a drawn eye with a falcon's cheek-line, cut in faience and carnelian from the Old Kingdom onward. Around the eastern Mediterranean it becomes a bead: after glass-bead production got going in the region around 1500 BCE, blue-and-white concentric eye beads spread among Phoenicians, Persians, Greeks, Romans, Arabs and Ottomans, and that bead is what a shop in Istanbul or Athens sells today.

What is striking is what stands in for the eye where the eye is not drawn. Illyrians used shapes of the phallus, the hand, the leg and animal teeth against the same harm. Romans used the fascinum, a winged phallus. Southern Italy still cuts a horn. *Inference —* the substitutions have one thing in common: each is a thing that catches a glance. The mechanism carriers describe is interception, and anything startling enough to take a look can do the job. That is why this atlas files the horn, the hand and the fist as kin of the eye rather than as unrelated signs.

*Tradition holds —* the harm is usually attributed to envy, and often to admiration that has not been qualified. That is why the eye is put on children, on livestock and on new houses more than on anything else.

names.name: The fish
names.th: ปลา

text.what: A fish in outline, usually two curved strokes crossing at the tail. In Christian use the Greek letters ΙΧΘΥΣ are sometimes written inside it. In China it is cast as a coin charm shaped like a fish and hung on a child. In Aotearoa the related shape is not a fish but the hook that catches one.
text.story:
The Christian fish is an acrostic before it is an animal. ΙΧΘΥΣ spells out Ἰησοῦς Χρῑστός Θεοῦ Υἱός Σωτήρ — Jesus Christ, God's Son, Saviour. It appears in Christian art and literature from the second century CE and is widespread by the late second to fourth. It is found in the Catacombs of Saint Sebastian and the Catacomb of Priscilla, in the marble ruins of Ephesus, and on funerary stelae carrying inscriptions such as ΙΧΘΥϹ ΖΩΝΤΩΝ, fish of the living.

The story most people have heard about it is disputed. Robert Mowat proposed in 1900 that it was a secret sign among persecuted Christians, arguing from silence. Modern scholarship disputes that: Rasimus lists it among solutions that were once popular, and no early Christian source ties the fish to persecution. The connections the early sources do make are to baptism, to the Eucharist and to the feeding of the multitude.

The fish also turns up on a dated amulet with a word square on its back. The earliest Sator square with explicit Christian imagery is a sixth-century bronze amulet from Asia Minor: two fish turned towards one another on one side, the Sator square in Greek characters on the other, and ICHTHUS written above the square. It is in the Berlin State Museums.

China's fish is a coin. Among the shapes Chinese numismatic charms took as they separated from circulating coinage were spades, locks, fish, peaches and gourds, and fish and lock charms were worn mainly by young children and infants — daily wear rather than festival wear.

*Inference —* this atlas has not found a source connecting the Christian fish and the Chinese fish charm, and does not connect them. A fish is a common animal and an easy outline; two traditions reaching for it is not evidence of contact.

names.name: The fig fist
names.said: in Italian, mano fica or far le fiche; in Spanish, higa; in Portuguese and Galician, figa
names.th: กำปั้นฟิก (มาโนฟิกา)

text.what: A closed fist with the thumb pushed up between the index and middle fingers, carved or cast small and hung at the neck. In jet it is black and matte; in coral it is red; in silver it is the size of a thumb joint. The gesture it copies is obscene, and that is the working part.
text.story:
Rome called it the manus fica. The pater familias made it during the Lemuria to turn away the spirits of the dead. Early Christians called the same shape the manus obscena, the obscene hand. Greeks wore amulets of the gesture at the neck against the evil eye and drew it in their art; what they took to be an overtly sexual gesture was expected to distract harm from its target.

The fist also fused with another sign. Roman soldiers carried the fist-and-phallus amulet — a phallic pendant with a clenched fist at the base of the shaft, facing away from the glans, several of them making the fig sign. The largest known collection of them comes from Camulodunum, Roman Colchester. Some examples carry vulvar imagery as well.

The insult and the amulet never separated. In Italy the gesture was rude enough that Dante uses it in Inferno XXV; it has long since fallen out of use there. In Russia, Belarus and Ukraine it is shish, kukish or dulya, a flat refusal. In Turkey it is the equivalent of the middle finger. In Poland it means no. In Croatia, Serbia and Slovenia a fig hidden in a pocket marks a false oath.

In Portugal, Brazil and parts of Spain — Galicia and Asturias — the same hand is a wish of good luck and a guard against the evil eye. Asturian ones are made of jet and it is usual to give them to young children; Spanish calls them higas, Galician and Portuguese figas, Asturleonese ciguas. *Inference —* the same shape reads as a curse in one country and a christening present in the next, which is the clearest case in this atlas of a sign whose meaning is entirely local. In Britain, Ireland, France, Germany and North America it survives mainly as the game where an adult pretends to have stolen a child's nose.
text.today: Jet figas are still made and sold in Asturias and at Santiago de Compostela, where the jet trade grew up around pilgrims at the end of the Middle Ages. Brazilian figas are sold in wood, horn and gold.

names.name: The footprint
names.th: รอยพระพุทธบาท

text.what: The print of a foot, or of two feet side by side, cut in stone or wood or painted. A dharmachakra is often set at the centre of the sole, or the 32, 108 or 132 auspicious signs of the Buddha are engraved or painted across it. There are two kinds and the tradition distinguishes them: prints found in stone or rock, and prints made by hand.
text.story:
The footprint is a way of showing a person by showing where they stood. As a sculptural object it starts in India, in the pre-Greco-Buddhist phase, at sites like Sanchi and Bharhut — that is, in the period when the Buddha was represented by signs rather than by a body. Many of the prints found in rock are acknowledged within the tradition not to be prints of the Buddha's foot but replicas or representations, which can count as cetiya, relics.

The count is large. The Japanese scholar Motoji Niwa found more than 3,000 footprints, about 300 of them in Japan and more than 1,000 in Sri Lanka. The named sites include Sri Pada in Sri Lanka and Phra Phutthabat in Thailand, with more in Cambodia and Burma. In China, the discovery of a large footprint of the Buddha at Chengzhou during the Tang led the Empress Wu Zetian to declare a new era name in 701 CE — a footprint that reset the calendar.

One of the marks on the sole is a sign in its own right elsewhere in this atlas. In Buddhism the swastika is read as standing for the auspicious footprints of the Buddha, and a left-facing one is often imprinted on the chest, feet or palms of Buddha images. Theravada communities in Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia commonly associate the sign with the Buddha's footprints.

Portable versions exist. A Lanna buddhapada of the late fifteenth to early sixteenth century is teak decorated with mother of pearl and glass.

*Inference —* this is the only sign in this batch that is an absence rather than a thing: the shape of somebody who is no longer standing there. Whether it belongs among amulets at all depends on whether a thing you visit counts beside a thing you carry, and this atlas files it here because the small ones are carried.

text_th.what: รอยเท้าข้างเดียว หรือสองข้างเคียงกัน สลักบนหินหรือไม้ หรือวาดด้วยสี กลางฝ่าพระบาทมักมีธรรมจักร หรือมีมงคล 32, 108 หรือ 132 ประการของพระพุทธเจ้าสลักหรือวาดไว้ทั่วฝ่าพระบาท มีสองประเภท และประเพณีแยกแยะไว้ชัด: รอยที่พบบนหินหรือโขดหิน และรอยที่ทำขึ้นด้วยมือ
text_th.story:
รอยพระพุทธบาทเป็นวิธีแสดงถึงบุคคลหนึ่งด้วยการแสดงที่ที่ท่านเคยยืน ในฐานะวัตถุประติมากรรม เริ่มต้นในอินเดียในช่วงก่อนพุทธศิลป์แบบกรีก ที่แหล่งอย่างสาญจีและภารหุต — กล่าวคือ ในยุคที่พระพุทธเจ้าถูกแทนด้วยสัญลักษณ์ ไม่ใช่ด้วยพระวรกาย รอยจำนวนมากที่พบบนหินได้รับการยอมรับภายในประเพณีเองว่าไม่ใช่รอยจากพระบาทของพระพุทธเจ้า แต่เป็นรอยจำลองหรือรูปแทน ซึ่งนับเป็นเจติยะ (cetiya) หรือสิ่งเคารพบูชาได้

จำนวนนั้นมาก นักวิชาการญี่ปุ่น โมโตจิ นิวะ (Motoji Niwa) พบรอยพระพุทธบาทกว่า 3,000 รอย ราว 300 รอยอยู่ในญี่ปุ่น และกว่า 1,000 รอยอยู่ในศรีลังกา แหล่งที่มีชื่อได้แก่ศรีปาทะในศรีลังกา และพระพุทธบาทในประเทศไทย และมีอีกในกัมพูชาและพม่า ในจีน การค้นพบรอยพระพุทธบาทขนาดใหญ่ที่เฉิงโจวในสมัยราชวงศ์ถัง ทำให้จักรพรรดินีบูเช็กเทียน (Wu Zetian) ทรงประกาศชื่อรัชศกใหม่ใน ค.ศ. 701 — รอยพระบาทที่ตั้งปฏิทินใหม่

เครื่องหมายหนึ่งบนฝ่าพระบาทเป็นเครื่องหมายที่มีระเบียนของตัวเองอยู่ที่อื่นในแอตลาสนี้ ในพระพุทธศาสนา สวัสดิกะถูกอ่านว่าหมายถึงรอยพระพุทธบาทอันเป็นมงคล และสวัสดิกะแบบหันซ้ายมักประทับไว้ที่พระอุระ พระบาท หรือฝ่าพระหัตถ์ของพระพุทธรูป ชุมชนเถรวาทในเมียนมา ไทย และกัมพูชา มักเชื่อมโยงเครื่องหมายนี้กับรอยพระพุทธบาท

มีแบบที่พกพาได้ด้วย รอยพระพุทธบาทล้านนาสมัยพุทธศตวรรษที่ 21 (ปลายคริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 15 ถึงต้นคริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 16) ทำจากไม้สักประดับมุกและกระจก

*ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* นี่คือเครื่องหมายเดียวในชุดนี้ที่เป็นร่องรอยของการไม่อยู่ มากกว่าเป็นสิ่งของ: รูปร่างของผู้ที่ไม่ได้ยืนอยู่ตรงนั้นแล้ว มันควรอยู่ในหมวดเครื่องรางหรือไม่ ขึ้นอยู่กับว่าสิ่งที่คุณเดินทางไปสักการะนับรวมกับสิ่งที่คุณพกติดตัวได้หรือไม่ และแอตลาสนี้จัดไว้ที่นี่เพราะรอยขนาดเล็กถูกพกติดตัว

names.name: The hand
names.th: มือ

text.what: A human hand, cast or cut flat and hung where it can be seen. It comes in three postures this atlas keeps apart: the palm open with five fingers spread, the fist with the thumb pushed between two fingers, and two fingers extended with the thumb folded over. Each is a gesture first and an object second — the metal copies something a living hand does.
text.story:
Open-hand motifs run through the ancient Near East. Von Kemnitz records amulets of the hand of Ishtar used in Mesopotamia and Babylon to keep evil or disease from entering a building. At Khirbet el-Qom in Judah an Iron Age tomb carries an engraved hand beside an inscription; what it meant is argued over, and the usual reading is a protective sign in a funerary setting. One of the first appearances of the hand as the amulet now called the hamsa is in Israelite tombs of around 800 BCE.

The name it travels under is not one name. Khamsa is Arabic for five. Hand of Fatima is a label Europeans popularised in French colonial North Africa, not an Arabic term. Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews call it the hand of Miriam; Levantine Christians call it kef Miryam, the hand of Mary; in Berber languages afus is simply hand. One shape, five communities, five names, and the argument over which name to print is live.

In al-Andalus the hand is well documented from the thirteenth century onward. Among Moriscos in Granada, khamsa pendants were described as large engraved medals with a hand inscribed with letters, likely Qur'anic. A reform council banned them in 1526 as Islamic symbols and ordered crosses in their place; the Synod of Guadix renewed the ban in 1554. Christians wore them anyway — a Nasrid-period gold pendant is inscribed Ave Maria gratia plena.

*Inference —* filing the open palm, the fist and the horned hand as one family is this project's decision, not a claim any of their carriers make. What they share is a gesture arrested in metal and aimed outward. Each has its own record here.

names.name: The horn
names.th: เขา (คอร์นิเชลโล)

text.what: A single twisted horn, tapering to a point, hung at a neck or a rear-view mirror. Gold, silver, plastic, bone, terracotta, or the red coral that is the version Naples is known for. A few centimetres long. The hand version — the mano cornuta, two fingers extended and held pointing downward with a swivelling motion — is the same sign made of fingers.
text.story:
The horn is worn against the malocchio, the evil eye, and against bad luck generally, and historically for fertility and virility. It is a regional amulet before it is an Italian one: most often worn by men in southern Italy, above all in Campania, then Lazio, Apulia and Basilicata, and less in Sicily and Calabria.

What the horn is a horn of is an open question. Cornicelli are thought to be modelled on an eland horn. The red ones look like a chili pepper, and dried chilies are hung in some southern Italian houses against the malocchio — but chilies reached Europe only after the Columbian exchange, so the resemblance is younger than the shape. The classical lines pull in several directions at once: the cornucopia broken from a goat by Zeus; coral sacred to Venus; silver sacred to Luna; the phallic outline and the red pointing to Priapus; the horn itself to Pan.

What the harm is said to reach is specific. The malocchio is described as harming nursing mothers and their babies, fruiting trees, milking animals and the sperm of men — the forces of generation, in that order.

The horn moved from the animal to the machine without changing shape. Cornicelli hang from rear-view mirrors now, which the sources trace to the older custom of hanging them on draft horses.

*Inference —* this atlas files the horn beside the eye rather than as an unrelated sign, because the logic its carriers describe is the same interception: a thing conspicuous enough to take the look meant for somebody else.
text.today: Made in gold and silver for jewellers, and in plastic by the tray for the tourist trade. San Gregorio Armeno in Naples sells both, on the same street, a few metres apart.

names.name: The key
names.th: กุญแจ

text.what: A key, drawn or hung. Nobody in this record carries one to open anything. The sign works on the idea that somewhere there is a door, that somebody holds the key to it, and that showing the key shows whose side you are on.
text.story:
Haiti keeps the clearest statement of it. Most lwa are matched to Roman Catholic saints by an analogy between their functions, and Papa Legba, as the key to the spirit world, is typically associated with Saint Peter, who traditionally holds keys in Roman Catholic imagery. That is not a resemblance somebody noticed later; it is the documented mechanism by which Vodou and Catholicism were joined, and the key is the hinge of the pairing.

Manila carries the keys on a building. Quiapo Church, built in the Baroque style, had a quatrefoil window in the centre of its pediment sealed up in the late 1980s and replaced with a relief of the crossed keys and tiara of the pope, marking its status as a minor basilica. The keys sit above a plaza where amulets and remedies are sold from stalls.

Naples hangs one on a sprig. The cimaruta's branches sprout small charms in combinations that vary by region, and the cited account gives one example outright: a cimaruta might bear the collective imagery of a key, dagger, blossom and moon.

Egypt supplies a key that is not one. The ankh is known in English as the ankh or as the "key of life", the second name based on its meaning rather than its shape; the sign is a T topped by a droplet loop, it wrote the three consonants of the word for life, and it appears in Egyptian art as an object held by deities and handed to the pharaoh. *Inference —* the key reading came from outside. Nothing in the account of the sign's Egyptian use involves a lock, a door or an opening; the loop over a bar was named a key by people who already had a sign for a key and wanted one here. This atlas files it under this motif because that is the name the ankh now travels under, and marks where the name came from.

So: one documented loan, one badge of rank, one component on a compound charm, and one English gloss. The Neapolitan key sits inside the same Catholic world as the papal keys, and it would be easy to join them; no source read here does, and neither does this record.
text.notes: A short record, and short on purpose. Four appearances, two traditions, and one of the four is a translator's name rather than a carrier's. It is filed under the tool family, added to the vocabulary for it; house would fit it about as well, since half of what a key means here is the door it belongs to.

names.name: The knot
names.th: ปม

text.what: A tie, either made in cloth and thread or copied in stone and metal. Two kinds sit under one heading: the knot that is actually tied — a red string on a wrist, a thousand stitches in a soldier's belt, rushes woven on a feast day — and the knot that is depicted, cut in jasper or drawn as a hieroglyph, with nothing to untie.
text.story:
Egypt gives the depicted knot its clearest case. The tyet resembles a knot of cloth and may have started as a bandage to absorb menstrual blood. An early example comes from a First Dynasty tomb at Helwan, excavated by Zaki Saad in the 1940s — old enough to predate the first written references to Isis, whom it was later tied to. From the early New Kingdom, roughly 1550 BCE, tyet amulets went into the wrappings, usually on the upper torso, and from then to the end of dynastic Egypt few people were buried without one. Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead calls for a tyet of red jasper at the mummy's neck and says the power of Isis will protect the body and drive away whoever would commit a crime against it. Green faience examples were made too, the colour standing for renewed life. The tyet can be compared with the Minoan sacral knot at Knossos — a knot with a projecting loop — and the comparison is offered as a resemblance, not a descent.

The tied knot is a different object with a different working part: somebody's hands did it, at a named time, and it can be undone. Bulgarian and Macedonian martenitsi are twisted red and white yarn, given never bought, worn from 1 March and taken off at the sight of a stork or a blossoming tree — sometimes tied then onto a fruit tree. Romanian mărțișor uses the same two threads and is described by observers as funia anului, the year's rope, winding summer into winter. Irish Brigid's crosses are woven from straw or rushes on 1 February and hung in the rafters. Japanese senninbari carry a thousand knots, each made by a different woman, for a soldier going to war.

Undoing is part of the grammar. Islamic hadith describe a charm worked against Muhammad; in one variant he is cured only after the charm — a knot — is taken and taken apart. *Inference —* a knot is the one amulet form that carries its own cancellation in its shape, which is why so many traditions put a date on when it comes off.

names.name: The lion
names.th: สิงโต

text.what: A lion's head on a human body, a lioness's paws on a hippopotamus, or a lion reared up on its hind legs. The sign is a predator set between a person and whatever is coming, and it is nearly always attached to something else — this is a face and a set of paws borrowed onto another body rather than a whole animal drawn on its own.
text.story:
Egypt put the lion in the birth room. The two gods most frequently invoked in Egyptian household apotropaic ritual were Taweret and Bes, and Bes is described in that account as the lion-deity, developed from the earlier dwarf god Aha, 'fighter'. James Romano, Egyptologist and former Curator of Egyptian Art at the Brooklyn Museum, holds that in its earliest inception Bes was a representation of a lion rearing up on its hind legs. Taweret takes the form of a female hippopotamus with the tail of a Nile crocodile and the paws of a lioness, features that parallel other ferocious protective deities, in her case Sekhmet the lioness goddess; her predatory form is what lets her ward evil away from the innocent.

Mesopotamia gave the face to the thing being warded off. Lamashtu has "the head of a lion, the teeth of a donkey, naked breasts, a hairy body, hands stained (with blood?), long fingers and fingernails, and the feet of Anzû", and her amulets vary: a canine or leonine face, talons, wings. An obsidian amulet in the Metropolitan Museum of Art gives her a lion-griffin-like head, raised clawed hands and the feet of a bird of prey. The lion is also overhead — the astral-medical text LBAT 1597 reads, "If (the moon is) in the region of Leo, lamaštu, labašu, and ahhazu-demons, the seized-by-lamaštu(-disease), seized by lamaštu day-and-night(-disease), the god is a lion related to a belligerent god, Ištar, and Hand of the Ghost-disease, (in the region of) Venus and Leo."

This is one of the few families in the atlas where transmission is argued from excavated objects rather than from resemblance. Some scholars hold that Bes is a counterpart of the Mesopotamian Pazuzu: both are protector demons of the home, both have lion parts, wings, a long phallus and similar facial features, both sit similarly on protective amulets, and both are associated with protecting pregnant women and mothers. The contact is physical. A possible Pazuzu figure has been found in Egypt and Bes amulets at sites in Iran, and in a seventh-century-BCE fort at Nimrud five Pazuzu heads were found near a Bes amulet. The derivation, though, stays open: one theory connects both names to the king name Bazi, and the cited account states that neither Pazuzu's name has been shown to come from Bazi nor Bes's name proved to be foreign.

Late antiquity mixed the head into a composite. E. A. Wallis Budge, describing the figure that carries the name Abraxas on magical gems, wrote that "as a Pantheus, i.e. All-God, he appears on the amulets with the head of a cock (Phœbus) or of a lion (Ra or Mithras), the body of a man, and his legs are serpents which terminate in scorpions, types of the Agathodaimon." On other gems Abraxas stands upon a lion borne by a crocodile, and departed spirits ride the back of a crocodile or a lion on the journey to judgment. Budge's gloss names the borrowing outright: the lion head is read as Ra or Mithras, which is a syncretism rather than a coincidence.

The last dated appearance here is an instruction rather than an object. The Pseudo-Aristotelian Sirr al-Asrar, in the Arabic Hermetica perhaps dating to the ninth century CE, gives a kings' talisman that keeps harm away: under certain astrological marks, a ruby-red stone is carved on a Thursday with a winged, crowned man riding a lion with a flag, six hairless men bowing beneath his hands, and the stone is then burned in an extended ritual.
text.notes: No source read here documents a living lion amulet, so this record closes in the ninth century CE rather than at the present day. That is a gap in the sources, not a statement that the sign died; it is marked so a later pass can fill it.

names.name: The number square
names.said: wafq al-aʿdād, 'harmonious disposition of the numbers'; in Hebrew, kamea; in Chinese, Luoshu
names.th: ตารางตัวเลข (ตารางมหัศจรรย์)

text.what: A grid of numbers in which every row, every column and both diagonals add to the same total. The order is the number of cells along a side; the total is the magic constant. Written on paper, engraved on metal, sewn into a shirt, cut into a temple wall. The 3×3 and the 4×4 do most of the amulet work.
text.story:
This one has to be told four times, because four traditions arrived at the same grid and gave four accounts of what it was for.

China has it first. The 3×3 square was known to Chinese mathematicians as early as 190 BCE, in a text called Shushu jiyi, and is given explicitly by the first century CE in the Da Dai Liji. That earliest use is for divination and astrology. Chinese mathematicians called it the Nine Halls; the identification with the legendary Luoshu chart — the pattern of dots on a turtle's shell that rose out of the river Lo while King Yu was channelling a flood — was only made in the twelfth century, after which it was called the Luoshu square.

India's first uses are medical and practical. The 3×3 square first appears in the Gargasamhita, recommended to pacify the nine planets, the navagraha; the oldest version of that text is from 100 CE, though the planetary passage cannot be earlier than 400 CE. The first dateable 3×3 in India is in a medical text, Vrnda's Siddhayog of about 966 CE, prescribed to women in labour for an easy delivery. The oldest dateable fourth-order square in the world is in Varahamihira's Brhat Samhita of about 550 CE, and it is not a charm at all: it is a recipe grid for making perfumes from sixteen substances, with no magical properties attributed. A 4×4 square was inscribed on the wall of the Parshvanath temple at Khajuraho around the twelfth century, and is called the Chautisa Yantra after its magic sum of 34. Narayana Pandit, writing in 1356, says the point of studying these squares is to construct yantra, to deflate bad mathematicians, and for the pleasure of good ones.

The Islamic world produced the mathematics and then the amulets. The first dateable 3×3 in Arabic appears in Jābir ibn Hayyān's Kitab al-mawazin al-Saghir, tied to alchemy; the Arabic name, wafq al-aʿdād, means the harmonious disposition of the numbers, and the earliest treatises are purely mathematical. Squares of orders 3 to 9 appear in the Baghdad encyclopedia Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa of about 983. From the thirteenth century the squares were increasingly put to occult purposes: the Algerian Ahmad al-Buni, around 1225, attributed mystical properties to them in Shams al-Ma'arif and described how to construct them. The 3×3 was described as a child-bearing charm from its first literary appearances in Jābir and in al-Ghazālī, and it kept that role in the tradition of the planetary tables. The pairing of seven squares with the seven heavenly bodies first appears in Ibn Zarkali's Kitāb tadbīrāt al-kawākib, in eleventh-century al-Andalus, and survives in Greek, Arabic and Latin versions. In Islamic talismanic practice the 3×3 with the constant 15 was often associated with the four archangels; 6×6 squares are attested by the late tenth century but did not enter the magical vocabulary until the thirteenth. Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Kishnawi wrote on their theory in eighteenth-century West Africa.

Europe got them last, as occult objects, and had to rediscover the mathematics. They came through Spain and Italy; Ibn Zarkali's work was translated as Libro de Astromagia in the 1280s under Alfonso X. The magic square of three was discussed numerologically by Abraham ibn Ezra of Toledo in the early twelfth century, which influenced later Kabbalists. Around 1315 Manuel Moschopoulos wrote a mathematical treatise that left the mysticism out. Agrippa gave the planetary squares in De occulta philosophia in 1531; Paracelsus reproduced them in garbled form in 1567; Dürer put a 4×4 into Melencolia I in 1514. By the eighteenth century the earlier mysticism had gone and the subject was recreational mathematics.

*Inference —* the same grid carries a Chinese divination, an Indian childbirth charm, an Islamic archangel invocation and a Renaissance planetary correspondence. Transmission is documented for some of those links and not for others; where it is not documented, this record says so rather than assuming.

names.name: The mirror
names.said: bāguà jìng, the eight-trigram mirror; in Mongolian, toli
names.th: กระจก

text.what: A disc of polished metal, worn or hung so it faces outward. Two well-documented kinds: the Chinese bagua mirror, octagonal or circular, with the eight trigrams ringed around a flat, convex or concave glass, fixed above a door or window; and the Mongolian and Buryat toli, a round brass, copper or bronze mirror ornamented on one face and polished on the other, worn at a shaman's neck or sewn in quantity onto the deel or apron.
text.story:
The bagua mirror is a feng shui remedy rather than a feng shui instrument, and its users are clear about the difference: a luopan measures, this one acts. Modern ones descend from ancient bronze-cast versions used by Taoist masters to perform mirror techniques, 鏡術, said to reveal or destroy evil spirits and to overcome natural calamities. The three shapes do three jobs in the tradition's own account: flat reflects, convex disperses, concave converges or absorbs external sha qi — poison arrows — and so changes the feng shui of a house.

What counts as a poison arrow is concrete: the sharp corner of a neighbouring building, or an open road running at your front door. Hang a mirror above the door or window facing it and the arrow is turned away. The problem is where it goes. Anything reflected is understood to be sent in the direction the mirror faces, so pointing a bagua mirror at a neighbour's house is offensive and is a feng shui taboo. The mirrors are cheap and self-installed, which makes them easy to misuse; feuds over offensively aimed mirrors are well known in Hong Kong and other dense Chinese communities, and have been parodied in popular culture. *Inference —* this is the only charm in this atlas whose standard grievance is that somebody else used one correctly.

The toli is worn, not hung. Shamans in parts of Mongolia and in the Republic of Buryatia wear them at the neck or on the ritual costume, which is often called armour, because these pieces protect the shaman from hostile spirit attack. Among the Daur the front and back of the costume were covered with small toli laid like overlapping scales, with up to eight large mirrors on the front and a medium one over the heart — the neker-toli, sometimes plated in nickel. The mirrors are also said to collect and store the power called wind horse, to house helper spirits, and to purify water or vodka. Among the Daur the number a shaman owns says how powerful they are.

*Inference —* a polished disc worn outward does the same physical thing in both traditions: it sends back whatever arrives. The explanations attached to it are not the same, and this record keeps them apart rather than writing one logic across both.

names.th: ฝ่ามือเปิด (ฮัมซา)

text.what: A flat hand, palm forward, five fingers spread and usually symmetrical — the two outer fingers drawn as thumbs so the sign reads the same either way up. Cast in silver or brass, cut in gold, pressed in glass. An eye is often set in the middle of the palm. It hangs at a neck, over a door and off a mirror from Morocco to Iraq.
text.story:
Five is the count and the name. The standard Arabic term is khamsa, five, with Maghrebi khmisa beside it. Hand of Fatima is a French colonial nickname, popularised by Europeans in North Africa rather than used in Arabic; in colonial-era French, fatma meant a Muslim or Arab woman. Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews say hand of Miriam. Levantine Christians say kef Miryam, hand of Mary. Berber afus just means hand.

Inside the Islamic world the amulet's documented use sits in the west — the Maghreb and historic al-Andalus — and is sparse in the Mashriq, where a hand in ritual use more often belongs to Shi'i iconography and not to this tradition. Von Kemnitz traces the route: Berbers brought the khamsa to al-Andalus; the expelled Muslim and Jewish population carried it back to North Africa with new motifs and techniques. In al-Andalus its use as an amulet is well documented from the thirteenth century.

The sign has an Egyptian claimant too. One account connects the khamsa with the Mano Pantea, an amulet Egyptians knew as the Two Fingers, where the two fingers stand for Isis and Osiris and the thumb for their child Horus, invoking a parent's protection over a child. *Inference —* that is a theory of origin, offered as one among several, and this atlas prints it as a theory.

In Jewish use the hand doubles as the letter shin, first letter of Shaddai, a name of God — one sign carrying two readings at once. It decorates ketubot and Torah pointers. It largely dropped out of Ashkenazi use by the mid-twentieth century and stayed in Sephardi and Mizrahi practice throughout.
text.today: Sold everywhere on the Mediterranean rim and online, in silver, in enamel, on phone cases and on keyrings, worn by people with no tie to any of the five naming communities. Whether a mass-produced khamsa is the same object as a Moroccan silversmith's is an argument with named people on both sides; this atlas reports it and does not settle it.

names.name: The word that reads both ways

text.what: Writing arranged so its shape is part of the instruction. Two forms carry most of it. ABRACADABRA is written as a triangle, a letter dropped from each line, worn on parchment at the neck. The Sator square is a 5×5 grid of five five-letter Latin words — SATOR AREPO TENET OPERA ROTAS — using eight letters, that reads the same across, down, backwards and upwards.
text.story:
ABRACADABRA is first attested in the second century CE, in the Liber Medicinalis of Serenus Sammonicus, physician to the emperor Caracalla. In chapter 52 he prescribes that sufferers from malaria wear an amulet with the word written in the form of a triangle; he claimed the amulet makes lethal diseases go away. The origin of the word is unknown. Conjectures point to an Aramaic phrase meaning 'I create like the word', to abraxas, or to the first four letters of the Greek alphabet, and the Oxford English Dictionary says no documentation has been found to support any of them. The historian Don Skemer suggests the Hebrew ha brachah dabarah. The Aramaic linguist Steve Caruso argues it cannot be Aramaic at all, and traces the popular Aramaic etymology to a long thread on an early internet message board.

The Gnostics of the sect of Basilides used it as a formula to call beneficent spirits against disease and misfortune, and it is found on Abraxas stones worn as amulets. Its use spread past them. A sick person wore the triangle on parchment at the neck, and the explanation recorded is that written that way it worked like a funnel, driving the sickness out of the body. A sixteenth-century Jewish codex from Italy, Ets ha-Da'at, gives it as an amulet and describes it as a cure from heavens for all sorts of fevers, for consumption and for fire. Not everyone agreed: the Puritan minister Increase Mather dismissed the word as having no power in it, and Daniel Defoe wrote dismissively about Londoners who posted it on their doorways during the Great Plague. Today it is mostly a stage-magic word.

The Sator square has harder dates and no agreed meaning. The oldest known one was found in November 1936, in ROTAS form, etched on column LXI of the Palestra Grande near the amphitheatre at Pompeii; graffiti on those columns predates the earthquake of AD 62. A second at the house of Publius Paquius Proculus, found in October 1925, dates between AD 50 and AD 79. Four were found at Dura-Europos in Syria in 1931–32, on the walls of military buildings, dated about AD 200. One was scratched on plaster at Cirencester in Roman Britain, found 1868; one on a roof tile at Aquincum near Budapest, found 1954; one on Roman pottery at Manchester, about AD 185; one on an unfired brick at Conímbriga in Portugal, second century. The earliest square with explicit Christian imagery is a sixth-century bronze amulet from Asia Minor with two fish facing one another on one side and the square in Greek characters on the other, the word ICHTHUS written above it, now in the Berlin State Museums. After more than a century of research there is no consensus on where the square came from or what it means.

What it was used for is much better documented than what it says. In medieval Germany the square was inscribed on disks thrown into fires to put them out; an edict of 1743 by Duke Ernest Auguste of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach required every settlement to make them. By the fifteenth century it was a touchstone against fire at the Château de Chinon and the Château de Jarnac. It appears as a remedy during labour in the twelfth-century Trotula, where the instruction is to write the names on cheese and butter and give them to the woman to eat, and a thirteenth-century parchment from Aurillac gives a Sator chant for women in childbirth. It was widely cited against dog bites and rabies, the cure administered by eating bread inscribed with the words. Jean du Choul in 1555 describes a man from Lyon who recovered from insanity after eating three crusts of bread inscribed with the square, then reciting five paternosters for the five wounds of Christ. In Bosnia it was used against fear of water; in Iceland it was etched into the fingernails against jaundice. In nineteenth-century Brazil it was used against dog and snake bites; among German settlers in the Allegheny Mountains it was used to prevent fire, stop fits and prevent miscarriages. It appears in eighteenth-century Pennsylvania Dutch Pow-wow books such as The Long Lost Friend.

*Inference —* both forms share a property their users describe out loud: the writing is doing something by its shape, not by its sense. The triangle funnels; the square holds whichever way you read it. Neither needs to be understood by the person wearing it, and in the Sator's case nobody understands it yet.

names.name: The phallus
names.th: สัญลักษณ์รูปลึงค์

text.what: An erect phallus, modelled in bronze, bone or wood and worn, hung or fixed. Roman versions are frequently winged, and turn up as pendants, finger rings, relief carvings, lamps and wind chimes. Thai palad khik are small carved rods worn at the waist. The sign is not decorative and was not treated as decorative.
text.story:
In Roman religion the fascinus was the divine phallus. Pliny called it a medicus invidiae — a doctor, or remedy, for envy and for the look that carries it. The Vestal Virgins tended the cult of the fascinus populi Romani, and when a general celebrated a triumph they hung an effigy of it under his chariot to protect him from invidia. Augustine, drawing on Varro, records a phallic image carried in procession at the festival of Father Liber to keep enchantment off the fields.

Who wore one is a narrower question than it looks. There are very few Roman images of people wearing a phallic charm. Varro notes the custom of hanging one at a baby's neck, and phallus-bearing rings have been found too small for anyone but a child. A 2017 experimental archaeology project suggested some types were designed to stay pointing outwards, in the wearer's direction of travel, so as to face whatever was coming.

The explanation Roman writers give is not only fertility. The protective function is usually tied to the regenerative power of an erect phallus, but in most cases what diverts the look is the shame or the laughter that obscenity produces. The victory is sometimes drawn literally: a phallus ejaculating at a disembodied eye, a motif known from reliefs at Leptis Magna in present-day Libya and from several places on Hadrian's Wall, and from a first-century BCE terracotta of two small phallus-men sawing an eyeball in half.

Soldiers carried a compound version, the fist-and-phallus amulet, with a clenched fist at the base of the shaft — often making the fig sign. The largest known collection is from Camulodunum.

The sign is not only Roman. In Thailand the palad khik is carved, blessed and worn at the waist, and Thai practice has its own account of what it is for, which this atlas records in that amulet's own file rather than folding into Rome's.

text_th.what: รูปลึงค์ที่แข็งตัว ปั้นหรือแกะจากสำริด กระดูก หรือไม้ แล้วนำมาสวม แขวน หรือติดตั้งไว้ แบบของโรมันมักมีปีก และพบในรูปจี้ห้อยคอ แหวน ภาพสลักนูน ตะเกียง และกระดิ่งลม ปลัดขิกของไทยเป็นแท่งแกะสลักขนาดเล็กที่สวมไว้ที่เอว สัญลักษณ์นี้ไม่ใช่เครื่องประดับ และไม่ได้ถูกปฏิบัติเหมือนเป็นเครื่องประดับ
text_th.story:
ในศาสนาโรมัน ฟัสซินุส (fascinus) คือลึงค์ศักดิ์สิทธิ์ พลินี (Pliny) เรียกมันว่า เมดิคุส อินวิดิไอ (medicus invidiae) คือหมอ หรือยารักษา สำหรับความริษยาและสายตาที่พาความริษยามา หญิงพรหมจารีแห่งเวสตา (Vestal Virgins) เป็นผู้ดูแลลัทธิบูชาฟัสซินุสแห่งประชาชนโรมัน (fascinus populi Romani) และเมื่อแม่ทัพฉลองชัยชนะ พวกนางจะแขวนรูปจำลองของมันไว้ใต้รถศึกของเขา เพื่อคุ้มครองเขาจากอินวิดิอา (invidia ความริษยา) ออกัสติน (Augustine) ซึ่งอ้างวาร์โร (Varro) บันทึกว่ามีการแห่รูปลึงค์ในเทศกาลของเทพลิเบอร์ผู้เป็นบิดา (Father Liber) เพื่อกันมนตร์สะกดไม่ให้ตกต้องไร่นา

ใครเป็นผู้สวมนั้นเป็นคำถามที่แคบกว่าที่เห็น ภาพของชาวโรมันที่แสดงคนสวมเครื่องรางรูปลึงค์มีน้อยมาก วาร์โรกล่าวถึงธรรมเนียมการแขวนไว้ที่คอทารก และมีการพบแหวนที่มีรูปลึงค์ซึ่งเล็กเกินกว่าจะสวมได้นอกจากเด็ก โครงการโบราณคดีเชิงทดลองในปี ค.ศ. 2017 เสนอว่าบางแบบออกแบบให้ชี้ออกด้านนอกเสมอ ไปในทิศทางที่ผู้สวมเดิน เพื่อหันหน้าเข้าหาสิ่งที่กำลังมา

คำอธิบายที่นักเขียนโรมันให้ไว้ไม่ได้มีเพียงเรื่องความอุดมสมบูรณ์ หน้าที่คุ้มครองมักผูกกับพลังแห่งการให้กำเนิดของลึงค์ที่แข็งตัว แต่ในกรณีส่วนใหญ่ สิ่งที่เบี่ยงสายตาออกไปคือความอับอายหรือเสียงหัวเราะที่ความหยาบโลนก่อให้เกิด บางครั้งชัยชนะนี้ถูกวาดออกมาตรงตัว คือลึงค์ที่หลั่งน้ำอสุจิใส่ลูกตาที่ไม่มีร่างกาย ลวดลายที่รู้จักจากภาพสลักนูนที่เลปติสแมกนา (Leptis Magna) ในลิเบียปัจจุบัน และจากหลายจุดบนกำแพงเฮเดรียน (Hadrian's Wall) และจากรูปปั้นดินเผาในศตวรรษที่ 1 ก่อน ค.ศ. ที่แสดงมนุษย์ลึงค์ตัวเล็กสองตนกำลังเลื่อยลูกตาผ่าครึ่ง

ทหารพกแบบผสม คือเครื่องรางกำปั้นและลึงค์ ซึ่งมีกำปั้นอยู่ที่โคนลำ มักทำท่ามือมะเดื่อ (fig sign) คอลเลกชันที่ใหญ่ที่สุดเท่าที่รู้จักมาจากคามูโลดูนุม (Camulodunum)

สัญลักษณ์นี้ไม่ได้มีแต่ในโรมัน ในประเทศไทย ปลัดขิกถูกแกะสลัก ปลุกเสก และสวมไว้ที่เอว และธรรมเนียมไทยมีคำอธิบายของตนเองว่ามีไว้เพื่ออะไร ซึ่งแอตลาสนี้บันทึกไว้ในแฟ้มของเครื่องรางชิ้นนั้นเอง แทนที่จะนำไปรวมไว้กับของโรม

names.name: The red thread
names.th: ด้ายแดง

text.what: A length of red wool or silk tied round a wrist. In the Jewish folk custom it is thin scarlet wool worn as a bracelet or band. In Bulgaria and North Macedonia red is twisted with white into a martenitsa, usually as two small dolls, Pizho in white and Penda in red. In Romania and Moldova the same two threads make a mărțișor with a charm hung from them.
text.story:
The thread's Jewish version is a folk custom, and the sources are careful about how thin its textual footing is. A scarlet thread tied about the wrist appears at Genesis 38, when Tamar gives birth to twins. As early as Rabbi Shmuel ben Hafni Gaon, commentators noted that a red string on the hand may be a good omen, and some say it could go round a finger; one early commentary, Aggadas Bereishis, says Joseph's coat was the same as his brothers' except that Jacob put a red string on the cuffs. But there is no written requirement in the Torah, in halacha or in Kabbalistic texts to tie a red string on a wrist, and it is not clear the mentions of red string as a good omen describe a widespread practice. The one public exhortation on record is from the 1490s: when Jews were barred from wearing tefillin, Rabbi Abraham Saba recommended wearing a red string on the hand instead, to remember the commandment.

The modern trade is documented. Elderly women sell scarlet thread to pilgrims and visitors in Israel, especially in the Old City of Jerusalem. Outside Israel it became popular in the late 1990s with celebrities, many of them not Jewish — Madonna and her children, Leonardo DiCaprio, Michael Jackson, Ariana Grande, Tucker Carlson, Jared Kushner — and the wider popularity is often linked to Philip Berg's Kabbalah Centre. Whether that is the same object as the thread a Jerusalem woman sells is an argument with named parties on both sides; the Kabbalah Centre's critics include the Kabbalist Michael Laitman, who holds that practical Kabbalah has no use for red strings.

The Balkan thread runs on a calendar instead. Martenitsi are given, never bought for oneself, from Baba Marta Day on 1 March, and worn pinned to clothing or at the wrist or neck until the wearer sees a stork or a swallow back from migration, or a tree in blossom — then taken off, and in some places tied to the branch of a fruit tree to give the tree health and luck. Red and white are read as a wish for good health; white for the purity of melting snow, red for the setting sun and for life. Both martenitsa and mărțișor are inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

*Inference —* the red string is worn on wrists in Jewish, Hindu and Chinese practice, and the Jewish source itself says so without claiming a link between them. This atlas reports the three and does not draw a line between them, because nothing read here draws one.

names.name: The beetle
names.th: ด้วง (สคารับ)

text.what: A dung beetle seen from above — head, wing case and legs indicated, the underside left flat so it can be engraved. Usually identified as Scarabaeus sacer. Standard ones run between 6 mm and 40 mm long, most between 10 mm and 20 mm, drilled end to end for a thread or a swivel ring. It is the only sign in this atlas that doubles as a signature: the flat base takes a name, a title or a motto and prints it in clay.
text.story:
The reading Egyptians gave the beetle is stated in the sources: Khepri rolls the sun across the sky at daybreak the way the beetle rolls a ball of dung, so the sign stands for the sun's journey, for rebirth and for regeneration. The beetle-shaped amulet became enormously popular by the early Middle Kingdom, around 2000 BCE, and stayed popular for the rest of the pharaonic period and beyond. By the end of the First Intermediate Period, about 2055 BCE, scarabs had become extremely common and largely replaced cylinder seals and circular button seals with simple geometric designs.

The sign travelled as an object, not as an idea. From the middle Bronze Age other peoples of the Mediterranean and the Middle East imported scarabs from Egypt and made their own, in Egyptian or in local styles, especially in the Levant. A scarab inscribed with Nefertiti's name was among the luxury goods on the Uluburun wreck off Turkey. *Inference —* a portable seal that also functions as a charm is unusually easy to export, and the Levantine copies are evidence of trade in the thing rather than of the Egyptian theology travelling with it.

What is cut on the base changed over time. Pharaohs' names in the Middle Kingdom, then officials' names and titles used as administrative seals, then short prayers or mottoes in the New Kingdom and Third Intermediate Period, which are hard to translate. Some carry hunting scenes. Commemorative scarabs were made for political purposes, notably the large ones of Amenhotep III.

Materials are the other half of the story. Most were carved from steatite — a soft stone that hardens when fired — or moulded in Egyptian faience, then glazed blue or green and fired. Hardstone examples are green jasper, amethyst and carnelian. Most were originally green or blue; weathering has left most steatite ones looking white or brown, so a museum tray reads paler than the original trade did.
text.today: Scarabs are made by the thousand as souvenirs in Egypt, and the shape is standard jewellery and tattoo flash worldwide. The ancient ones are also the most forged class of Egyptian antiquity this atlas covers, which is a matter for the long read on authentication rather than for this page.

names.name: The serpent
names.th: งู

text.what: A snake, drawn coiled, reared, entwined in pairs, or hooded above a head. It is cut into rings and pendants, cast on the branches of Neapolitan silver charms, hooded in stone over Angkorean doorways, and worn as the cobra on an Egyptian crown. Nothing else in this atlas is so evenly split between a thing to be guarded against and a thing that does the guarding.
text.story:
Snakes make good guardians for a reason their observers state plainly: a cornered cobra or rattlesnake holds its ground, displays, and fights rather than retreating. So it gets set where something cannot be moved out of harm's way. At Angkor, hooded multi-headed nāgas guard temples in stone, and from about the twelfth century CE a favourite subject was the Buddha meditating on the coils of a nāga whose flared hood shields him — the story of Mucalinda, who came up from the roots of a tree when the storm began.

Egypt puts the snake at the top. Wadjet, the Egyptian cobra, is from the earliest records the patron and protector of the country, of the other gods and of the pharaohs, worn entwined around the papyrus staff and set in the crown. Nehebkau, the two-headed serpent, guarded the entrance to the underworld, and charms against snakes were inscribed or chanted invoking him — which is the whole ambivalence in one deity: the snake keeps snakes off.

The entwined pair is older than the caduceus. The oldest known representation of two snakes coiled round a rod is the Sumerian god Ningizzida, later a god of healing and magic; a green steatite vase carved for King Gudea of Lagash, dated variously to 2200–2025 BCE, carries an inscription dedicated to him and is in the Louvre. The Greek physician Asclepius carries the single-snake staff that modern medicine still uses. Moses set a serpent on a pole, the Nehushtan, at Numbers 21:8.

Europe kept a domestic version. German popular belief records the house snake that looks after the cows and the children, whose appearance is an omen of death, and whose life is often held to be bound to the master's and the mistress's.

*Inference —* the snake turns up in this role on every inhabited continent, and the sources read here do not show one tradition teaching another. Where the same posture appears — reared, hooded, entwined — the likeliest account is that people in many places watched the same animal do the same thing.

text_th.what: งูที่วาดเป็นขด ชูตัว พันกันเป็นคู่ หรือแผ่พังพานเหนือศีรษะ ถูกสลักลงบนแหวนและจี้ หล่อไว้บนกิ่งของเครื่องรางเงินแบบเนเปิลส์ แผ่พังพานในงานหินเหนือประตูสมัยพระนคร (Angkor) และสวมเป็นงูเห่าบนมงกุฎอียิปต์ ไม่มีสิ่งใดในแอตลาสนี้ที่แบ่งครึ่งเท่ากันขนาดนี้ ระหว่างสิ่งที่ต้องป้องกัน กับสิ่งที่ทำหน้าที่ป้องกัน
text_th.story:
งูเป็นผู้พิทักษ์ที่ดีด้วยเหตุผลที่ผู้สังเกตกล่าวไว้ตรง ๆ: งูเห่าหรืองูหางกระดิ่งที่จนมุมจะยืนหยัด ขู่ และสู้ แทนที่จะถอย ดังนั้นมันจึงถูกวางไว้ในที่ที่มีบางสิ่งไม่อาจเคลื่อนย้ายหนีอันตรายได้ ที่เมืองพระนคร นาคหลายเศียรแผ่พังพานเฝ้าปราสาทไว้ในรูปหิน และตั้งแต่ราวคริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 12 เรื่องที่นิยมคือพระพุทธเจ้าประทับสมาธิบนขนดของนาคที่แผ่พังพานกำบังพระองค์ (พระนาคปรก) — เรื่องของพญามุจลินท์ ผู้ขึ้นมาจากรากไม้เมื่อพายุเริ่มขึ้น

อียิปต์วางงูไว้ที่จุดสูงสุด วาเจต (Wadjet) งูเห่าอียิปต์ ปรากฏตั้งแต่บันทึกแรกสุดในฐานะผู้อุปถัมภ์และผู้คุ้มครองประเทศ คุ้มครองเทพองค์อื่น ๆ และฟาโรห์ ปรากฏพันรอบไม้เท้าต้นปาปิรัส และประดับไว้บนมงกุฎ เนเฮบคาว (Nehebkau) งูสองหัว เฝ้าทางเข้าสู่ยมโลก และมีการจารึกหรือสวดคาถากันงูโดยอัญเชิญเทพองค์นี้ — ซึ่งคือความก้ำกึ่งทั้งหมดอยู่ในเทพองค์เดียว: งูกันงู

คู่งูพันกันเก่ากว่าคทาคาดูเซียส (caduceus) ภาพงูสองตัวพันรอบไม้ที่เก่าที่สุดที่รู้จักคือเทพนิงกิชซิดา (Ningizzida) ของสุเมเรียน ซึ่งภายหลังเป็นเทพแห่งการรักษาและเวทมนตร์ แจกันหินสบู่สีเขียวที่สลักถวายพระเจ้ากูเดอา (Gudea) แห่งลากาช ซึ่งกำหนดอายุไว้ต่าง ๆ กันระหว่าง 2200–2025 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. มีจารึกอุทิศแด่เทพองค์นี้ และอยู่ที่พิพิธภัณฑ์ลูฟวร์ แอสคลีเพียส (Asclepius) แพทย์ชาวกรีก ถือไม้เท้างูตัวเดียวที่การแพทย์สมัยใหม่ยังใช้อยู่ โมเสสตั้งงูไว้บนเสา คือ เนหุชทาน (Nehushtan) ในกันดารวิถี 21:8

ยุโรปเก็บฉบับในบ้านไว้ ความเชื่อพื้นบ้านของเยอรมันบันทึกถึงงูประจำบ้านที่ดูแลวัวและเด็ก ๆ การปรากฏตัวของมันเป็นลางมรณะ และมักถือกันว่าชีวิตของมันผูกอยู่กับชีวิตของนายบ้านและแม่บ้าน

*ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* งูปรากฏในบทบาทนี้ในทุกทวีปที่มีคนอาศัย และแหล่งข้อมูลที่อ่านในที่นี้ไม่ได้แสดงว่าธรรมเนียมหนึ่งสอนอีกธรรมเนียมหนึ่ง ในที่ที่ท่าทางเดียวกันปรากฏ — ชูตัว แผ่พังพาน พันกัน — คำอธิบายที่เป็นไปได้มากที่สุดคือ ผู้คนในหลายที่เฝ้าดูสัตว์ชนิดเดียวกันทำสิ่งเดียวกัน
