names.name: Inheriting
names.th: การสืบทอดเครื่องราง

text.what: A charm that passes from one person to the next and gathers weight as it goes. The object is the same object; what changes is that it now carries a line of people. Traditions that inherit charms tend to have rules about who may receive one, which is what separates an heirloom from a second-hand purchase.
text.story:
Java files the inherited blade under a word of its own. A kris is revered as tosan aji, sacred heirloom weapon, and counted a pusaka. Heirloom blades were handed down through successive generations and worn at weddings and other ceremonies; a fighter might carry three — his own, one from his father-in-law and one that was the family's. A pusaka kris given by a Javanese king to a noble or a subject stood for the king's confidence in the receiver and counted as a great honour. When Prince Diponegoro was defeated and detained at the end of the Java War and had to hand his kris to the Dutch in 1830, the event marked the disarming of the kris among the Javanese populace; its ceremonial life as heirloom and personal amulet continued.

Fiji keeps its whale teeth out of the market on purpose. Tabua are not sold, but traded as gifts at weddings, birthdays and funerals, and were traditionally given for atonement or esteem in sevusevu and in negotiations between rival chiefs. Age shows on them: contact with the oils in human hands darkens the tooth. The law now constrains the handing on — removal from Fiji is capped at 225 exports a year, requires permits from the Ministry of iTaukei Affairs and CITES papers, and in 2007 New Zealand returned 146 tabua seized for lacking valid export permits.

Māori hei-tiki pass through the ground. Hei-tiki are taonga, treasures, usually of pounamu, and Horatio Gordon Robley recorded two main readings of them: memorials to ancestors, or representations of Hineteiwaiwa, goddess of childbirth. Under the first, they were often buried when their kaitiaki — their guardian — died, and retrieved later to be kept somewhere special and brought out at tangihanga. Under the second, a hei-tiki was often given to a woman by her husband's family when she was having trouble conceiving.

Rome is the counter-case. A freeborn Roman boy wore his bulla until he came of age, and before putting on the toga virilis he placed it in the care of the household gods, the Lares. It went sideways into the house's keeping, not down to a son.

*Inference —* inheritance and the market pull against each other in every one of these cases, and the pull is visible in prices. Ancient dzi beads reach hundreds of thousands of US dollars, with beads carrying more eyes and the iron-inclusion marks called bloodspots worth more; new dzi run from about ten to two thousand US dollars depending on quality and lustre. An object that can be inherited can be sold, and the rules that make inheriting possible — who may receive, from whom — are exactly the rules a sale breaks.
text.how: By the tradition's own rule: down a male line, from a father-in-law at a marriage, from a king to a subject, out of the ground after a guardian's death, or as a gift at a funeral. Several traditions attach maintenance to receipt — a kris inherited is a kris that has to be cleaned yearly.
text.today: Live, and regulated. Tabua move within Fiji as gifts and across borders only with permits. Kris are worn as part of Javanese ceremonial dress and kept as family pusaka. Dzi beads are traded at high prices alongside machine-made copies sold by the strand for less than two US dollars, which the trade distinguishes by whether the decoration penetrates the bead's core.

restricted.note: Among Arrernte groups, ownership of sacred tjurunga was determined by a person's conception site within a patrilineal totemic clan, and access was limited to a small number of people. names.name: Inscribing
names.th: การลงอักขระ

text.what: Writing the words that do the work. Lead scratched with a stylus, parchment ruled and lettered with a quill, silver foil punched with a blessing, metal foil incised with Khom Pali, paper painted with strokes nobody is meant to read. In most of these traditions the writing is the charm and the material is packaging: get the letters wrong and there is no object, only a blank.
text.story:
The oldest dated example in this atlas is two silver scrolls found in 1979 in a Judahite burial chamber at Ketef Hinnom, southwest of Jerusalem's Old City, in a site first reported by Gabriel Barkay in 1975. They carry portions of the Priestly Blessing from Numbers, date from around 600 BCE, and took three years to unroll without destroying. They are the oldest surviving texts from the Hebrew Bible known, and they were worn.

Jewish practice still treats the letters as the object. A mezuzah's klaf is written by a qualified scribe, a sofer stam, trained in the law and in the calligraphy of Ktav Stam, in indelible black ink with a quill made from a feather or, rarely now, a reed; tearing or damaging the wording invalidates it. Tefillin are stricter still: 3,188 letters across the parchments, as long as fifteen hours of a scribe's work for a set, and the letters must be written in order — find a mistake later and it cannot be corrected, because the replacement letter would have been written out of sequence.

The Greek and Roman world wrote to bind rather than to bless. Curse tablets — tabella defixionis, katadesmos — are thin lead sheets scratched in tiny letters, then rolled, folded or pierced with nails. Writers added palindromes, boustrophedon lines and otherwise meaningless words such as Bazagra or Bescu, and professionals sometimes prepared tablets in advance with a space left for the customer's name. Mesopotamian incantation bowls run their text in a spiral from the outer rim inward, so that, in John Charles Arnold's description, demons following the charms would be caught in the centre.

China took the logic to its end and made the writing unreadable on purpose. Fulu are talismanic script — strokes that resemble Chinese characters without being them. Ge Hong noted in the Baopuzi, in the Eastern Jin (317–420), that a talisman worked whether or not its user could decipher it, and Fudan University's Ge Zhaoguang describes the illegibility as deliberate archaism, a veil that leaves only qualified clergy able to produce them. Thai yant are written in Khom Pali, a Thai variant of Khmer script, or in Lan Na Tai Tham in the north. Islamic talismanic shirts carry Quranic verses, names of God and of prophets, and numbers; the earliest surviving examples were made in or near the fifteenth century.

*Inference —* two opposite strategies run through all of this. One camp writes to be read by a power that reads: the blessing, the verse, the name. The other writes to be unreadable by anyone: the meaningless words on a lead sheet, the Taoist strokes, the letters that only a scribe's hand can form. Both are ways of putting the text beyond the ordinary user's reach.
text.how: Materials first, because they decide the tool: lead takes a stylus, parchment takes a quill and a ruled line, silver takes a punch, metal foil takes a stylus and then rolls, paper takes a brush. Then the text, in a script the tradition specifies. Then, in several traditions, a check: many observant Jews have a scribe examine mezuzah parchments for tears and faded letters at least twice every seven years.
text.today: Still a paid trade. Scribes write mezuzot and tefillin to order, and sellers who supply a photocopied text on paper with a decorated case are selling a case: a valid mezuzah has to be handwritten on parchment by a qualified scribe. Thai and Cambodian masters still write yant on metal, cloth and skin. Chinese folk healers still use zhuyou, the talismanic branch of healing, which traditional Chinese medicine rejects and which was reinterpreted in the twentieth century as a local counterpart to hypnosis.

text_th.what: การเขียนถ้อยคำที่ทำหน้าที่ ตะกั่วที่ขีดด้วยเหล็กจาร แผ่นหนังที่ตีเส้นแล้วเขียนตัวอักษรด้วยปากกาขนนก แผ่นเงินบางที่ตอกคำอวยพรลงไป แผ่นโลหะบางที่จารอักขระขอมบาลี กระดาษที่ระบายด้วยเส้นที่ไม่มีใครตั้งใจให้อ่าน ในประเพณีส่วนใหญ่เหล่านี้ ตัวเขียนคือเครื่องราง และวัสดุเป็นเพียงหีบห่อ: เขียนตัวอักษรผิด ก็ไม่มีวัตถุ มีแต่ของเปล่า
text_th.story:
ตัวอย่างที่มีวันที่เก่าที่สุดในแอตลาสนี้คือม้วนเงินสองม้วน ซึ่งพบใน ค.ศ. 1979 ในห้องฝังศพของชาวยูดาห์ที่เคเทฟฮินโนม (Ketef Hinnom) ทางตะวันตกเฉียงใต้ของเมืองเก่าเยรูซาเล็ม ในแหล่งที่กาเบรียล บาร์กาย (Gabriel Barkay) รายงานครั้งแรกใน ค.ศ. 1975 ม้วนทั้งสองมีบางส่วนของพรของปุโรหิตจากหนังสือกันดารวิถี มีอายุราว 600 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. และใช้เวลาสามปีในการคลี่ออกโดยไม่ให้เสียหาย ม้วนทั้งสองคือข้อความจากคัมภีร์ฮีบรูที่เก่าที่สุดที่หลงเหลือมาเท่าที่รู้จัก และเคยถูกสวมใส่

การปฏิบัติของชาวยิวยังคงถือว่าตัวอักษรคือวัตถุ แคลฟ (klaf) หรือแผ่นหนังในเมซูซาห์ เขียนโดยอาลักษณ์ผู้มีคุณสมบัติ เรียกว่าโซเฟอร์ สตัม (sofer stam) ซึ่งได้รับการฝึกทั้งด้านกฎหมายศาสนาและการเขียนอักษรวิจิตรแบบคทาฟ สตัม (Ktav Stam) ด้วยหมึกดำที่ลบไม่ออก และปากกาที่ทำจากขนนก หรือซึ่งปัจจุบันพบน้อยแล้ว จากต้นอ้อ การฉีกหรือทำให้ถ้อยคำเสียหายทำให้เมซูซาห์นั้นใช้ไม่ได้ เทฟิลลินเข้มงวดยิ่งกว่า: ตัวอักษร 3,188 ตัวบนแผ่นหนังทั้งหมด งานของอาลักษณ์นานถึงสิบห้าชั่วโมงต่อหนึ่งชุด และตัวอักษรต้องเขียนตามลำดับ — หากพบข้อผิดพลาดภายหลังก็แก้ไม่ได้ เพราะตัวอักษรที่เขียนแทนจะกลายเป็นตัวที่เขียนนอกลำดับ

โลกกรีกและโรมันเขียนเพื่อผูกมัดมากกว่าเพื่ออวยพร แผ่นสาปแช่ง — ตาเบลลา เดฟิกซิโอนิส (tabella defixionis) หรือคาทาเดสมอส (katadesmos) — คือแผ่นตะกั่วบางที่ขีดเขียนด้วยตัวอักษรเล็กจิ๋ว แล้วม้วน พับ หรือตอกตะปูทะลุ ผู้เขียนเติมคำพาลินโดรม (คำที่อ่านจากหน้าไปหลังหรือหลังไปหน้าได้เหมือนกัน) บรรทัดที่เขียนสลับทิศไปกลับ และคำที่ไม่มีความหมายอย่างบาซากรา (Bazagra) หรือเบสกู (Bescu) และมืออาชีพบางครั้งเตรียมแผ่นไว้ล่วงหน้าโดยเว้นที่ไว้ให้เติมชื่อของลูกค้า ชามคาถาของเมโสโปเตเมียเขียนข้อความวนเป็นเกลียวจากขอบนอกเข้าด้านใน เพื่อที่ตามคำบรรยายของจอห์น ชาลส์ อาร์โนลด์ (John Charles Arnold) ปีศาจที่ตามคาถาเข้าไปจะถูกจับไว้ตรงกลาง

จีนนำตรรกะนี้ไปจนสุดทาง และทำให้ตัวเขียนอ่านไม่ออกโดยเจตนา ฝูลู่ (fulu) คืออักษรยันต์ — เส้นที่คล้ายอักษรจีนแต่ไม่ใช่อักษรจีน เก่อหง (Ge Hong) บันทึกไว้ในเป้าผูจื่อ (Baopuzi) สมัยราชวงศ์จิ้นตะวันออก (ค.ศ. 317–420) ว่ายันต์ใช้ได้ผลไม่ว่าผู้ใช้จะถอดความได้หรือไม่ และเก่อจ้าวกวง (Ge Zhaoguang) แห่งมหาวิทยาลัยฟู่ตั้น บรรยายว่าการอ่านไม่ออกนั้นเป็นการจงใจคงรูปโบราณไว้ เป็นม่านที่ทำให้มีเพียงนักบวชผู้มีคุณสมบัติเท่านั้นที่สร้างยันต์ได้ ยันต์ไทยเขียนด้วยอักขระขอมบาลี ซึ่งเป็นอักษรเขมรแบบไทย หรือด้วยอักษรธรรมล้านนาในภาคเหนือ เสื้อเครื่องรางของอิสลามมีโองการอัลกุรอาน พระนามของพระเจ้าและนามของนบี และตัวเลข ตัวอย่างที่หลงเหลือเก่าที่สุดทำขึ้นในหรือราวคริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 15

*ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* ยุทธศาสตร์สองแบบที่ตรงข้ามกันแล่นผ่านเรื่องทั้งหมดนี้ ฝ่ายหนึ่งเขียนเพื่อให้อำนาจที่อ่านได้อ่าน: คำอวยพร โองการ พระนาม อีกฝ่ายเขียนเพื่อให้ไม่มีใครอ่านออก: คำไร้ความหมายบนแผ่นตะกั่ว เส้นยันต์เต๋า ตัวอักษรที่มีแต่มืออาลักษณ์เท่านั้นที่เขียนได้ ทั้งสองแบบเป็นวิธีวางข้อความไว้ให้พ้นเอื้อมของผู้ใช้ธรรมดา
text_th.how: วัสดุมาก่อน เพราะวัสดุเป็นตัวกำหนดเครื่องมือ: ตะกั่วใช้เหล็กจาร แผ่นหนังใช้ปากกาขนนกและเส้นบรรทัด เงินใช้เหล็กตอก แผ่นโลหะบางใช้เหล็กจารแล้วม้วน กระดาษใช้พู่กัน จากนั้นคือข้อความ ในอักษรที่ประเพณีกำหนด จากนั้น ในหลายประเพณี คือการตรวจ: ชาวยิวที่เคร่งครัดจำนวนมากให้อาลักษณ์ตรวจแผ่นหนังเมซูซาห์ว่ามีรอยฉีกหรือตัวอักษรซีดจางหรือไม่ อย่างน้อยสองครั้งในทุกเจ็ดปี
text_th.today: ยังเป็นอาชีพที่มีค่าจ้าง อาลักษณ์เขียนเมซูซาห์และเทฟิลลินตามสั่ง และผู้ขายที่ให้ข้อความถ่ายเอกสารบนกระดาษมาในกล่องประดับ ก็คือขายกล่อง: เมซูซาห์ที่ใช้ได้ต้องเขียนด้วยมือบนแผ่นหนังโดยอาลักษณ์ผู้มีคุณสมบัติ อาจารย์ชาวไทยและกัมพูชายังคงลงยันต์บนโลหะ ผ้า และผิวหนัง หมอพื้นบ้านจีนยังคงใช้จู้โหยว (zhuyou) ซึ่งเป็นสายการรักษาด้วยยันต์ ที่การแพทย์แผนจีนปฏิเสธ และถูกตีความใหม่ในคริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 20 ว่าเป็นสิ่งที่เทียบได้กับการสะกดจิตในแบบท้องถิ่น

th_fields.dating.period: ยุคเหล็กถึงปัจจุบัน
th_fields.dating.note: กำหนดอายุจากม้วนเงินเคเทฟฮินโนม (Ketef Hinnom) ราว 600 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. ซึ่งเป็นเครื่องรางมีจารึกชิ้นแรกสุดที่แอตลาสนี้ระบุปีได้ การเขียนลงบนเครื่องรางย่อมเก่ากว่านั้นแน่นอน นี่คือสิ่งที่มีวันที่
th_fields.object.made_by: อาลักษณ์ นักบวช หรืออาจารย์ที่ประเพณีรับรองให้ทำได้ — โซเฟอร์ สตัม (sofer stam) สำหรับข้อความของชาวยิว นักพรตเต๋าสำหรับฝูลู่ (fulu) และอาจารย์ยันต์ในเอเชียตะวันออกเฉียงใต้ภาคพื้นทวีป
th_fields.object.inscription: แตกต่างไปตามประเพณี: พรของปุโรหิต บทเชมา (Shema) โองการอัลกุรอานและพระนามของพระเจ้า คาถาบาลี และสูตรผูกมัดที่กล่าวต่อพลูโต (Pluto) คารอน (Charon) เฮคาที (Hecate) หรือเพอร์เซโฟนี (Persephone)
th_fields.against.0.who: ชามคาถาภาษาอราเมอิกและภาษาซีเรียกเอง ซึ่งกล่าวต่อปีศาจที่ระบุชื่อไว้
th_fields.against.1.who: ลูกค้าชาวกรีกและโรมัน ซึ่งแผ่นจารึกของพวกเขามอบตัวเป้าหมายให้แก่เทพแห่งยมโลก
th_fields.against.1.note: ในกรณีนี้ ตัวเขียนคือการโจมตี ไม่ใช่โล่ — งานช่างเดียวกันที่หันไปอีกทาง
th_fields.against.2.who: ฮุร์เรม สุลต่าน (Hürrem Sultan) ผู้ทูลสุลต่านสุไลมานผู้เกรียงไกร (Suleiman the Magnificent) ว่าจารึกบนเสื้อเครื่องรางที่พระนางถวายจะคุ้มครองพระองค์จากกระสุน
th_fields.against.2.quote: จารึกบนเสื้อนั้นจะคุ้มครองพระองค์จากกระสุน
th_fields.against.3.who: หมอรักษาแบบจู้โหยว (zhuyou) ของลัทธิเต๋า ซึ่งใช้กันในจีนมาตั้งแต่อย่างน้อยสมัยราชวงศ์ฮั่นตะวันออก
th_fields.restricted.note: อักษรยันต์ของลัทธิเต๋าถ่ายทอดกันอย่างลับจากนักพรตสู่ศิษย์ และคาถากับท่ามือที่ใช้ก็แตกต่างกันไปในแต่ละนิกาย แอตลาสนี้พิมพ์ว่าการปฏิบัตินี้มีไว้เพื่ออะไรและใครเขียนได้ และไม่นำเส้นของยันต์หรือถ้อยคำที่กล่าวกำกับมาแสดงซ้ำ

dating.label: c. 600 BCE to now
dating.note: Dated from the Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls, c. 600 BCE, the earliest inscribed amulet this atlas can put a year on. Writing on charms is certainly older; this is what is dated.

object.made_by: a scribe, a priest or a master the tradition licenses — sofer stam for Jewish texts, a Taoist priest for fulu, a yant master in mainland Southeast Asia
object.inscription: varies by tradition: the Priestly Blessing, the Shema passages, Quranic verses and names of God, Pali gatha, binding formulae addressed to Pluto, Charon, Hecate or Persephone
object.script: Palaeo-Hebrew, Ashuri Hebrew, Arabic, Khom Pali, Lan Na Tai Tham, Greek, Latin, Taoist talismanic script

restricted.note: Taoist talismanic script is transmitted in secret from priest to disciple, and its incantations and hand-forms differ from sect to sect. This atlas prints what the practice is for and who may write it, and does not reproduce a talisman's strokes or the words that accompany them.
restricted.who_says: Ge Zhaoguang, Fudan University, and the accounts of fulu transmission summarised with him

against.who: the Aramaic and Syriac incantation bowls themselves, addressed to the demons they name
Greek and Roman clients, whose tablets hand the target over to underworld gods
against.note: here the writing is the attack, not the shield — the same craft pointed the other way

against.who: Hürrem Sultan, who told Suleiman the Magnificent the inscriptions on the talismanic shirt she gave him would protect him from bullets
against.quote: its inscriptions would protect him from bullets

against.who: Taoist zhuyou healers, in use in China since at least the Eastern Han

names.name: Knotting
names.said: tying the thing shut, or tying it on
names.th: การผูกปม

text.what: Tying, as the whole of the charm. A knot needs no words, no metal and no kiln — two colours of wool twisted together, a leather strap knotted into the shape of a letter, a thousand stitches pulled tight by a thousand different hands. Where a knot is the object, the tying is the making, the charging and often the giving all at once.
text.story:
Egypt made the knot a sign. The tyet, the knot of Isis, resembles a knot of cloth and may have begun as a bandage; an early example comes from a First Dynasty tomb at Helwan, excavated by Zaki Saad in the 1940s. Tyet amulets started going into burials in the early New Kingdom, from the reign of Amenhotep III, and from then to the end of dynastic Egypt few people were buried without one in the wrappings, usually on the upper torso. Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead calls for a tyet of red jasper at the mummy's neck, saying the power of Isis will be the protection of the body and that the amulet will drive away whoever would commit a crime against it.

In the Balkans the knot is worn for a month and then untied by the calendar. A martenitsa is twisted from white and red yarn, usually as two small wool dolls, Pizho and Penda, and is put on at Baba Marta Day on 1 March. It comes off when the wearer first sees a stork, a swallow or a tree in blossom — then it is tied to the branch of a fruit tree, or put under a stone so that whichever creature is nearest it the next day reads the coming year: a worm or larva for health and success, an ant for success won by hard work, a spider for trouble. Photios' Lexicon records an older Greek version in which priests wrapped a red thread, kroke, around the right hand and foot; ethnographers who trace the custom back that far do so tentatively, and the tradition itself names Thracian, Hellenic or Roman origins without settling on one. The practice is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Jewish practice knots leather into letters. The head-tefillin strap's knot forms the letter dalet or a double dalet, the arm strap's knot forms a yud, and with the shin on the head box those three letters spell Shaddai, one of the names of God. A separate folk custom ties a thin scarlet wool thread round the wrist against the evil eye; there is no requirement for it in the Torah, in halakha or in kabbalistic texts, and the only public exhortation to wear one that the sources name is from the 1490s, when Rabbi Abraham Saba recommended it to Jews forbidden to wear tefillin, as a reminder of the commandment.

Japan counted knots. A senninbari, a thousand-person-stitch belt, was decorated with a thousand knots or stitches, each normally made by a different woman; the custom began in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95, when the earliest versions were handkerchief-sized squares knotted to strengthen the cloth, the implication being that the strength passed to the man carrying it.

*Inference —* knots are the cheapest charm in this atlas and the most evenly distributed. That is worth saying plainly rather than reading as a single ancient custom travelling: thread is everywhere, tying is learned by every child, and a knot is the one amulet a person with nothing can make.
text.how: Twist, tie, or stitch. Martenitsi are twisted from red and white wool and pinned to clothing or tied at the wrist or neck. Brigid's crosses are woven from rushes or straw gathered the evening before. Senninbari stitches were solicited one at a time from women passing a temple, a train station or a department store, with a woman born in a Tiger year entitled by custom to sew twelve stitches or as many as her years; some belts were lined with women's hair, a practice the sources trace to folk belief on Okinawa, and coins were sewn in as well.
text.today: Martenitsi are worn every March in Bulgaria and North Macedonia and given, never bought for oneself, with modern versions adding coloured beads. Red wrist threads are sold by elderly women to pilgrims and tourists in the Old City of Jerusalem and were taken up in the late 1990s by celebrities with no connection to the custom, a spread often traced to Philip Berg's Kabbalah Centre. Tefillin knots are tied the same way every weekday morning.

text.what: A charm with an expiry date. The old one is taken down, returned, burnt, buried or tied to a tree, and a new one takes its place on a fixed day. The date is usually a turn in the calendar — a new year, a saint's feast, the first day of spring — and the swap is the practice, not the object.
text.how: Take it off or take it down; return it, burn it, bury it or leave it on a branch; obtain the replacement; put it where the old one was. In Java the equivalent is not replacement but cleaning: jamasan, the yearly cleaning of a kris, is required by the tradition and has left ancient blades worn thin.
text.story:
Japan does this at scale and gives a reason. Japanese practice places great weight on purity and newness — tokowaka, eternal youth — and it is on that ground that annual replacement of ofuda and omamori is encouraged. New ofuda are obtained before the end of the year or during the New Year season; the old ones are returned to the shrine or temple where they came from as a form of thanks, though most Shinto shrines in practice accept talismans from other shrines. Omamori are customarily replaced once a year and returned on or shortly after the New Year, so that the coming year starts with a fresh one. Old ones are not thrown away: they are burnt at a ceremony called Sagichō or Dondoyaki held at the Little New Year, on 14 or 15 January.

Daruma dolls date the system precisely. Charms drawn at Shorinzan Daruma Temple in Takasaki were given with an effectiveness of one year, so parishioners needed new ones every year; the ninth priest, Togaku, handled the demand by giving the people wooden block moulds and letting them make their own papier-mâché charms, near the beginning of the Meiwa period, 1764–72. Takasaki now produces eighty per cent of Japan's daruma, and the city's annual Daruma Doll Festival draws, by the city's own account, more than 400,000 people buying the year's dolls.

Bulgaria and North Macedonia run a spring version. Martenitsi go on at Baba Marta Day, 1 March, and come off when the wearer first sees a stork, a swallow or a blossoming tree — or at the end of March. The old one is tied to the branch of a fruit tree, giving the tree the health and luck the wearer had while wearing it, or put under a stone to be read the next day by whichever creature is nearest it. Ireland weaves a new Saint Brigid's cross on 1 February from rushes gathered the evening before; crosses were either taken down annually and replaced or left to accumulate between feasts, and discarded ones were burned or buried, with burial preferred because of Brigid's associations with agriculture.

Jewish practice keeps a different clock and it is worth naming as a contrast. A mezuzah is not replaced annually; many observant Jews have a qualified scribe check the parchments for tears and faded lettering at least twice every seven years. The object is meant to last, and the maintenance is inspection rather than replacement.

*Inference —* the parallel between a Japanese year-end burning, a martenitsa on a March branch and a yearly kris cleaning is real at the level of structure: each treats potency as something that runs down and has to be topped up on a date the calendar sets, not on a date the owner picks. What is this project's own reading, and not any tradition's claim, is the further step of grouping them — the reasons given differ completely, purity in one case, the return of spring in another, upkeep of a blade in a third, and no source read here connects them.
text.today: Live, and commercially organised. Japanese shrines and temples stock the year's talismans in quantity and hold the January fires; Takasaki's daruma market runs annually. Martenitsi are sold across Bulgaria and North Macedonia every February and hang on fruit trees through April. Mezuzah checking is a paid scribal service.

text.what: Putting the charm inside the cloth rather than on a cord. A pouch is stitched shut over what it holds; coins and hair are sewn into a belt; a charm is quilted into a bedcover; a shirt is itself the charm, worn under armour. Once stitched, the object cannot be checked without being destroyed, which is the point and the problem.
text.story:
The gris-gris came out of the Muslim Mande communities of far West Africa: a small cloth pouch, inscribed with verses from an ancestor and holding a ritual number of small objects, worn on the person. The Atlantic slave trade carried it to the Americas, where it became a significant practice in Haitian Vodou and in the Louisiana tradition the cited account calls "Louisiana Voodoo", and where the earliest legal mentions of that Louisiana tradition are New Orleans court cases of 1773, in which enslaved people were convicted of using gris-gris against those who held them. A 1982 survey in Senegal found gris-gris among the three methods of contraception best known to women there, alongside abstinence and roots and herbs.

The Kongo-derived mojo bag took the same shape in the United States and then went into bedding. African American quilt makers sewed mojo hands into quilts for protection — a practice the sources trace to Central African peoples such as the Bakongo, who adapted nkisi practice into the 'Pineapple quilt', and which spread from Mississippi and Alabama to Connecticut.

Japan sewed the charm into a belt and then sewed things into the belt. A senninbari was stitched a thousand times, usually one stitch per woman; some were lined with a woman's hair, or several women's, a form of added protection the sources trace to folk belief on Okinawa, and coins were sewn in as well. Some senninbari were never worn at all: they were folded and placed inside helmet liners, pockets or packs.

The Islamic world put the writing on the garment itself. Talismanic shirts — tılsımlı gömlek in Turkish, pirâhan telesmat in Persian — are found across the Muslim world in Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal and West African types, the earliest surviving examples made in or near the fifteenth century, inscribed with Quranic verses, names of God and of prophets, and numbers. Most seem intended as a shield in battle. Hürrem Sultan gave one to Suleiman the Magnificent and told him its inscriptions would protect him from bullets.

*Inference —* sewing solves a problem the cord cannot. A pendant announces itself and can be taken off you; a stitched charm passes a search, survives a change of owner's rules, and travels in a garment that has an innocent reason to exist. The practice is heaviest exactly where carrying a charm openly was dangerous.
text.how: A pouch is cut, filled and stitched shut; a belt is embroidered and its lining closed over coins or hair; a quilt takes the charm between its layers; a shirt is written on before it is made up. In hoodoo practice the filled bag is then fixed and fed — smoked over incense or candles, breathed on, prayed over, and dressed with a liquid — which is a separate step this atlas files under feeding the charm.
text.today: Gris-gris are worn across Senegalese society, by, in the words of the cited account, everyone from wrestlers to soldiers to housewives. Conjure shops sell made-up mojo bags and the materials to make them; Dr Jim Jordan, a conjure doctor in North Carolina, ran a Hoodoo store and a paid practice through the Jim Crow era and became a multi-millionaire doing it. Senninbari stopped being made at scale with the end of the Second World War and are now a collectors' category, catalogued and sold.

text.what: The charm put into the skin, where it cannot be dropped, stolen, sold or taken off. A long needle drives ink under the surface in a design that is often script — Pali phrases in Khom, Khmer, Lao Tham, Shan, northern Thai or Tai Lu letters, wrapped around animals and deities. The bearer carries the object and the obligations together, because in several of these traditions the tattoo works only while its rules are kept.
text.story:
Sak yant names its own mechanics. Sak, from a Proto-Mon-Khmer root meaning to prick, is a native Khmer word — Chuon Nath's 1967 dictionary holds that it is not a loan from Sanskrit or Pali — and yant comes from Sanskrit yantra, from yam, to hold or sustain, plus tra, instrument. The practice originated in the Khmer Empire around the ninth century, on indigenous mainland Southeast Asian animist tattooing that the cited account traces back as far as 2,500 BCE, with the designs drawn from Indian yantras. It runs today in Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and parts of Burma, and the script changes with the country: Khmer in Cambodia, Khom in central Thailand, Shan or northern Thai or Tai Lu in the north, Lao Tham in Laos.

What the tattoo is said to do splits three ways in the tradition's own account: effects that benefit the bearer, such as making them more eloquent; effects that ward off evil and hardship, taken up by soldiers, police, taxi drivers and people in other jobs they judge dangerous; and effects on other people, such as invoking fear. The same designs are applied to cloth and metal and put in a house, a temple or a vehicle instead of on skin.

Elsewhere the mark is the membership. Many Copts have the cross tattooed on the inside of the right arm at the wrist as a sign of faith. Catholic Croats in Bosnia used sicanje, tattooing, for protection against conversion to Islam under Ottoman rule. Ancient Egyptians tattooed dedication to a deity, and the marks were held to carry divine protection. Among Austronesian societies tattoos were regarded as magical wards against evil spirits and illness as well as records of raids and status, and the Chimu of coastal Peru wore them for magic and medical purposes; tattoos on Chancay bodies of around 1250 CE have been studied with lasers by researchers at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.

*Inference —* the tattoo is the limit case of everything else in this atlas. Every other charm here can be lost, pawned, inherited or buried; this one is disposed of only with the person. That is also why it is the practice most tightly governed by rules attached to the bearer rather than to the object.
text.how: Public structure only. A master applies the design with a long needle, in a rite that the tradition holds transfers spirits into the design — in the words of the cited study, spiritual tattooing functions as the bridge between the wearer and gods or wild spirits. The practice is defined by strict rules meant to maintain the tattoos' power, and the tattoo confers its powers only so long as the bearer observes those rules and taboos, such as abstaining from a certain type of food. What the master says, and which design is given to whom, are the master's, and this record stops there.
text.today: Both a living practice and a trade selling to visitors. Hollywood attention has moved the market: Angelina Jolie was tattooed by Ajahn Noo Kanpai with Old Khmer script sak yant in Thailand, and took a Bengal tiger yantra in 2004 to mark acquiring Cambodian citizenship. Buddhist images and figures used as tattoos by visitors who do not follow local rules about the respectful display of such images have caused public controversy in Buddhist countries. Both of those are arguments the traditions are having about themselves, and this atlas reports them rather than settling them.

text_th.what: เครื่องรางที่ใส่ลงไปในผิวหนัง ซึ่งทำหล่นไม่ได้ ถูกขโมยไม่ได้ ขายไม่ได้ และถอดออกไม่ได้ เข็มยาวพาหมึกลงไปใต้ผิวเป็นลวดลาย ซึ่งหลายครั้งเป็นตัวอักษร คือคาถาภาษาบาลีที่เขียนด้วยอักษรขอม เขมร ธรรมลาว ไทใหญ่ ธรรมล้านนา หรือไทลื้อ พันล้อมรูปสัตว์และรูปเทพ ผู้ถือแบกทั้งวัตถุและข้อผูกมัดไว้ด้วยกัน เพราะในหลายธรรมเนียม รอยสักจะให้ผลก็ต่อเมื่อรักษาข้อห้ามข้อปฏิบัติของมันไว้
text_th.story:
ชื่อ สักยันต์ บอกกลไกของตัวเองไว้ในชื่อ คำว่า สัก มาจากรากศัพท์มอญ-เขมรดั้งเดิมที่แปลว่าจิ้มหรือแทง เป็นคำเขมรดั้งเดิม พจนานุกรมของชวน ณาต (Chuon Nath) ฉบับ ค.ศ. 1967 ถือว่าคำนี้ไม่ได้ยืมมาจากภาษาสันสกฤตหรือบาลี ส่วนคำว่า ยันต์ มาจากภาษาสันสกฤต ยนฺตฺร (yantra) ซึ่งมาจาก ยมฺ แปลว่ายึดไว้หรือค้ำจุน รวมกับ ตฺร แปลว่าเครื่องมือ การปฏิบัตินี้กำเนิดในอาณาจักรเขมรราวคริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 9 บนพื้นฐานการสักตามคติผีของชนพื้นเมืองในภาคพื้นทวีปเอเชียตะวันออกเฉียงใต้ ซึ่งแหล่งข้อมูลที่อ้างถึงสืบย้อนไปได้ไกลถึง 2,500 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. โดยลวดลายได้มาจากยันตระของอินเดีย ปัจจุบันยังมีการสักในกัมพูชา ลาว ไทย และบางส่วนของพม่า และอักษรเปลี่ยนไปตามประเทศ กัมพูชาใช้อักษรเขมร ภาคกลางของไทยใช้อักษรขอม ภาคเหนือใช้อักษรไทใหญ่ อักษรธรรมล้านนา หรืออักษรไทลื้อ ลาวใช้อักษรธรรมลาว

สิ่งที่กล่าวกันว่ารอยสักทำได้ แบ่งเป็นสามทางตามคำอธิบายของธรรมเนียมเอง ได้แก่ ผลที่เป็นประโยชน์ต่อผู้ถือ เช่น ทำให้พูดจาคล่องแคล่วน่าฟัง ผลที่ปัดเป่าสิ่งชั่วร้ายและความทุกข์ยาก ซึ่งทหาร ตำรวจ คนขับแท็กซี่ และผู้ที่ทำงานอื่นที่ตนเห็นว่าเสี่ยงอันตรายนิยมสัก และผลที่เกิดกับผู้อื่น เช่น ทำให้เกิดความเกรงกลัว ลวดลายเดียวกันนี้ยังลงบนผ้าและโลหะ แล้วนำไปไว้ในบ้าน ในวัด หรือในรถ แทนที่จะลงบนผิวหนัง

ในที่อื่น เครื่องหมายบนผิวคือการเป็นสมาชิก ชาวคอปต์จำนวนมากสักรูปไม้กางเขนไว้ที่ด้านในของแขนขวาตรงข้อมือ เป็นเครื่องหมายแห่งศรัทธา ชาวโครแอตคาทอลิกในบอสเนียใช้ซิชาเนีย (sicanje) หรือการสัก เพื่อป้องกันการเปลี่ยนไปนับถือศาสนาอิสลามภายใต้การปกครองของออตโตมัน ชาวอียิปต์โบราณสักเพื่อแสดงการอุทิศตนแด่เทพองค์หนึ่ง และถือกันว่ารอยสักเหล่านั้นมีการคุ้มครองจากเทพอยู่ในตัว ในสังคมออสโตรนีเซียน รอยสักถูกมองว่าเป็นเครื่องป้องกันทางไสยศาสตร์จากภูตผีร้ายและความเจ็บป่วย และเป็นบันทึกของการออกรบและสถานะทางสังคมด้วย ชาวชิมู (Chimu) แห่งชายฝั่งเปรูสักเพื่อจุดประสงค์ทางไสยศาสตร์และการรักษาโรค รอยสักบนร่างของชาวชังไก (Chancay) ซึ่งมีอายุราว ค.ศ. 1250 ได้รับการศึกษาด้วยเลเซอร์โดยนักวิจัยของมหาวิทยาลัยจีนแห่งฮ่องกง

*ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* รอยสักคือกรณีสุดขอบของทุกสิ่งในแอตลาสนี้ เครื่องรางอื่นทุกชิ้นที่นี่อาจหาย ถูกจำนำ ตกทอดเป็นมรดก หรือถูกฝังได้ แต่ชิ้นนี้จะจากไปก็ต่อเมื่อคนผู้นั้นจากไปเท่านั้น นี่จึงเป็นเหตุผลด้วยว่าทำไมการปฏิบัตินี้จึงถูกกำกับด้วยกฎที่ผูกกับตัวผู้ถือ มากกว่าผูกกับวัตถุ อย่างเข้มงวดที่สุด
text_th.how: บันทึกนี้กล่าวถึงเฉพาะโครงสร้างที่เปิดเผยต่อสาธารณะ อาจารย์สักลวดลายด้วยเข็มยาว ในพิธีที่ธรรมเนียมถือว่าเป็นการถ่ายทอดวิญญาณลงไปในลวดลาย ตามถ้อยคำของงานศึกษาที่อ้างถึง การสักทางจิตวิญญาณทำหน้าที่เป็นสะพานเชื่อมระหว่างผู้ถือกับเทพเจ้าหรือวิญญาณในป่า การปฏิบัตินี้มีกฎเกณฑ์เคร่งครัดที่มีไว้เพื่อรักษาอานุภาพของรอยสัก และรอยสักจะให้อานุภาพก็ต่อเมื่อผู้ถือรักษากฎและข้อห้ามเหล่านั้น เช่น การงดกินอาหารบางประเภท สิ่งที่อาจารย์กล่าว และลวดลายใดให้แก่ผู้ใด เป็นของอาจารย์ และบันทึกนี้หยุดไว้เพียงเท่านี้
text_th.today: เป็นทั้งการปฏิบัติที่ยังมีชีวิตอยู่และการค้าที่ขายให้ผู้มาเยือน ความสนใจจากฮอลลีวูดทำให้ตลาดเปลี่ยนไป แองเจลินา โจลี (Angelina Jolie) ได้รับการสักยันต์ด้วยอักษรเขมรโบราณจากอาจารย์หนู กันภัย ในประเทศไทย และสักยันต์เสือเบงกอลในปี พ.ศ. 2547 (ค.ศ. 2004) เพื่อเป็นเครื่องหมายว่าได้รับสัญชาติกัมพูชา การที่ผู้มาเยือนซึ่งไม่ได้ปฏิบัติตามธรรมเนียมท้องถิ่นว่าด้วยการแสดงรูปศักดิ์สิทธิ์อย่างเคารพ นำรูปพระพุทธเจ้าและรูปทางพระพุทธศาสนามาสัก ได้ก่อให้เกิดข้อถกเถียงในที่สาธารณะในประเทศที่นับถือพระพุทธศาสนา ทั้งสองเรื่องเป็นข้อถกเถียงที่ธรรมเนียมเหล่านี้กำลังถกกันเองเกี่ยวกับตัวเอง และแอตลาสนี้รายงานไว้ ไม่ได้ตัดสิน

names.name: Washing off the ink
names.said: the charm is taken, not worn
names.th: การล้างหมึก

text.what: The charm written and then destroyed on purpose, so that a person can take it. Words are written inside a bowl, water is poured in, the writing comes off into the water, and the water is drunk. What was an object for a minute becomes a dose. Nothing survives, which is why almost no museum drawer holds an example of the practice that may be the commonest use of written charms alive.
text.story:
Islamic legal writing draws a fine line through this. Remke Kruk, summarising how close the approved and disapproved practices sit, notes that dissolving Quranic texts written on paper in water is forbidden, while the well-known Wahhabi-oriented cleric Wahid 'Abd al-Salam Bali recommends, in the cited account's words, writing in bowls with ink that is washed off by the water poured into the bowl. The same body of practice records treating a stomach ache by drinking water over which Quranic passages have been recited, and prescribes, for the condition called sihr al-nazif, drinking water over which an incantation has been recited and bathing in it for three days.

The Philippines has a swallowed branch of its own. An agimat can take the form of consumable enchanted mud, putik in Tagalog, and a mutya — described in one account as a drop of liquid taken from the heart of a banana tree at midnight — is ingested rather than worn.

*Inference —* this practice is the reason a survey of amulets built from museum collections will always undercount written charms. A takrut rolled into metal lasts a thousand years; the same verse written to be washed off lasts a minute and leaves a person, not an object. Where a tradition uses both, the collections show one and not the other.

It is worth marking what this record does not claim. Mesopotamian incantation bowls, which are the other famous case of writing inside a bowl, were buried face down under thresholds in the accounts read here, not washed and drunk, and nothing in those accounts connects the two customs.
text.how: Public structure only: a text is written on a surface chosen so the ink will lift — the inside of a bowl, a wooden slate — water is poured on, and the water is drunk or used for washing. Which text is written, and by whom, is the part the traditions govern, and this record does not set it out.
text.today: Live and contested inside Islam. The practices of healers who claim to speak with jinn to cure or prevent the evil eye are held by some conservative Muslims to be shirk, a serious sin; the cited account sets out how narrow the difference between approved and disapproved practice can be, with the washing-off method on the approved side of the line drawn by the cleric it names. This atlas reports that disagreement between Muslim authorities and takes no side in it.

names.name: Wearing hidden
names.said: kept out of sight, on purpose
names.th: การสวมเครื่องรางแบบซ่อน

text.what: The rule that a charm is not to be seen. Hoodoo mojo bags are made for one person and kept on that person, out of sight: men in a trouser pocket, women clipped to the bra, either pinned to clothing below the waist. Catholic devotional scapulars hang front and back under the outer clothes and are designed to be unobtrusive. A Thai takrut goes under the shirt at the chest or the waist. The charm that hides and the charm that stares out from a windscreen are doing opposite jobs.
text.story:
Concealment has a legal history in hoodoo. Some conjurers hid their charms and others, who made a living from conjure, wore their mojo bags on the outside of their clothes — the cited account records both, and the trade sign and the private charm were different objects. Where the mojo holds a love working, practitioners sometimes specify that it be worn next to the skin; the hiding place is treated as part of whether it works.

Catholic practice built hiding into rule. The Carmelite constitution of 1281 required the scapular to be worn even in bed, under penalty of serious fault, and the constitution of 1369 attached automatic excommunication to a Carmelite saying Mass without one. Short devotional scapulars given to people outside the orders were designed to disappear under ordinary clothes at home and at work. John Paul II said he received his first Brown Scapular at ten and wore it into his papacy.

Thailand hides the object and also fixes its height. The rule reported in the amulet literature is not to wear Buddhist amulets below the waist: they go at the neck or above the waist, out of respect for the Buddha, while takrut, which carry no Buddha image, may go in trouser pockets. Japan hides the contents rather than the object: omamori are carried openly on a bag or a phone strap and customarily never opened, so that the packet is visible and its inside is not.

*Inference —* two opposite logics run through this atlas and they meet here. The eye, the horn and the hand work by being seen — they intercept a look. The sewn bag, the scapular and the takrut work by being unseen. A collection that files both as amulets is filing two different mechanisms under one word, and the clearest way to tell them apart in a museum tray is to ask where the object sat on the body.
text.how: Under the shirt on a cord; pinned inside clothing; in a pocket; sewn into a lining; clipped where another person will not look. Several traditions add a height rule, a side rule or a no-opening rule on top of the hiding.
text.today: Live everywhere the practice is. Scapulars are still worn under work clothes; mojo bags are still made to order and concealed; Thai amulets are worn under the shirt in cased frames and lifted out to be examined by dealers with loupes, which is the moment the private object becomes a traded one.

text_th.what: ข้อปฏิบัติว่าเครื่องรางต้องไม่ให้ใครเห็น ถุงโมโจ (mojo bag) ของฮูดู (hoodoo ธรรมเนียมพื้นบ้านของชาวแอฟริกันอเมริกัน) ทำขึ้นสำหรับคนคนเดียว และเก็บไว้กับตัวคนนั้นโดยไม่ให้เห็น: ผู้ชายใส่ในกระเป๋ากางเกง ผู้หญิงหนีบไว้กับเสื้อชั้นใน หรือจะกลัดไว้กับเสื้อผ้าต่ำกว่าเอวก็ได้ สกาปูลาร์ (scapular) เพื่อความศรัทธาของคาทอลิกห้อยไว้ด้านหน้าและด้านหลังใต้เสื้อผ้าชั้นนอก และออกแบบมาให้ไม่สะดุดตา ตะกรุดของไทยอยู่ใต้เสื้อ ที่หน้าอกหรือที่เอว เครื่องรางที่ซ่อนตัว กับเครื่องรางที่จ้องออกมาจากกระจกหน้ารถ ทำหน้าที่ตรงข้ามกัน
text_th.story:
การซ่อนมีประวัติทางกฎหมายในฮูดู ผู้ประกอบเวทบางคนซ่อนเครื่องรางของตน ส่วนคนอื่นที่ทำมาหากินด้วยเวทมนตร์ สวมถุงโมโจไว้นอกเสื้อผ้า — บันทึกที่อ้างอิงเล่าไว้ทั้งสองแบบ และป้ายบอกอาชีพกับเครื่องรางส่วนตัวเป็นวัตถุคนละชิ้นกัน ในกรณีที่ถุงโมโจบรรจุการทำเสน่ห์ความรัก ผู้ปฏิบัติบางครั้งกำหนดให้สวมแนบเนื้อ ที่ซ่อนถูกถือเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของการที่มันจะได้ผลหรือไม่

ธรรมเนียมคาทอลิกบรรจุการซ่อนไว้ในกฎ ธรรมนูญของคณะคาร์เมไลท์ ค.ศ. 1281 กำหนดให้สวมสกาปูลาร์แม้ขณะนอน มิฉะนั้นถือเป็นความผิดร้ายแรง และธรรมนูญ ค.ศ. 1369 กำหนดโทษบัพพาชนียกรรม (การตัดออกจากพระศาสนจักร) โดยอัตโนมัติ แก่นักบวชคาร์เมไลท์ที่ถวายมิสซาโดยไม่สวมสกาปูลาร์ สกาปูลาร์เพื่อความศรัทธาแบบสั้นที่มอบให้บุคคลนอกคณะนักบวช ถูกออกแบบให้หายไปใต้เสื้อผ้าธรรมดาทั้งที่บ้านและที่ทำงาน สมเด็จพระสันตะปาปายอห์น ปอลที่ 2 ตรัสว่าทรงได้รับสกาปูลาร์สีน้ำตาลครั้งแรกเมื่อพระชนมายุสิบพรรษา และทรงสวมต่อมาจนถึงสมัยที่ทรงเป็นพระสันตะปาปา

ประเทศไทยซ่อนวัตถุ และยังกำหนดระดับความสูงด้วย ข้อปฏิบัติที่รายงานไว้ในงานเขียนเรื่องพระเครื่องคือ ไม่สวมพระเครื่องต่ำกว่าเอว: พระเครื่องอยู่ที่คอหรือเหนือเอว ด้วยความเคารพต่อพระพุทธเจ้า ส่วนตะกรุดซึ่งไม่มีพระพุทธรูป ใส่ในกระเป๋ากางเกงได้ ญี่ปุ่นซ่อนสิ่งที่อยู่ข้างใน ไม่ใช่ตัววัตถุ: โอมาโมริ (omamori) ถูกพกอย่างเปิดเผยบนกระเป๋าหรือสายห้อยโทรศัพท์ และตามธรรมเนียมจะไม่เปิดดูเลย ห่อจึงมองเห็นได้ แต่ข้างในมองไม่เห็น

*ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* ตรรกะสองแบบที่ตรงข้ามกันวิ่งผ่านแอตลาสนี้ และมาพบกันที่นี่ ดวงตา เขาสัตว์ และมือ ทำงานด้วยการถูกมองเห็น — มันสกัดสายตาไว้ ถุงที่เย็บ สกาปูลาร์ และตะกรุด ทำงานด้วยการไม่ถูกมองเห็น คอลเลกชันที่จัดทั้งสองแบบไว้ในหมวดเครื่องรางเหมือนกัน กำลังจัดกลไกสองแบบที่ต่างกันไว้ใต้คำเดียว และวิธีที่ชัดที่สุดในการแยกแยะเมื่ออยู่ในถาดของพิพิธภัณฑ์ คือการถามว่าวัตถุนั้นเคยอยู่ตรงไหนของร่างกาย
text_th.how: ใต้เสื้อโดยห้อยเชือก กลัดไว้ด้านในเสื้อผ้า ในกระเป๋า เย็บไว้ในซับใน หนีบไว้ในที่ที่คนอื่นจะไม่มอง หลายธรรมเนียมเพิ่มข้อกำหนดเรื่องความสูง เรื่องข้าง หรือเรื่องห้ามเปิด ซ้อนไว้บนการซ่อนอีกชั้นหนึ่ง
text_th.today: ยังปฏิบัติอยู่ทุกแห่งที่มีธรรมเนียมนี้ สกาปูลาร์ยังสวมใต้ชุดทำงาน ถุงโมโจยังทำตามสั่งและซ่อนไว้ พระเครื่องไทยสวมใต้เสื้อในกรอบเลี่ยม และถูกหยิบออกมาให้เซียนพระส่องด้วยกล้องส่องพระ ซึ่งเป็นช่วงเวลาที่วัตถุส่วนตัวกลายเป็นวัตถุในตลาดเช่าหา

restricted.note: Among Arrernte groups, tjurunga were kept apart from the camp in a sacred place closed to women and to uninitiated men, and in the period described only initiated men could see or touch them. Australian collecting institutions hold material of this kind under access restrictions set by the relevant communities. This atlas prints the restriction and holds no description of those objects or their keeping places.
restricted.who_says: Arrernte practice as described in the cited account, and AIATSIS, which restricts access to culturally sensitive collection items to those with the permission of the relevant Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander community

names.name: Akodessawa fetish market
names.said: a-ko-des-SA-wa; the French name is mar-SHAY day fay-tee-SHUR
names.th: ตลาดเครื่องรางอาโกเดสซาวา

text.what: A supply market in the Akodessawa district of Lomé, Togo, for the materials used in Vodun practice. The stock is animal: monkey heads, skulls, dried birds, crocodiles, skins. Sellers work from tables, buyers come with a need, and a practitioner puts the material together for them. The encyclopedia calls it "the world's largest voodoo market", using a spelling this atlas otherwise keeps out of its own sentences.
text.story:
Vodun is long established in Togo, and the route it took is a loop rather than a line. Enslaved people carried Yoruba gods to the Caribbean and South America; there the gods were joined to Catholic saints and church symbols and changed meaning; when freed people and their families came back to West Africa, they built a Vodun practice in the country their families had left.

The word in the market's French name is the difficult one. A fetish here is comparable to an orisha: it may be a god, or a person, a plant, an animal or a material, depending on the rite and the situation, and in the rite it is activated and strengthened. Some are held to have been particular people.

This atlas does not print rite detail. What a practitioner does with a material bought at these tables is the practitioner's to publish, and the sources read for this record do not publish it. What is on the record is the trade: a district, a named market, sellers, stock, and customers who come for a specific thing.

*Inference —* the market is photographed more than it is documented. This project found no published price list, no seller interview and no survey it could cite; the record therefore stays with what the encyclopedia states and says plainly that the rest is missing rather than filling it from a travel column.

names.name: The Barkhor
names.th: บาร์คอร์

text.what: A ring of street about a kilometre round, circling the Jokhang temple in the old city of Lhasa. It is at once the city's commercial centre and a circuit walked as devotion. Traffic goes one way, clockwise, and some of the people on it are not walking but measuring the ring out in full-body prostrations.
text.story:
The circuit came from the temple. Songtsen Gampo and Princess Wencheng led the move to Lhasa and built the Jokhang; people began to turn around the temple, and the path their feet wore became a road. That road is one of the three circumambulation routes of Lhasa — the others are the Lingkhor and the Woesor — and it is the oldest street in the city, dated in origin to the 7th century CE and still carrying the plan of the old town.

Tibetans call it the holy road. The direction is not decorative: you walk with the turning of the prayer cylinder, which is to say clockwise, right shoulder to the temple.

The street is also the busiest commercial one in the old city. *Inference —* the objects this atlas is about are made and worn across this region — the agate dzi bead, the amulet box at the throat, the printed cloth flag — but no source read for this record itemises a Barkhor stall, and this record does not furnish one. On the street's present policing and regulation this atlas has read nothing it can cite, and it does not speculate.
text.today: In use as both a market street and a kora, on the published accounts this project has read. No day is marked open or closed below.

names.name: Room 1: Enlightenment, the British Museum
names.th: ห้อง 1: ยุคเรืองปัญญา พิพิธภัณฑ์บริติช

text.what: One long room off the Great Court, lined with tall wall presses and galleried in dark wood. The museum calls it the oldest room in the present building, put up for King George III's library and now holding a permanent display of eighteenth-century collecting. The objects are not grouped by country. They are grouped in seven disciplines an eighteenth-century collector would have recognised — the natural world, the birth of archaeology, art and civilisation, classifying the world, ancient scripts, ritual and religion, trade and discovery — so a Pacific shield, a Sumerian tablet and an astrolabe stand within a few steps of each other.
text.story:
This is the room about how the rest of the museum filled up. Sir Hans Sloane's cabinets are here; the museum's own gallery text says his collection, with several additional libraries, became the foundation of the British Museum, established by Act of Parliament on 7 June 1753.

The museum does not hedge about what else the period was. Its own page for this room says the Enlightenment "witnessed the aggressive global expansion of European colonialism and the transatlantic slave trade" and that "This room's displays reflect the close connection between Enlightenment and empire." Under Ritual and religion it writes that "Christian mistrust of superstition and idols, rituals and magic led to ignorance about other religions", that scholars set out to dispel that by studying the religions they met, collecting religious artefacts and grouping gods into families — and that "Much of this activity took place within the context of colonialism." Under Trade and discovery it names the East India and Royal Africa Companies, "whose wealth was made possible through the use of enslaved labour".

One object in this room carries a live claim. The museum's catalogue places a bark-and-wood shield, registration number Oc1978,Q.839, on display in Room 1, Trade & Discovery, Wall Press 96; it was donated by the Lords of the Admiralty and first registered and given a Q number in 1978. Rodney Kelly, a Gweagal man from Bermagui, began campaigning for the shield's return after it appeared in the exhibition Encounters at the National Museum of Australia, 27 November 2015 to 28 March 2016, and travelled to Britain three times, once in 2016 and twice in 2017; the chair of the La Perouse Local Aboriginal Land Council, Noeleen Timbery, has backed the return. The British Museum has refused, on the ground that British law does not permit it to hand the object over.

The identification is itself contested, and the museum says so on its own object page. Its curator's comments open: "Once thought to have been obtained on Captain Cook's first voyage to the Pacific, when he visited Botany Bay near present day Sydney, New South Wales, in 1770." The record now dates the shield "1771 (or earlier)" and finds the match with Sydney Parkinson's and John Frederick Miller's drawings only an apparent one. *Inference —* an object whose owner and whose date are both argued over is the right object to meet first in a museum, and this room is where a reader of this atlas should start before walking to the Egyptian cases.
text.today: Open with the rest of the museum, free, and unchanged in layout. The museum's own warning stands beside its hours: "Occasionally we may need to close galleries at short notice." This project has not stood in the room.

text.what: The head shrine of Inari, at the foot of a 233-metre mountain in Fushimi-ku, Kyoto. Paths climb four kilometres to smaller shrines, roofed most of the way by torii gates — roughly 10,000 of them, each one paid for by a Japanese business, about 800 set close enough together to make a tunnel. Tens of thousands of rock altars, otsuka, stand along the way, set up by private people and cut with their own names for Inari.
text.story:
The shrine was formally founded in 711 CE by the Hata clan, immigrants from the Korean peninsula who brought irrigation, sericulture and sake brewing into Yamashiro. The Yamashiro fudoki tells it as an arrow, a rice cake that turned into a white bird, and rice growing where the bird came down. Inari began as the kami of rice and agriculture and stays that; merchants took Inari up as the patron of business, which is why the gates are donated by companies.

Donating a torii to have a wish granted, or in thanks for one granted, spread from the Edo period onward and has not stopped. Unlike most Shinto shrines, this one leaves the main object of worship — a mirror — in open view. Foxes stand at the gates as Inari's messengers, often with a granary key in the mouth.

The shrine was in the first rank of state-supported shrines from 1871 to 1946. Police counted 2.69 million worshippers over three days of the new year in 2006, the largest count in western Japan. Around 32,000 branch shrines carry Inari elsewhere in the country.

On the approach, sweet shops sell tsujiura senbei, a folded fortune cracker documented at least to the 19th century and argued to be the ancestor of the American fortune cookie.

*Inference —* an omamori bought at a shrine gate is the shrine's own object, and a head shrine of this size is one of the places the practice runs at scale. This atlas has read no published stock list for this shrine's own counter, so the charm records below are linked as kin rather than as inventory.

text.what: A roofed market of 61 streets and more than 4,000 shops on 30,700 square metres in the walled city of Istanbul, between the Beyazit and Nuruosmaniye mosques. Traders of one good still hold one street, the way the guilds arranged it. Two domed stone halls, the bedestens, sit at the centre; the eye beads a visitor carries out are sold in the jewellers' and souvenir lanes around them.
text.story:
Mehmed II started it in the winter of 1455/56, months after taking Constantinople, with a building for textiles and jewels: the Cevahir Bedesten, the Bedesten of Gems, finished in the winter of 1460/61 and endowed to the waqf of Hagia Sophia. A second hall, the Sandal Bedesten, followed. Sellers filled the ground between them, and a quarter grew that did nothing but trade.

By the 17th century the shape was fixed: 67 named streets, 18 gates opened at dawn and shut at dusk, 3,000 shops plus 300 in the surrounding hans. Evliya Çelebi described it around 1638. Until the repairs that followed the 1894 earthquake there were no shops as western Europe knew them — a merchant sat on a wooden divan in a space six to eight feet wide and three to four feet deep, the precious stock kept in cabinets rather than displayed, and the day ended by drawing a drape across it.

The eye bead is the market's smallest export. In Turkey it is the nazar boncuğu; in Greece the same object is the máti. It is blue glass with white, black and yellow at the centre, a design whose written record and surviving examples run back to about 1500 BCE, and it is now, in the encyclopedia's flat phrase, a popular choice of souvenir with tourists.

*Inference —* a market that concentrated one trade per street for five centuries is the reason the bead has a fixed look at all. Mass production did not flatten this design; a guild had already fixed it.
text.today: Employs 26,000 people and takes between 250,000 and 400,000 visitors a day. Wikipedia's account, read on 16 September 2026, states the complex opens each day except Sundays and bank holidays, from 9:00 to 19:00. This project has not read that timetable on the bazaar's own page, so no day is marked open or closed below.

names.th: อินซาดง

text.what: A neighbourhood of Jongno District, Seoul, 12.7 hectares of galleries, antique shops, paper and brush shops and tea houses along Insadong-gil and the alleys off it. It holds 40 per cent of South Korea's antique shops and art galleries and 90 per cent of its traditional stationery shops — which means it is where the brush, the ink and the paper a talisman is written on are bought.
text.story:
The antique trade here began as a forced sale. During the Japanese occupation wealthy Korean residents were made to move and to sell their belongings, and the district became the place that trade happened. After the Korean War it turned into a centre of artistic life and cafés; foreign visitors in the 1960s called it Mary's Alley; the 1988 Olympics brought the international trade. In 2000 the area was renovated, and after protest its rapid modernisation was halted for two years.

The temple in the neighbourhood is Jogyesa, a principal Korean Buddhist temple; the central temple of Cheondoism stands nearby, finished in 1921. Calligraphy is demonstrated on the street daily.

The Korean protective charm does not come from a shop here, and the distinction is the point of this record. A pujŏk — bujeok — is produced by a mudang, a shaman, usually built out of hanja characters, handed to clients at the end of a rite and stuck to the inside wall of a house. Mudang are concentrated in Seoul more thickly than anywhere else in the country except Jeju; a late 20th-century Korean Gallup survey found 38 per cent of South Korean adults had consulted one. *Inference —* what Insadong sells is the material and the antique, not the charm; the charm is commissioned, and this atlas has read no source that puts a bujeok counter on this street.
text.today: Trading, with the backstreets gentrified into cafés and guest houses. About 100,000 visitors on a Sunday were reported in 2000. No day is marked below: the shops keep their own hours and nobody publishes them as one timetable.

names.th: ทาเมล

text.what: A commercial neighbourhood of narrow alleys in Kathmandu, about 1.4 kilometres north of Durbar Square. Shops run wall to wall: trekking gear, handicrafts, woollens, music, groceries, guest houses. It is the district a visitor to Nepal buys things in, which makes it the counter across which most Himalayan protective objects leave the country.
text.story:
The name comes from Tha Bahi, which places the district's root in the Newar community, the indigenous people of the Kathmandu Valley. Thamel has been the centre of Kathmandu's tourist trade for over four decades, since the years of the overland hippie route, and it is now the valley's densest concentration of shops aimed at outsiders.

What the shops stock is where this atlas has to be careful. The encyclopedia's account lists food, trekking gear, music, handicrafts, souvenirs and woollens, and itemises no charm. *Inference —* prayer flags, rudraksha strings, dzi beads and gau boxes are what a Himalayan souvenir lane carries, and this project has read no survey of Thamel's stalls, so the objects below are linked as kin of the district rather than asserted as stock.

What can be cited is where the materials come from. Rudraksha — the seed of Elaeocarpus ganitrus, strung and counted by Shaivites — is cultivated in the Himalayan foothills, and the most popular varieties are found around Kathmandu and the Arun Valley. Printed cloth prayer flags reached Nepal and Tibet through the Indian monk Atisha, who died in 1054. Dzi beads are found in Tibet and in neighbouring Nepal, Bhutan, Ladakh and Sikkim, and Tibetans treat them as hereditary gems rather than as purchases.
text.today: Trading, and the pre-base camp for mountaineering: gear shops, money changers, agents, guest houses. No day is marked below, because the alleys keep shop hours and nobody publishes them.

names.th: ข่านเอลคาลีลี

text.what: Cairo's bazaar quarter, in the medieval city between al-Muizz Street, al-Muski Street and the mosque and shrine of al-Hussein. Shops sit at ground level in the walls of old khans — multi-storey merchant inns built round a courtyard — with workshops above and behind them. Goldsmiths hold their own souq inside it, and it is the goldsmiths' lane that matters to this atlas: a charm in Cairo is usually something small, stamped or cast in metal, and bought where metal is sold.
text.story:
The quarter is named after a stable-master. During Sultan Barquq's first reign, between 1382 and 1389, his amir akhur Jaharkas al-Khalili pulled down the Fatimid royal mausoleum that stood here — the Turbat az-Za'faraan, the Saffron Tomb — and put up a large khan in its place. He is reported to have thrown the bones of the Fatimid caliphs onto the rubbish hills east of the city. The khan took his name, then the whole district did.

Sultan al-Ghuri, the last effective Mamluk sultan, demolished al-Khalili's building and rebuilt it in 1511, laying out a souq with monumental stone gates. Two of those gates still stand on Sikkat al-Badistan. By the end of the Mamluk period there were 21 khans and wikalas here; by the end of the 18th century, some 39. El-Fishawy's coffeehouse, still in the lanes, was established in 1773.

The present trade is aimed at visitors and at Cairenes in different lanes. Shops sell souvenirs, antiques and jewellery; the goldsmiths' souq still serves locals; crafts workshops run in the courtyards and upper floors. The scholar Remke Kruk found books on magic and sorcery well represented in street stalls and bookshops across the Muslim world around 2005, from Marrakesh to Cairo to Yemen, alongside religious pamphlets condemning the practices those books describe — an argument conducted stall to stall, in print, in the same streets.

*Inference —* the pharaonic amulet shapes a visitor buys here — scarab, wedjat eye, ankh — are jewellery made now, not survivals. This atlas has read no source that surveys what the Khan's stalls actually stock, so the record stops at what the goldsmiths' souq and the workshops are documented to be.

The market has twice been attacked. A suicide bombing on 7 April 2005 killed 21 people; a second attack on 22 February 2009 killed a 17-year-old French visitor and injured 22 people.
text.today: Trading, and oriented to tourism in its best-known lanes, as of the most recent published account this project has read. No day is marked open or closed below: the district's hours are the individual shopkeepers' and nobody publishes them as a timetable.

text.what: The market streets of the Marrakesh medina, running north from the square called Jemaa el-Fnaa into the old city. The lanes follow the road that once linked the Almoravid stone fortress to the city's first Friday mosque, and they still hold the main axis of the souks. Each lane is one trade.
text.story:
Marrakesh was founded in 1070. Its two focal points were the Ksar el-Hajjar, the fortress of stone, and the first Friday mosque; the souk streets grew along the roads between them and have kept that line ever since. At the fortress end lay a large open space for temporary and weekly markets, called Rahbat al-Ksar, then as-Saha al-Kubra, the grand square. That space is today's Jemaa el-Fnaa, and the souk is edged along one side by it.

What the square sells changes by the hour. By day: orange juice, water sellers with leather bags and brass cups, snake charmers. Later the charmers leave and the square fills with storytellers, musicians, magicians and peddlers of traditional medicines; after dark, food stalls. UNESCO's programme for intangible heritage began with people worried about exactly this square, and the label followed.

The written trade is documented across the region rather than lane by lane. The scholar Remke Kruk found books on magic and sorcery well represented in street stalls and bookshops from Marrakesh to Cairo to Yemen around 2005; from about 1990 religious pamphlets condemning those practices sold beside them.

*Inference —* the herbalists' stalls are what most visitors come away describing, and this atlas has not yet read a source it can cite for them. The record therefore names the square's medicine peddlers, which is published, and stops there rather than furnishing the lanes from guidebooks it could not open.
text.today: Trading. The square went into a renovation programme from May 2025, budgeted at 160 million dirhams and scheduled to finish by the end of that year, to rework infrastructure and reorganise the public and commercial space. Hours are the stallholders' own; none are marked below.

text.what: A run of stalls on Calle Linares in the El Rosario neighbourhood of La Paz, spilling into Jiménez, Santa Cruz and Illampu. Stock: medicinal plants, retama, amulets, talismans, powders, dried frogs, armadillos, and the sullus — dried llama foetuses — that are buried under the foundations of Bolivian houses as an offering to Pachamama.
text.story:
The market's Spanish name was chosen to be recognisable to foreigners, which is a fact about naming rather than about what is sold. Most of the stallholders are Aymara women, the chifreras. The yatiri who work here are identifiable by their black hats and coca pouches, and the pouches hold amulets, talismans and powders sold for luck, beauty and fertility; they also read fortunes and take commissions for love work and for curses.

The year has a shape. October is the busiest month, because Pachamama offerings cluster there — sellers put roughly 60 per cent of the year's sales in that one month — and February, at Carnival, is the other peak.

One street over in the calendar sits Alasitas. From 24 January, for a month, La Paz holds a fair for Ekeko, the Aymara god of abundance, where people buy miniature versions of what they want — food, tools, a house, a car, a diploma — to give to somebody else, on the understanding that the full-sized version follows within the year. Men and, less often, women acting as shaman bless the miniatures; at midday on 24 January the Catholic Church blesses them too, at the cathedral. The name is Aymara for buy from me.

In 2019 the market was named Intangible Cultural Heritage of La Paz. *Tradition holds —* many of the rituals served here have been adapted to an urban setting, which the encyclopedia attributes to the long aftermath of colonisation rather than to tourism.
text.today: Trading, on published accounts. October and Carnival are the peaks. No day is marked open or closed below; stall hours are the sellers' own.

text.what: A row of esoteric stalls inside the Gamarra clothing district of La Victoria, Lima, along Avenida Aviación. Medicinal plants, bottled preparations in coloured glass, amulets, incense, black and white candles, and sprays sold for money. Readers work the same aisle, taking tarot and palm.
text.story:
Gamarra is Lima's garment quarter — blocks of textile workshops and wholesalers — and the esoteric market sits inside it rather than apart from it. Daniela Ramos described the trade for Nexos, the Universidad de Lima's magazine, on 31 October 2024: herbalists, curanderos and readers working side by side, a reader named Timbaya among them, selling plants, potions, amulets and cleansings.

The prices in that account are worth recording with their date. Herbal remedies at 10 to 30 soles; a potion for attracting love at 30; a tarot reading from 10 up to 120; an energy cleansing at 1,200. All in Peruvian soles, in October 2024.

What customers ask for is not what the market's name implies. Ramos reports that money, not love, is the most common request — prosperity formulas outsell love potions at the stalls she stood at.

*Inference —* an esoteric market inside a garment wholesaling district is a market serving traders, not tourists. Ramos's account is of a working aisle in a working quarter; this project has read no visitor survey and does not claim one.

text.what: A municipal covered market in Colonia Merced Balbuena, southeast of Mexico City's historic centre: one long metal nave, narrow aisles, traders grouped by what they sell. Pottery in one section, party supplies in another, live animals in a third. Two aisles at the back carry medicinal plants and the goods for ritual — candles, amulets, oils, soaps, powders — and those two aisles are why the market is known outside the city.
text.story:
The city built it. Mercado de Sonora opened on 23 September 1957, one of a set of public markets set up to organise and regulate retail trade, descended from the pre-Hispanic tianguis, the street market. At the market's fiftieth anniversary in 2007 the party included mariachis and a limpia, a cleansing, to clear the building of bad energy.

Herbal medicine and ritual goods are not two trades here but one, because Mexican herbal medicine has been tied to religious and magical practice for centuries. Avocado leaves for inflammation, chiranthodendron for the heart, jacaranda flowers for the stomach. Dried rattlesnake against cancer. Crosses of ocote wood for luck; chains of garlic against harm; and a seed called deer's eye — ojo de venado — against the evil eye. Candles come in sizes, shapes and colours, each colour with its own function.

The traffic is countable. An estimated 2,000 people come each weekend specifically for that section, which is one of the city's centres for Santería and for the veneration of Santa Muerte. The most popular goods are for love: candles, oils, amulets, soaps, needles, lotions, herbs, and services — spell casting, cleansings — sold under names like ven a mi, come to me, and miel de amor, honey of love.

Prices carry their moment. During the H1N1 scare of 2009 trade fell by about half, but a ten-herb blend against flu — eucalyptus, bougainvillea, tejocote — kept herb sellers solvent at 80 pesos a kilo; Santa Muerte sellers reported moving white dresses for the images, white being the colour of health.

The market carries its costs in public. Street peddlers fill what is left of the car park and spill into the surrounding lanes on Saturdays; the building leaks, its floors and ramps are in poor condition, and market representatives put that down to borough corruption and to officials extorting traders. Police have raided the animal aisles over protected species.
text.today: Trading, with Saturday the busiest day and the widest stock. The Linares family, five generations of cartonería makers and the inventors of the alebrije, still work in workshops just behind the market. No day is marked open or closed below: stall hours are the traders' own.

text.what: An open-air market covering several square miles of the Addis Ketema district of Addis Ababa, and the name of the neighbourhood it fills. An estimated 13,000 people work in about 7,100 business entities. Most of it is wholesale, sorted into sections the traders call terras: coffee, spices, scrap metal, furniture, electronics. Coffee is the main good passing through.
text.story:
The market is a product of occupation policy. Addis Ababa's older market stood near St George's Church, where the City Hall is now; the Italian occupiers of the 1930s moved it west, to land around the premises of Fitawrari Habte Giyorgis Dinagde, and kept the old site — renamed Piazza, with European-style shop windows — for Europeans. The Arab traders of Piazza moved half a mile west after them; local shopkeepers displaced those traders in turn, and since the 1960s Merkato has been a mostly local market. It grew without a plan.

This record has to state a gap rather than fill it. The Ethiopian protective object in this atlas is the talismanic scroll — the ketab, written in Ge'ez on hide — and it is not a market good. A scroll is commissioned by the patient from a dabtara, an unordained figure in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, who cuts it to the patient's own measure: to the height of the body for head-to-toe protection, longer to hang on a wall. The making includes a sacrifice of the animal whose hide is used, standing for the person the scroll is for. Activation needs a third party literate in Ge'ez to read it aloud.

*Inference —* that is why a market this size is thin in this atlas. A commissioned object made to a body's measurements does not have a stall. This project searched for a published source placing the scroll trade inside Merkato and found none it could cite; the record says so instead of inventing an aisle.
text.today: Trading, as Africa's largest open-air market. It is not primarily a tourist market: most sections are wholesale. No day is marked open or closed below.

names.name: The Egyptian galleries, the Metropolitan Museum of Art
names.th: ห้องจัดแสดงอียิปต์ พิพิธภัณฑ์ศิลปะเมโทรโพลิแทน

text.what: A chain of rooms along the museum's north side, running from the predynastic material through to Roman Egypt and ending at the Temple of Dendur in its glass hall. For this atlas it is the densest walkable run of amulets anywhere: wedjat eyes in faience, carnelian, obsidian and gold, scarabs, cippi, and trays of small figures, laid out in numbered galleries a visitor can name. Faience, which the labels use constantly, is crushed quartz fired with a glaze that comes out of the kiln blue or green.
text.story:
The Met's Egyptian collection was not mostly bought. The department's own page says the museum's three decades of archaeological work in Egypt began in 1906, and the encyclopedia account puts almost half the present collection down to the excavation seasons of 1906 to 1941. That is why a Met amulet more often carries a find-spot than a dealer's name: a small gold amulet in Gallery 109, accession 22.1.58, is credited to MMA excavations, 1920–22, from the Memphite Region.

The size of the collection is published two ways and this record prints both. The Wikipedia account gives more than 26,000 pieces across forty galleries, almost all on display; the department's own page, read on 17 September 2026, says "approximately 30,000 objects". Neither is wrong on its own terms and this project has not read a reconciliation.

Walk it and the amulets sort themselves by gallery. Gallery 120 holds a run of faience wedjat eyes from about 1386–1347 BCE, entered in 1911 on the Rogers Fund. Gallery 127 holds one cut in gold, 332–30 BCE, and one in obsidian. Gallery 130 holds a long faience-and-aragonite wedjat, 6.5 centimetres, bought in 1926 on the Edward S. Harkness Gift. Gallery 128 holds the Metternich Stela, catalogued as Magical Stela with Horus the Child, 360–343 BCE, and Gallery 134 a shelf of smaller cippi in steatite, soapstone and faience — the same design shrunk from 83.5 centimetres to under 5.

How the objects got here is still being worked out in public, and not always by the museum first. In September 2022 New York law enforcement seized 27 objects on three warrants for return to Italy and Egypt. The museum has since published a statement on collecting practices and hired a provenance-research manager with a team of three. *Inference —* an excavation credit line is a stronger provenance than a purchase, and the 1906–1941 seasons are the reason this room reads differently from a room filled by a dealer; it is not the same thing as saying every object here arrived cleanly.

The licence is the other half of why this atlas keeps pointing here. Since 2017 every Met image of a public-domain work carries a Creative Commons Zero dedication, which is on Wikimedia Commons' accepted list. A photograph of a Met wedjat can be reproduced, cropped and altered with no permission asked. The dedication covers the museum's photographs. It says nothing about who the objects belong to.
text.today: Open six days a week; closed Wednesdays. General admission on 17 September 2026 is US$30 for adults, US$22 for seniors and for visitors with a disability, US$17 for students and free for children 12 and under, with pay-what-you-wish admission for New York State residents and for New York, New Jersey and Connecticut students. The museum lists the Ancient West Asia and Ancient Cyprus galleries as closed for renovation as of that date; the Egyptian galleries are not on that list. This project has not stood in them.

text.what: A flea-market neighbourhood in the old town of Athens, built round Monastiraki Square and running along Pandrossou and Adrianou streets. Clothing, souvenirs and specialist shops; a metro station on the square; and, in the souvenir windows, trays of the blue glass eye.
text.story:
The district takes its name from the square, and the square from the Church of the Pantanassa standing in it. It is one of Athens's main shopping districts and its best-known bargain quarter.

The object this atlas comes for has a Greek name. The bead a Turkish seller calls nazar boncuğu is máti in Greek, the eye, and it belongs to a tradition Greek authors were already describing in classical antiquity: Hesiod, Callimachus, Plato, Theocritus and Plutarch all mention the harmful look, and Peter Walcot's Envy and the Greeks listed more than a hundred ancient works that do. Greeks hung talismans in the house and wore amulets; Peisistratus hung a grasshopper figure before the Acropolis, a few hundred metres uphill from this square.

The trade is not a museum piece. A 2015 Pew survey of central and eastern Europe found a median of 48 per cent of adults reporting belief in the evil eye, with 66 per cent in Greece — the joint highest figure in the survey. The bead is also, in the encyclopedia's phrase, a popular choice of souvenir with tourists, and both those sentences describe the same stall.

*Inference —* the Monastiraki article itemises no charm, and this record does not claim a particular shop. What it claims is the pairing: the densest souvenir trade in Athens, in a country where two adults in three report the belief the object answers.
text.today: Trading, as a flea market and a tourist quarter. No day is marked open or closed below; the shops keep their own hours and no timetable is published for the district.
