names.name: The amulet and charm cases, Pitt Rivers Museum
names.th: ตู้เครื่องรางและของขลัง พิพิธภัณฑ์พิตต์ริเวอร์ส

text.what: Eight glass-topped cases on the Court, the ground floor of the museum, with deep drawers under them. The museum's own guide names them: C26A, C27A and C28A hold Amulets and Charms; C29A, Amulets, Charms, and Divination; C30A, Charms against the Evil Eye; C30B, Amulets, Cures, and Charms; C31A, Magic and Trial by Ordeal; C31B, Amulets and Charms for Animals. A Neapolitan silver cimaruta, a blue glass eye bead from Hebron, a Japanese glass hy-o-tan, a string of blue beads that hung round a donkey's neck in Istanbul and an Algerian sheep's shoulder blade written on in Arabic all sit within arm's reach of one another, because they answer the same problem.
text.story:
The museum publishes the total: almost 6,000 amulets and charms in the collections, though not all of them are on display. They come from everywhere, England included.

The largest single block arrived by sale and then by transfer. Adrien de Mortillet, 1853–1931, son of the archaeologist Gabriel de Mortillet and later a lecturer and chair at the School of Anthropology in Paris, built an amulet collection drawn from five continents and from antiquity to the early twentieth century. In 1931, a few months before he died, he sold it to Henry Wellcome's museum in London. It was transferred to the Pitt Rivers Museum in 1985. In 2012 the museum catalogued more than 2,500 of them under a project called Small Blessings, funded by Arts Council England's Designation Development Fund and running February to September that year, and put the records online.

The English cases owe a bank cashier. Edward Lovett swapped alpine plants grown in seashells for the charms Londoners had in their pockets and gave the results to Oxford; the museum's own England: The Other Within project counts 216 objects from him, 55 of them English, accessioned 1893 to 1911 — the encyclopedia gives the span as 1896 to 1911, and this record prints both rather than choosing. Walter Leo Hildburgh's amulets, bought across Europe, Asia and the Middle East, came by the same 1985 route out of Wellcome.

The cases are grouped by what an object does, not by where it is from, because the founder's 1884 Deed of Gift requires it: a clause says changes to the displays "shall not affect the general principle originated by Augustus Henry Lane Fox Pitt Rivers". The museum states plainly that this evolutionary approach to material culture is no longer appropriate in the modern display paradigm, and that it has kept the arrangement because the Deed does.

So it has gone at the labels instead. Labelling Matters, led by the director Laura Van Broekhoven with the research associate Marenka Thompson-Odlum and funded through the TORCH Heritage Seed Fund and Knowledge Exchange, reviews the language of the permanent displays; its stated aim is to "identify areas of improvement and to trial ways of changing our public texts where derogatory and other problematic language is used". In 2020 the museum took human remains off display, including the tsantsas shown since the 1940s. With the Museum of Natural History it returned the remains of 17 Aboriginal Australians to the Australian government in 2022, and in 2026 agreed to repatriate Naga skeletal remains, some of which had been shown in a case titled Treatment of Dead Enemies. That last one reaches these cases directly: the museum's own amulets guide describes an object made to be put in the spring of the Rengma Naga village of Tesophenyu, and lists what its wrappings hold.

The guide is careful about the claims and this atlas keeps its wording. It defines an amulet with the Oxford English Dictionary — "Anything worn about the person as a charm preventative against evil, mischief, disease, witchcraft, etc." — and explains sympathetic magic as meaning "that the appearance of an object resembles, in some way, the cure or protection it is believed to offer". Of the Maasai ivory amulet hung round a cow's neck it reports the Maasai term inkonyek, people with 'eyes', whose envious glance is held to be deadliest to young children and calves. Of a Yoruba ori box it records that the original owner assured the collector it was filled with 'juju' but could not say what was inside.

*Inference —* a case that puts a Naples cimaruta next to a Nagaland packet is making an argument, and the museum now argues with its own furniture.
text.today: On the Court floor, free, and still laid out on the founder's principle while the museum rewrites what is written on the cards. Displays are rotated, and the guide this record leans on was revised in March 2010 by Kate White, then Head of Access and Public Relations, so a case number is the museum's last published word and not a promise about today. This project has not stood in the Court.

names.name: Quiapo Church
names.native: Basilika Menor at Pambansang Dambana ni Jesus Nazareno
aliases: Minor Basilica and National Shrine of Jesus Nazareno
Parish of Saint John the Baptist
names.th: โบสถ์กีอาโป

text.what: A Catholic basilica in the Quiapo district of Manila, housing the Jesús Nazareno, a dark statue of Christ carrying the cross. Outside it, on Plaza Miranda and in the streets around the building, stalls sell herbs, oils, candles and amulets. Two systems trade at one address, and both have said so in public.
text.story:
The church has burnt, fallen and been rebuilt since 1588: destroyed by Limahong's men in 1574, burnt in 1603, damaged by the British in 1762, burnt in 1791 with the image spared, thrown down by the earthquake of 1863, burnt again in 1929. The present reinforced-concrete building, by the architect Juan Nakpil, was finished in 1935 and expanded in 1984-86. Pope John Paul II raised it to a minor basilica in 1987; it was declared a national shrine in December 2023.

The devotion is enormous. The feast of the Traslación on 9 January re-enacts the image's transfer from Intramuros, and 6.5 million devotees took part in 2024. Every Friday is Quiapo Day, with a novena and thousands in attendance; devotees climb a narrow stair to kiss the statue's foot or wipe it with a handkerchief they bring each visit. Men who carry the image walk under a panata, a vow. In October 2024 the Archbishop of Manila decreed the church's name changed to the Minor Basilica and National Shrine of Jesus Nazareno, dropping the usual English name to shift attention from the image's colour to the name of Christ.

The plaza trade is the other half. Agimat — anting-anting in its folklorised form — is the Filipino word for an amulet, and the practice that goes with it: most bear Latin inscriptions, most come with a small book of incantations to be read on Good Friday. Agimat merchants set up near churches, in the courtyard or the marketplace alongside, and Quiapo is the district the encyclopedia names when it names one. Filipino fighters wore anting-anting against the Spanish and the Americans; Macario Sakay wore a vest of religious images and Latin phrases.

The church has not been quiet about what else the stalls sell. Published accounts record peddlers of unsafe abortifacients and untested herbal remedies working the vicinity, and the Archdiocese of Manila condemning practices connected with them; Cardinal Gaudencio Rosales issued canonical excommunications in relation to abortion near the shrine. Abortion is illegal in the Philippines, and the accounts tie the trade to people who cannot afford a surgical procedure.
text.today: In use as a basilica and a national shrine, with the plaza trade running alongside it. This project has not read the basilica's own published timetable, so no day is marked open or closed below — the Friday novena is a cited fact about the week, not a statement that other days are shut.

names.name: Via San Gregorio Armeno
names.th: ถนนซานเกรโกริโออาร์เมโน

text.what: A narrow street in the old centre of Naples, lined with workshops that make figures for the presepe, the Neapolitan nativity scene. Terracotta heads, wired limbs, cloth, cork and plaster; shepherds beside this year's footballers and politicians. Coral and silver horns hang in the same windows, because the trade that models a figure by hand is the trade that cuts a charm by hand.
text.story:
The street is a stenoporos, one of the narrow cross-lanes of the Greek grid Neapolis was laid out on, running between the two main streets of the ancient city — today's Via dei Tribunali and Spaccanapoli — and crossing at the old agora.

The figures have a long root in the same ground. A temple of Ceres stood on this street in classical times, and citizens offered her small terracotta figurines made in the workshops nearby. The church of San Gregorio Armeno was founded around 930 on that temple's foundations. The Neapolitan nativity scene itself is much later, from the end of the 18th century. The workshops now run all year, with the main displays from early November to 6 January.

Naples is also a capital of the horn. The cornicello — curniciello in Neapolitan — is a twisted horn charm in gold, silver, bone, terracotta, plastic or red coral, worn against the malocchio and hung from rear-view mirrors, a custom the article traces back to protecting draught horses. Coral is the material that carries it, and coral is sacred to Venus.

Edward Lovett, the London folklorist, published a paper in 1909 called Amulets from Costers' Barrows in London, Rome, and Naples. He was reading three street trades as one subject, and this street is the one still working.

*Inference —* a lane whose craftsmen have modelled votive figures on the same ground for two thousand years is the clearest case in this atlas of a workshop outliving the religion it started in. Both halves of that sentence are cited; the joining of them is this project's.
text.today: Workshops produce figures year-round, traditional and topical. The heavy display season runs from early November to 6 January. No weekday is marked open or closed below: the shops set their own hours and no timetable is published for the street.

names.name: Sensō-ji
names.th: วัดเซนโซจิ

text.what: Tokyo's oldest-established Buddhist temple, in Asakusa, dedicated to Kannon, the bodhisattva of compassion. You reach the main hall through two gates and a shopping street: the Kaminarimon with its 700-kilogram red lantern, then Nakamise-dōri, 250 metres and about 72 shops, then the Hōzōmon. Omikuji stalls stand inside the precinct and along the approach — shake a numbered stick from a metal canister, read the answer out of one of a hundred drawers.
text.story:
The temple's origin story is a statue in a net: in 628 two brothers fishing the Sumida pulled up an image of Kannon, and the village headman turned his house into a temple for it. The first documented mention is later, in the Kamakura-period Azuma Kagami, which has Asakusa carpenters called to Kamakura in 1181. Tokugawa Ieyasu made it an official place of prayer for the shogunate in 1590.

The shops came with permission. In 1685 the temple licensed businesses on the main approach in exchange for their cleaning the grounds, and Nakamise has been a selling street ever since — cleared by government order in May 1885, rebuilt in brick that December, flattened by the 1923 earthquake, rebuilt in concrete in 1925, burnt out in the firebombing of 10 March 1945. The main hall went in that raid too and was rebuilt between 1951 and 1958, now under a titanium roof.

The temple is the 13th stop on the Bandō Sanjūsankasho pilgrimage route and the most visited religious site in the world, at over 30 million people a year. For a suggested donation of 100 yen a visitor may consult the omikuji oracle.

*Tradition holds —* the shops on a temple approach are not a later commercial layer but a continuous trade in selling to pilgrims who walked here, which is the encyclopedia's own framing of Nakamise.
text.today: Open, with the Nakamise shops on the approach and the omikuji stalls in use. This project has not read the temple's published timetable, so no day is marked open or closed below.

names.name: Mana Whenua, Te Papa
names.th: มานาเฟนูอา ที่พิพิธภัณฑ์เตปาปา

text.what: Te Papa's permanent Māori exhibition, on Level 4 of the Wellington waterfront building. The museum's own description: taonga tuku iho — treasures handed down — "ranging from weaving, carving, and pounamu pendants, to waka and whare". A whare is a house; the whare here is Te Hau ki Tūranga, a carved meeting house standing inside the gallery. A waka is a canoe; Teremoe, a waka taua or war canoe from the Whanganui region used in the wars of the mid-1800s, is in the same room. Photography is not allowed. The lighting is deliberately low.
text.story:
These are not curios, and the museum does not frame them as any. Its collections page states the principle it works under: "Mana Taonga is a recognition of the power of taonga to communicate deep truths about our people." It counts more than 30,000 taonga registered in the Taonga Māori collection, from ancestral carvings, personal ornaments, garments and weaponry through to flaked stone, bird bone and shell from excavations, and it says the Mana Taonga principle guides its approach to access and research, aiming at "the reconnection of people to their tribal taonga".

The hei-tiki make the point about how objects travel. Te Papa holds over 200 of them, the largest single group anywhere; the British Museum has about fifty. Some were exchanged or given to European travellers and sailors at the earliest point of contact, and, in the encyclopedia's flat phrasing, "the majority were stolen or improperly obtained through colonial processes". The stone itself is now legally Māori: in 1997 the Crown handed ownership of all naturally occurring pounamu back to the South Island iwi Ngāi Tahu as part of their Claims Settlement. Pounamu is nephrite jade and bowenite, found only in the South Island, and Māori classify it by colour — kahurangi, īnanga, kawakawa, tangiwai.

The whare at the centre of the gallery is the clearest case in the building. Te Hau ki Tūranga is a nineteenth-century Rongowhakaata carved meeting house, confiscated by the Crown in 1867 and later held by Te Papa; ownership was returned to Rongowhakaata through the iwi's Treaty settlement, and the house stayed in the museum while the iwi-in-residence exhibition Ko Rongowhakaata: Ruku i te Pō, Ruku i te Ao ran from September 2017 to February 2022. The museum kept the object and gave back the title.

Te Papa also does the asking. Karanga Aotearoa is, in the museum's own words, "the government mandated authority that negotiates the repatriation of Māori and Moriori ancestral remains on behalf of Māori and Moriori"; Cabinet agreed in May 2003 that Te Papa should act for the government in returning kōiwi and kōimi tangata — ancestral skeletal remains — and toi moko, preserved tattooed heads held in institutions abroad. Between 1 July 2003 and 1 May 2024 it repatriated 850 Māori and Moriori ancestral remains from overseas institutions, from Australia, Austria, Canada, France, Germany, Sweden, the United Kingdom, the United States and elsewhere, and returned 76 to iwi within New Zealand. A Repatriation Advisory Panel oversees it, and iwi representatives set the place, the time and the details of each return.

From 29 August 2026 the carving argument is on show at scale. He Toi Whakairo: The Art of Māori Carving, running to August 2031 inside Mana Whenua on Level 4, puts more than 140 whakairo — carvings — from seven centuries in one place, many never exhibited before, under the whakataukī he toi whakairo, he mana tangata: the art of carving is the dignity of people.
text.today: Open every day, 10am to 6pm, except Christmas Day. Entry is free for New Zealanders and people living in New Zealand and NZ$35 for international visitors aged 16 and over, as published on 17 September 2026; some exhibitions and experiences are ticketed on top. Mana Whenua is free with museum entry, is listed as wheelchair accessible, has variable lighting, and carries a no-photography rule. This project has not stood on Level 4.

restricted.note: Photography is not permitted in Mana Whenua, on the museum's own rule. names.name: Tha Phrachan amulet market
names.native: ตลาดพระเครื่องท่าพระจันทร์
names.th: ตลาดพระเครื่องท่าพระจันทร์

text.what: Bangkok's main amulet market, running in the lanes beside Thammasat University and the Chao Phraya river pier of the same name. Stalls are trays and glass-topped cases; buyers arrive with jeweller's loupes and go over a two-centimetre clay tablet the way a coin dealer goes over a coin.
text.story:
Tha Phrachan is the market Thai writing on amulets names first when it names any. Wikipedia's account puts it plainly: famous markets for amulets include Tha Phrachan Market next to Thammasat University, and rare pieces often require expert authentication because forgeries are common.

What the loupes are for is the trade's central problem. A phra khrueang is valued by which temple pressed it, which monk consecrated it, and when — facts that live in the clay's texture, the mould's flaws and a certificate, not in the image on the front. *Tradition holds —* the specialist who reads those tells for a fee is as much a part of this market as the seller.

The scale is not small. When the Jatukham Rammathep amulet peaked in 2007, that single type's market reached twenty billion baht in a year before the bubble burst in late 2007, leaving stock that could be had cheap. *Inference —* a market that can move that much in twelve months is a financial market with devotional objects in it, and the argument over which of those two things it mainly is runs among Thai commentators, not between Thais and outsiders.
text.today: Still trading as of the most recent published accounts this project has read. Hours are not published as a timetable: stalls keep their own, the lanes are busiest in daylight, and weekends draw the collectors. This project has not stood there, so no day is marked either way below.

text_th.what: ตลาดพระเครื่องหลักของกรุงเทพฯ ตั้งอยู่ในตรอกข้างมหาวิทยาลัยธรรมศาสตร์และท่าเรือริมแม่น้ำเจ้าพระยาที่มีชื่อเดียวกัน แผงพระเป็นถาดและตู้กระจก ผู้เช่าหามาพร้อมกล้องส่องพระ และพิจารณาพระเนื้อดินขนาดสองเซนติเมตร อย่างที่ผู้ค้าเหรียญพิจารณาเหรียญ
text_th.story:
ท่าพระจันทร์คือตลาดแรกที่งานเขียนเรื่องพระเครื่องของไทยเอ่ยชื่อ เมื่อจะเอ่ยถึงตลาดใดก็ตาม บทความในวิกิพีเดียกล่าวไว้ตรง ๆ ว่า ตลาดพระเครื่องที่มีชื่อเสียงรวมถึงตลาดท่าพระจันทร์ข้างมหาวิทยาลัยธรรมศาสตร์ และพระหายากมักต้องให้ผู้เชี่ยวชาญตรวจพิสูจน์ เพราะพระปลอมมีอยู่ทั่วไป

กล้องส่องพระมีไว้เพื่ออะไร นั่นคือปัญหาใจกลางของการค้านี้ พระเครื่ององค์หนึ่งถูกตีค่าจากว่าวัดไหนกดพิมพ์ พระสงฆ์รูปใดปลุกเสก และเมื่อใด — ข้อเท็จจริงที่อยู่ในเนื้อดิน ตำหนิของแม่พิมพ์ และใบรับรอง ไม่ใช่ในรูปด้านหน้า *ตามคติที่เล่าสืบกันมา —* ผู้ชำนาญที่อ่านร่องรอยเหล่านั้นโดยคิดค่าบริการ เป็นส่วนหนึ่งของตลาดนี้พอ ๆ กับเจ้าของแผงที่ปล่อยเช่า

ขนาดของตลาดไม่เล็ก เมื่อพระจตุคามรามเทพถึงจุดสูงสุดใน พ.ศ. 2550 (ค.ศ. 2007) ตลาดของพระแบบนั้นเพียงแบบเดียวมีมูลค่าถึงสองหมื่นล้านบาทในหนึ่งปี ก่อนฟองสบู่จะแตกในปลายปี พ.ศ. 2550 ทิ้งพระค้างแผงที่หาได้ในราคาถูก *ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* ตลาดที่เคลื่อนไหวได้มากขนาดนั้นในสิบสองเดือน คือตลาดการเงินที่มีวัตถุแห่งศรัทธาอยู่ในนั้น และข้อถกเถียงว่ามันเป็นอย่างไหนเป็นหลัก เกิดขึ้นในหมู่นักวิจารณ์ชาวไทยเอง ไม่ใช่ระหว่างคนไทยกับคนนอก
text_th.today: ยังเปิดทำการค้าอยู่ ตามรายงานที่เผยแพร่ล่าสุดที่โครงการนี้ได้อ่าน เวลาเปิดทำการไม่ได้เผยแพร่เป็นตาราง: แต่ละแผงมีเวลาของตนเอง ตรอกคึกคักที่สุดในเวลากลางวัน และวันหยุดสุดสัปดาห์นักสะสมจะมากัน โครงการนี้ยังไม่เคยไปยืนอยู่ที่นั่น จึงไม่ได้ระบุวันใดไว้ข้างล่างว่าเปิดหรือปิด

names.name: The Lovett charms at Wellcome Collection
names.th: เครื่องรางของโลเวตต์ที่เวลคัมคอลเลกชัน

text.what: An address rather than a room. Walk into 183 Euston Road today and there is no case of Edward Lovett's London charms to look at: the permanent show of Henry Wellcome's own collecting, Medicine Man, closed for good on 27 November 2022 after fifteen years, and the permanent exhibition now is Being Human. What Wellcome still holds under Lovett's name is paper — a collection dossier in the archive of the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum, catalogued as 'Lovett Collection', reference WA/HMM/CM/Col/64, a summary sheet dated to about the 1980s — and two exhibitions' worth of history.
text.story:
Lovett collected by swap. He was chief cashier at a bank in the City, lived in Croydon and later Caterham, and spent his free time asking dockers, costermongers and sailors' families what they carried and why, trading them alpine plants grown in seashells for it. He wrote it up in "Magic in Modern London" in 1925 and he did not theorise: he recorded who gave him the thing and what they said about it, and left the explaining alone. That restraint is why his labels still work a century later.

He and Henry Wellcome corresponded for years. In 1916 Lovett curated an exhibition, 'Folklore of London', at the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum at 54a Wigmore Street. In 1930, three years before Lovett died, Wellcome's museum bought from his collection of British amulets and charms: a mole's foot from Downham Market in Norfolk, carried loose in a pocket in the 1890s or 1900s, is still catalogued with that purchase note and is now in the Science Museum Group collection as A79966.

Wellcome's own writing on those objects reports the claims and names the claimants. In "Moles' feet, dried frogs and other folk medicines", published on its website by Kate Wilkinson on 21 May 2019, it gives the reasoning as its owners gave it: "the digging-foot of a mole (with its cramped appearance) is thought to be a cure for cramp". A dried frog in a silk bag was carried against fits; snake vertebrae were strung against pain in the lower back; a coil of eel skin was wound round the fingers, in Scotland, against cramp; a potato was the one people were still carrying, in a pocket, against rheumatism. An old woman in Devonshire used quartzite on warts.

The charms themselves went to Oxford. When Wellcome Collection showed them again in 'Charmed Life: The solace of objects', 6 October 2011 to 26 February 2012, the museum's own page says the 1,400 amulets the artist Felicity Powell worked with were "borrowed from Oxford University's Pitt Rivers Museum" — the same building Lovett had been giving to since the 1890s. Powell was one of few people to have had access to them; the page describes her as caught by the silent witness they bore to personal stories now lost. Her films and medals hung beside them.

The institution has since said how the wider collecting worked. In 2021 Wellcome Collection acknowledged that Henry Wellcome's collecting was shaped by colonialism, that many objects bought at auction around the turn of the twentieth century carried no record of how they had been got, and that they may have been "unjustly taken"; in 2025 it returned a group of Jain manuscripts to India. *Inference —* Lovett sits oddly inside that account, because his method was a trade on a street with the owner present, and this project has not read a Wellcome statement that treats his material as contested. Saying so is not a defence of it; it is a note about what is and is not on the record.
text.today: The galleries, library, café and shop at 183 Euston Road are free, and the building's own line is that "All our permanent and temporary exhibitions, and most of our events, are free." Photography is allowed for personal use in most exhibitions except where signs say otherwise. To see a Lovett charm you go to Oxford or to the Science Museum Group catalogue; to read his file you book the library here.

text_th.what: เป็นที่อยู่มากกว่าห้องจัดแสดง หากเดินเข้าไปที่เลขที่ 183 ถนนยูสตัน (Euston Road) ทุกวันนี้ จะไม่มีตู้เครื่องรางลอนดอนของเอ็ดเวิร์ด โลเวตต์ให้ชม นิทรรศการถาวรว่าด้วยการสะสมของเฮนรี เวลคัม (Henry Wellcome) เอง ชื่อเมดิซินแมน (Medicine Man) ปิดถาวรเมื่อวันที่ 27 พฤศจิกายน ค.ศ. 2022 หลังจัดมาสิบห้าปี และนิทรรศการถาวรในปัจจุบันคือบีอิงฮิวแมน (Being Human) สิ่งที่เวลคัมยังเก็บไว้ภายใต้ชื่อโลเวตต์คือเอกสาร ได้แก่แฟ้มคอลเลกชันในหอจดหมายเหตุของพิพิธภัณฑ์การแพทย์ประวัติศาสตร์เวลคัม ลงรายการว่า ‘คอลเลกชันโลเวตต์’ (Lovett Collection) เลขอ้างอิง WA/HMM/CM/Col/64 เป็นแผ่นสรุปที่ระบุอายุไว้ราวทศวรรษ 1980 และประวัติของนิทรรศการสองครั้ง

names.name: Alan Dundes
names.th: อลัน ดันดีส

text.what: American folklorist, 1934–2005, who taught at the University of California, Berkeley for forty-two years. For this atlas he matters for one book: "The Evil Eye: A Casebook", University of Wisconsin Press, 1992, which he edited — a gathering of the arguments about the eye rather than a single account of it. He also gave the field the working definition of 'folk' that lets a charm carried by an office or a football team count as folklore at all.
text.story:
Dundes studied English at Yale, spent two years maintaining artillery on a ship in the Mediterranean, then took a folklore doctorate at Indiana under Richard Dorson. Berkeley hired him into anthropology in 1963 and he stayed until he collapsed while teaching a graduate seminar on 30 March 2005.

His definition is the part that reaches into these records. Dundes wrote in 1969 that any group of people sharing a common linking factor, an urban group such as a labor union for instance, can and does have folklore, and that 'folk' is a flexible concept which can refer to a nation or to a single family. The critical issue, he said, is which groups in fact have traditions. *Inference —* that is the sentence that lets a challenge coin, a phone charm and an exam charm sit in the same atlas as a Middle Kingdom scarab without special pleading.

He insisted that collecting without theory is wasted work, and said so to his own field at the American Folklore Society in 2004. His students in the introductory course each had to collect, identify and analyse forty items; about 500,000 items are housed in the Berkeley Folklore Archives as a result.

He was also the most publicly argued-with folklorist of his generation. His 1980 presidential address on German culture, published as "Life is Like a Chicken Coop Ladder", drew a reaction strong enough that he stayed away from the society's annual conference for years, and the linguist Anatol Stefanowitsch in 2012 called it "unstructured, poorly argued and flimsily sourced" and "methodologically flawed because he only looked for evidence supporting his theory, and not — as even a folklorist should — for evidence against his theory". His psychoanalytic essay on American football earned him death threats. This atlas reports the quarrel and does not take a side in it.
text.today: The casebooks he edited are still the fastest way into a contested subject — the evil eye in 1992, the walled-up wife in 1996, the blood libel legend in 1991 — because each prints the opposing readings side by side instead of choosing. A donation from an anonymous former student endowed a Distinguished Professorship of Folkloristics at Berkeley, which is why the subject survived his retirement.

names.name: Augustus Pitt Rivers
aliases: Augustus Henry Lane Fox Pitt Rivers
names.th: ออกัสตัส พิตต์ ริเวอร์ส

text.what: English soldier and archaeologist, 1827–1900, who arranged objects by what they are for rather than by where they came from. He gave more than 20,000 of them to the University of Oxford in 1884 on conditions that still bind the display. Every amulet case in this atlas that groups a Japanese charm beside a Neapolitan one is standing inside his idea.
text.story:
He was commissioned into the Grenadier Guards on 16 May 1845 and served until 1882, ending as a Lieutenant-General. His combat was limited — the Battle of the Alma in 1854 — and most of his service went on musketry instruction; he founded the Hythe School of Musketry and published "On the improvement of the rifle as a weapon for general use" in 1858. Testing rifle after rifle is where the method comes from: he was already comparing small variations in a made object for a living.

Reading Darwin and Herbert Spencer, he arranged his collection typologically and, within types, chronologically, meaning to show progression in design and evolution in human culture from the simple to the complex. He treated archaeology as an extension of anthropology and built matching archaeological and ethnographic collections so the two could be read together.

In 1880 he inherited estates in Cranborne Chase carrying Roman and Saxon material and excavated them over seventeen seasons, from the mid-1880s until his death, insisting that everything be collected and catalogued rather than only what looked worth keeping. Under the Ancient Monuments Protection Act 1882 he became the first Inspector of Ancient Monuments, and put railings round sites including Kit's Coty House in Kent.

The 1884 gift to Oxford came with conditions: a permanent lecturer in anthropology, which made Edward Burnett Tylor the first lecturer in anthropology in the United Kingdom in 1885, and a building for the collection used for no other purpose. A further clause says changes to the displays "shall not affect the general principle originated by Augustus Henry Lane Fox Pitt Rivers".

That clause is why the argument about his method is still live rather than historical. The museum's own account states that this evolutionary approach to material culture is no longer appropriate in the modern display paradigm for archaeological and anthropological objects, and that it has broadly retained the typological organisation because the Deed of Gift requires it.
text.today: The museum he founded holds more than 600,000 items, nearly all acquired by donation from colonial officials, travellers, scholars and missionaries. In September 2020 it removed human remains from display, including the shrunken heads shown since the 1940s; the director said exhibiting them "reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking that goes against the museum's core values". *Inference —* a bequest that fixes a nineteenth-century argument into the furniture is a different kind of object from the things inside the cases, and it is the one the museum cannot deaccession.

names.name: Campbell Bonner
names.th: แคมป์เบลล์ บอนเนอร์

text.what: American classicist, 1876–1954, of the University of Michigan, who wrote the book that made carved magical gems a subject with a method. "Studies in Magical Amulets, Chiefly Graeco-Egyptian", Ann Arbor, 1950, described and classified the engraved stones of the late Roman eastern Mediterranean — the ones cut with Abraxas, the reaper, the womb-symbol, strings of vowels — and set out how to read the images and the inscriptions together.
text.story:
Bonner was born in Nashville, Tennessee, on 30 January 1876 and died in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on 11 July 1954. His published work runs from 1921 and covers magical papyri as well as gems; the amulets sat inside a wider study of popular religion in the late pagan and early Christian world.

The gems are small, hard and portable, cut in haematite, jasper, carnelian and chalcedony, and they carry a mixture nobody else had sorted: Egyptian gods, Greek vowels, Hebrew divine names, Roman medical language. Bonner's 1950 volume is where that mixture stopped being a curiosity list and became a corpus with types.

*Inference —* the tell of a corpus that worked is that it grew after its author died. The Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest runs the Campbell Bonner Magical Gems Database, named for him, launched in 2010, and it estimates the entire corpus at around 5,600 pieces. That is a number nobody could have counted before the material had a shared vocabulary.
text.today: The database at the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest carries his name and, in its own words, has "the primary aim ... to bring the entire corpus of magical gems online". This project has not read a published academic criticism of Bonner's framing and does not assert that none exists.

text.what: American classicist, born 1955, Edward Olson Distinguished Service Professor in Classics at the University of Chicago. He works on Greek poetry, religion and magic, and wrote "The transformation of Greek amulets in Roman imperial times" in 2018 — a study of how the Greek protective object changed shape, material and claim once Rome was running the Mediterranean.
text.story:
Faraone's first book, "Talismans and Trojan horses: guardian statues in ancient Greek myth and ritual", 1992, took the largest protective objects the Greeks made: statues buried or set up to guard a city. "Ancient Greek Love Magic" followed in 2001, on the other end of the same practice — the spells and objects aimed at one person rather than a wall.

The 2018 book is the one an amulet record reaches for. *Inference —* its subject is change rather than origin, and that is the useful move: the Greek amulet did not simply persist into the Roman empire, it acquired new stones, new inscriptions and new customers, and a record that dates an object by its shape alone will get it wrong.

He founded and directed the University of Chicago's Center for the Study of Ancient Religions from 2008 to 2018, and co-edited "Masks of Dionysius" with Thomas H. Carpenter in 1993 and "Prostitutes and Courtesans in the Ancient World" with Laura K. McClure in 2006.
text.today: He holds the Edward Olson chair from the 2021–22 school year. His honours include a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1995, a National Endowment for the Humanities Fellowship in 2013, a fellowship at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 2021, and the Charles J. Goodwin Award of Merit from the Society for Classical Studies in 2024.

names.name: Edward Lovett
names.th: เอ็ดเวิร์ด เลิฟเวตต์

text.what: English folklorist, July 1852 – 1933, who collected charms off London streets while working as a chief cashier at a bank in the City. He gathered the things people were actually carrying — a mole's foot, a dried frog, a blue bead, a caul — and wrote them up in "Magic in Modern London" in 1925. His material is now spread across the Pitt Rivers Museum, the Cuming Museum in Southwark, the Wellcome collection and two museums of childhood.
text.story:
Lovett collected on his walks. He lived in Croydon and later Caterham, and worked the London streets, Sussex and Surrey in his spare time — costers' barrows, dock workers, sailors' families — asking what people had in their pockets and why. He grew alpine plants in seashells and traded the small specimens for amulets from the people he met. That is the whole method: a swap, on a street, recorded on the spot.

He donated to the Pitt Rivers Museum between 1896 and 1911. He joined the Folklore Society in 1900 and published in its journal: "The Modern Commercial Aspect of an Ancient Superstition" in 1902, "Superstitions and Survivals amongst Shepherds" and "Amulets from Costers' Barrows in London, Rome, and Naples" both in 1909. In a 1906 Museums Journal article he set out a plan for a folk museum of Britain and campaigned for it into the early 1920s. It was never built.

He corresponded with Henry Wellcome, and in 1916 curated an exhibition, 'Folklore of London', at the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum. In 1914 he showed over five hundred dolls at the National Museum of Wales, meaning to give adults what he called a "scientific history of the doll, from the standpoints of ethnography and folklore". His theory that the coffin dolls found on Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh in the 1830s were substitution burials for sailors lost at sea has not been supported by recent scholarship.

What separates him from most collectors of his generation is what he did not do. Lovett did not venture into theorising on folklore, confining his research to the collection of talismans and other objects with claims attached. *Inference —* that restraint is why his labels still work: he wrote down who gave him the thing and what they said about it, and left the explaining to other people.
text.today: The Wellcome Collection showed his amulets in 'Charmed Life: The solace of objects', 6 October 2011 to 26 February 2012, alongside new work by the artist and curator Felicity Powell. Wellcome also publishes an online piece on his collections, "Moles' feet, dried frogs and other folk medicines", by Kate Wilkinson, dated 21 May 2019.

names.name: Flinders Petrie
names.th: ฟลินเดอร์ส พีทรี

text.what: English Egyptologist, 1853–1942, who dug Egypt for half a century and sorted what came out of it. He held the first chair of Egyptology in the United Kingdom, at University College London, and in 1914 published a catalogue of amulets that arranged them into classes museums still shelve by. He also argued for eugenics in print, and the same books that fixed the amulet classes carry that argument.
text.story:
Petrie taught himself to survey before he could vote. At nineteen he produced the most accurate survey of Stonehenge then made; in 1880 he went to Giza to measure the pyramids and found the place, in his words, "a house on fire, so rapid was the destruction". He called his own job that of a "salvage man".

From November 1884 he dug almost continuously — Tanis, Tell Nebesheh, the Fayum, Amarna from 1891, Tell el-Hesi in Palestine in 1890, the Merneptah stele at Luxor in 1896, the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim in the winter of 1904–5. He cut the foreman out of his digs and paid the workmen direct, which he said stopped finds being pulled out fast and sloppily. In 1904 he set the method down in Methods and Aims in Archaeology. In 1913 he sold his Egyptian collection to University College London, where it is the Petrie Museum.

The amulet book is the one this atlas leans on. Amulets: illustrated by the Egyptian collection in University College, London, Constable, 1914, runs to 190 pages and sorts the material by what Petrie took the object to be doing — amulets of power, of property, protective amulets, the human-headed gods, the animal gods, the properties of stones. *Inference —* a museum drawer labelled by function rather than by find-spot is a drawer laid out on that scheme, and a visitor reading a case label in London, New York or Cairo is usually reading Petrie's categories at one remove.

The other half of the record is dated too. Petrie has been denounced for his pro-eugenics views; he was a dedicated believer in the superiority of the Northern peoples over the Latinate and Southern peoples, and he put the argument into his 1906 series Question of the day, blaming England's social problems on racial degeneration. It ran into his Egyptology: he held that Egyptian civilisation came from an invading "Dynastic Race" that conquered what he called in 1895 an "inferior, exhausted mulatto" population. E. A. Wallis Budge argued against him that Egyptian religion was of a piece with the religions of northeastern and central Africa; most of their colleagues at the time sided with Petrie.
text.today: The Petrie Museum at University College London holds the excavated amulet series he sold it in 1913. UCL marked the centenary of his 1923 knighthood by asking, in its own words, "Between investigations on eugenics, decolonial practice, and calls for repatriation, what has become of Flinderella?" *Inference —* both halves of him are still in the room: the typology is working equipment, and the racial theory it was written beside is now the subject of the museum's own labels.

text.what: English philologist and antiquary, 1830–1907, of Wellington in Somerset. He wrote the two books that pulled the evil eye and its answering objects together as one subject in English — "The Evil Eye" in 1895 and "Horns of Honour" in 1900 — and he bought the objects while he was writing, in Spain, Italy and elsewhere. His collection went to the Somersetshire Archaeological Society's museum at Taunton after his widow's death.
text.story:
Elworthy came to writing late. A woollen manufacturer's eldest son, schooled privately at Denmark Hill, he made his first name as a dialect scholar: "The Dialect of West Somerset", published for the English Dialect Society by Trübner between 1875 and 1886, in two volumes with a grammar and a word-book.

Then he turned to the eye. "The Evil Eye: an account of this ancient and widespread superstition", John Murray, 1895, gathered what he had seen on the road — the coral horn in Naples, the hand, the crescent, the amulets sold at street barrows — and set them beside Roman and Greek material. "Horns of Honour", the same publisher, 1900, took the horn on its own. He drew, and he drew well; the plates are his.

His obituarist in the Dictionary of National Biography wrote that in the course of those travels he made "perhaps the finest collection of charms, amulets, and such-like trinkets in existence". That sentence is the record of a whole period's vocabulary, and this atlas prints it as a quotation rather than borrowing it. Elworthy's own subtitle does the same work. The word he put on his title page is the verdict the book starts from, and everything inside is described by somebody who had already decided what the practice was.

*Inference —* what survived the framing is the evidence. Elworthy recorded which object was sold on which street, what a seller said it did, and what shape it took in one town against the next; those observations are still checkable and are still cited, including in this atlas, wherever a Mediterranean charm needs a dated nineteenth-century sighting.
text.today: His 1895 and 1900 books are out of copyright and circulate freely as scans, which keeps both the observations and the vocabulary in wide reach. The Pitt Rivers Museum's 'The Other Within' project, by Alison Petch, carries a biographical page on him as one of the collectors behind English ethnographic holdings.

names.name: Joseph Naveh
names.th: โยเซฟ นาเวห์

text.what: Israeli epigrapher and palaeographer, 1928–2011, who read the writing on the amulets. With Shaul Shaked he published the Aramaic texts of late antique metal amulet strips and of the clay incantation bowls — the objects buried upside down under house floors in Babylonia — in editions that print the text, the translation and the object together.
text.story:
Naveh was born in Mukachevo, then Czechoslovakia, on 21 January 1928. He worked for the Israel Department of Antiquities from 1955 to 1971 and was a district archaeologist from 1958, then taught in the Department of Ancient Semitic Languages at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem from 1971 to 1991. His field was West Semitic epigraphy: the shapes of letters, and what the shapes date.

That is the skill the amulet material needs. A rolled silver or bronze lamella and a bowl written in a spiral both carry script and nothing else datable — no stratigraphy in a bowl bought on a market, no style in a thin strip of metal. "The Development of the Aramaic Script", his 1970 dissertation, and "Early History of the Alphabet", 1997, are the tools; the amulet volumes are what he used them on.

With Shaked he produced "Amulets and Magic Bowls: Aramaic Incantations of Late Antiquity" and then "Magic Spells and Formulae" in 1993. *Inference —* the dating in this atlas for any Aramaic amulet or bowl rests on that letter-by-letter work, whether or not the record says so.

He was elected to the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities in 1994. He died on 21 November 2011.
text.today: The bowls keep arriving on the antiquities market without find-spots, which is the reason his palaeography stays load-bearing and also the reason the objects are contested. This project has not read a published provenance study of the bowl corpus and does not assert what share of it was excavated.

names.name: Shaul Shaked
names.th: ชาอูล ชาเกด

text.what: Israeli Iranist and philologist, 1933–2021, of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. He read the Aramaic incantation bowls and metal amulets of late antique Babylonia alongside Zoroastrian and Middle Persian material, which is why his editions catch what the Jewish, Christian, Mandaean and Iranian texts borrowed from one another.
text.story:
Shaked was born in Debrecen, Hungary, on 5 March 1933. He took his doctorate in Iranian languages at SOAS in 1964 and taught at the Hebrew University in Indian, Iranian and Armenian Studies and in Comparative Religion, holding the Schwarzman chair. He was elected to the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities in 1985 and chaired its humanities division from 1995 to 2001. He won the Israel Prize for Linguistics in 2000 and the Sándor Scheiber Prize in 2012.

His listed research interests are Zoroastrianism, Middle Persian lexicography, early Judaeo-Persian, Aramaic magical texts, and Aramaic and Arabic loan words in Iranian. The bowls sit at the join of all of those. A Babylonian bowl written in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic and buried under a floor names demons with Iranian names and formulas with Jewish ones; a reader who knows only one side of that misses half the text.

With Joseph Naveh he published "Amulets and Magic Bowls: Aramaic Incantations of Late Antiquity" and "Magic Spells and Formulae" in 1993. He continued the corpus with others — "Aramaic Bowl Spells: Jewish Babylonian Aramaic Bowls", with James N. Ford and Siam Bhayro, volume one from Brill in 2013 and volume two in 2022. He died on 27 October 2021.
text.today: The bowl corpus is still being edited volume by volume, and the later volumes are appearing after his death. *Inference —* an amulet class whose standard edition is unfinished is a class whose dating and readings will move, so this atlas's Aramaic bowl records are marked as provisional wherever they lean on a text rather than on an object.

names.name: Siegfried Seligmann
names.th: ซีกฟรีด เซลิกมันน์

text.what: German ophthalmologist and independent scholar, 1870–1926, who wrote the largest survey of the evil eye anybody has attempted. "Der böse Blick und Verwandtes", two volumes, 1910, collects the belief and its objects across languages and centuries; German scholarship still calls it an indispensable standard work. He assembled a collection of more than 1,500 amulets while writing it.
text.story:
Seligmann was born at Wandsbek on 12 June 1870 and practised in Hamburg. An eye doctor writing about the eye that harms is a coincidence he does not seem to have made much of; what he did was read everything. "Der böse Blick und Verwandtes" in 1910 was followed by "Die Zauberkraft des Auges und das Berufen" in 1922 and, after his death on 10 November 1926, by "Die magischen Heil- und Schutzmittel aus der unbelebten Natur" in 1927 — the protective and healing materials drawn from the mineral world.

He married Alice Bettina Warburg in 1904, and the family connection shows in where his papers went. His ethnological library was taken into the Warburg Kulturwissenschaftliche Bibliothek in Hamburg; since 1987 his papers have been held by the Warburg Institute in London. The amulet collection itself was bought in 1927 for Hamburg's ethnological museum.

The German Wikipedia entry records that his Hamburg residence later became a Judenhaus — one of the buildings into which Jewish residents were forced under Nazi persecution. That happened after his death.

*Inference —* the reason this atlas cites Seligmann rather than paraphrasing him is that his footnotes name sources this project can chase; he was compiling, not theorising, and the compilation is what has lasted.
text.today: The books are in German and mostly untranslated, which is why English writing on the eye tends to reach for Elworthy's 1895 volume first even though Seligmann's is larger and later. His collection and his papers sit in two different cities and two different countries, which is the ordinary fate of a private amulet collection.

names.name: E. A. Wallis Budge
aliases: Sir Ernest Alfred Thompson Wallis Budge
names.th: อี. เอ. วอลลิส บัดจ์

text.what: English Egyptologist and Orientalist, 1857–1934, Keeper of Egyptian and Assyrian Antiquities at the British Museum from 1894 to 1924. He bought for that museum across Egypt, Sudan and Iraq, wrote over a hundred books, and in 1930 published a 543-page compendium of amulets and talismans that is still the volume a second-hand shop is likeliest to have. Egyptologists who use it warn about it in the same breath.
text.story:
Budge left school at twelve and clerked at W. H. Smith for eight years, studying Assyrian in his lunch hours at St Paul's until the cathedral organist raised money to send him to Cambridge. He entered the British Museum in 1883 and stayed forty-one years.

Between 1886 and 1892 he made three missions to Mesopotamia and then went to Egypt almost yearly and to Sudan five times. He came back with cuneiform tablets, Syriac, Coptic and Greek manuscripts and hieroglyphic papyri — the Papyrus of Ani among them, and the Amarna letters. On the 1888 Baghdad trip his baggage was searched under new Ottoman customs rules; he got the Tell Amarna tablets out by bribery, and said so himself in his 1920 memoir By Nile and Tigris. Museum officers of the period, Budge included, moved antiquities in diplomatic pouches and paid customs officials to look away. The archaeologist Brian M. Fagan has called him "one of the major illegal looters of antiquities".

The amulet book is "Amulets and superstitions", Oxford University Press, 1930: xxxix plus 543 pages, twenty-two plates, and a subtitle that lists what it covers — Egyptian, Sumerian, Assyrian, Hebrew, Christian, Gnostic and Muslim amulets and talismans, the evil eye, the pentagon, the swastika, the cross, the properties of stones, rings, divination, numbers, the Kabbalah, ancient astrology. It is the widest single sweep anybody attempted, and it was assembled by one man who had handled most of the objects.

The warnings are on the record and they are specific. The Egyptologist James Peter Allen writes that Budge's books "were not too reliable when they first appeared and are now woefully outdated". Wikipedia's own summary says the writing style of his era — a lack of clear distinction between opinion and incontrovertible fact — is no longer acceptable in scholarly works. Adam H. Becker's article "Doctoring the Past in the Present: E. A. Wallis Budge, the Discourse on Magic, and the Colonization of Iraq", in History of Religions 44:3 (2005), puts the vocabulary Budge used for other people's religions next to the politics of the occupation he wrote it under.

On one point his colleagues were wrong and he was not: Budge argued that Egyptian religion had grown out of the religions of northeastern and central Africa. That was regarded as impossible at the time, when nearly everyone followed Flinders Petrie's invading "Dynastic Race".
text.today: Because Budge's books entered the public domain they have stayed continuously in print and are scanned in full online, so his translations and his framing reach far more readers than any corrected edition does. *Inference —* a search for almost any amulet term still lands on him first, which is why this atlas cites him for what he saw and not for what he concluded.

names.name: Walter Leo Hildburgh
names.th: วอลเตอร์ ลีโอ ฮิลด์เบิร์ก

text.what: American collector and art historian, 1876–1955, who bought amulets in vast numbers across Europe, Asia and the Middle East and then wrote about them. His amulet collection was left to the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum and transferred to the Pitt Rivers Museum in 1985; his English medieval alabasters went to the Victoria and Albert Museum, 300 of them in 1946 for his seventieth birthday.
text.story:
Hildburgh took a doctorate at Columbia on alternating current, then spent his life on objects. The University of London gave him a D.Litt. in the History of Art in 1937. He gave or bequeathed over 5,000 objects to the Victoria and Albert Museum alone, and further material reached the British Museum, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Cooper Hewitt and the UCL Institute of Archaeology.

The amulets are the part that concerns this atlas, and they are also the part that moved. They went first to Henry Wellcome's museum, and in 1985 the whole Wellcome amulet material was transferred to Oxford. *Inference —* that means a tray of Spanish hands or Japanese charms catalogued as Pitt Rivers material may have been bought by an American in a Madrid street in 1906, passed through a pharmaceutical fortune's private museum in London, and only reached Oxford eighty years later. The label says Pitt Rivers. The object's history says four other things first.

He published on what he bought rather than only accumulating it: articles on cowrie shells as amulets, on hand images as amulets in Spain, and on the psychology he thought underlay amulet use in Europe.
text.today: Hildburgh's amulets are the bulk of what a visitor to the Pitt Rivers charm cases is looking at, and the Wellcome connection is why the same names recur in both institutions' catalogues. This project has read no published account of how individual pieces were acquired, and does not assert that any particular object was bought fairly or unfairly.

names.name: Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies
names.th: สถาบันการศึกษาชาวอะบอริจินและชาวเกาะช่องแคบทอร์เรสแห่งออสเตรเลีย (AIATSIS)

text.what: Australian Government statutory authority in Canberra, founded in 1964 as the Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies and renamed under the AIATSIS Act 1989. It collects, publishes and researches, and it holds over a million cultural items — roughly 42,000 hours of audio, around 700,000 photographs and about six million feet of film. Part of that collection is secret or sacred, and AIATSIS publishes the rules for handling it. Those rules are why this atlas leaves Australia largely blank.
text.story:
The founding purpose was salvage, in the vocabulary of its time: to record language, song, art, material culture, ceremonial life and social structure before those traditions perished in the face of European ways. No Aboriginal people attended the 1961 conference that planned the institute. Before 1970 there had never been an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander member on its council. The 1989 Act changed the arithmetic: a council of nine, of whom the Act requires that at least five be Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, with one of the Minister's appointees a Torres Strait Islander.

The collection was built by donation, gift, purchase and fieldwork, and also by deposit — an arrangement that permits the original owners to assign access and use conditions appropriate to the cultural information in the items. That clause is the hinge. It means an item can sit in a national collection and still be governed by the people it came from.

The handling rules follow from it. AIATSIS holds material that is sensitive and/or secret/sacred to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and under its founding Act adheres to strict protocols when processing it. Restricted visual media are stored separately from the rest of the collection. Audio and moving-image items are not played until cultural requirements have been checked. Restricted material is digitised in secured conditions such as enclosed booths, by staff who can meet the protocols of the item being digitised. The institute also supports the protocols of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Library, Information and Resource Network.

On the research side, AIATSIS published the Guidelines for Ethical Research in Australian Indigenous Studies in 1999, updated them in 2012, and replaced them in 2020 with the AIATSIS Code of Ethics for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Research. The Code rests on four principles: Indigenous self-determination, Indigenous leadership, impact and value, and sustainability and accountability.
text.today: A new precinct, Ngurra, is planned on the shore of Lake Burley Griffin at a stated A$316.5 million, to include a resting place for ancestral remains of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people that cannot be returned to Country. AIATSIS Central Australia opened in Alice Springs / Mparntwe on 2 February 2024. The institute's Australian Indigenous Language Collection is registered in UNESCO's Memory of the World programme — a different UNESCO instrument from the intangible-heritage lists.

text_th.what: หน่วยงานตามกฎหมายของรัฐบาลออสเตรเลียในกรุงแคนเบอร์รา ก่อตั้งในปี ค.ศ. 1964 ในชื่อสถาบันการศึกษาชาวอะบอริจินแห่งออสเตรเลีย (Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies) และเปลี่ยนชื่อตามพระราชบัญญัติ AIATSIS ปี ค.ศ. 1989 สถาบันนี้รวบรวม เผยแพร่ และทำวิจัย และมีวัตถุทางวัฒนธรรมกว่าหนึ่งล้านรายการ — เสียงบันทึกราว 42,000 ชั่วโมง ภาพถ่ายราว 700,000 ภาพ และฟิล์มภาพยนตร์ราวหกล้านฟุต ส่วนหนึ่งของคอลเลกชันเป็นของลับหรือของศักดิ์สิทธิ์ และ AIATSIS เผยแพร่กฎสำหรับการจัดการของเหล่านั้น กฎเหล่านี้คือเหตุที่แอตลาสนี้ปล่อยออสเตรเลียว่างไว้เกือบทั้งหมด

restricted.note: AIATSIS holds material that is secret or sacred to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and restricts access to it: restricted visual media are stored apart from the rest of the collection, audio and moving-image items are not played until cultural requirements are checked, and depositors may set access and use conditions on what they deposit. This atlas prints those conditions and stops. It does not reconstruct restricted Australian designs, objects or rites from other sources, and does not fill the gap with a neighbouring tradition's practice.

names.name: The British Museum
names.th: พิพิธภัณฑ์บริติช (บริติชมิวเซียม)

text.what: London museum of human history, founded by act of parliament in 1753 and open to the public since 15 January 1759. It was the world's first public national museum and charges no admission except for loan exhibitions. For this atlas it is the largest single holding of Egyptian and Mesopotamian amulets in one building, and the institution whose keeper wrote the most-reprinted book about them.
text.story:
The museum began with Sir Hans Sloane's 71,000 objects, bought for the nation for £20,000 after his death in 1753 — far under the £50,000 or more his collection was then reckoned at. Among them were 160 Egyptian objects, which is where the Egyptian collection starts. In 1802 George III presented the Rosetta Stone. Henry Salt, British consul in Egypt, supplied much of the rest from 1818 onward.

E. A. Wallis Budge ran the Egyptian and Assyrian department as keeper from 1894 to 1924 and did the buying, in Egypt, Sudan and Iraq. His methods are on the record in his own memoir and in later assessment: the archaeologist Brian M. Fagan has called him "one of the major illegal looters of antiquities".

The collection's size is stated two ways in the same account: eight million artefacts in the permanent collection, and over 13 million objects in total. This record gives both rather than picking one.

The museum's published position on returns rests on statute. It argues that the British Museum Act 1963 prevents any object from leaving the collection once it has entered it — "The Museum owns its collections, but its Trustees are not empowered to dispose of them" — and that the "restitutionist premise, that whatever was made in a country must return to an original geographical site, would empty both the British Museum and the other great museums of the world". It has nevertheless returned Tasmanian Aboriginal burial remains where legislation allowed, and it has a published policy on human remains. The Parthenon sculptures claimed by Greece, the Benin Bronzes claimed by Nigeria and the Ethiopian tabots are the standing claims; preliminary talks with the Greek government began in late 2022.
text.today: On 28 April 2020 the museum put over 1.9 million images of its collection online. Most images that are © The Trustees of the British Museum carry a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International licence: free to share and adapt for non-commercial use with a credit to the museum, and a separate licence from British Museum Images for anything the museum deems commercial. *Inference —* that licence is not on Wikimedia Commons' accepted list, because Commons requires that commercial use be allowed. So this atlas can link to a British Museum image and cannot host one, and that is a fact about the licence, not a judgement about the museum.

names.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
names.th: พิพิธภัณฑ์ศิลปะเมโทรโพลิทัน (เดอะเมต)

text.what: New York museum founded in 1870, holding about 1.5 million works across seventeen curatorial departments. Its Egyptian department runs to more than 26,000 pieces, almost all of them on display across forty galleries, and almost half of those came out of the museum's own excavations between 1906 and 1941. Since 2017 every image of a public-domain work in the collection has carried a CC0 dedication.
text.story:
The New York State Legislature incorporated the museum on 13 April 1870; an 1893 act required that the collections be kept open and accessible free of charge throughout the year. The Egyptian holdings began as private collections and were then built by digging: the excavation seasons from 1906 to 1941 supply almost half the current collection, which is why a Met amulet more often has a find-spot than a bought one does.

The Michael C. Rockefeller Wing, opened in 1982 around Nelson Rockefeller's gift of more than 3,000 pieces, holds over 11,000 works from sub-Saharan Africa, the Pacific and the Americas. The museum's own account notes what changed with that wing: the material was now shown as art, in a Western art museum, where before objects from those regions had been treated as ethnographic work.

The acquisition record is contested and documented. The Euphronios Krater, bought with deaccession proceeds under Thomas Hoving, proved to be looted and went back to Italy in 2006. In September 2022 New York law enforcement seized 27 objects on three warrants for return to Italy and Egypt; in March 2023 fifteen more tied to Subhash Kapoor; in December 2023 the museum announced the return of fourteen Khmer sculptures to Cambodia and two to Thailand. In April 2023 ProPublica reported on the museum's Indigenous American holdings and on a loan-versus-own distinction that kept objects outside the reach of NAGPRA, since objects on loan do not trigger the repatriation process. The museum has since issued a statement on collecting practices and hired a provenance-research manager with a team of three.
text.today: The Open Access initiative began at the start of 2017. In the museum's own words six months in: "It's been six months since the Met launched its Open Access initiative, which made available all 375,000+ images of public-domain works in the Met collection under Creative Commons Zero (CC0)." Open access images and data have since been viewed over 1.2 billion times with over 7 million downloads. CC0 is on Wikimedia Commons' accepted list, so a Met amulet photograph can be hosted, reused and altered here with no permission sought. The dedication covers the museum's images of public-domain works; it says nothing about who the objects belong to.

text_th.what: พิพิธภัณฑ์ในนิวยอร์กที่ก่อตั้งใน ค.ศ. 1870 มีผลงานราว 1.5 ล้านชิ้นในแผนกภัณฑารักษ์สิบเจ็ดแผนก แผนกอียิปต์มีวัตถุมากกว่า 26,000 ชิ้น เกือบทั้งหมดจัดแสดงอยู่ในห้องจัดแสดงสี่สิบห้อง และเกือบครึ่งหนึ่งของจำนวนนั้นมาจากการขุดค้นของพิพิธภัณฑ์เองระหว่าง ค.ศ. 1906 ถึง 1941 ตั้งแต่ ค.ศ. 2017 ภาพของผลงานที่เป็นสาธารณสมบัติทุกภาพในคอลเลกชันมีการอุทิศแบบ CC0 กำกับไว้
text_th.story:
สภานิติบัญญัติรัฐนิวยอร์กจดทะเบียนจัดตั้งพิพิธภัณฑ์เมื่อวันที่ 13 เมษายน ค.ศ. 1870 กฎหมาย ค.ศ. 1893 กำหนดให้คอลเลกชันต้องเปิดและเข้าถึงได้โดยไม่เสียค่าใช้จ่ายตลอดทั้งปี คอลเลกชันอียิปต์เริ่มจากคอลเลกชันส่วนบุคคล แล้วจึงเติบโตขึ้นด้วยการขุด: ฤดูการขุดค้นระหว่าง ค.ศ. 1906 ถึง 1941 ให้วัตถุเกือบครึ่งของคอลเลกชันในปัจจุบัน ซึ่งเป็นเหตุที่เครื่องรางของเดอะเมตมักมีจุดที่พบมากกว่าชิ้นที่ซื้อมา

ปีกไมเคิล ซี. ร็อกกีเฟลเลอร์ (Michael C. Rockefeller Wing) ซึ่งเปิดใน ค.ศ. 1982 โดยมีของบริจาคจากเนลสัน ร็อกกีเฟลเลอร์มากกว่า 3,000 ชิ้นเป็นแกน มีผลงานกว่า 11,000 ชิ้นจากแอฟริกาใต้สะฮารา แปซิฟิก และทวีปอเมริกา คำบอกเล่าของพิพิธภัณฑ์เองระบุถึงสิ่งที่เปลี่ยนไปพร้อมกับปีกนี้: วัตถุเหล่านี้ถูกจัดแสดงในฐานะศิลปะ ในพิพิธภัณฑ์ศิลปะแบบตะวันตก ในขณะที่ก่อนหน้านั้นวัตถุจากภูมิภาคเหล่านี้ถูกปฏิบัติในฐานะงานด้านชาติพันธุ์วรรณนา

ประวัติการได้มาของวัตถุเป็นเรื่องที่มีข้อโต้แย้งและมีเอกสารยืนยัน คราเตอร์ยูโฟรนิออส (Euphronios Krater) ซึ่งซื้อด้วยเงินจากการจำหน่ายวัตถุออกจากคอลเลกชันในสมัยโทมัส โฮวิง (Thomas Hoving) ปรากฏว่าเป็นของที่ถูกปล้นมา และถูกส่งคืนอิตาลีใน ค.ศ. 2006 ในเดือนกันยายน ค.ศ. 2022 เจ้าหน้าที่บังคับใช้กฎหมายของนิวยอร์กยึดวัตถุ 27 ชิ้นตามหมายสามฉบับ เพื่อส่งคืนอิตาลีและอียิปต์ ในเดือนมีนาคม ค.ศ. 2023 ยึดอีกสิบห้าชิ้นที่เชื่อมโยงกับสุภาษ กปูร์ (Subhash Kapoor) ในเดือนธันวาคม ค.ศ. 2023 พิพิธภัณฑ์ประกาศส่งคืนประติมากรรมเขมรสิบสี่ชิ้นแก่กัมพูชา และสองชิ้นแก่ประเทศไทย ในเดือนเมษายน ค.ศ. 2023 โปรพับลิกา (ProPublica) รายงานเกี่ยวกับวัตถุของชนพื้นเมืองอเมริกันในพิพิธภัณฑ์ และเกี่ยวกับการแยกระหว่างการยืมกับการเป็นเจ้าของ ซึ่งทำให้วัตถุอยู่นอกขอบเขตของกฎหมายแนกพรา (NAGPRA กฎหมายคุ้มครองและส่งคืนหลุมศพชนพื้นเมืองอเมริกัน) เนื่องจากวัตถุที่ยืมมาไม่ทำให้เกิดกระบวนการส่งคืน นับแต่นั้นพิพิธภัณฑ์ได้ออกแถลงการณ์เรื่องแนวทางการสะสม และจ้างผู้จัดการด้านการวิจัยที่มาของวัตถุพร้อมทีมงานสามคน
text_th.today: โครงการเปิดการเข้าถึง (Open Access) เริ่มต้นเมื่อต้นปี ค.ศ. 2017 ในถ้อยคำของพิพิธภัณฑ์เองเมื่อผ่านไปหกเดือน: “ผ่านไปหกเดือนแล้วนับตั้งแต่เดอะเมตเปิดตัวโครงการเปิดการเข้าถึง ซึ่งทำให้ภาพผลงานสาธารณสมบัติในคอลเลกชันของเดอะเมตทั้งหมดกว่า 375,000 ภาพ เปิดให้ใช้ได้ภายใต้ครีเอทีฟคอมมอนส์ศูนย์ (CC0)” นับแต่นั้นภาพและข้อมูลแบบเปิดถูกเข้าชมไปกว่า 1.2 พันล้านครั้ง และดาวน์โหลดกว่า 7 ล้านครั้ง CC0 อยู่ในรายการสัญญาอนุญาตที่วิกิมีเดียคอมมอนส์ยอมรับ ดังนั้นภาพถ่ายเครื่องรางของเดอะเมตจึงนำมาเผยแพร่ ใช้ซ้ำ และดัดแปลงในที่นี้ได้โดยไม่ต้องขออนุญาต การอุทิศนี้ครอบคลุมภาพที่พิพิธภัณฑ์ถ่ายผลงานสาธารณสมบัติ แต่ไม่ได้กล่าวอะไรเลยว่าวัตถุเหล่านั้นเป็นของใคร

names.name: The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act
names.th: รัฐบัญญัติคุ้มครองและส่งคืนหลุมฝังศพชนพื้นเมืองอเมริกัน (NAGPRA)

text.what: United States federal law, Pub. L. 101–601, enacted on 16 November 1990. It requires federal agencies and any institution receiving federal funding to return Native American cultural items — human remains, funerary objects, sacred objects and objects of cultural patrimony — to lineal descendants and to culturally affiliated tribes, Alaska Native villages and Native Hawaiian organizations. It also makes trafficking in those items a criminal offence.
text.story:
The Act has three sets of provisions, and the difference between them decides most arguments about it. The repatriation provisions reach backwards: they apply to remains or objects discovered at any time, before or after 1990, wherever found, so long as the holder receives federal funding. The disposition provisions govern discovery or excavation on federal or tribal land after 16 November 1990, and they do not apply to private or state land outside a reservation boundary. The criminal provisions make trafficking an offence.

Maria Pearson is generally credited as the first catalyst. In the early 1970s her husband, an Iowa Department of Transportation engineer, told her that road construction at Glenwood had turned up both white and Native American remains: twenty-six white burials were reburied quickly, while the remains of a Native American mother and child went to a lab. She sat outside Governor Robert D. Ray's office in traditional dress until he saw her. "You can give me back my people's bones and you can quit digging them up." The Iowa Burials Protection Act of 1976 followed, then a decade of lobbying, then the looting of the Slack Farm mound in Kentucky in 1987 and the protests at Dickson Mounds in Illinois, and then the federal Act.

It has moved a great deal of material: the remains of about 32,000 individuals, nearly 670,000 funerary objects, 120,000 unassociated funerary objects and 3,500 sacred objects. It is also slow, and the burden of proving cultural affiliation falls on tribes, which is hardest in California, where many small bands were extinguished before they could be federally recognised. Some archaeologists object that remains untraceable to a historic tribe are being put beyond study. The Act itself says Congress meant to strike a balance between scientific examination and the fact that Native Americans, like people from every culture, hold their ancestors' remains in religious and spiritual reverence.

Penalties were raised in 2022. A first conviction for trafficking Native American human remains went from twelve months to one year and one day, which makes it a felony, and a subsequent conviction from five years to ten. A first conviction for trafficking cultural items remains a misdemeanour of up to one year; a subsequent one went from five years to ten.
text.today: Revised Interior Department regulations took effect on 12 January 2024 and state that museums and federal agencies "must defer to the Native American traditional knowledge of lineal descendants, Indian Tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations". The gaps are still real. ProPublica reported in April 2023 that the Metropolitan Museum of Art had held Indigenous American objects on long-term loan rather than owning them, and objects on loan do not trigger the repatriation process. *Inference —* the law is a US statute with a funding hook; it does nothing about a private collector, a foreign museum or an object sold abroad before 1990, and a reader should not treat it as a general rule about who owns a charm.

text.what: Oxford museum of archaeology and anthropology, founded in 1884 on Augustus Pitt Rivers' gift of about 22,000 objects and now holding more than 600,000. It is arranged by what things are for rather than by where they are from, so charms from a dozen continents share a case. Nearly the whole collection came in by donation from colonial officials, travellers, scholars and missionaries.
text.story:
The Deed of Gift set the terms. Oxford had to appoint a permanent lecturer in anthropology — Edward Burnett Tylor, in 1885, the first in the United Kingdom — and had to put up a building used for nothing else. Construction ran 1885 to 1886. A further clause says changes to the displays "shall not affect the general principle originated by Augustus Henry Lane Fox Pitt Rivers".

That is why the typological layout survived its own justification. The museum's account states that this evolutionary approach to material culture is no longer appropriate in the modern display paradigm for archaeological and anthropological objects, and that the original organisation has broadly been kept because the Deed requires it.

The amulet material arrived by two routes and they matter. Edward Lovett donated London street charms between 1896 and 1911. Walter Leo Hildburgh's amulets, bought across Europe, Asia and the Middle East, were bequeathed to the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum and transferred here in 1985.

Since 2020 the museum has changed what it shows. During the COVID closure it removed human remains from display, including the tsantsas shown since the 1940s; the director said that exhibiting them "reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking that goes against the museum's core values". It is meeting originating communities to correct its records and discuss returns — the Living Cultures work with the Maasai group Oltoilo Le Maa and InsightShare among them. With the Museum of Natural History it returned the remains of 17 Aboriginal Australians to the Australian government in 2022, and in 2026 agreed to repatriate Naga skeletal remains, some of which had been displayed in a case titled Treatment of Dead Enemies.
text.today: Collections Online is browsable and its images are not openly licensed. The museum's terms allow images to be used for non-commercial educational and community purposes and state that they "cannot be used freely or without permission for commercial purposes"; publication needs a licence application to photographic services, and credit must read "© Pitt Rivers Museum, University of Oxford" with the object's accession number. No Creative Commons licence is named. *Inference —* this atlas can therefore cite a Pitt Rivers accession and link to it, and cannot host the picture.

text.what: Paris museum of the arts and cultures of Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas, opened to the public on 23 June 2006 in a Jean Nouvel building beside the Seine. It holds more than a million objects and shows about 3,500 at a time. It is also where the French argument about returning colonial-era collections is loudest, because 70,000 of France's 90,000 sub-Saharan objects are here.
text.story:
The museum was assembled out of two older ones with incompatible purposes: the 25,000 objects of the Musée national des Arts d'Afrique et d'Océanie, created for the Colonial Exposition of 1931, and the 250,000-object ethnology collection of the Musée de l'Homme, created for the Paris Exposition of 1937. One was run by art historians, the other by anthropologists. The new museum was put under two ministries to match, and ten thousand further objects were bought.

Critics went at it from both directions on opening. Michael Kimmelman in the New York Times, 2 July 2006, called it "a missed opportunity and an inexplicable exercise" and asked whether religious, ceremonial and practical objects, never intended as art in the modern Western sense, would be showcased "like baubles, with no context". James Clifford wrote that in this museum "'illusion' and the 'work of art' coexist uneasily with the realism of ethnography and history". Others praised the same building: the Financial Times called the layered galleries an "animated, occasionally jarring dreamscape", the Washington Post called it visually stunning.

The returns argument has a paper trail. In 2016 the French government refused objects requested by the president of Benin on the ground that the national collections are inalienable. In 2018 the report Emmanuel Macron commissioned from Bénédicte Savoy and Felwine Sarr argued that artefacts taken unlawfully in the colonial period should go back when asked for. Macron then promised Benin 26 pieces taken by force from Dahomey; no French law then existed to permit it. By late 2021 the objects were ready and the museum staged a final exhibition around them. Separately, after a change in French law in 2010, the museum returned mokomokai — Māori tattooed heads — to New Zealand on 23 January 2012.
text.today: In December 2025, 77 works from the museum's Louvre selection were installed in the Louvre's new Gallery of the Five Continents, shown alongside Western art. This project has not read the museum's own image-rights statement and makes no claim about whether its collection photographs are openly licensed; the safe assumption for this atlas's picture pipeline is that they are not.

text.what: New Zealand's national museum, in Wellington, established by the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa Act 1992 and opened on 14 February 1998. Te Papa is Māori for 'the treasure box'. It runs on a bicultural philosophy built into the building's design process through the Treaty of Waitangi, and it is the institution that asks other museums, worldwide, for Māori ancestral remains back.
text.story:
Te Papa came out of a merger — the National Museum of New Zealand and the National Art Gallery, whose own line runs back to the Colonial Museum of 1865. The design process was led by Cliff Whiting with Cheryll Sotheran and Ken Gorbey and followed bicultural principles; Pete Bossley of Jasmax was the architect. The cultural collections hold Māori taonga and Pacific material alongside photography.

Since 2003 the museum has run a programme requesting the return of Māori remains held in institutions around the world. The clearest case in this atlas's range is the Musée du quai Branly: initially reluctant, it was able to move after a change in French law in 2010, and the mokomokai — tattooed preserved heads — were formally returned to New Zealand on 23 January 2012. They are held at Te Papa and are not on display.

The museum also draws the line inside its own building, and the argument about that is public. In 2010 it advised pregnant and menstruating women to avoid a behind-the-scenes tour of some collections; a spokeswoman said the policy was in place because of Māori beliefs surrounding the taonga collection included in the tour, "for their own safety". The advice generated outrage and claims that the museum was overbearing. This atlas reports both the reason given and the objection, and adjudicates neither.
text.today: Entry is free for New Zealanders and NZ$35 for international visitors as of September 2024. Collections Online publishes images under two rights statements, named on the museum's own page: some images are openly available with no restrictions on reuse, and others carry a Creative Commons Attribution – Non-Commercial – No Derivatives licence. For taonga the museum asks something further — that images of taonga be used only for research, study, personal and educational purposes, because the material holds significant cultural importance to iwi. *Inference —* that request is not a licence term, and this atlas treats it as binding anyway.
