names.name: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
aliases: Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage
names.th: มรดกทางวัฒนธรรมที่จับต้องไม่ได้ของยูเนสโก

text.what: The UNESCO programme run under the 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage. It lists practices, not objects. A charm cannot be inscribed; the craft of making it, the festival it is sold at or the rite it belongs to can be. States Parties nominate, and an intergovernmental committee meets annually and decides.
text.story:
Article 2 of the Convention defines intangible cultural heritage as traditions or living expressions inherited from our ancestors and passed on to our descendants — oral traditions, performing arts, social practices, rituals, festive events, knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universe, and the knowledge and skills to produce traditional crafts. Those are the five domains.

Two statements in the Convention's own summary matter more than the lists. The first is that intangible cultural heritage is "traditional, contemporary and living at the same time" — it is not a survival, and an element does not have to be old. The second is that it is "community-based: intangible cultural heritage can only be heritage when it is recognized as such by the communities, groups or individuals that create, maintain and transmit it". A state cannot inscribe a practice over the heads of the people doing it.

There are three registers: the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding, and the Register of Good Safeguarding Practices. The committee meets annually to evaluate nominations proposed by States Parties and decide whether or not to inscribe them.
text.today: What inscription is not: a ranking, a mark of quality, a property title, a trademark, or a bar on anyone making or selling anything. UNESCO's own wording is that intangible cultural heritage "is not merely valued as a cultural good, on a comparative basis, for its exclusivity or its exceptional value". *Inference —* this atlas therefore counts an inscription as attention paid and never as a verdict, and it never reads an absence from the lists as evidence that a practice is less real. Most of the practices in these records have never been nominated by anybody.

text_th.what: โครงการของยูเนสโกที่ดำเนินการภายใต้อนุสัญญาว่าด้วยการสงวนรักษามรดกทางวัฒนธรรมที่จับต้องไม่ได้ ค.ศ. 2003 โครงการนี้ขึ้นทะเบียนการปฏิบัติ ไม่ใช่วัตถุ เครื่องรางขึ้นทะเบียนไม่ได้ แต่งานช่างที่สร้างมัน เทศกาลที่ขายมัน หรือพิธีที่มันสังกัด ขึ้นทะเบียนได้ รัฐภาคีเป็นผู้เสนอ และคณะกรรมการระหว่างรัฐบาลประชุมทุกปีเพื่อตัดสิน
text_th.story:
มาตรา 2 ของอนุสัญญานิยามมรดกทางวัฒนธรรมที่จับต้องไม่ได้ว่าคือประเพณีหรือการแสดงออกที่ยังมีชีวิต ซึ่งสืบทอดมาจากบรรพบุรุษและส่งต่อไปยังลูกหลาน — ประเพณีมุขปาฐะ ศิลปะการแสดง แนวปฏิบัติทางสังคม พิธีกรรม งานเทศกาล ความรู้และการปฏิบัติเกี่ยวกับธรรมชาติและจักรวาล และความรู้และทักษะในการผลิตงานช่างฝีมือดั้งเดิม นั่นคือห้าขอบเขต

ข้อความสองข้อในบทสรุปของอนุสัญญาเองสำคัญกว่าบัญชีรายชื่อ ข้อแรกคือมรดกทางวัฒนธรรมที่จับต้องไม่ได้ "เป็นทั้งประเพณี ร่วมสมัย และยังมีชีวิตอยู่ในเวลาเดียวกัน" — มันไม่ใช่สิ่งหลงเหลือจากอดีต และองค์ประกอบหนึ่งไม่จำเป็นต้องเก่า ข้อที่สองคือมัน "ตั้งอยู่บนชุมชน: มรดกทางวัฒนธรรมที่จับต้องไม่ได้จะเป็นมรดกได้ก็ต่อเมื่อชุมชน กลุ่มคน หรือบุคคลที่สร้าง รักษา และถ่ายทอดมัน ยอมรับว่าเป็นเช่นนั้น" รัฐไม่อาจขึ้นทะเบียนการปฏิบัติหนึ่งข้ามหัวคนที่ปฏิบัติมันอยู่

มีสามบัญชี: บัญชีรายชื่อตัวแทนมรดกทางวัฒนธรรมที่จับต้องไม่ได้ของมนุษยชาติ บัญชีรายชื่อมรดกทางวัฒนธรรมที่จับต้องไม่ได้ที่ต้องได้รับการสงวนรักษาอย่างเร่งด่วน และทะเบียนแนวปฏิบัติที่ดีในการสงวนรักษา คณะกรรมการประชุมทุกปีเพื่อประเมินข้อเสนอที่รัฐภาคีเสนอมา และตัดสินว่าจะขึ้นทะเบียนหรือไม่
text_th.today: สิ่งที่การขึ้นทะเบียนไม่ใช่: การจัดอันดับ เครื่องหมายคุณภาพ เอกสารสิทธิ์ เครื่องหมายการค้า หรือข้อห้ามไม่ให้ใครทำหรือขายสิ่งใด ถ้อยคำของยูเนสโกเองคือ มรดกทางวัฒนธรรมที่จับต้องไม่ได้ "ไม่ได้มีคุณค่าเพียงในฐานะสินค้าทางวัฒนธรรม บนพื้นฐานของการเปรียบเทียบ เพราะความเป็นของเฉพาะหรือคุณค่าอันโดดเด่นของมัน" *ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* แอตลาสนี้จึงนับการขึ้นทะเบียนเป็นความสนใจที่ได้รับ ไม่เคยนับเป็นคำตัดสิน และไม่เคยอ่านการที่ไม่มีชื่ออยู่ในบัญชีว่าเป็นหลักฐานว่าการปฏิบัตินั้นจริงน้อยกว่า การปฏิบัติส่วนใหญ่ในระเบียนเหล่านี้ไม่เคยถูกใครเสนอชื่อเลย

names.name: Wellcome Collection
names.th: เวลคัมคอลเลกชัน

text.what: London museum and library at 183 Euston Road, opened to the public in June 2007 and part of the Wellcome Trust. It rests on what Sir Henry Wellcome, 1853–1936, bought: books, paintings and objects on the history of medicine worldwide, gathered on a scale no individual has matched since. Its holdings are described as including 17,500 magic-medical amulets, talismans and charms that Wellcome picked up in Islamic North Africa and elsewhere.
text.story:
Wellcome's museum came first — the Wellcome Historical Medical Museum at 54a Wigmore Street. Edward Lovett curated an exhibition there in 1916, 'Folklore of London'; the two men corresponded for years. Wellcome bought at auction on an industrial scale, and Walter Leo Hildburgh's amulets were bequeathed into the same collection.

The institution has published its own account of how that buying worked. In 2021 the Collection acknowledged that Wellcome's collecting was shaped by colonialism: many objects bought at auction in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century carried no documentation of how they had been acquired, and may have been "unjustly taken" from communities across Europe, Asia, Africa and the Middle East. It has committed to working with communities on provenance, and in 2025 returned a group of Jain manuscripts to India after researchers found they had been acquired without the consent of the communities they belonged to.

The display has moved too. Medicine Man, the permanent show of part of Wellcome's own collection, closed permanently on 27 November 2022 after fifteen years; the closure was perceived to follow concerns over racist, sexist and ableist theories and language.

The amulets themselves have been on the move for longer. Hildburgh's amulet material was transferred out of Wellcome to the Pitt Rivers Museum in 1985. The figure of 17,500 magic-medical amulets is published as a description of the Wellcome holdings; this record prints the two statements side by side and does not reconcile them, because it has not read a catalogue that says what stayed and what left.
text.today: Wellcome is digitising and openly licensing its collection: as of January 2020 over 40 million images from 325,000 items were available on wellcomecollection.org and through third-party services. The licensing is mixed, per item — in the Collection's own words, digitised materials "can be accessed and downloaded for use under a variety of Creative Commons non-commercial, attribution and Public Domain licences, depending on the material". *Inference —* attribution and public-domain items clear Wikimedia Commons; non-commercial ones do not, so the licence has to be read on the item and never assumed from the institution. Its exhibition 'Charmed Life: The solace of objects', 6 October 2011 to 26 February 2012, showed Lovett's amulets beside new work by Felicity Powell.

text.what: Media repository run by the Wikimedia Foundation, launched on 7 September 2004, holding over 147 million free-to-use files as of September 2026. Every picture in this atlas comes from here or from a source under the same terms. That is a constraint on what this atlas can show, and it shapes which museums are visible in it.
text.story:
Commons takes only files that are out of copyright or published under a free licence, and its definition of free is strict: a licence must specifically and irrevocably allow anyone to use the material for any purpose. Republication and distribution must be allowed. Commercial use must be allowed. The licence must be perpetual and non-revocable. A file must also be free of copyright restrictions in both the United States and the source country of the work.

What that admits: CC0, public domain, Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY), Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike (CC BY-SA), the Free Art License, and free software licences. What it refuses: CC BY-NC, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-NC-ND, and fair use — in Commons' own words, it "does not accept fair use justifications", and material licensed exclusively under non-commercial-only licences is not accepted either.

*Inference —* run that rule across the museums in this atlas and the map goes uneven. The Metropolitan Museum of Art put its public-domain images under CC0 in 2017, so a Met amulet can be shown here. The British Museum released 1.9 million images in 2020 under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, which bars commercial use, so a British Museum amulet cannot. The Pitt Rivers Museum names no Creative Commons licence at all. Wellcome Collection licenses per item, so each picture has to be checked on its own page.

The consequence is worth stating plainly rather than hiding in a caption: a reader looking at this atlas is looking at the collections that chose an open licence, not at the collections that hold the most material.
text.today: This atlas accepts CC0, public domain, CC BY, CC BY-SA and the Free Art License, and nothing else. Every image record carries its file name, its licence, its licence URL and its author, and a picture whose licence cannot be read is not published. Candidate files are listed on each record before they are fetched, so the licence is checked at the point of collection rather than at the point of publication.

names.name: abracadabra
names.th: อาบราคาดาบรา

etymology.root: Origin unknown. Wikipedia's article reports the Oxford English Dictionary's position: 'no documentation has been found to support any of the various conjectures'.
etymology.first_attested: the second century CE, in Serenus Sammonicus's Liber Medicinalis (also known as De Medicina Praecepta Saluberrima), chapter 52
etymology.note: This is the rare case in this batch where the first appearance of the word is also the first description of the object it was written on: an amulet worn against fever.
etymology.folk: Labelled folk etymology, all of it. An Aramaic phrase meaning 'I create like the word' (אברא כדברא); a link to abraxas; a resemblance to the first four letters of the Greek alphabet, alpha-beta-gamma-delta. The historian Don Skemer suggests the Hebrew phrase ha brachah dabarah. The Aramaic linguist Steve Caruso argues the word cannot be Aramaic at all, and traces the spread of that claim to an extended discussion on an early internet message board which credits rabbi Lawrence Kushner with publishing a modern etymology.

text.what: A word that was an object. Written out as a shrinking triangle on a piece of parchment and hung at the neck, it was a prescription — the earliest surviving instruction for it is a doctor's, for fever. It is now what a stage magician says at the end of a trick, which is a demotion with a date.
text.story:
Serenus Sammonicus, physician to the Roman emperor Caracalla, wrote in chapter 52 of the Liber Medicinalis that a sufferer from malaria should wear an amulet with Abracadabra written on it in the form of a triangle. He claimed the amulet makes lethal diseases go away. Other emperors who followed his medical teaching — Geta and Severus Alexander — may have used the formula too.

The form was understood to do the work. Written in the shrinking triangle, the word was taken to act like a funnel, driving the sickness out of the body. That is a claim about a shape, not about a language, which fits a word nobody could translate then either.

It was picked up by the Gnostics of the sect of Basilides, who used it invoking beneficent spirits against disease and misfortune, and it is found on Abraxas stones worn as amulets. From there its use spread past the Gnostics.

It kept turning up on parchment. A sixteenth-century Jewish codex from Italy, Ets ha-Da'at (The Tree of Knowledge), a collection of magical spells, carries it as an amulet described as a 'cure from heavens' for 'all sorts of fever[s]', consumption and fire.

It was also argued with, in print, for centuries. The Puritan minister Increase Mather dismissed the word as bereft of power. Daniel Defoe wrote dismissively about Londoners who posted it on their doorways to keep sickness out during the Great Plague of London.

By the early 1800s it had become an example of what magicians say, and that is where it stayed; today it is the tag line at the end of a trick. Aleister Crowley took it back the other way, adapting it into Abrahadabra in The Book of the Law, the central text of Thelema.

*Inference —* the arc is from a prescription written by a named imperial physician to a punchline, with the shape doing the work at one end and the sound doing it at the other. Very few objects in this atlas can be dated to a chapter number.

names.name: amulet
names.th: อะมูเล็ต

etymology.root: Latin amuletum > Middle French amulette > English amulet
etymology.first_attested: mid-15th century in English, as amalettys, then not recorded again until c. 1600 (Online Etymology Dictionary)
etymology.note: Pliny's Natural History describes an amuletum as an object that protects a person from trouble. Where the Latin word itself came from is not settled: the Online Etymology Dictionary calls its origin uncertain and offers a possible link to amoliri, 'to avert, to carry away, remove'.
etymology.folk: Labelled folk etymology: an Arabic source is sometimes claimed for amuletum. The Online Etymology Dictionary's entry rejects an Arabic origin.

text.what: The English cover-word for a protective object, and the word this atlas is written in. English-language museums, catalogues and scholarship use it as the wide category and file everything else inside it — Wikipedia's article calls amulet the proper, inclusive term and puts good luck charm and devotional article underneath it as subsets. Other writers split the pair: an amulet turns harm away, a talisman brings fortune in. The same encyclopedia carries both positions, one article apart. Which sense a reader meets depends on who wrote the label in front of them.
text.story:
Pliny's Natural History pins the Latin word to a thing: an amuletum is an object that protects a person from trouble. Beyond that the Latin is dark. The Online Etymology Dictionary calls its origin uncertain, floats a link to amoliri, 'to avert, to carry away', and turns down the Arabic derivation that gets repeated in popular writing.

English took the word late, and then dropped it. The Online Etymology Dictionary records amalettys in the middle of the fifteenth century, probably through French, and then nothing again until about 1600. A hundred and fifty years of silence, and then it came back to stay.

The split with talisman is the argument the word carries. Wikipedia's amulet article states flatly that talismans and amulets have interchangeable meanings, and in the next breath that an amulet is generally worn for protection and made from a durable material. Its talisman article keeps the functions apart: protection against evil on one side, good fortune on the other. Museum labels follow one convention or the other without announcing which.

*Inference —* the category is European and it was laid over the world from outside. An Egyptian wore a wedjat; a Bangkok collector buys a phra khrueang by temple and by monk; a visitor to a Kyoto shrine takes home an omamori. None of them reaches for a word meaning amulet-in-general. The wide word belongs to the cataloguer, and it is the word on the spine of this project. Saying so is the least the reader is owed.

text_th.what: คำครอบคลุมในภาษาอังกฤษสำหรับวัตถุคุ้มครอง และเป็นคำที่แอตลาสนี้ใช้เขียน พิพิธภัณฑ์ บัญชีรายการ และงานวิชาการภาษาอังกฤษใช้คำนี้เป็นหมวดใหญ่ และจัดทุกอย่างไว้ข้างใน บทความในวิกิพีเดียเรียกอะมูเล็ตว่าเป็นคำที่ถูกต้องและครอบคลุม และจัดเครื่องรางนำโชคกับวัตถุเพื่อความศรัทธาไว้ใต้คำนี้เป็นหมวดย่อย นักเขียนคนอื่นแยกคู่คำนี้ออกจากกัน อะมูเล็ตหันภัยออกไป ทาลิสแมนนำโชคเข้ามา สารานุกรมเดียวกันมีทั้งสองจุดยืน ห่างกันเพียงบทความเดียว ผู้อ่านจะพบความหมายแบบไหนขึ้นอยู่กับว่าใครเขียนป้ายที่อยู่ตรงหน้า

names.name: apotropaic
names.th: อะโพโทรเพอิก (กันภัย)

etymology.root: Greek apo 'away' + tropos 'turn' > apotrepō (ἀποτρέπω) 'to turn away, to ward off' > apotropaios (ἀποτρόπαιος) 'averting' > English apotropaic
etymology.note: Wiktionary's English entry dates the adjective's use from 1883; this project has not read the citation behind that date, so it is reported and not asserted. Wikipedia's article glosses the Greek verb directly as 'to ward off', which is why the two English words sit on one shelf here.

text.what: The scholar's adjective, and nobody's own. No wearer calls a bead apotropaic. It is the word a museum label, an excavation report and a doctoral thesis use for anything meant to turn harm aside — and its one virtue is that it names a purpose without taking a view on whether the purpose is met. This atlas uses it for that reason and no other.
text.story:
Greek did not need one word, because it had a crowd of them. The ancient sources carry apotropaia, probaskania, periammata, periapta, profylaktika, phylaktiria, antipharmaca, alexicaca, alexipharmaca and alexima pharmaca, all for protective objects, with no one of them dominant.

The gods came in matching sets. Offerings went to the apotropaioi theoi, the averting gods, and to the Apopompaioi theoi, who send evil away, and the Apōsikakoi theoi, the evil-averting gods. Zeus, Apollo, Heracles and Leucothea all carried the epithet Alexicacus, averter of evil; Heracles was also Keramyntes, another averter.

English boiled the crowd down to one adjective and handed it to the academy. *Inference —* that reduction is why an Egyptian birth tusk, a Roman fascinum, an Irish Brigid's cross and a Japanese ofuda can hang on one wall under one heading. The category is a translation choice, made once, in Greek, and then carried by people writing in English about everybody else.

*Tradition holds —* the practices the word covers rarely describe themselves as a category at all. A household rite in Egypt, spitting into the folds of a garment in Greece, a grasshopper hung before the Acropolis by Peisistratus: these were separate acts to the people doing them, and the adjective that gathers them is ours.

names.name: charm
names.th: ชาร์ม (charm)

etymology.root: Latin carmen 'song, verse, enchantment, religious formula' (from canere 'to sing') > Old French charme 'magic charm, magic spell, incantation; song, lamentation' > Middle English charme > English charm
etymology.first_attested: c. 1300 in English, meaning an incantation (Online Etymology Dictionary)
etymology.note: The senses arrive in order and the dates are on record: 1590s for any item worn to avert evil; a pleasing quality by the seventeenth century; 1865 for what the Online Etymology Dictionary glosses as a “small trinket fastened to a watch-chain, etc.” Wiktionary adds that charm displaced the native Old English lybb.

text.what: A word that has been three things in sequence and is still all three. A charm is a said or sung formula; a charm is a small object worn against harm or for luck; charm is what a person has who is pleasant to be near. English keeps no marker between them, so charm bracelet, charm offensive and charm against toothache are the same word doing different work.
text.story:
It started as the words themselves. Latin carmen is a song, a verse, a formula — from canere, to sing — and Old French charme is the spell spoken aloud. English has it by about 1300 in that sense only: an incantation. There is no object in the word yet.

The object arrives around 1590, when charm starts to mean any item worn to avert evil. The pleasing-person sense follows in the seventeenth century, and the weaker sense of being highly pleasing in the early eighteenth. The bracelet sense is the newest of the four and can be dated: 1865, for a small object fastened to a watch-chain.

*Inference —* the drift is from what is said, to what is worn, to what is admired, and the hinge is the same idea each time — a thing with the power to move somebody who is not choosing to be moved. That is also why this atlas files a spoken formula and a hung pendant under one heading without apology: English already did.

*Tradition holds —* the older English charm was as often spoken over an injury as hung round a neck, and the practical difference between a verse and an object narrows to nothing once the verse is written down and folded into a case.

names.name: fetish
names.th: เฟติช

etymology.root: Latin facticius 'made by art, artificial' (William Pietz points instead to facere, 'to make') > late medieval Portuguese feitiço 'spell' > sixteenth-century pidgin Fetisso on the West African coast > French fétiche > English fetish
etymology.first_attested: 1610s in English, as fatisso (Online Etymology Dictionary)
etymology.note: The Latin root is itself disputed. Pietz points to facere; the philosopher Charles de Brosses, who is credited as the source of the term fetishism, traced it to fatum, fanum and fari. Some scholars read that instability as symptomatic of the concept's own confusion between what is enchanted and what is manufactured.

text.what: A European word, applied from outside, to objects Europeans met on the West African coast and could not file. This atlas carries the word for its own history and for nothing else: no object anywhere in this project is described as a fetish. What the word describes is an act of labelling, and the labelling had consequences — it supplied the bottom rung of a ladder of religions that European writers then climbed, with themselves at the top.
text.story:
William Pietz, whose 1994 ethno-historical study is the standard account, argues the term originated on the coast of West Africa in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, in the encounter itself. He keeps two things apart: actual African objects that Europeans called fetishes, together with the local theories of those objects, and 'fetish' as an idea about a kind of object. The second is European property.

He traces the chain in one sentence: from the late medieval Portuguese feitiço, to the sixteenth-century pidgin Fetisso on the African coast, to various northern European versions of the word by way of the 1602 text of the Dutchman Pieter de Marees. The Portuguese developed the concept for objects used in West African religious practice. What went into the category was then decided by exclusion: objects were classed as fetishes indiscriminately because, from a European standpoint, they did not fit anywhere else.

The travel literature spread it. Ramusio's Viaggio e Navigazioni of 1550, de Bry's India Orientalis of 1597, Purchas's Hakluytus Posthumus of 1625, Churchill's Collection of Voyages and Travels of 1732, Astley's A New General Collection of Voyages and Travels of 1746, Prevost's Histoire générale des voyages of 1748: these are the books the eighteenth-century theorists read.

Then it became a theory. Charles de Brosses popularised the term around 1760, in Du culte des dieux fétiches, comparing West African religion with the magical side of ancient Egyptian religion. Auguste Comte put fetishism first in his sequence of religious development, ahead of polytheism and monotheism. G. W. F. Hegel, in Lectures on the Philosophy of History, held that Africans were incapable of abstract thought and that a fetish object could therefore be anything arbitrarily given 'imaginary powers'. Modern scholarship reads the whole sequence as colonial: the Portuguese, Dutch and British deployed the category to criticise how colonised people dealt with material objects, and built European rationality by contrast.

The word then kept moving away from the coast. Around 1837 it meant an object of blind devotion among the New England Transcendentalists. In 1897 Havelock Ellis fixed the psycho-sexual sense, which is the sense most English speakers now hear first.

And it did not stay only in European mouths. The market at Akodessawa, a district of Lomé in Togo, carries the word in its own French name: Marché des Féticheurs. Wikipedia's account of it says the market sells fetishes used in vodún religious practice. *Inference —* a word coined about people can be taken up by them, for trade, for tourism, or because it is the word the customer knows. That does not undo the coinage, and this atlas still does not use it to describe an object.

*Tradition holds —* the objects themselves have their own names in their own languages — nkisi among Kikongo speakers is the clearest case — and those names are what this project files them under.

names.name: fu
names.th: ฝู (福)

etymology.root: Chinese 福 (fú) 'fortune, good luck'. A different character, 符 (fú), means a tally or talismanic graph and gives fulu (符籙), 'talismanic script'; 籙 (lù) is a registry of priests' memberships and of the skills they are trained in.
etymology.note: Two characters, one romanisation, and a reader has to watch the character rather than the sound. 福 is the New Year fortune-word pasted at a door; 符 is the Taoist talisman-graph that stands behind the Japanese ofuda and the Korean bujeok. No dated first attestation is given here for either; the practice of mounting 福 is dated instead.

text.what: One character, printed on a square of red paper and pasted at the entrance, usually turned upside down. Fú means fortune or good luck; it is also the name of a god, one of the trio of star gods Fú, Lù and Shòu, who is often shown as a figure carrying the character. Mounted fu appear at the doors of Chinese homes worldwide at New Year, and the practice runs across every level of income.
text.story:
The custom is old enough to date: mounting the character goes back at least to the Song dynasty, 960 to 1279 CE.

The upside-down part is a pun, and the pun is the mechanism. In nearly all varieties of Chinese the word for upside-down and the word for to arrive are homophones — dào, written 倒 and 到. 'Upside-down fu' therefore sounds all but identical to 'good luck arrives', so pasting the character inverted on a door or doorpost states a wish that prosperity descends on the house.

A second story explains the same thing differently. It puts the origin with the family of a nineteenth-century Qing prince: on a New Year's Eve the prince's servants pasted fu characters through the house as a joke, one illiterate servant put his on upside down, and when the prince was furious another servant saved him by pointing out that the mistake announced prosperity arriving. Two accounts, one practice; the encyclopedia carries both without choosing.

The sound does further work. Bats — 蝠 — are among the most common of Chinese symbols and carry the same sound as fu, which is why textiles and ceramics show bats in flight, sometimes more than a hundred at once. Bran, 麩子, fūzi, is a rarer match.

The other fu is a different trade. In Taoist practice, 符 are instructions to deities and spirits, symbols for exorcism, and recipes for potions and cures, written by priests of the fulu pai. Their illegibility is not a failure: Ge Hong noted in the Baopuzi, by the Eastern Jin dynasty of 317 to 420, that successful use did not depend on the user's being able to read the script, and scholars including James Robson and Gil Raz argue the incomprehensibility is central to the talisman's authority.

The fortune character now has a code point: Unicode 10, in 2017, added a rounded version at U+1F260 🉠 ROUNDED SYMBOL FOR FU.

names.th: กรีกรี (gris-gris)

etymology.root: From the Mande languages spoken by Mandinka and Bambara people in West Africa; Wikipedia's article reports the sense 'magic'. Carried to the Americas with enslaved Muslims and into Louisiana and Haitian French.
etymology.note: No dated first attestation was read for this record, in any language, so none is given. English spellings on record include grigri, gregory and gerregery. In West Africa, written charms worn by non-Muslims were called saffis.

text.what: A word that names a small cloth sack worn on the person, holding Qur'anic verses written on paper and a set number of small objects. It began in Muslim Mande communities of far West Africa and crossed the Atlantic with enslaved people. On the western side of the ocean the same word carries two opposite charges, and which one a speaker means depends on where they are standing.
text.story:
The trade route came first. Travellers through the Volta Basin, in what is now Ghana, reported Mande speakers such as the Dyula as central to making and distributing Islamic charms, which they called gris-gris. From them the practice spread to other Muslim groups — the Dagomba, who wrote extensive Arabic manuscripts 'with magic formulae and prescriptions for preparing amulets'. The sacks held Qur'an verses on paper with herbs, worn at the neck. Sometimes the written charm alone counted, carried by priests. Non-Muslims in the region wore them too, under the name saffis.

The makers are named. Among Mande Muslims, scholars of the mystical division called siri, 'path', are marabouts, and they are the ones who produce gris-gris; scholars of seli, 'prayer', are karamokos, who study Qur'anic law. Some cross over. The whole practice is Karamokobara.

In the United States the word turned. Enslaved people used gris-gris against their owners, and the word came to name harm done to a target; some were found in burials; there are period reports of people cutting, drowning or otherwise handling somebody else's gris-gris to injure them. New Orleans court cases in 1773 convicted enslaved people of using gris-gris to kill enslavers — among the earliest legal mentions of Louisiana's tradition. Enslaved conjure women made gris-gris to start rebellions, and the bags were held to guide people to freedom on the Underground Railroad. By the 1800s the word was used in Louisiana to mean both bewitch and the object itself. In October 1849 authorities arrested an enslaved man carrying a human finger wrapped in flannel that he held brought good luck; people in New Orleans sought human remains from tombs for conjure and gris-gris, and gravesites were disturbed for it. In Cajun communities the word reads as harm and ill-fortune. In the Louisiana Creole community, Gris-Gris doctors have worked for centuries and are looked on favourably by the Black community at large.

In Haiti, on the same account, the word kept its West African sense: an amulet with good intentions. In Hoodoo a gris-gris is taken to represent the self.

It is also current and ordinary. A 1982 survey put gris-gris among the top three methods of contraception known to women in Senegal, alongside abstinence and roots and herbs; over sixty per cent of women reported knowing such traditional methods, against a little over forty per cent for the pill. They are worn, in the article's own words, 'from wrestlers to soldiers to housewives, and can feature anything from monkey to snake to mouse.'

etymology.root: Arabic khamsa (خمسة) 'five' > English hamsa; Maghrebi variants khmisa; Hebrew hamesh (five) in Jewish usage; Berber afus, 'hand', names a similar motif
etymology.note: The standard name of the object is a number, not a hand and not a person. Every named version — Hand of Fatima, Hand of Miriam, Hand of Mary — is a later label attached by somebody, and the Arabic phrase yad Fatima is rare in pre-modern usage.

text.what: A word that is a number. Five — for the fingers — is what the object is called in Arabic, and hamesh, also five, in Hebrew usage. The names a shopper meets in Europe and America are all attachments: 'Hand of Fatima' (French Main de Fatma) was popularised by Europeans in French colonial North Africa and is a colonial nickname rather than an indigenous Arabic term. In Sephardi and Mizrahi Jewish contexts it is the Hand of Miriam. Levantine Christians call it kef Miryam, the hand of Mary.
text.story:
The number is in the curses too, which is the strongest sign that the counting came first. Khamsa fi ainek — 'five [fingers] in your eye' — is said with the right hand raised, palm out, fingers slightly apart, to blind the aggressor. Khamsa wa-khamis, 'five and Thursday', is said without any gesture; Thursday, the fifth day, is held favourable for rites and for pilgrimages to saints' tombs against the evil eye. And there is the spitting formula: 'Khamsa, Khamsa, Khamsa, tfu, tfu, tfu', which Wikipedia's article compares to knocking on wood.

The name has been legislated against. Among the Morisco population of Granada and nearby regions, khamsa pendants were popular and described as 'large engraved medals ... with a hand inscribed with letters'. A reform council banned khamsas as Islamic symbols in 1526 and ordered crosses in their place; the Synod of Guadix renewed the prohibition in 1554; an episcopal committee convened by Emperor Charles V decreed a ban on the Hand of Fatima and all open right-hand amulets in 1526. They went on being worn, including by Christians — a Nasrid-period gold pendant survives inscribed Ave Maria gratia plena.

It is argued over now from inside as well. Eva-Maria von Kemnitz, citing Bruno Barbatti, calls it the most important averting sign in the Islamic world; Salafi authorities reject it, and a fatwa states it is impermissible to hang the 'Khamsa', with hands of Fatima listed among prohibited amulets. The hamsa is also a national symbol of Algeria and appears in its emblem.

*Inference —* a name that is a number is very hard to suppress: you cannot ban five. What actually displaced the Arabic word in most of the world's shops was not a prohibition but a French colonial nickname, and that is the name on the label a buyer in London or Los Angeles reads today.

names.name: juju
names.th: จูจู

etymology.root: Contested. Two proposals are in print and neither has won. Wikipedia's article reports an origin in Hausa, where the term means 'evil spirit'. The same article, and the Online Etymology Dictionary, report a derivation from French joujou, 'toy, plaything' — the dictionary calls it supposed.
etymology.note: This project reports both proposals with their proposers and picks neither. The two pull opposite ways: one African and grave, one French and diminishing.

text.what: In central West Africa — Nigeria, Benin, Togo, Cameroon, Ghana — juju names a body of practice and the objects and spells inside it. In looser English it means magical properties dealing with luck, good or bad. Across the West African diaspora the word covers charms made in African traditional and African diaspora religions generally. Wikipedia's article records the practitioner's title plainly: a juju man is any man vetted by local traditions and well versed in traditional spiritual medicines.
text.story:
The word reached English print through colonial officials. James George Frazer published it in Folk-Lore volume XXVI under the title 'A Priest-King in Nigeria', from a communication he received from P. A. Talbot, District Commissioner in southern Nigeria. Talbot described the dominant Ju-Ju of Elele, a town in the north-west of the Degema district, as a Priest-King elected for a term of seven years, and wrote: 'The whole prosperity of the town, especially the fruitfulness of farm, byre, and marriage-bed, was linked with his life. Should he fall sick, therefore, it entailed famine and grave disaster upon the inhabitants ...'

Others were already writing it down. Le Comte C. N. de Cardi documented the practice among Igbo, Ibibio and Yoruba people of the Niger Delta in an article of 1899; Alan Maxwell Boisragon in a book of 1897.

On what the word covers, Wikipedia's article is careful and worth quoting rather than paraphrasing: according to some authors, 'It is neither good nor bad, but it may be used for constructive purposes as well as for nefarious deeds.' Its commonest reported use is the treatment of physical and spiritual complaints — insect and animal bites, and the countering of curses. It is also used to bind a contract or secure compliance, with the practitioner paid for the service. Used against somebody, it is reported as a means of revenge and of causing misfortune.

*Inference —* the etymological fight matters because of what each answer implies. Hausa 'evil spirit' makes the word a local name for a serious thing. French joujou makes it a European joke about somebody else's religion. Which root a nineteenth-century writer preferred has usually said more about the writer than about the word, and the sources have not settled it.

text_th.what: ในแถบตอนกลางของแอฟริกาตะวันตก — ไนจีเรีย เบนิน โตโก แคเมอรูน กานา — จูจูหมายถึงระบบการปฏิบัติ รวมทั้งวัตถุและคาถาที่อยู่ในนั้น ในภาษาอังกฤษแบบหลวม ๆ หมายถึงคุณสมบัติทางเวทมนตร์ที่เกี่ยวกับโชค ทั้งดีและร้าย ในหมู่ชาวแอฟริกาตะวันตกพลัดถิ่น คำนี้ครอบคลุมเครื่องรางที่ทำขึ้นในศาสนาดั้งเดิมของแอฟริกาและศาสนาของชาวแอฟริกันพลัดถิ่นโดยทั่วไป บทความในวิกิพีเดียบันทึกตำแหน่งของผู้ประกอบพิธีไว้ตรง ๆ ว่า จูจูแมน (juju man) คือชายใดก็ตามที่ผ่านการรับรองตามธรรมเนียมท้องถิ่น และเชี่ยวชาญยาทางจิตวิญญาณแบบดั้งเดิม

names.name: luck
names.th: ลัก (luck, โชค)

etymology.root: Middle Low German, Dutch or Frisian luk, a short form of gelucke (Middle High German gelücke) > English luck
etymology.note: It likely entered English as a gambling term, and the context of gambling stays detectable in the word's connotations. Before it, Old and Middle English said speed (Old English spēd, Middle English spede) for good fortune — a word of fate or divine help, not of chance: 'Christ be our speed', in William Robertson's Phraseologia generalis of 1693. Chance itself is a Latin loanword through Old French cheance, from Late Latin cadentia, 'falling', taken into Middle English from the late thirteenth century. Wikipedia's article also compares old Slavic lukyj and old Russian luchaj.

text.what: The word the whole 'good luck charm' category hangs on in English, and a late arrival that came in through a card game. Wikipedia's article sets out three conditions for it: luck is good or bad, luck is the result of chance, and luck applies to a sentient being. Nothing in that definition involves a god, which is exactly what changed when the word arrived.
text.story:
English managed without it until the 1480s. What it had instead was speed — Old English spēd — which meant good fortune and also prosperity, profit and abundance, and which named help rather than chance. A bestower of success could be called a speed. Then luck came in from Low German, Dutch or Frisian, probably at a gaming table, and it named something else: a personal chance event, with nobody behind it.

The idea it needed had arrived a couple of centuries earlier. Chance, from Old French cheance and Late Latin cadentia, literally describes an outcome as a falling — as of dice — and English took it from the late thirteenth century. Fortuna, the Roman goddess, was a popular medieval allegory, and learned writers of the High Middle Ages made her a servant of God distributing success and failure in a fickle way, which is how chance was fitted into a Christian frame without being given a will of its own.

The symbols the word gathers are local and contradictory. Seven is a lucky number in Christian-influenced cultures, eight in Chinese-influenced ones. In Chinese and Japanese, four is unlucky because it sounds like the word for death. Greek practice counts entering and leaving a house by different doors, and breaking a mirror, as unlucky; Navajo practice counts throwing rocks into a whirlwind. In Western practice, opening an umbrella indoors may be counted unlucky partly because it can poke somebody in the eye, and shaking hands with a chimney sweep counted lucky partly because it is a kind but unpleasant thing to do.

The gods stayed on for a while beside it: Fortuna and Felicitas in Roman religion, Dedun in Nubian religion, the Seven Lucky Gods in Japan, Lakshmi and her inauspicious counterpart Alakshmi in Hinduism.

*Inference —* the arrival of luck is the arrival of the idea that the outcome is nobody's decision. An object bought against that is a different object from one bought to petition somebody, even when it is the same object on the same string. Half the arguments in this atlas about whether a charm is devotional or commercial are really arguments about which of those two words the buyer is using.

names.name: mascot
names.th: มาสคอต

etymology.root: Provençal masco 'sorceress, witch' > French mascotte 'lucky charm' > English mascot
etymology.first_attested: first recorded in 1867; entered English in 1881 (Wikipedia's Mascot article)
etymology.note: Wikipedia's article credits the word's popularity to Edmond Audran, whom it calls a French composer, and to La mascotte, performed in December 1880; it calls the work an opera. The piece is also widely described as an operetta, and this project has not read a source that settles the label, so both are reported and neither asserted. Before 1880 the word was gamblers' slang in France, and before the nineteenth century it attached to inanimate objects — a lock of hair, a ship's figurehead.

text.what: The only word in this batch whose modern sense is a job. A mascot is a human, an animal or an object thought to bring luck, or anything that stands for a group with a common public identity — a school, a team, a society, a military unit, a brand. The luck sense is still the first one the word carries; the costume is a twentieth-century addition.
text.story:
The route is short and well-marked: masco, a Provençal word for a sorceress, into French mascotte meaning a lucky charm, used for anything that brought luck to a household. Wikipedia's article dates the first record to 1867 and the arrival in English to 1881, in the sense of a specific living creature attached to a human organisation as a symbol or live logo. What moved it from French gamblers' slang into general use was a stage piece: Edmond Audran's La mascotte, performed in December 1880.

Before all that the word sat on objects of a kind this atlas is full of — a lock of hair, a figurehead on a sailing ship.

The costume came later, and it came from puppetry. Animals were used first, by sports organisations, to entertain spectators and to unsettle opponents. Stylistic changes in American puppetry in the middle of the twentieth century, including the work of Jim Henson and of Sid and Marty Krofft, were adapted to sports mascots, and the three-dimensional costumed character followed — the Phillie Phanatic, the Flyers' Gritty, the Seattle Kraken's Buoy, the Washington Commanders' Major Tuddy. Marketers took the form from there.

The live argument attached to the word is over mascots based on human likenesses. Mascots using Native American tribes are contested, and many argue they are offensive exploitations of an oppressed culture. Several tribes have taken the other position: the Utah Utes and the Central Michigan Chippewas are sanctioned by local tribes, and Florida State's use of Osceola and Renegade is supported by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, though the university declines to call them mascots. Both sides are named here and neither is joined.

names.name: mojo
names.th: โมโจ

etymology.root: Contested, and African on both proposals. Wikipedia's mojo bag article derives it from Kikongo mooyo, glossed as referring to the spirits that dwell within magical charms, and names the cavity of an nkisi where the charm's materials are kept. The Online Etymology Dictionary says 'probably of Creole origin' and points to Gullah moco, 'witchcraft', and Fula moco'o, 'medicine man'.
etymology.first_attested: 1920s in English in the sense 'magic' (Online Etymology Dictionary)
etymology.note: Both proposals are reported here with their sources and neither is preferred. The dictionary also records a 1935 underworld slang sense for narcotics.

text.what: In Hoodoo, the African American spiritual tradition, mojo is both the conjure work and the bag that holds it — Wikipedia's article calls a mojo bag a prayer in a bag, a spell that can be carried on the body. Outside that, in general American English, mojo means sexual potency, then drive, then momentum in a meeting. The same word, one century, two rooms.
text.story:
Both proposed roots point at the same shelf. On Wikipedia's account the Kikongo mooyo names the spirits inside a charm and the cavity of an nkisi where the charm's materials sit — so the word starts as the inside of a container. On the Online Etymology Dictionary's account it is Creole, beside Gullah moco and Fula moco'o. Neither source claims the other is wrong.

The object has an ancestry that is not contested. Bakongo people of the Congo River region made medicine bags of leather or cloth holding feathers, animal parts, roots and herbs; when Bakongo people were enslaved in the United States the practice continued and became a custom of Hoodoo. Nkisi bags looked like mojo bags and are named as their ancestor. The philosophy came with them: in Bakongo religion, simbi spirits can inhabit an nkisi bag, and the nganga makes the bag for a person with ingredients specific to a particular simbi.

The bag has other American names — toby, lucky hand, nation sack, conjure bag, package — and the word hand in that list has its own contested origin: from finger and hand bones of the dead used in the bags, or from lucky hand root, favoured by gamblers, or from the hand of cards the mixed ingredients resemble.

Then the word left. Wikipedia's account is blunt about it: mojo underwent a semantic change in American popular culture at the beginning of the twentieth century and came to refer to sexuality and virility, as musicians began to use the word outside its original context within African American culture. From there it became motivation in general.

*Inference —* this is the sharpest case in this batch of a word walking away from the people who made it. A term for the spirit inside a container now means the thing a commentator says a footballer has lost and an investor says a start-up has found. The bag is still made; the word on top of it now belongs to everybody.

names.th: นาซาร์

etymology.root: Arabic naẓar (نَظَر) 'sight, surveillance, attention' > borrowed into Albanian, Azerbaijani, Bengali, Hebrew, Hindi-Urdu, Kurdish, Pashto, Persian, Punjabi, Sindhi and Turkish
etymology.note: The word names the look, not the object. Turkish nazar boncuğu compounds it with boncuk, Turkic for bead, so the Turkish for the object is literally 'nazar bead' — the borrowed word plus a native one. Greek does not borrow at all: the object there is máti (μάτι), 'eye'.

text.what: A word for a glance that has ended up as the name of a glass disc. Naẓar in Arabic is sight, surveillance, attention. Across a dozen languages it names the harmful look — in India and Pakistan nazar lag gai says somebody has been struck by it — and by extension the bead sold against it. Persian and Afghan usage says cheshm nazar or nazar qurbāni; Turkish says nazar boncuğu, the nazar bead; Greek, which did not borrow the word, says máti.
text.story:
The phrase that keeps it away is its own small piece of evidence. In India and Pakistan the Hindi-Urdu chashm-e-baddoor — 'may the evil eye keep away' — is said aloud, without any object involved at all. The bead is the same sentence in glass.

What the bead is is described the same way by everyone selling it: handmade glass, concentric circles or teardrops in dark blue, white, light blue and black, sometimes edged yellow or gold. Wikipedia's article quotes the recipe as “a mixture of molten glass, iron, copper, water, and salt, ingredients that are thought to shield people from evil”, and reports the colour logic in a wearer's terms: 'According to Turkish belief, blue acts as a shield against evil and even absorbs negativity.' It also carries the argument from rarity — in the Middle East and the Mediterranean, blue eyes are uncommon, and light-eyed people were held able to curse with a look.

The bead is old and the word is not the oldest thing about it. The Turkish boncuk, the blue glass eye bead, is a design of great antiquity; written documentation and surviving beads date from as early as the sixteenth century BCE, and glass beads were made and used from Mesopotamia to Egypt, from Carthage to Greece, from Phoenicia to Persia and through the Roman imperial period.

And it now has a code point. Unicode added U+1F9FF 🧿 NAZAR AMULET in 2018. *Inference —* that is the moment the word finished its journey: a name for a look, then a bead, then a character available on every phone on earth, sent by people who have never heard the Arabic.

*Tradition holds —* wearers say a bead that breaks has taken a strong nazar and stored it, and broken in order to protect the person wearing it.

names.th: โอมาโมริ

etymology.root: Japanese mamoru 'to protect' > noun mamori (守り) 'protection' > honorific prefix o- (御) + mamori = omamori (御守/お守り)
etymology.note: Omamori is the sonkeigo — honorific — form of the ordinary word for protection. The grammar is doing work: the honorific is aimed at the kami or the Buddhist figure the charm is dedicated to, not at the object or its buyer. No dated first attestation was read for the word itself.

text.what: The Japanese word for a shrine or temple charm, and a rare case of a name that says who is doing the protecting rather than what the thing is made of. Omamori are sold at Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples alike, with few exceptions, to anybody, regardless of religious affiliation — and are mainly understood as a donation to the shrine or temple the buyer is visiting, with the object as the receipt.
text.story:
The word takes a compound for every need, which is how a reader can tell what a given charm is for without opening it: kōtsū-anzen for traffic safety, yaku-yoke for avoiding evil, kaiun for opening fortune, gakugyō-jōju for study and passing examinations, shōbai-hanjō for business, en-musubi for finding a partner and marrying, anzan for a safe pregnancy and delivery, kanai-anzen for the household's safety and peace.

The object is a brocade bag over paper or wood carrying a written prayer. Custom says not to open it — opening it loses the benefit — so the inscription is a thing the owner owns and does not read. Charms are customarily replaced once a year, returned to the shrine or temple they came from, and burnt rather than thrown away, as respect to the deity that helped through the year. Most returns come on or just after the Japanese New Year.

Yanagita Kunio, writing in 1969, put the dating carefully: 'Japanese have probably always believed in amulets of one kind or another, but the modern printed charms now given out by shrines and temples first became popular in the Tokugawa period or later, and the practice of a person wearing miniature charms is also new. The latter custom is particularly common in cities.'

The word is now on objects a shrine never touched. Materials have widened from paper and wood to bumper decals, bicycle reflectors and credit cards. Where popular shrines cannot meet demand they turn to factories, and priests have complained about the “quality and authenticity” of factory products. Shops sell generic omamori with Mickey Mouse, Hello Kitty, Snoopy or Kewpie on them, not issued by any shrine or temple and not presented as religious. Both of those are called omamori, by their sellers and their buyers. This atlas reports that and leaves the argument where it is.

names.name: periapt
names.th: เพริแอปต์ (เครื่องรางแขวนคอ)

etymology.root: Greek peri- 'around' + haptos (ἅπτος) 'fastened' > períaptos 'hung round' > períapton (περίαπτον) 'amulet' > Middle French periapte > English periapt
etymology.first_attested: Wiktionary marks the English noun from the 16th century; the earliest dated quotation on that page is Walter Scott, The Talisman, 1825
etymology.note: The gap between the marked century and the earliest quotation this project read is real and is left open here rather than closed with a guess.

text.what: An English word for an amulet worn hung round the neck, defined by the hanging rather than by the shape or the material. It is close to dead. It survives in antiquarian writing, in medical history, and in translations out of Greek, where the plural periapta sits in the ancient list of protective objects.
text.story:
The Greek says what it is: períaptos, hung round. Not carved, not blessed, not written — fastened on. Ancient Greek sources list periapta among apotropaia, probaskania, periammata, phylaktiria and the rest, none of them the single dominant term.

The English quotations Wiktionary carries are all of a type. Walter Scott, in The Talisman in 1825, writes that the Persians were perhaps most remarkable for their unshaken credulity in amulets, spells, periapts and similar charms. Thomas Oswald Cockayne, in Leechdoms, Wortcunning, and Starcraft in 1864, records that the occipital bone of an ass's head in a skin is also a good periapt. Charles William King's The Natural History of Precious Stones of 1867 distinguishes a decoration from a periapt, for it was suspended round his neck by golden chains. Fielding H. Garrison's An Introduction to the History of Medicine of 1921 has a formula that became a charm for intractable haemorrhage, written on the part affected or worn as a periapt.

*Inference —* the word survived exactly where the Greek did — in the Victorian antiquarian's English, and in the vocabulary of men writing about other people's practices at a distance. It never made it onto a shop sign.

*Tradition holds —* the distinction the word preserves is worth keeping even if the word is not: an object that hangs is a different object from one sewn in, buried under a threshold or nailed to a door, and every one of those is in this atlas.

names.name: phylactery
names.th: ฟิแล็กเทอรี (phylactery)

etymology.root: Greek phylaktērion (φυλακτήριον) 'guarded post, safeguard, security', in later Greek 'amulet' or 'charm' > the Greek New Testament, where it occurs once > Latin and the languages of Europe > English phylactery
etymology.first_attested: the Greek New Testament, at Matthew 23, in the accusative plural; the word passed from there into the languages of Europe
etymology.note: Neither Aquila nor Symmachus uses phylacteries in their translations, so the New Testament occurrence carries the whole transmission on its own. Wikipedia's amulet article also uses phylactery as a general synonym for any unspecified amulet.

text.what: Three words wearing one spelling, and a reader has to know which is meant. In Bible translation and in older Jewish scholarship, phylactery is the English word for tefillin — the leather boxes of Torah text bound to arm and head. In general English it is a loose synonym for any amulet. In tabletop gaming it names the object a lich hides its life force in, which is where most English speakers under forty meet the word first.
text.story:
The Greek starts as architecture and police work. Phylaktērion is a guarded post, a safeguard, a security; only in later Greek does it mean an amulet. The New Testament uses it once, at Matthew 23, for the boxes worn by Jews — a Greek word for a Jewish object, chosen by a Greek-writing author — and from that single occurrence it entered the European languages. Tefillin itself is a different word with a different history: the Targumim and the Peshitta are the first texts to use it, and Jastrow connects it to a Syriac word for attachments or hangings.

The archaeology and the word meet: finds at Qumran and the reference in Matthew 23 together show that by the first century CE many Jews were wearing some physical form of the object.

The third stage is datable and recent. The term appears in the first-edition Advanced Dungeons & Dragons Monster Manual in 1977, where a lich holds its status by conjurations, enchantments and a phylactery, and the nature and function of that phylactery is not explained. By the second edition in 1989 the object explicitly stores the lich's life force. The third-edition Monster Manual, in 2000, describes it as resembling a Jewish tefillin, and notes it can also be a ring or an amulet.

That borrowing has been argued with. Eric Silver has criticised the gaming term for its Jewish religious origin and proposed talisman as the neutral word instead. Wizards of the Coast has not retired the term; Paizo Publishing stopped using it in 2021, and its liches now keep their souls in a soul cage.

*Inference —* the arc is one word carried three times by people who were not its owners: a Greek writer naming a Jewish practice, European translators keeping his choice, and a game designer reaching past both for a container that sounded old.

names.name: talisman
names.th: ทาลิสแมน

etymology.root: Greek teleō 'I complete, perform a rite' (from telos 'end, fulfilment') > Byzantine Greek telesma 'completion, religious rite, payment' > Arabic ṭilsam (طِلَسْم, plural ṭalāsim) > French talisman > English talisman
etymology.first_attested: 1630s in English, for a magical figure cut or engraved on stone or metal under certain observances (Online Etymology Dictionary)
etymology.note: A figurative sense — any means of attaining extraordinary results — follows by 1784. The Arabic word was also taken into Turkish, Persian and Hindi, so a reader meets it again in each of those languages before it ever reached English.

text.what: The word for a made object whose power the maker claims to have put in it. Where amulet turns harm away, talisman brings fortune in — that is the split most English writers use, and Wikipedia's talisman article states it as the key difference. Its amulet article, one click away, says the two have interchangeable meanings. Both are in print. The Arabic ṭilsam behind the English word carries something the English lost: a sense of manufacture under conditions, made at a particular hour for a particular end.
text.story:
The root is a verb about finishing a rite. Greek teleō, 'I complete, perform a rite'; telesma, the completion or the payment. Arabic took it as ṭilsam, French took it from Arabic, English took it from French in the 1630s.

What the Arabic word names is a craft with a timetable. The tenth-century Abbasid mathematician Thabit ibn Qurra was held to be the expert; in one of his texts on talismans he wrote, 'The noblest part of astronomy is the science of talismans.' In John of Seville and Limia's twelfth-century version of ibn Qurra's De imaginibus, talismans and astronomy matter more to wisdom than geometry or philosophy do. Adelard of Bath's translation of the same text insists on knowledge of both astronomy and astrology, because a talisman has to be made at the moment of an auspicious celestial event — and because, in that text, a maker who is distracted or in doubt produces a powerless one.

The instructions are specific about material. Adelard's translation specifies lead, iron, bronze, gold or silver for a talisman meant to earn love from a king, a family member or a peer; pitch and tar, bitumen and aloes for one meant to set people against each other, take money, defend or destroy a place, or win a legal case.

*Inference —* the English word kept the object and dropped the clock. A modern English speaker who calls a lucky coin a talisman is using a word that once meant a thing timed to a sky.

etymology.root: Arabic verb ʿawwadha 'to fortify someone with an amulet or incantation' > noun taʿwīdh (تعويذ) 'amulet, charm' > Urdu and Hindi ta'wiz (تعویز, तावीज़)
etymology.note: The noun is built from a verb about the act, not from a word for an object — the name says what is done to a person, not what is hung on them. No dated first attestation was read, so none is given here.

text.what: The word across the Muslim world for a worn written charm and, by extension, for the object it is folded into: a pendant, letters carved on metal, a framed prayer. What goes inside is text — Qur'anic verses, hadith, the ninety-nine names of God, the names of prophets and their companions, or a religious narrative. The word and the permission arrive together, which is the whole argument: Wikipedia's article reports that Sunni Muslims are permitted to wear ta'wiz as long as it consciously strengthens their bond with Allah and does not come from a belief the ta'wiz itself cures or protects.
text.story:
The verb underneath the noun is the point. ʿawwadha is to fortify somebody with an amulet or an incantation — the grammar makes the wearer the object of the action and the text the instrument.

What gets written is specific and named. The word Allah is especially common; touching it or seeing it is held to turn evil away. The names of prophets and religious figures connect the wearer to the person named, and the favoured figures are Solomon, Ali ibn Abi Talib and his sons Hasan and Husain, and the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus. Written accounts of those lives are also used, sometimes illustrated.

The clearest dated use is military. Scrolls carrying Qur'anic quotations, prophetic references and sacred symbols were common in war in the Ottoman Empire, with verses such as 'victory is from God and conquest is near' (Qur. 61:13) found on ta'wiz worn in combat. Texts packaged in tawiz were most often pre-made when used by the public; a literate wearer could change the verse at their own discretion.

*Inference —* that last detail is the useful one. A charm whose text a literate wearer can swap is a charm whose owner is also its author, and it puts the taweez in a different class from an object a specialist alone may make. This atlas files it as written, not as consecrated.

*Tradition holds —* objects of this kind are also criticised from inside the religion, and the criticism is about where the power is located rather than about the paper. The permission Wikipedia records carries its own limit in the same sentence.

etymology.root: Fon vodún, from the Gbe languages of the Niger-Congo family, translating as 'spirit', 'God', 'divinity' or 'presence' > Haitian Creole Vodou
etymology.first_attested: 1658, in the Doctrina Christiana, where the Fon word Vôdoun is first recorded (Wikipedia's Haitian Vodou article)
etymology.note: In Haitian Creole, Vodou first designated a style of dance and drumming, and outsiders then adopted it as a general term for Afro-Haitian religion. Many practitioners describe their tradition as Ginen instead — a moral philosophy and a code for how to live and serve the spirits. The West African religion is usually written Vodún, or Vodu, to keep it distinct; the anthropologist Timothy R. Landry argues vodúnsínsen, 'spirit worship', is the more accurate name for it.

text.what: Two religions and one misspelling. Vodún is the religion of Aja, Ewe and Fon people in Benin, Togo, Ghana and Nigeria, with priesthoods, initiatory societies and the divination system Fá. Vodou is Haiti's: formed in the mid-eighteenth century out of Fon, Kongo and Yoruba traditions under colonial Saint-Domingue, with Roman Catholic and Masonic material absorbed into it, and carrying temples (ounfò), priests and priestesses (oungan and manbo), four grades of initiation, a liturgy of drum, song and dance, and a diaspora in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, France, Canada and the United States. Vodou is the spelling used by scholars, by official Haitian Creole orthography and by the United States Library of Congress. Some scholars prefer Vodoun, Voudoun or Vodun; French also carries vaudou and vaudoux. The two-o spelling, on Wikipedia's account, “is now generally avoided by practitioners and scholars when referring to the Haitian religion”.
text.story:
The word is older than any of the arguments about it. The Fon Vôdoun is first recorded in 1658, in the Doctrina Christiana, and in the kingdom of Dahomey it meant a spirit or a deity. Ouidah was a major slave embarkation point from the 1670s to the 1860s, and Vodún practitioners were among those shipped; with Kongo religion, theirs became one of the two main influences on what formed in Haiti. Many Haitian terms, the word Vodou included, come out of Fon.

What happened to the spelling in English has a date and an address. The United States occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934, and the occupation produced tourist shows and a literature — Faustin Wirkus and William Seabrook wrote the books that reached American readers. Seabrook's The Magic Island was published on 3 January 1929 by Harcourt, Brace & Company; it is described as the first popular English-language work to describe the concept of a zombie, which Seabrook defined as “a soulless human corpse, still dead, but taken from the grave and endowed by sorcery with a mechanical semblance of life”. Time said it “introduced 'zombi' into U.S. speech”. The book inspired the 1932 stage play Zombie and fed Victor Halperin's 1932 film White Zombie, with Bela Lugosi — the first feature-length zombie film, and the one that “originated several fictional tropes”, chiefly the zombie as a mindless henchman under an evil magician's spell. Jacques Tourneur's I Walked with a Zombie followed in 1943. The film “London Voodoo” of 2004 is named on the same list of works that sensationalise the religion.

The doll most people picture belongs to that literature and not to either religion. Wikipedia's article states it plainly: “The voodoo doll is not prominent in either” Haitian Vodou or “Louisiana Voodoo”.

Who objects is on record. Scholars describe Vodou as one of the world's most maligned and misunderstood religions; Christians in Haiti have presented it as Satanic, and in Anglophone and Francophone writing generally it has been tied to sorcery and black magic, attitudes “sometimes linked with anti-black racism”. In U.S. popular culture Haitian Vodou is usually portrayed as destructive and malevolent, and the absence of any central Vodou authority has made those representations hard to answer. Practitioners answered anyway: after attacks on Vodouists following the overthrow of Jean-Claude Duvalier in 1986, they formed the civil rights groups Zantray and Bode Nasyonal. Haiti's 1987 constitution guaranteed freedom of religion, and President Jean-Bertrand Aristide granted Vodou official recognition in 2003. Hostility did not stop: Protestants blamed Vodou in part for the 2010 earthquake, and mobs attacked Vodouists afterwards.

So this atlas's word list bans the two-o spelling outside quotations and proper nouns, and the validator fails any record that uses it loose. The reason is not squeamishness about an old spelling. That spelling reached English through an occupation and an entertainment industry, and what it names in English is a thing those industries built — a zombie, a pin-stuck doll, a film villain. Calling a religion with clergy, liturgy, a constitution's protection and six million estimated practitioners by the name of its own caricature is the error the rule exists to stop. The exceptions are real and stay: “Louisiana Voodoo” is the proper name of a distinct tradition, and a quotation keeps its speaker's words.

text_th.what: สองศาสนาและการสะกดผิดหนึ่งแบบ โวดุน (Vodún) คือศาสนาของชาวอายา เอเว และฟอน ในเบนิน โตโก กานา และไนจีเรีย มีคณะนักบวช สมาคมที่ต้องผ่านพิธีรับเข้า และระบบการทำนายฟา (Fá) โวดู (Vodou) คือศาสนาของเฮติ ก่อตัวขึ้นในกลางคริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 18 จากธรรมเนียมของชาวฟอน คองโก และโยรูบา ภายใต้อาณานิคมแซ็ง-โดมิงก์ (Saint-Domingue) โดยซึมซับองค์ประกอบจากโรมันคาทอลิกและฟรีเมสันเข้าไว้ด้วย และมีวิหาร (อุนโฟ, ounfò) นักบวชชายและหญิง (อุงกันและมันโบ, oungan และ manbo) การรับเข้าสี่ขั้น พิธีกรรมที่ประกอบด้วยกลอง เพลง และการร่ายรำ และมีชุมชนพลัดถิ่นในคิวบา สาธารณรัฐโดมินิกัน เปอร์โตริโก ฝรั่งเศส แคนาดา และสหรัฐอเมริกา Vodou เป็นตัวสะกดที่นักวิชาการใช้ ที่อักขรวิธีทางการของภาษาครีโอลเฮติใช้ และที่หอสมุดรัฐสภาสหรัฐอเมริกาใช้ นักวิชาการบางคนนิยม Vodoun, Voudoun หรือ Vodun ภาษาฝรั่งเศสมีทั้ง vaudou และ vaudoux ส่วนตัวสะกดที่มีตัว o สองตัว ตามคำของวิกิพีเดีย "ปัจจุบันผู้ปฏิบัติและนักวิชาการโดยทั่วไปหลีกเลี่ยงเมื่อกล่าวถึงศาสนาของเฮติ"

names.th: วอร์ด (ปัดเป่า)

etymology.root: Proto-Germanic *wardōną 'to guard' > Old English weardian 'to watch, guard, keep, protect' (noun weard 'watching, ward, protection, guardianship') > Middle English warden > English ward; English guard is the same word returned through Old French
etymology.note: Wiktionary marks ward and guard as doublets and glosses the transitive verb 'To fend off, to repel, to turn aside', usually with off. No dated first attestation is given there, so none is claimed here.

text.what: The English verb for what the carriers of every object in this atlas say it does. Ward off: fend off, repel, turn aside. It is the plainest word available for the job, it is older in English than amulet or talisman, and it has no scholarly air at all — which is why the adjective apotropaic, whose Greek verb means exactly this, is the one that ended up on museum labels.
text.story:
Old English weardian is to watch, to guard, to keep, to protect; the noun weard is the watching itself. The Norman conquest sent the same Germanic root back across the Channel and returned it as guard, so English carries the word twice, once early and Germanic and once late and French, and uses the two for different registers.

The noun went somewhere the verb did not. In law a ward is not the thing that protects but the person protected: a minor or an incapacitated adult placed under a guardian or a court. That sense runs out of feudal wardship, where custody of a minor heir's lands, of the heir, and of the heir's choice of marriage partner were rights that got sold to the highest bidder or granted as a favour. Henry VIII sponsored the Statute of Uses in 1535 to protect his income from wardship and established the Court of Wards and Liveries in 1540. The court lost its function in 1646 with the abolition of feudal tenure in England and Wales, and was abolished in 1660.

The word then travelled with the common law. In Australia, New Zealand and the United States a child is a ward of the court; in Ireland and the United Kingdom, a ward of court with no article; in Canada, a permanent ward, except in Ontario, which says Crown ward. In France a pupille de l'État is a minor under the responsibility of the state.

*Inference —* one root, two ends that face each other. The horseshoe over a door wards. The child inside the house is a ward. English has kept both without ever needing to notice.

etymology.root: Sanskrit root yam 'to sustain, support' + the instrumental suffix -tra > yantra (यन्त्र), 'instrument, machine, contraption'
etymology.note: In Rigvedic Sanskrit yantra is an instrument for restraining or fastening — a prop, a support, a barrier. The literal sense is still live in Sushruta's medical vocabulary, where it names blunt surgical instruments such as tweezers or a vice. The sense 'mystical or occult diagram' arises in the medieval period, in the Kathasaritsagara and the Pancharatra.

text.what: A machine. That is the word's plain sense and it has never gone away: yantra is an instrument, a thing built to hold and to do work. The diagram sense — concentric triangles, circles, hexagons, lotus petals and an outer square with doors at the four directions, radiating from a central point called the bindu — is a later specialisation of the same idea. A yantra that has not been energised with its mantra is held by practitioners to be lifeless, which is consistent with the root: an instrument that is not driving anything is not doing its job.
text.story:
The word travelled east and kept its shape. Sak yant, the tattooing practice of Cambodia, Thailand and Laos, splits into sak — a native Khmer word meaning to tattoo, from a Proto-Mon-Khmer root meaning to prick, which Chuon Nath's 1967 dictionary establishes is not a Sanskrit or Pali loan — and yant, the Sanskrit yantra arriving with Indian designs. One indigenous word, one borrowed one, welded into the name of a practice.

Gudrun Bühnemann sorts the diagrams into three kinds by use: those that a ritual implement such as a lamp or a vessel stands on; those used in regular worship, like the Sri Yantra of the goddess Tripura Sundari; and those made for a specific desire-driven rite, often on birch bark or paper, sometimes with flowers, rice paste or ashes worked in.

The dating of the form is where this record has to go carefully. Wikipedia's article says representations of the yantra in India 'have been considered to date back to 11,000–10,000 BCE', and in the next sentence reports that the Baghor stone, found in an Upper Palaeolithic context in the Son River Valley, was dated by G. R. Sharma, who excavated it, to 25,000–20,000 BCE, and that Kenoyer, also on the excavation, associated it with Shakti. Those two ranges do not agree with each other, and neither is a date for the word. *Inference —* what can be said is that a triangular engraved stone was excavated and read by its excavators as related to goddess worship; reading it as a yantra is an interpretation laid over an object by people who already had the word.

*Tradition holds —* the diagrams are consecrated and energised by a priest, using mantras tied to the particular deity, and in Sri Lankan Buddhism a practitioner is required to hold the yantra of the deity once that deity has shown acceptance of their prayer.

text_th.what: เครื่องจักร นั่นคือความหมายตรงตัวของคำนี้ และไม่เคยหายไปไหน: ยันตระคือเครื่องมือ สิ่งที่สร้างขึ้นเพื่อยึดไว้และเพื่อทำงาน ความหมายในแง่แผนภาพ — สามเหลี่ยม วงกลม และหกเหลี่ยมซ้อนกัน กลีบบัว และกรอบสี่เหลี่ยมด้านนอกที่มีประตูทั้งสี่ทิศ แผ่ออกจากจุดศูนย์กลางที่เรียกว่า พินทุ (bindu) — เป็นความหมายเฉพาะที่เกิดทีหลังของแนวคิดเดียวกัน ผู้ปฏิบัติถือว่ายันตระที่ยังไม่ได้รับพลังจากมนต์ของมันนั้นไร้ชีวิต ซึ่งสอดคล้องกับรากศัพท์: เครื่องมือที่ไม่ได้ขับเคลื่อนสิ่งใดก็ไม่ได้ทำหน้าที่ของมัน
text_th.story:
คำนี้เดินทางไปทางตะวันออกโดยยังคงรูปเดิม สักยันต์ การสักของกัมพูชา ไทย และลาว แยกได้เป็น สัก — คำเขมรดั้งเดิมที่แปลว่าสัก มาจากรากศัพท์มอญ-เขมรดั้งเดิม (Proto-Mon-Khmer) ที่แปลว่าทิ่มแทง ซึ่งพจนานุกรมของจวน ณาต (Chuon Nath) ฉบับ ค.ศ. 1967 ยืนยันว่าไม่ใช่คำยืมจากสันสกฤตหรือบาลี — กับ ยันต์ คือคำสันสกฤต ยันตระ ที่มาพร้อมลวดลายจากอินเดีย คำพื้นเมืองหนึ่งคำ คำยืมหนึ่งคำ เชื่อมเข้าด้วยกันเป็นชื่อของการปฏิบัติ

กุดรุน บึห์เนอมันน์ (Gudrun Bühnemann) แบ่งแผนภาพออกเป็นสามประเภทตามการใช้: แบบที่เครื่องใช้ในพิธีอย่างตะเกียงหรือภาชนะตั้งอยู่บนนั้น แบบที่ใช้ในการบูชาเป็นประจำ เช่น ศรียันตระของพระแม่ตรีปุรสุนทรี และแบบที่ทำขึ้นสำหรับพิธีเฉพาะที่มุ่งให้สมความปรารถนา มักทำบนเปลือกต้นเบิร์ชหรือกระดาษ บางครั้งมีดอกไม้ แป้งข้าว หรือเถ้าผสมลงไป

การกำหนดอายุของรูปแบบนี้คือจุดที่บันทึกนี้ต้องระมัดระวัง บทความในวิกิพีเดียกล่าวว่าภาพแทนยันตระในอินเดีย 'ถูกพิจารณาว่ามีอายุย้อนไปถึง 11,000–10,000 ปีก่อน ค.ศ.' และในประโยคถัดมารายงานว่าศิลาบาโฆร์ (Baghor stone) ซึ่งพบในบริบทยุคหินเก่าตอนปลายในหุบเขาแม่น้ำโสน ได้รับการกำหนดอายุโดย จี. อาร์. ชาร์มา (G. R. Sharma) ผู้ขุดค้น ไว้ที่ 25,000–20,000 ปีก่อน ค.ศ. และเคโนเยอร์ (Kenoyer) ซึ่งอยู่ในการขุดค้นด้วย เชื่อมโยงศิลานี้กับพระศักติ ช่วงเวลาทั้งสองนี้ไม่ตรงกัน และไม่มีช่วงใดเป็นอายุของตัวคำ *ข้อสันนิษฐาน —* สิ่งที่พูดได้คือ มีการขุดพบหินสลักรูปสามเหลี่ยม และผู้ขุดค้นตีความว่าเกี่ยวข้องกับการบูชาเทพี การอ่านหินนั้นว่าเป็นยันตระ คือการตีความที่ผู้ซึ่งมีคำนี้อยู่แล้ววางทับลงบนวัตถุ

*ตามคติที่เล่าสืบกันมา —* แผนภาพเหล่านี้ได้รับการปลุกเสกและเสริมพลังโดยนักบวช ด้วยมนต์ที่ผูกกับเทพองค์นั้นโดยเฉพาะ และในพุทธศาสนาแบบศรีลังกา ผู้ปฏิบัติต้องถือครองยันตระของเทพองค์นั้น เมื่อเทพแสดงว่ารับคำอธิษฐานของเขาแล้ว

text.what: Twenty-two plates and three hundred in-text illustrations bound into a 543-page book: E. A. Wallis Budge's "Amulets and superstitions", published in London and New York by Oxford University Press and H. Milford in 1930. The Wellcome Collection's catalogue record gives the collation as xxxix, 543 pages with illustrations, plates and facsimiles, 25 cm tall. A single plate will set an Egyptian scarab beside a Babylonian cylinder, a Hebrew amulet and a Gnostic gem, drawn or photographed to no common scale.
text.story:
The subtitle is the argument. Budge's runs to a paragraph — Egyptian, Sumerian, Assyrian, Hebrew, Christian, Gnostic and Muslim amulets and talismans and magical figures, with chapters on the evil eye, the origin of the amulet, the pentagon, the swastika, the cross, the properties of stones, rings, divination, numbers, the Kabbâlâh and ancient astrology. Nobody had put that list on one shelf before, and the plates are the list made visible: this atlas's own habit of setting a Cairo object beside a Naples one descends directly from pages laid out like these.

The books have a reputation and it is not a good one. The Egyptologist James Peter Allen writes that Budge's books "were not too reliable when they first appeared and are now woefully outdated". The archaeologist Brian M. Fagan has called Budge "one of the major illegal looters of antiquities": as the British Museum's buyer he smuggled cuneiform tablets out of Iraq by bribery, and gave his own account of one such trip in By Nile and Tigris.

*Inference —* the plates and the text fail differently, and the difference matters to a reader. A plate records what an object looked like in 1930, which is checkable. The caption records what Budge thought it meant, which is often not. So this atlas cites these pictures for shape and cites almost nothing here for meaning.
text.today: The Wellcome Collection's record for the 1930 edition carries the rights statement "In copyright. It is possible this item is protected by copyright and/or related rights." So the plates are not reproduced here, and no candidate image file is listed below. Later reprints of Budge circulate widely and have kept his readings in print long after Egyptology dropped them.
